name_vi: Tư duy ngược — muốn thành công thì tránh thất bại trước
definition: Solve a hard problem by flipping it around and asking what would guarantee failure instead of success.
mechanism: Inversion works because the mind notices obstacles more clearly than paths to success. Losses, embarrassments, and disasters feel concrete, so listing them surfaces hidden risks that optimism hides. Removing one clear cause of failure often improves odds more than chasing a brilliant new idea. It also breaks fixation on a single plan by forcing you to consider the opposite direction, which reveals assumptions you did not know you were making.
classic_example: German mathematician Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi, who died in 1851, was famous for the advice to invert, always invert when facing a hard problem. Charlie Munger later adopted the same habit at Berkshire Hathaway meetings, asking what could ruin an investment before asking what could make it succeed, and credited inversion with avoiding many costly mistakes over decades of decisions.
modern_example: Before launching a new content channel, a creator lists everything that would make viewers quit in the first week, such as confusing titles, slow openings, and inconsistent posting. Fixing those specific failure points before launch proves easier than guessing a viral formula, and the checklist becomes a simple quality gate for every video the team publishes afterward.
failure_mode: Inversion can turn into pure pessimism if you only hunt for dangers and never act. Some problems also have no clear opposite, so forcing a flip produces trivial advice. Use it to clear obvious landmines, then still make a positive plan and commit resources to actually building something worthwhile.
apply_steps: State the goal in one clear sentence
List everything that would guarantee failure
Rank the failure causes by impact
Remove or guard the top causes first
Revisit the list before committing resources

situation_notes.deciding-under-stress: Inversion reveals the few panic driven moves most likely to cause lasting damage so you can rule them out first.
situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: Inversion shows which audiences topics and formats would almost certainly waste your limited time before you commit months to building.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: Inversion exposes the bottlenecks hiring mistakes and cost jumps that would break the business if growth suddenly doubled next quarter.

case_seeds: Jacobi's invert always invert maxim in nineteenth century mathematics
Munger's inversion habit in Berkshire Hathaway investment reviews
lab_spec: The user enters a goal and the tool prompts them to list everything that would guarantee failure, then rank each cause by impact. A visual checklist turns the top risks into prevention actions and shows which dangers remain open before they commit.
origin: German mathematician Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi, who worked in the nineteenth century, was credited with the maxim to invert, always invert, when a direct proof stalled. Charlie Munger popularised the habit outside mathematics in his talks and in Poor Charlie's Almanack, turning a problem-solving trick from analysis into a general discipline for investing, business, and everyday planning.
mechanism_deep: Inversion has several distinct sub-moves that are often collapsed into one slogan. The first is goal negation: instead of describing success in vague positive terms, you describe failure in concrete, observable terms, because failure usually has fewer, sharper signatures than success. A business can succeed in hundreds of ways, but it reliably dies from running out of cash, losing trust, or depending on one fragile customer. The second sub-move is causal reversal. You work backwards from the imagined disaster and ask what chain of earlier choices would have to be true for that disaster to happen, which exposes intermediate causes that forward planning skips over because each step looks harmless on its own. The third is obstacle prioritisation. Not every possible failure deserves equal attention, so inversion forces a ranking by two dimensions at once: how likely the cause is, and how irreversible its damage would be. A frequent small annoyance and a rare ruinous event demand completely different responses, and confusing them wastes the limited attention inversion is meant to save. Underneath these moves sits an asymmetry in human cognition. Losses and threats are processed more vividly than equivalent gains, a pattern psychologists call negativity bias, so the inverted question recruits stronger attention and more honest answers than the optimistic question does. People who will happily brainstorm ten ways to grow will often, when asked how to guarantee collapse, immediately name the embarrassing truth nobody wanted to say aloud, such as a founder conflict or a product nobody actually needs. Inversion also changes the emotional politics of a group, because criticising a hypothetical failure plan feels safer than criticising a colleague's actual proposal, so dissent surfaces earlier. The boundary conditions matter. Inversion works best when failure modes are enumerable and at least partly preventable, as in safety, investing, operations, and personal health. It works poorly when the problem is exploratory and the main risk is not a known obstacle but an unknown possibility, because listing known failures cannot reveal an opportunity nobody has imagined yet. It also degrades when the inverted list becomes a ritual of anxiety, where teams keep adding exotic disasters to avoid deciding. Used well, inversion is therefore a filter placed before positive planning, not a replacement for it: first delete the moves that reliably lose, then spend creative energy only on the plans that survive that deletion, and revisit the failure list whenever stakes, scale, or incentives materially change.
examples_extra: During the Second World War, statistician Abraham Wald was asked where to add armour to American bombers based on bullet holes in returning aircraft. Wald inverted the question: the holes showed where a plane could be hit and still return, so the missing aircraft implied the fatal areas were the ones with no holes. Armour belonged on the engines and cockpit, exactly where survivors showed the least damage. The insight depended entirely on the aircraft that never came back.

Psychologist Gary Klein developed the premortem for project teams, later described in the Harvard Business Review in 2007. Before launch, a team imagines the project has already failed a year later and each member writes down why. Klein argued the exercise legitimises doubt and surfaces risks that politeness suppresses in normal planning meetings, especially risks known privately by junior staff who would otherwise stay silent. The format is now standard in many product and engineering teams.
misconceptions: Many people think inversion means being negative about everything — in reality, it is a brief, structured search for preventable failure before positive planning begins.
Many people think avoiding obvious stupidity guarantees success — in reality, it only removes common causes of loss; you still need a positive source of advantage.
Many people think inversion is the same as risk listing — in reality, it works backwards from a guaranteed failure, which produces sharper and more honest causes than a generic risk register.
practice: Premortem on paper: Take a current project, write 'It is twelve months later and this failed completely' at the top of a page, then spend ten minutes listing every plausible cause without stopping to argue. Circle the two causes you can prevent this week and write one concrete prevention for each.

Failure shopping list: For a personal goal such as saving money, write ten behaviours that would guarantee failure, then check which ones you did in the last seven days. Stop the single most frequent one for the next week and note what changes.
cross_domain: The same backward logic appears in aviation safety, where accident investigators reconstruct a crash chain and then design checklists and interlocks that make each link impossible to repeat, and in medicine, where morbidity and mortality conferences examine how a patient was harmed in order to remove the step that allowed it. In both fields the gain comes not from exhorting excellence but from systematically deleting a known path to disaster. Investing applies it when a buyer first lists how a company could permanently lose money before modelling any upside at all.

quote.text: All I want to know is where I'm going to die so I'll never go there.
quote.author: Charlie Munger

name_vi: Tư duy bậc hai — và rồi điều gì xảy ra tiếp theo
definition: Look past the immediate result of a decision and ask what that result will then cause next.
mechanism: Most decisions trigger chains of reactions from other people, markets, and systems, and those reactions often matter more than the first effect. Second-order thinking works by extending the timeline and asking who responds, how incentives shift, and what new problems the solution creates. It slows down seductive quick wins and exposes delayed costs while there is still time to redesign the move or prepare for its consequences.
classic_example: In 1935 cane toads were released in Queensland, Australia to eat beetles damaging sugar cane crops. The toads largely ignored the beetles, spread rapidly across the country, and poisoned native predators that tried to eat them. A solution chosen for its immediate effect became a long term ecological problem that authorities are still trying to contain many decades later.
modern_example: A manager cuts the support team to save money this quarter and profits briefly rise. Within months response times worsen, angry customers cancel, and the sales team spends its days apologising instead of selling. The first order saving was real, but the second order losses were larger, slower, and much harder to reverse once experienced staff had already left.
failure_mode: Chains of consequences are endless, so tracing them too far produces speculation rather than insight and can paralyse simple decisions. Effects beyond two or three steps are usually too uncertain to plan around precisely. Use this model for consequential and hard to reverse choices, not for everyday low stakes calls.
apply_steps: Write down the expected immediate result
Ask what that result causes next
Ask who reacts and how
List delayed costs and new problems
Redesign the move to soften bad effects

situation_notes.market-panic: Second order thinking reveals how forced selling falling prices and fear feed each other after the first shock hits your portfolio.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: Second order thinking shows how rapid hiring changes culture quality and communication long after the first exciting growth numbers appear publicly.
situation_notes.competitor-price-war: Second order thinking reveals how rivals customers and suppliers will respond after your first price cut resets expectations across the market.

case_seeds: Introduction of cane toads in Queensland, Australia, 1935
Howard Marks on second level thinking in The Most Important Thing, 2011
source_ref: Howard Marks — The Most Important Thing
lab_spec: The user enters a decision and its expected first result, and the tool builds an expanding chain diagram of likely second and third effects. Each branch can be tagged positive or negative, revealing which delayed consequences deserve a plan before acting.
origin: The habit has no single inventor and grew out of systems thinking, economics, and ecology during the twentieth century. Economist Frederic Bastiat anticipated it in 1850 with his distinction between what is seen and what is not seen. Investor Howard Marks gave it its modern popular name, second-level thinking, in The Most Important Thing in 2011, contrasting it with superficial first-level reactions in markets.
mechanism_deep: Second-order thinking can be broken into a chain with at least four links that each need separate attention. First comes the direct effect, which is usually fast, visible, and easy to measure, and therefore dominates headlines, dashboards, and performance reviews. Second comes the response of other actors. People are not passive material; customers, competitors, employees, and regulators observe the first effect and change their own behaviour to protect or advance their interests, often cancelling part of the intended benefit. A price cut that wins buyers this month teaches those buyers to wait for discounts and invites rivals to match, so the market resets at a worse level for everyone. Third comes adaptation over time, where the system settles into a new equilibrium that nobody explicitly chose. Congestion pricing, rent controls, and performance bonuses all produce settled behaviours that differ from the behaviour in the first excited weeks. Fourth comes the side effect on stocks rather than flows: trust, skills, soil, reputation, and morale are accumulated reserves that a decision can quietly deplete while its flow numbers still look good, which is why damage often appears suddenly and late. The underlying driver is that most interesting environments are reflexive and delayed. Causes feed back into themselves, and the delay between action and consequence breaks the brain's simple learning loop, so intuition trained on immediate feedback systematically underweights later effects. That is also why second-order thinking pairs naturally with incentives: asking who gains, who loses, and what each party will do next month is more reliable than asking what a policy intends. The boundary conditions are uncertainty and depth. Each additional step multiplies assumptions, so a third or fourth order claim should be held much more loosely than a second order one, and for small reversible decisions the cost of tracing chains exceeds any benefit. The model is most valuable exactly where decisions are large, hard to reverse, affect many adaptive actors, or create precedents, because precedents are themselves a powerful second-order effect: every exception you grant teaches everyone watching what the real rule is. A practical discipline follows from this structure. For any significant move, write the first-order effect in one line, then force three further entries: the response of the party most affected, the response of the party who profits from that response, and the state of the system after everyone has adjusted. Each entry must name an actor and an incentive, not just an event, because vague chains invite storytelling. Where an entry cannot be named, mark it as the point of greatest ignorance and design the move so that point is monitored or reversible.
examples_extra: When Prohibition banned alcohol sales in the United States in 1920, the first-order aim was to reduce drinking and its harms. Second-order effects included a large illegal market, organised crime built around bootlegging, and drinkers shifting toward stronger spirits because concentrated alcohol was easier to smuggle. The policy was repealed in 1933 after those unintended consequences became politically impossible to ignore. Congress eventually accepted that the cure had created a larger criminal economy than the drinking it suppressed.

In sports, the introduction of the three-point line in the NBA in 1979 at first rewarded a few long-range shooters. Over decades, second-order adaptation transformed training, player selection, and court spacing, as teams realised efficient offences should generate many three-point attempts. A rule change aimed at adding excitement eventually reshaped what skills young basketball players everywhere were taught to develop. Coaches now teach shooting form and spacing to children who may never play professionally.
misconceptions: Many people think second-order thinking means predicting the distant future precisely — in reality, it means naming the most likely next reactions and preparing for them, not forecasting exactly.
Many people think every decision needs deep chain analysis — in reality, it is reserved for consequential, hard-to-reverse choices; small reversible calls should stay fast.
Many people think a good first-order result proves a decision was good — in reality, the result that matters includes how others respond and what the system settles into afterwards.
practice: And-then-what chain: Write a pending decision at the top of a page, then draw three boxes labelled 'and then what happens?' For each box, name who reacts and how, not just what changes. Stop after three boxes and circle any effect you could soften with a small design change today.

Precedent test: Before granting an exception at work or at home, write one sentence completing 'If I do this once, everyone who sees it will expect...' If that sentence worries you, redesign the exception or refuse it explicitly rather than letting it set the rule silently.
cross_domain: Ecology shows the pattern when removing predators lets prey multiply until vegetation collapses, a sequence documented in many rewilding and overhunting cases, while public health shows it when a drug that suppresses one symptom pushes patients to stop other treatments they still need. In both fields the intervention works exactly as designed at step one, and the harm arrives through the responses and adaptations that step one triggers. The pattern is identical even though the substances, actors, and timescales differ completely.

name_vi: Nguyên lý nền tảng — bóc vấn đề về sự thật gốc
definition: Break a problem down to its basic proven facts and rebuild your answer from those facts upward.
mechanism: Most beliefs are inherited analogies copied from other people, prices, and traditions, which quietly cap what seems possible. First principles thinking strips away those conventions until only verifiable facts remain, such as physical limits, real costs, and human needs. Rebuilding from that floor exposes which constraints are genuine and which were merely habits, often revealing solutions that look unreasonable only because nobody questioned the inherited assumptions underneath them.
classic_example: When Elon Musk founded SpaceX in 2002, conventional wisdom held that rockets were unavoidably expensive. Musk instead listed the raw materials a rocket is made from and what those materials cost on commodity markets, concluding that the materials were only a small fraction of the finished price. That gap convinced him that reusable rockets built in house could change launch economics.
modern_example: A freelancer assumes a professional website must cost a large fee because agencies charge that much. Breaking the job into its parts, a domain, simple hosting, a template, and a few pages of text, shows the real costs are modest. She builds a basic version herself in a weekend and spends the saved money on photography that actually wins clients.
failure_mode: Rebuilding everything from scratch is slow and exhausting, and for most everyday problems accumulated expert knowledge is reliable and far cheaper to use. First principles reasoning also fails when your supposed basic facts are wrong. Reserve it for expensive, stagnant, or strategically important problems where conventional answers clearly disappoint.
apply_steps: State the problem and current standard answer
List every assumption behind that answer
Reduce each part to verified facts
Rebuild a solution using only those facts
Compare cost and results against convention

situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: First principles thinking separates real audience needs and your actual skills from trendy niches everyone copies without questioning the underlying fit.
situation_notes.pricing-a-product: First principles thinking rebuilds price from real costs customer value and alternatives instead of copying whatever competitors happen to charge today.
situation_notes.learning-from-zero: First principles thinking identifies the few foundational concepts that everything else rests on so beginners stop memorising disconnected tips and tricks.

case_seeds: Founding of SpaceX and its raw material cost analysis, 2002
Aristotle's first principles in ancient Greek philosophy
origin: The term descends from ancient Greek philosophy, especially Aristotle in the fourth century BCE, who defined a first principle as the first basis from which a thing is known. The method was later central to Descartes and to physics, and was popularised for business and engineering readers in the twenty-first century through Elon Musk's repeated explanations of how SpaceX and Tesla reasoned about costs.
mechanism_deep: First-principles work proceeds through distinct layers that are easy to describe and hard to do honestly. The top layer is the inherited solution, complete with its price, timeline, and prestige, all of which arrived from other people's constraints rather than from the problem itself. Beneath it sits a layer of conventions: industry markups, standard components, regulatory habits, and phrases such as 'that is how it is done,' which mix genuine constraints with pure historical accident. Only at the bottom sit the true primitives for a given problem, which differ by domain: in physical products they are materials, energy, and manufacturing steps; in services they are human time, attention, and trust; in learning they are the small set of concepts on which all later material depends. The causal engine of the model is that each layer above the primitives quietly multiplies cost and narrows options, so removing even one unjustified layer can change what is possible by an order of magnitude rather than by a small percentage. Rebuilding then becomes a design act, not just an analysis act: you recombine primitives under the real constraints and accept ugly, nonstandard intermediate forms, because a rebuilt solution rarely resembles the polished inherited one. Two disciplines protect the process from self-deception. The first is verification of the primitives themselves, since a wrong 'basic fact' produces a confidently wrong rebuild, which is worse than copying experts. The second is selective use: analogy and expert practice encode enormous compressed experience, so discarding them everywhere wastes the very knowledge that makes most daily work efficient. The boundary is therefore economic. Use first principles where the inherited answer is expensive, stagnant, strategically decisive, or visibly absurd compared with its underlying costs, and use analogy where the problem is routine, cheap, and well served by people who have solved it many times before. A further subtlety is that primitives change over time: battery cells, bandwidth, and computation all became radically cheaper within a generation, so a rebuild that was impossible a decade ago may be trivial now, and yesterday's first-principles conclusion expires just as surely as yesterday's convention does. There is also a social cost that explains why the method stays rare. A rebuilt solution usually looks amateur beside the polished inherited one, lacks prestigious references, and forces its author to defend every step personally rather than pointing to standard practice. Organisations punish that exposure, so competent people rationally copy. The method therefore needs protection: a sponsor, a prototype budget, or a deadline by which the rebuild must beat the inherited answer on a stated measure. Without such protection, first-principles projects are typically abandoned at the first embarrassing intermediate stage, before the recombination that makes them valuable has had time to appear.
examples_extra: In medicine, Semmelweis in the 1840s questioned why women died of childbed fever far more often in the doctors' ward of the Vienna General Hospital than in the midwives' ward. Reducing the problem to what actually differed between the wards, including doctors coming directly from autopsies, led him to require hand disinfection with chlorinated lime, after which deaths in his ward fell sharply, even though germ theory did not yet exist to explain why.

Chef and writer J. Kenji Lopez-Alt rebuilt the problem of a better homemade burger from primitives in The Food Lab, testing grind size, salt timing, and heat transfer separately instead of copying restaurant lore. His experiments showed, for example, that salting ground beef only on the exterior preserves a looser texture, a conclusion reached by isolating variables rather than by imitating famous chefs' finished recipes.
misconceptions: Many people think first-principles thinking means ignoring all experts — in reality, it means verifying which expert claims rest on facts and which rest only on tradition.
Many people think it is always the smartest approach — in reality, it is slow and costly, so it should be reserved for expensive or stagnant problems.
Many people think breaking a problem down is the whole method — in reality, the value comes from rebuilding a new solution from the verified pieces, not from the teardown alone.
practice: Cost teardown: Pick one product or service you pay for, list its physical or human ingredients, and look up or estimate the cost of each ingredient separately. Write down the gap between ingredient cost and price, then list three honest reasons that might justify the gap before judging it.

Assumption audit: Write a familiar claim such as 'I need a degree to do X' and list every assumption inside it. Mark each assumption F for verified fact or H for habit, then design one small test this week for the single H that matters most.
cross_domain: Cooking shows the same pattern when a cook stops copying recipes and reasons from heat, water, salt, and acid directly, gaining the ability to rescue unfamiliar dishes, while personal finance shows it when a saver rebuilds a budget from actual needs for housing, food, transport, and rest instead of copying percentage rules designed for a different income and city. In both cases the primitives are few, stable, and transferable once learned. Once the primitives are clear in either kitchen or budget, outside advice becomes far easier to judge.

name_vi: Thí nghiệm tưởng tượng — thử ý tưởng trong đầu trước
definition: Test an idea by imagining an extreme or impossible scenario and following its logic to the end.
mechanism: A thought experiment isolates one variable inside an imagined scene, removing cost, danger, and practical mess so the pure logic of an idea becomes visible. Pushing a claim to an extreme case reveals contradictions and hidden assumptions that ordinary discussion misses. Because the experiment runs entirely in the mind, you can test dozens of scenarios quickly before spending money or reputation in the real world.
classic_example: As a teenager in 1896, Albert Einstein imagined chasing alongside a beam of light and wondered what he would see. Pursuing that impossible picture on and off for years helped him see that the speed of light must stay constant for every observer. The line of questioning led directly toward his special theory of relativity, published in 1905.
modern_example: Before quitting her job, an office worker imagines her employer offering double pay to stay and notices she would still refuse. The experiment tells her the real problem is the work itself, not the salary. She stops negotiating for a raise and instead plans a careful move into a different role over the following six months.
failure_mode: Imagined scenarios obey your assumptions, so a flawed premise produces confident but useless conclusions. Thought experiments cannot replace real data when a question is empirical and testable. Treat them as tools for clarifying logic and generating hypotheses, then check the important ones against evidence, experiments, or small real world trials.
apply_steps: State the claim you want to test
Invent an extreme scenario around it
Follow the logic step by step
Note any contradiction or surprise
Decide what real evidence would settle it

situation_notes.career-pivot: A thought experiment like imagining double pay to stay reveals whether money or the work itself is driving your urge to leave.
situation_notes.decision-under-time-pressure: A quick thought experiment about the worst realistic outcome helps you see whether a rushed decision is truly dangerous or merely uncomfortable.
situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: Imagining a claim pushed to its extreme quickly exposes exaggerated promises in courses and headlines before you spend money believing them.

case_seeds: Einstein imagining chasing a beam of light, 1896
Schrödinger's cat thought experiment, 1935
origin: Imagined scenarios have been used since ancient philosophy, including Plato's cave and, much later, Galileo's falling-body arguments in the seventeenth century. The modern German term Gedankenexperiment was popularised in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and the method became famous through physics, where Einstein, Schrodinger, and others used imagined setups to expose what a theory truly committed them to before any laboratory test was possible.
mechanism_deep: A thought experiment works by constructing a stripped world in which only the variables under dispute are allowed to move, then running that world forward under strict logic until it yields agreement, absurdity, or a hidden premise. Its three useful forms should be distinguished. A destructive experiment pushes a claim into an extreme corner, such as zero friction or infinite time, to see whether it contradicts itself there. A constructive experiment shows that a seemingly impossible combination can be described coherently, which reopens a question people had closed by habit. A probing experiment changes one sympathy or identity, such as swapping who bears a cost, to reveal whether a judgement depends on the principle claimed or merely on who benefits. The engine underneath is that real-world tests entangle many causes at once, while an imagined test can hold everything else still, so a contradiction found there must belong to the idea itself rather than to messy conditions. The discipline that keeps the tool honest is to state the setup's assumptions in words, vary them one at a time to see whether the conclusion survives, and finally name what real observation would settle the question the imagination opened.
examples_extra: Philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson published a famous thought experiment in 1971 imagining a person waking up medically connected to an unconscious violinist whose life depends on staying connected for nine months. The scenario was designed to test arguments about abortion by separating questions about rights and obligations from the biological details of pregnancy, and it remains widely discussed and criticised in ethics teaching.

Economist and philosopher Amartya Sen and earlier writers used imagined famines with adequate total food to probe distribution: if grain exists in a country while one region starves, the scenario forces attention onto prices, wages, and entitlements rather than harvest size alone. Sen's analysis of the Bengal famine of 1943 in Poverty and Famines applied that lens to a real catastrophe.
misconceptions: Many people think a persuasive thought experiment proves its conclusion — in reality, it clarifies what a claim implies; empirical questions still need real evidence.
Many people think extreme scenarios are cheating — in reality, extremes are the point, because contradictions that hide at normal values become visible at the edges.
Many people think thought experiments are just daydreaming — in reality, a disciplined one states assumptions, changes one variable, and follows logic without quietly rewriting the setup mid-way.
practice: Extreme dial: Take a belief you hold, write it as one sentence, then imagine its key variable turned to zero and to maximum for two minutes each. Write down any point where your belief becomes absurd or changes meaning, and note what that reveals about the belief's real limits.

Identity swap: For a current dispute, rewrite the scenario with the names and roles swapped, keeping every fact identical. If your judgement changes, write down which principle actually changed; if none did, you have found a sympathy effect worth naming honestly.
cross_domain: Law uses hypothetical cases in classrooms and judgments to test whether a proposed rule produces acceptable results at its edges before it governs real people, while engineering uses imagined failure scenarios in design reviews to find weak points that prototypes have not yet reached. In both fields the imagined case is cheap, fast, and disposable, and its job is to fail safely so the real system does not have to.

name_vi: Dao cạo Occam — lời giải đơn giản nhất thường đúng nhất
definition: Prefer the explanation that needs the fewest new assumptions while still accounting for all the observed facts.
mechanism: Every extra assumption in an explanation is another chance to be wrong, so complex theories accumulate risk even when they sound impressive. The simplest account that fits all the evidence usually wins because it depends on fewer unproven claims. The razor works as a ranking tool rather than a proof, telling you which explanation to test first and which elaborate story needs stronger evidence before it deserves belief.
classic_example: William of Ockham, a Franciscan friar writing in fourteenth century England, argued that thinkers should not multiply entities beyond necessity. His principle pushed scholars to strip needless layers from theological and philosophical arguments. Centuries later the razor bearing his name became a standard tool in science for choosing between competing explanations that fit the same observations equally well.
modern_example: A small shop owner notices sales dropped this week and wonders about competitors, algorithms, and the economy. The simplest check comes first, and it turns out a road closure diverted traffic from the street. Instead of launching an expensive rebrand, she adds delivery options for two weeks and sales recover once the road reopens.
failure_mode: Reality is sometimes genuinely complicated, and the simplest explanation can be a comforting story that ignores inconvenient facts. The razor also misleads when the simple answer is familiar rather than truly assumption free. Use it to order your investigation, never as an excuse to stop investigating before the evidence is actually checked.
apply_steps: List the competing explanations honestly
Count the assumptions each one needs
Check which fits all the facts
Test the simplest explanation first
Upgrade only when evidence demands complexity

situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: Occam's razor favours the boring explanation that a course seller profits from hype over elaborate claims of secret methods nobody else found.
situation_notes.team-conflict: Occam's razor suggests checking workload confusion and unclear instructions before assuming a teammate is deliberately sabotaging the project or disrespecting you personally.
situation_notes.channel-not-growing: Occam's razor points first to weak topics and packaging rather than shadow bans or conspiracies when a channel stalls without any evidence.

case_seeds: William of Ockham's writings on parsimony, fourteenth century
Copernican heliocentrism displacing elaborate epicycle models, 1543
origin: William of Ockham, an English Franciscan friar and scholastic philosopher writing in the early fourteenth century, repeatedly favoured explanations and arguments that avoided unnecessary plurality. He did not coin the exact modern slogan attributed to him; later writers distilled his repeated parsimony arguments into the principle now called Occam's razor. It became a standard heuristic in science and philosophy over the following centuries.
mechanism_deep: The razor operates through probability, testing order, and cognitive economy, and each mechanism needs separating. Probabilistically, every independent assumption in an explanation must be true for the whole explanation to hold, so assumptions multiply risk in the same way that a chain is only as strong as the product of its links. An account requiring one familiar cause is therefore, before testing, more likely than an account requiring that cause plus a hidden motive plus a coincidence plus a cover-up, even if the elaborate account feels more satisfying as a story. As a testing order, the razor is a queueing rule rather than a verdict: investigate the explanation that is cheapest to check and needs fewest new entities first, because most everyday anomalies really do come from mundane causes such as a typo, a closed road, a dead battery, or a misunderstood instruction. Only when the simple account fails to fit a stubborn fact should complexity earn its place, and then it should earn it one justified assumption at a time. Cognitively, the razor protects against a known weakness: human minds prefer explanations with agents, intentions, and drama, so elaborate theories feel insightful precisely because they entertain. Parsimony is a deliberate counterweight to narrative appetite. There are important refinements. Simplicity must be measured in assumptions, not in sentence length or familiarity; a familiar conspiracy can be verbally short while smuggling in many hidden assumptions, and a strange physical theory can be verbally long while assuming very little. Simplicity also competes with completeness, because an explanation that ignores a real observation is not simple, it is merely incomplete. The boundary cases are domains where the underlying system is genuinely many-caused, such as chronic illness, organisational failure, and historical events, where the razor should rank hypotheses for testing but should never be used to declare that only one cause is allowed to exist. Used at the right strength, the razor keeps inquiry fast and honest; used as a slogan to end arguments, it becomes the very kind of unexamined shortcut it was meant to cut away. A useful refinement is to count assumptions in public. When two explanations compete, write each one's assumptions as a numbered list and require the longer list to justify every extra entry with evidence the shorter list cannot explain. This turns the razor from a taste into an audit, and it often reveals that the real dispute is over a single assumption both sides had buried in prose. It also exposes the opposite abuse, where a supposedly simple account quietly assumes the very thing it claims to prove, a circularity that paragraph form hides and list form makes embarrassingly visible.
examples_extra: In medicine, doctors are taught a version of the razor through the saying that when you hear hoofbeats, think of horses, not zebras, attributed to physician Theodore Woodward in the 1940s. A patient with a cough and fever in winter is tested first for common infections, not for a rare tropical disease, because common causes explain most presentations and rare ones are considered when the common account fails to fit.

In 1859, astronomers noticed Mercury's orbit shifting in a way Newton's laws did not fully predict, and some proposed a hidden planet, Vulcan, to explain it. The extra planet was never found. Albert Einstein's general relativity, published in 1915, accounted for the shift without adding a new planet, and the simpler-in-entities explanation prevailed once its other predictions were confirmed. The episode is now a standard caution against inventing unseen entities too quickly.
misconceptions: Many people think Occam's razor says the simplest explanation is always true — in reality, it only says which explanation to prefer and test first when both fit the facts.
Many people think simple means short or familiar — in reality, simplicity is counted in assumptions, and a familiar story can hide many unproven ones.
Many people think the razor proves elaborate theories wrong — in reality, complex explanations win whenever the evidence demands them; they just need stronger evidence.
practice: Assumption count: Write the two explanations you are torn between for a current problem, then list the assumptions under each as bullet points. Test the explanation with fewer assumptions first this week, and only move to the other if a specific fact refuses to fit.

Boring cause first: The next time something at home or work breaks, write down the most boring possible cause and check it physically before searching for a deeper theory. Log how often the boring check solves it over the next month.
cross_domain: Software debugging follows the razor when engineers check a typo, a stale cache, or an unplugged service before redesigning an architecture, because most outages trace to mundane recent changes, while criminal investigation follows it when detectives prioritise the statistically common explanations for a disappearance before entertaining elaborate plots. In both fields the discipline is identical: spend the first, cheapest investigative effort where base rates and fewest assumptions point. Both professions are paid for conclusions, yet both save money by exhausting the mundane first.

name_vi: Dao cạo Hanlon — đừng vội quy cho ác ý
definition: Avoid blaming malice for a mistake when carelessness or misunderstanding can explain what actually went wrong.
mechanism: People naturally explain others behaviour by character while excusing their own by circumstance, which manufactures enemies out of ordinary errors. Hanlon's razor corrects that bias by ranking incompetence, overload, and miscommunication above deliberate harm, since honest mistakes are statistically far more common than plots. Starting from the kinder explanation keeps relationships repairable and directs your energy toward fixing the process that allowed the error instead of fighting a person.
classic_example: Robert Hanlon submitted the razor that bears his name for Arthur Bloch's Murphy's Law Book Two, published in 1980, offering it as a companion to Murphy's Law. The saying spread widely because workplaces kept proving it true. Similar sentiments had been attributed to Napoleon and Goethe, but Hanlon's crisp version became the one offices quoted when tempers rose over everyday blunders.
modern_example: A colleague misses the deadline for sending you figures and you assume he is undermining your project. A quick message reveals his laptop died and the file was never backed up. Annoying, but not sabotage. You agree a shared folder for drafts, and the same situation never causes a crisis again because the process, not the person, got fixed.
failure_mode: Some harm really is deliberate, and applying this razor blindly can make you naive around genuinely dishonest or hostile actors. Repeated identical mistakes after clear warnings also stop deserving the benefit of the doubt. Use it as your first hypothesis, then let patterns of behaviour, not single incidents, decide whether intent was actually malicious.
apply_steps: Pause before assigning bad intent
List innocent explanations for the behaviour
Check the facts with a neutral question
Fix the process that allowed the error
Escalate only if the pattern repeats

situation_notes.team-conflict: Hanlon's razor reframes a missed deadline as overload or confusion worth clarifying before accusations harden a small problem into lasting resentment.
situation_notes.reading-a-new-partner: Hanlon's razor warns against reading a slow reply or sloppy email as disrespect when a new partner may simply be overwhelmed.
situation_notes.idea-rejected-by-boss: Hanlon's razor suggests your boss rejected the idea from budget pressure or poor timing rather than personal dislike of you or your work.

case_seeds: Publication of Hanlon's razor in Murphy's Law Book Two, 1980
source_ref: Robert Hanlon via Arthur Bloch — Murphy's Law Book Two
origin: Robert J. Hanlon of Scranton, Pennsylvania submitted the saying for Arthur Bloch's Murphy's Law Book Two, published in 1980, and Bloch credited him by name. Similar sentiments had circulated earlier and were loosely attributed to figures such as Napoleon and Goethe without solid documentation, but Hanlon's version, never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity, is the documented modern source.
mechanism_deep: The razor exploits three well-established facts about error. First, base rates are lopsided: in any large organisation or busy life, forgetfulness, overload, broken tools, and garbled messages occur thousands of times for every one deliberate act of sabotage, so a rational first guess follows the frequencies rather than the drama. Second, human attribution is asymmetric: observers explain other people's failures by character and their own by circumstance, a pattern psychologists call the fundamental attribution error, so the feeling that an act was malicious is itself unreliable evidence generated by a known bias. Third, intent is expensive to verify while process is cheap to inspect, so the razor sequences your response productively: check the shared file, the ambiguous instruction, and the impossible deadline first, because those checks either solve the problem or produce the evidence that would justify suspecting intent later. There is also a strategic layer. The boundary is pattern and stakes. A single incident deserves the razor; identical harm after clear warnings, concealed actions, and personal benefit from the failure together shift the odds, and in domains involving money, safety, or abuse, protective action should not wait for charitable interpretation. The razor governs your first explanation, not your final judgement and never your precautions.
examples_extra: In January 2018, a Hawaii emergency employee sent a false ballistic missile alert to the state during a drill, causing widespread panic before a correction followed thirty-eight minutes later. Investigations by the Federal Communications Commission and the state attributed the event to confusing drill procedures, a poorly designed interface, and human error, not to sabotage, and the fixes that followed targeted procedure and software design rather than a supposed plot.

When Coca-Cola replaced its flagship drink with New Coke in 1985 and reversed course seventy-nine days later, a durable conspiracy theory claimed the launch had been a deliberate plot to rekindle love for the original formula. Company executives and later histories have consistently rejected this: it was a sincere, expensive blunder. The episode remains a standard case of a mistake being widely read as cunning.
misconceptions: Many people think Hanlon's razor says malice never happens — in reality, it only ranks error ahead of malice as the first hypothesis to check.
Many people think applying it means excusing the harm — in reality, the damage still needs fixing and consequences; only the explanation of intent changes.
Many people think it is about being nice — in reality, it is about base rates and evidence order; error is simply far more common than plotting.
practice: Three innocent causes: The next time someone's mistake angers you, write down three innocent explanations before contacting them, then ask one neutral question that would distinguish among all four explanations, including malice. Notice how often the first reply resolves the story without any accusation.

Process fix log: For one week, every time something goes wrong around you, record the process condition that allowed it, such as no backup, unclear owner, or no deadline reminder. At week's end, fix the single most repeated condition instead of blaming any individual.
cross_domain: Customer service operations apply the razor when a furious complaint is first routed as a likely shipping, billing, or instruction failure, because the overwhelming majority of cases resolve there without any villain, while cybersecurity teams apply its inverse discipline carefully: they investigate incidents as probable accidents first for triage, but isolate systems immediately because the cost of a real attack is too high for charity to delay containment.

quote.text: Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity.
quote.author: Robert J. Hanlon

name_vi: Bản đồ không phải lãnh thổ — mô hình không phải thực tế
definition: Remember that every model description or metric is only a simplified picture and never the full reality.
mechanism: Every map, model, and metric survives by leaving things out, and the omissions are exactly where surprises hide. Confusing the representation with reality makes people optimise numbers instead of outcomes and trust plans long after conditions change. Holding the distinction in mind keeps you checking the actual ground, updating the map when it disagrees with experience, and remembering that no single viewpoint captures everything that matters.
classic_example: Alfred Korzybski presented the idea that a map is not the territory in 1931 and developed it in his book Science and Sanity, published in 1933. He argued that language and models are abstractions layered on reality, and that confusing the two produces endless practical and psychological errors. His work founded general semantics and influenced later writers on thinking and communication.
modern_example: A marketing dashboard shows rising engagement, so the team celebrates while actual sales quietly fall. The metric was only a map of attention, not the territory of revenue. When the manager starts reviewing customer calls alongside the dashboard each week, the team discovers the new content attracts curious beginners who never buy, and the strategy changes completely.
failure_mode: Taken too far, this model becomes an excuse to dismiss all data and models as useless, leaving only gut feeling. Some maps are extremely accurate for their purpose, and ignoring them is worse than trusting them carefully. The point is to know what your map leaves out, not to navigate without one.
apply_steps: Name the map you are using
Ask what it deliberately leaves out
Compare it against direct observation
Update the map when reality disagrees
Keep a second viewpoint for important decisions

situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: A glossy forecast or backtest is only a map, and this model reminds you the real market will behave differently under stress.
situation_notes.presenting-to-leadership: This model helps you present metrics honestly by naming what the dashboard omits before leaders mistake a tidy chart for complete reality.
situation_notes.comparing-to-others: Social media profiles are heavily edited maps of a life, and this model stops you comparing your full reality against curated highlights.

case_seeds: Korzybski presents the map territory distinction, 1931
Science and Sanity published by Alfred Korzybski, 1933
origin: Polish-American thinker Alfred Korzybski, founder of general semantics, presented the distinction at a scientific meeting in 1931 and developed it in Science and Sanity in 1933. He was reacting against careless identification of words, labels, and models with the things they represent. The phrase later spread through linguistics, psychology, management, and investing, where Charlie Munger and others repeated it as a warning about models.
mechanism_deep: A map works because of three deliberate distortions, and understanding them turns a slogan into a usable inspection tool. The first distortion is selection: a map keeps only the features its maker judged relevant to one purpose, so a road map omits geology and a financial statement omits morale, not because those things are unreal but because they were outside the job the map was built for. Trouble begins when a map built for one job is silently used for another, such as using engagement metrics designed to sell advertising as if they measured learning or trust. The second distortion is compression: reality is continuous, changing, and many-dimensional, while any representation must freeze it into categories, averages, and snapshots. Compression hides variance, so an average customer, an average temperature, or a net promoter score can describe a population that no individual member actually resembles, and decisions aimed at the average can serve nobody. The third distortion is lag: maps are made from past observations, so they describe the territory as it was when surveyed, and the more stable the past looked, the more confidently people navigate a present that has already moved, a failure visible whenever a business plan assumes last year's platform rules still hold. Underneath all three sits a psychological pull toward reification, the tendency to treat an abstraction as a concrete thing once it has a name and a number. A credit score, an IQ figure, or a brand valuation starts as a summary and ends up being defended, gamed, and feared as if it were the person, the mind, or the company itself. The corrective is not to abandon maps, which would leave only unaided intuition, an even worse map that hides its own distortions. The corrective is a routine of triangulation: compare the map against direct contact with the territory, against a second map built for a different purpose, and against the testimony of people who live in the places the map flattens, then update or discard the representation when the territory disagrees, because in every such disagreement the territory is right by definition. The model also prescribes a maintenance rhythm. Every map should carry, at least informally, three labels: its purpose, its date, and its known blind spots, and it should be re-surveyed whenever decisions based on it start surprising their makers, because surprise is the territory signalling that the representation has drifted. Skilled practitioners therefore budget for contact with the ground itself: site visits, customer conversations, raw records read without aggregation. Such contact feels inefficient beside a clean dashboard, which is precisely why organisations cut it first and why their maps then age undisturbed until a crisis performs the re-survey at a far higher price.
examples_extra: During the Vietnam War, United States officials under Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara relied heavily on quantified measures such as enemy body counts to judge progress. Historians widely argue the numbers became a misleading map: they could rise while strategic and political reality on the ground deteriorated, and the pressure to produce favourable counts distorted reporting itself, a failure later called the McNamara fallacy.

In navigation, drivers following satellite directions have repeatedly driven into closed roads, construction zones, and unsuitable routes when the digital map lagged behind physical reality or misread a location. Navigation providers now add live user reports precisely because a static map, however detailed, cannot be the territory; the road as it exists today always outranks the road as recorded.
misconceptions: Many people think the model means all models and data are useless — in reality, it means every model omits something, so you must know its omissions and purpose.
Many people think a more detailed map is automatically a better one — in reality, extra detail can add lag, false precision, and clutter while still omitting what matters.
Many people think direct experience is pure truth with no map involved — in reality, memory and perception are also representations, just less explicit ones that need checking too.
practice: Omission audit: Take one dashboard, report, or profile you rely on and write three columns: what it shows, what it leaves out, and who could tell you about the left-out part. This week, get one left-out fact directly from that person or place before your next decision using the map.

Two-map check: For an important judgement, deliberately find a second representation built for a different purpose, such as customer calls alongside sales data, or a walk through a neighbourhood alongside its listings map. Write down one place where the two maps disagree and investigate that spot first.
cross_domain: Education shows the gap when a test score, built as a narrow sample of performance on one day, is treated as a student's whole ability, steering teaching toward the test itself, while finance shows it when a risk model summarising calm recent years is treated as the market's true behaviour and fails in a crisis. In both fields the summary was useful until institutions forgot it was a summary and began serving the number instead of the reality.

quote.text: The map is not the territory.
quote.author: Alfred Korzybski

name_vi: Vòng tròn năng lực — biết rõ mình giỏi và dốt ở đâu
definition: Know clearly which topics you truly understand and stay inside that boundary when making important decisions.
mechanism: Judgement quality collapses outside the areas where you have real experience and reliable feedback, but confidence often stays high, which is the dangerous combination. Defining your circle forces an honest inventory of what you know, what you merely recognise, and what you are guessing. Decisions then either stay inside proven ground or deliberately buy expertise, more time, and smaller stakes when stepping outside it becomes unavoidable.
classic_example: During the technology boom of the late 1990s, Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger openly admitted that internet businesses lay outside their circle of competence and refused to buy them. Commentators mocked Berkshire Hathaway as outdated while technology shares soared. When the dot com bubble burst in 2000, their restraint protected their capital while many celebrated technology investors lost heavily.
modern_example: An office worker who understands index funds gets pitched a complicated crypto leveraged product by an enthusiastic friend. She admits the product sits outside her circle and that she cannot explain how it makes or loses money. She declines, keeps her savings plan unchanged, and later watches the product collapse in a market downturn she never claimed to predict.
failure_mode: A circle drawn too tightly becomes an excuse never to learn, delegate, or grow, and competence boundaries are easy to misjudge in both directions. Some valuable opportunities require acting with partial knowledge alongside experts. Treat the circle as a guide for sizing risk and seeking help, not as a permanent fence around your ambitions.
apply_steps: List topics you understand from real experience
Mark topics you only recognise superficially
Write your boundary down explicitly
Stay inside it for large decisions
Shrink stakes or hire expertise outside it

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Your circle tells you whether you truly understand how a company earns money or are merely buying a story you cannot evaluate.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: Advice outside your circle cannot be judged properly, so this model pushes you to simplify the decision or refuse it entirely today.
situation_notes.what-to-learn-next: Mapping your circle shows which adjacent skill would expand it most usefully instead of scattering effort across fashionable topics with no foundation.

case_seeds: Buffett and Munger avoid technology stocks before the dot com crash, 2000
lab_spec: The user lists topics they invest or work in and rates their real experience, feedback quality, and ability to explain each one simply. The tool draws a visual circle map showing proven ground, shaky edges, and unknown territory, with warnings before they rate a topic too generously.
origin: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger developed and popularised the phrase at Berkshire Hathaway from the 1980s onward, with Buffett stating it most famously in his 1996 letter to shareholders. The underlying idea is older, rooted in Socratic awareness of ignorance and in craft traditions where masters knew the limits of their trade, but Buffett and Munger turned it into an explicit investing and decision discipline.
mechanism_deep: A real circle of competence is built from three ingredients that must all be present, and the absence of any one shrinks the circle far more than people expect. The first ingredient is a causal model: you can explain, in plain language and without notes, how the thing actually makes money, works, or fails, including who pays, why they pay, and what would have to change for the result to reverse. The second ingredient is lived feedback: you have made predictions or decisions in this area before and reality has corrected you, repeatedly and at a cost you actually felt, because only paid-for feedback burns away the confident errors that reading alone leaves intact. The third ingredient is boundary awareness, a specific and current list of adjacent questions you know you cannot answer, which is the part most people skip because it requires writing down ignorance in advance, before events expose it publicly. The dynamics around the circle explain its characteristic failures. Confidence expands faster than competence because recognition feels like knowledge: after watching many videos about a field you recognise its vocabulary and mistake that fluency for judgement, while your true circle has barely moved. Success also expands the apparent circle dishonestly, since a person who struck it rich in one industry is treated, and treats himself, as wise about unrelated industries, a transfer that wealth and status encourage and that has destroyed many fortunes on the second act. The circle interacts with stakes in a way that makes it practical rather than purist: outside the circle you are not forbidden to act, but the model demands compensation in the form of smaller stakes, larger margins of safety, independent expert help whose incentives you have checked, or a deliberate decision to treat the money as tuition. Over a lifetime the circle should grow, but it grows at its edges, through adjacent topics where existing feedback loops can extend, not through leaps into fashionable fields where you have neither model nor feedback and where your first lesson will be priced for experts. One more dynamic deserves emphasis: the circle is domain-specific at a finer grain than people assume. A brilliant investor in consumer brands may have no edge in biotechnology on the same exchange, and a superb clinician may be a poor judge of hospital budgets, because the feedback that built the circle was earned case by case in one narrow arena. Honest practitioners therefore speak of circles in the plural and distrust any reputation, including their own, that arrives pre-generalised. The practical test stays the same in every arena: predictions recorded in advance, outcomes reviewed without editing, and errors priced honestly.
examples_extra: In sport, elite tennis player Rafael Nadal built his career overwhelmingly on clay early on, winning his first French Open title in 2005 as a teenager, and was for years markedly stronger on that surface than on grass. Rather than pretending the circle was uniform, he and his team spent seasons specifically extending his grass game, and he went on to win Wimbledon in 2008 and 2010, an expansion earned at the edge, not assumed.

Surgeon and writer Atul Gawande has described in his books how surgical competence is procedure-specific: a surgeon excellent at one operation is a beginner again at a new one, and outcomes improve measurably with volume in that exact procedure. Hospitals that publish surgeon-specific volumes apply the circle idea institutionally, steering patients toward operators for whom this operation, not surgery in general, sits inside proven ground.
misconceptions: Many people think the circle is fixed by talent or education — in reality, it is built by feedback-rich experience and can be deliberately expanded at its edges.
Many people think staying in the circle means never acting with incomplete knowledge — in reality, it means adjusting stakes, safety margins, and help when you step outside it.
Many people think recognising a topic from news and videos puts it inside the circle — in reality, only explaining it causally and having been corrected by real feedback counts.
practice: Boundary letter: For one topic you spend money or time on, write three sentences: what I can explain without notes, what I have been wrong about before, and what I cannot judge at all. Keep the letter where you decide, and require yourself to reread it before any unusually large commitment in that topic.

Teach-back test: Choose a topic you believe is inside your circle and explain aloud, for two minutes without notes, how it makes money or works and how it could fail. Record yourself; every place you stall, use jargon as a substitute for explanation, or cannot name a failure mode marks real boundary, not inside.
cross_domain: Medicine institutionalises the circle through specialisation and referral, where a good general practitioner is valued partly for knowing which cases exceed general practice and belong to a specialist, while aviation does the same through type ratings that license a pilot for specific aircraft rather than for flying in general. In both fields the boundary is explicit, tested, and legally meaningful, which is exactly what personal decision-making usually lacks.

quote.text: The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital.
quote.author: Warren Buffett

name_vi: Tính có thể bác bỏ — khẳng định tốt phải kiểm chứng được
definition: A useful claim must be stated clearly enough that some possible evidence could prove it wrong.
mechanism: A claim that fits every possible outcome predicts nothing, because it rules nothing out. Falsifiability forces vague beliefs into precise statements with observable tests attached, which separates knowledge from storytelling. Each survived attempt at refutation genuinely strengthens a claim, while a claim protected from every test stays weak forever. The habit also exposes advice, courses, and strategies designed to sound right no matter what happens.
classic_example: Karl Popper published The Logic of Scientific Discovery in German in 1934, arguing that science advances by bold claims that evidence could refute. He contrasted Einstein's risky predictions with theories that explained everything after the fact and could never be proven wrong. His criterion reshaped philosophy of science and still shapes how researchers design studies and evaluate competing theories today.
modern_example: A course seller promises his trading method works but blames every losing student for weak mindset, so no result can ever count against it. Applying falsifiability, a buyer asks what outcome would prove the method flawed and gets no answer. She walks away and instead chooses a boring strategy whose past performance can actually be checked.
failure_mode: Not every valuable question is falsifiable, including ethics, taste, and many one off historical or strategic judgements. Demanding laboratory standards there produces false confidence in whatever happens to be measurable. Use falsifiability to screen empirical claims and advice, while accepting that some important decisions must rest on judgement rather than tests.
apply_steps: State the claim in precise words
Ask what evidence would prove it wrong
Set the test before seeing results
Run the cheapest honest test available
Drop or revise claims that fail

situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: Falsifiability exposes courses whose promises can never fail on paper because every bad result gets blamed on the student's mindset or effort.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: Asking what would prove a tipster wrong reveals whether their track record is genuinely testable or carefully worded to survive any market.
situation_notes.online-arguments: Falsifiability cuts through debates where both sides keep shifting definitions by asking each person what evidence would actually change their mind today.

case_seeds: Popper publishes The Logic of Scientific Discovery, 1934
Eddington's eclipse expedition tests Einstein's predictions, 1919
source_ref: Popper — The Logic of Scientific Discovery
origin: Austrian-British philosopher Karl Popper formalised the criterion in The Logic of Scientific Discovery, published in German in 1934 and in English in 1959. Popper was reacting against theories, including some versions of Marxist history and psychoanalysis, that could explain every outcome after the event. He proposed falsifiability as the line demarcating empirical science from non-science, reshaping twentieth-century philosophy of science.
mechanism_deep: Falsifiability works because of an asymmetry in logic: no pile of confirming examples can prove a universal claim, since the next case may differ, but a single genuine counterexample can refute it, so claims that expose themselves to that risk and survive carry real information. This produces a practical test for any assertion: before checking whether evidence supports it, ask what the world would have to look like for the claim to be wrong, and require the claimant, including yourself, to answer in advance, with observable terms and a deadline where relevant. The mechanism also disciplines testing itself. A test only counts if it could have gone the other way, so you must set the threshold before seeing the outcome, use a measure the claim actually implies, and refuse post-hoc rescues that rewrite the claim after failure, or at most allow a rescue that itself makes a new risky prediction. The limits are real and structural. Single historical events, ethical claims, and existential statements are not falsifiable in the laboratory sense, yet they are not therefore meaningless; Popper himself treated falsifiability as a boundary for empirical science, not for all worthwhile thought.
examples_extra: In 1919, Arthur Eddington and Frank Watson Dyson led eclipse expeditions to Principe and Brazil to measure whether starlight bent near the Sun by the amount Einstein's general relativity predicted. The prediction was risky and precise: different bending values would have supported Newton or no deflection instead. The announced results favoured Einstein and made his reputation, precisely because the test could have embarrassed him.

In business, the UK advertising regulator has repeatedly required marketers to withdraw health and earnings claims that could not be substantiated with testable evidence, applying a practical falsifiability standard: a claim must be stated specifically enough to be checked, and the seller must hold the checking evidence before advertising, rather than inventing explanations after complaints arrive.
misconceptions: Many people think falsifiable means already proven false — in reality, it means capable of being shown false if wrong; good scientific claims are falsifiable and so far unfalsified.

Many people think a claim supported by many examples must be strong — in reality, examples collected without any possible refuting test add little, because a claim that fits everything predicts nothing.
Many people think non-falsifiable claims are worthless in every sense — in reality, ethics, taste, and meaning fall outside the criterion; it only governs empirical claims.
practice: Refutation sentence: Take one belief guiding your spending or work and complete the sentence 'I would know I am wrong if, by [date], [observable result] happens.' If you cannot complete it, rewrite the belief more precisely until you can, then put the date in your calendar.

Guru audit: Pick one piece of advice you follow and write what its seller or author would accept as a failure of the advice itself, not of the follower. If every failure is blamed on followers' mindset or effort, downgrade the advice in your notes today.
cross_domain: Investing applies falsifiability when a written thesis includes explicit kill criteria, such as a debt level or market-share loss that would prove the thesis wrong and trigger a sale, while software product teams apply it when they pre-register a success metric and a ship-or-kill threshold before an A/B test. In both fields the pre-commitment is the whole point: the refuting condition must be fixed while hope and embarrassment cannot yet edit it.

quote.text: A theory which is not refutable by any conceivable event is non-scientific.
quote.author: Karl Popper

name_vi: Hàng rào Chesterton — hiểu lý do tồn tại trước khi phá bỏ
definition: Do not remove an existing rule or system until you understand why it was put there.
mechanism: Existing rules and routines often encode hard won lessons whose original reasons have been forgotten, so they look pointless precisely when their work is invisible. Chesterton's fence inserts a pause between seeing an apparently useless structure and destroying it. During that pause you investigate its history and purpose, which either reveals a real function worth preserving or confirms the rule is genuinely obsolete and safe to remove.
classic_example: Gilbert Keith Chesterton set out the principle in his 1929 book The Thing, imagining a reformer who wants to tear down a fence across a road without knowing why it was built. Chesterton argued the reformer should not be allowed to proceed until the fence's purpose is understood. The image became a lasting warning for policymakers, managers, and programmers alike.
modern_example: A new team lead wants to scrap a slow weekly approval step that delays every campaign. Asking around, she learns the step was added after an unapproved advert once caused a legal complaint and a fine. Instead of deleting it, she narrows the check to risky claims only, keeping the protection while removing most of the delay.
failure_mode: Investigating every legacy rule can stall necessary change, and some rules exist only because of rent seeking, habit, or long gone conditions. The fence principle can also be weaponised to defend anything old. Set a reasonable deadline for finding the purpose, and if none surfaces after honest effort, reform should proceed.
apply_steps: Pause before removing the rule
Ask who created it and when
Find the problem it originally solved
Check whether that problem still exists
Replace its function before deleting it

situation_notes.scaling-decision: Chesterton's fence stops you deleting informal checks that quietly held quality together before growth exposes why they existed in the first place.
situation_notes.users-but-no-revenue: An old paywall or signup step may look like friction yet exist to filter abusers, so understand it before removing it entirely.
situation_notes.asking-for-budget: Showing leadership you investigated why an existing process exists makes your request to change or fund it far more credible and persuasive.

case_seeds: Chesterton publishes The Thing with the fence parable, 1929
origin: English writer G. K. Chesterton stated the principle in his 1929 book The Thing, in a passage about a reformer who wants to remove a gate or fence across a road without knowing why it was erected. The image summarised an older conservative caution about reform, but Chesterton's formulation, that the reformer must first discover the fence's use, is the version later adopted by policymakers, engineers, and programmers.
mechanism_deep: The fence principle rests on the idea that surviving practices are compressed evidence. A rule that has operated for years has been shaped, however imperfectly, by accidents, complaints, lawsuits, shortages, and workarounds, most of which were never written down, so its current form carries information that no living person can fully recite. This creates an asymmetry of visibility that the principle is designed to counteract: the costs of a fence are continuous and conspicuous, in delays, forms, and frustrations everyone can point to, while its benefits are negative and invisible, consisting of disasters that did not happen and therefore left no stories. The investigative pause the model demands is therefore specific, not mystical: find who introduced the rule, what incident or fear prompted it, what breaks in its absence in comparable places, and whether the original condition still exists today. The boundary is equally specific. Some fences protect rents, exclude outsiders, or survive purely because removing them is nobody's job, and an honest investigation reveals those too. The principle sets a burden of inquiry proportional to irreversibility, not a veto: a reversible experiment with monitoring needs little archaeology, while abolishing a safety check, a legal safeguard, or a cultural norm deserves the full search before anyone swings the hammer.
examples_extra: In software engineering, teams repeatedly learn the fence lesson when deleting apparently dead code that turns out to be a workaround for a specific customer's workflow or an old regulatory case. Mature teams therefore use deprecation notices, usage telemetry, and staged rollouts, investigating why code exists before removal, a practice formalised in large codebases at companies such as Google, where owners must be consulted before deleting shared infrastructure.

In Britain, many apparently eccentric local rules, such as common grazing rights and ancient rights of way, have repeatedly survived reform attempts because investigation revealed living functions: drainage management, public access, and legal claims that would resurface expensively if abolished casually. Parliamentary reviews of rights of way treat historical evidence of use as substantive, not decorative, for exactly the compressed-evidence reason Chesterton described.
misconceptions: Many people think Chesterton's fence means never changing old rules — in reality, it means understanding a rule's function first, then reforming it with that function replaced or consciously accepted as a risk.
Many people think every old rule must have a wise purpose — in reality, some exist from rent-seeking or dead conditions; investigation is how you find out which kind you face.
Many people think the principle is only political — in reality, it applies equally to code, household routines, contracts, and any system whose reasons were never written down.
practice: Fence interview: Choose one annoying rule in your workplace or home and ask two people who were there before you: 'Do you know why this started?' Write down any incident they name. If nobody knows after honest asking, run a small reversible removal for two weeks with a clear check date.

Invisible benefit list: Before deleting a step from a routine, list three bad outcomes that step might be silently preventing, however unglamorous. For each, write how you would notice within a month if removal caused it, so the experiment has an alarm attached.
cross_domain: Medicine applies the fence when clinicians hesitate before stopping a long-standing medication, because its benefit may be the absence of events and its history may include a forgotten indication recorded in old notes, while urban planning applies it when a seemingly pointless alley or setback turns out to carry drainage, access, or fire-escape functions. In both fields the visible thing looks like clutter until its invisible job is traced.

name_vi: Đường phủ định — tốt lên bằng cách bỏ bớt điều hại
definition: Improve a situation by removing harmful or useless elements instead of adding more features or effort.
mechanism: Harmful elements usually have clearer, more reliable effects than beneficial additions, whose gains are speculative and often cancel each other out. Removing a bad habit, a toxic customer, or a needless step produces immediate, predictable improvement without new complexity. Subtraction also reduces the surface area for errors and interactions, which is why progress by removal is often more robust than progress by addition.
