In publishing, editors use category sales distributions, not one breakout title, to set realistic advances for new authors. In medicine, screening programmes start from population prevalence before any individual test result is allowed to move the clinical estimate.

name_vi: Lãi kép / Tăng trưởng kép
definition: Compounding happens when growth builds on earlier growth so small steady gains become surprisingly large over long periods.
mechanism: Compounding works because each period adds not only to the original amount but also to all previous gains. Early growth looks disappointingly slow because the base is small, which tempts people to quit or chase shortcuts. Over time the base grows, so the same percentage produces ever larger absolute gains. The key variables are rate, time, and consistency. Interrupting the process, especially through large losses or long breaks, destroys far more value than most people intuitively expect.
classic_example: Warren Buffett accumulated most of his wealth after age fifty because compounding needed decades to show its full effect. He and Charlie Munger purchased See's Candies in 1972 for 25 million dollars, and the business went on to generate many times that amount in profits over the following decades through steady reinvestment and pricing power.
modern_example: A marketer publishes one useful post each week for a small audience and sees almost no growth for six months. By the second year, older posts keep bringing search traffic while new posts reach a larger base. The channel grows faster without extra effort because past work keeps working, exactly like interest earning interest on earlier interest in a savings account.
failure_mode: Compounding misleads when people assume a high early growth rate will continue forever or ignore fees, taxes, and losses that compound negatively. Debt, bad habits, and reputational damage also compound. The model also fails for short time horizons where the curve still looks flat and linear effort may matter more than waiting for exponential effects.
apply_steps: Start early even with a small amount
Protect the base from large losses
Reinvest gains instead of spending them
Measure progress over years not weeks

situation_notes.idle-cash-decision: This model reveals the long term cost of leaving cash idle, because years without growth cannot be recovered later by small extra contributions.
situation_notes.what-to-learn-next: It shows why learning a foundational skill early matters, since that skill makes every later skill faster and cheaper to acquire.
situation_notes.channel-not-growing: It explains a flat early channel curve, revealing that consistent publishing builds a library that later grows traffic without proportional extra work.

case_seeds: Buffett and Munger purchase of See's Candies, 1972
Buffett wealth growth accelerating after age fifty
lab_spec: The user inputs a starting amount, monthly contribution, annual growth rate, and years. The tool draws two curves comparing simple growth versus compounding and highlights the crossover point where growth on past gains overtakes new contributions, with sliders to test fees and a late start.
origin: Charging interest is ancient, recorded in Mesopotamian practice, but compound growth was analysed mathematically in medieval and early modern finance. Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 helped spread such calculations in Europe, and Jacob Bernoulli, studying continuously compounded interest in 1683, uncovered the constant e. The modern mental model, however, was popularised for investors by Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger.
mechanism_deep: The engine is a single recursion: this period's ending balance becomes next period's starting base. That one change converts addition into multiplication, and multiplication repeated is exponentiation, which is why the curve stays deceptively flat before bending sharply upward. Three variables govern the bend. Rate sets the steepness, time sets how many multiplications occur, and consistency determines whether the chain survives unbroken. Time dominates in a way intuition resists: at a fixed rate, the final period alone can add more than the first decade combined, because it acts on the largest base. Interruption is correspondingly brutal. A fifty percent loss requires a one hundred percent gain just to return to the starting line, so avoiding large drawdowns protects compounding more than squeezing out extra return. Fees and taxes act as negative rates that compound just as faithfully; a one percent annual fee sounds trivial but consumes a large share of a multi-decade ending balance. There is also volatility drag: alternating gains and losses of the same percentage do not cancel, they shrink the base, so a steadier path can beat a wilder path with the same average return. Human intuition fails because it is linear, trained on effort-in and result-out relationships, so people quit during the flat early stretch precisely when patience is cheapest. The boundary conditions matter too. Compounding needs a reinvestment channel and a base that survives; skills, audiences, and reputations compound only while their owner keeps producing and does not destroy trust, which is the reputational equivalent of a catastrophic loss. A mathematical symmetry deepens the intuition: in pure doubling, the gain during the final doubling period equals the entire accumulated value from all previous periods combined. That is why the last decade of a forty-year savings plan can add more than the first three, and why starting five years earlier routinely beats doubling contributions later. Inflation runs the identical engine in reverse, quietly halving purchasing power on a schedule the Rule of 72 predicts from the inflation rate, which is why cash held under a mattress is not a neutral choice but a slowly compounding loss. Knowledge compounds through the same recursion when each idea makes the next easier to absorb: a reader with a latticework of models recognises patterns in a new book that a beginner cannot see, so identical reading hours yield widening returns. Relationships and trust compound identically, with each kept promise raising the base on which the next interaction builds. The shared boundary condition across money, skill, and reputation is that the exponent only works on what survives: a single catastrophic loss, a health collapse from neglected habits, or one act of dishonesty can reset the base to near zero, which is why every serious compounder, from Buffett onward, treats avoiding ruin as the first rule rather than an afterthought.
examples_extra: The chessboard legend tells of the inventor Sissa asking a king for wheat doubled on each square: one grain, then two, then four. By the final square the promised total exceeded harvests the kingdom could ever supply. The story is a legend, but it remains the cleanest illustration of why doubling feels harmless early and becomes impossible late.

Under ideal laboratory conditions, Escherichia coli bacteria can divide roughly every twenty minutes. A single cell's descendants therefore number in the billions within a day, which is why food contamination becomes dangerous so quickly and why early intervention, when the base is still tiny, matters far more than later effort. The same arithmetic explains why sterilising equipment and treating infections early deserve disproportionate effort inside hospitals and food supply chains.

formula.expression: FV = PV x (1 + r)^n ; doubling time is approximately 72 / (r in percent)
formula.variables: FV is the future value after compounding. PV is the present value, the starting base. r is the growth rate per period expressed as a decimal, and n is the number of periods the base is left to compound.
formula.worked_example: Invest 1,000 dollars at 8 percent per year for ten years: FV = 1,000 x 1.08^10 = about 2,159 dollars. The Rule of 72 predicts doubling in about 72/8 = 9 years.

misconceptions: Many people think compound interest was called the eighth wonder of the world by Einstein — in reality, that attribution is apocryphal, with no reliable record of Einstein saying it.
Many people think a higher average return always compounds better — in reality, large losses and volatile swings drag the geometric result below the simple average.
Many people think starting later can be fixed by contributing a bit more — in reality, lost early periods remove the multiplications that later contributions can never recreate.

practice.name: Two-start race
practice.instructions: Use a spreadsheet or calculator to grow 100 units at 10 percent yearly for forty years, starting now versus starting ten years from now with 200 units. Compare the endings and write down which input mattered more, the delay or the doubled contribution.

practice.name: Fee drag check
practice.instructions: Take a real or hypothetical investment and compute its thirty-year value at 7 percent growth, then again at 6 percent to simulate a one percent annual fee. Note the percentage of the ending balance the seemingly small fee consumed.

cross_domain: In epidemiology, infections compound when each case generates further cases, so early exponential phases decide whether an outbreak stays containable. In technology, network platforms compound value as each new user makes the service more useful to existing users. In personal health, sleep debt and cardiovascular fitness both accumulate gradually, rewarding consistency long before results become visible. In writing and research, an archive of earlier work compounds quietly as each new piece sends readers back into the older catalogue.

name_vi: Hoán vị và Tổ hợp
definition: Permutations and combinations are ways to count arrangements where order either matters completely or does not matter at all.
mechanism: Small sets explode into surprisingly large numbers of possible arrangements, and counting them correctly depends on whether order changes the outcome. A password, a race ranking, and a committee are different problems because swapping positions matters in the first two but not the third. Factorial growth explains why brute force guessing fails quickly and why variety in teams, schedules, or product options expands faster than intuition suggests. The model turns vague feelings about many possibilities into an exact count.
classic_example: In the seventeenth century, Blaise Pascal built his famous triangle of numbers to solve counting problems raised by gamblers in 1654. The triangle gave a systematic way to calculate combinations for dice and card games, replacing guesswork with a reliable method that later became central to probability, statistics, and computer science.
modern_example: A manager scheduling five team members for on call weekends assumes there are only a few arrangements. Counting permutations shows there are far more possible orders than she expected, which explains why manual scheduling feels endless. She switches to simple rules and rotation instead of trying to evaluate every arrangement by hand each month.
failure_mode: Counting arrangements misleads when real world constraints make many counted options impossible or meaningless in practice. It also wastes time when an approximate sense of scale is enough. People often apply the wrong version, counting ordered arrangements for a problem where order does not matter, and get a dramatically inflated answer.
apply_steps: Ask whether order changes the outcome
Count total positions and available choices
Use combinations when order does not matter
Check if constraints eliminate many arrangements

situation_notes.decision-under-time-pressure: This model reveals why trying to compare every possible option under time pressure fails, because arrangement counts explode far beyond human review capacity.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: It shows how adding team members or product variants multiplies coordination options, making simple rules more valuable than exhaustive manual planning.

case_seeds: Pascal's triangle and gambling problems, 1654
Lottery odds calculations using combinations
origin: Counting arrangements is ancient, appearing in Indian and Chinese mathematics for verse metres, dice, and lotteries, and in the work of medieval Islamic scholars. In Europe it was systematised during the seventeenth-century probability correspondence of Pascal and Fermat, and Jacob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi of 1713 gave combinations a central place in the new mathematics of chance.
mechanism_deep: Everything rests on the multiplication principle: if a task happens in stages with independent choices at each stage, the total count is the product of the stage counts. That product is why small increases explode; adding one more position multiplies the total rather than adding to it, and arranging n distinct items produces n factorial orders, a sequence that outruns exponentials with fixed bases. The central judgement is whether swapping two items creates a genuinely new outcome. If it does, you have a permutation and the raw product stands. If it does not, the same selection has been counted once for every internal arrangement, so you divide by that number of arrangements to get a combination. Most real errors are overcounting errors: identical items treated as distinct, the same committee counted in every order, or constraints ignored until the count includes impossible cases. Boundary cases matter as well: selections without replacement shrink the available pool at each step, while selections with replacement keep it constant, and confusing the two changes the answer dramatically. Human intuition fails because it extrapolates linearly from arranging three or four items, where counts feel manageable, to ten or twenty items, where the counts exceed the number of seconds in a human lifetime.
examples_extra: A standard Rubik's Cube can be arranged in about 43 quintillion permutations, a figure computed from the orientations and positions of its corner and edge pieces. That astronomical count from a small handheld toy explains why random twisting never solves it and why the puzzle rewards memorised algorithms instead.

Genetics runs on combinations: DNA codons are ordered triples drawn from four bases, giving 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 codons. That small counting fact underlies the genetic code, in which those 64 codons specify twenty amino acids plus stop signals during protein synthesis in cells.

formula.expression: nPr = n! / (n - r)! ; nCr = n! / (r! x (n - r)!)
formula.variables: n is the total number of items available to choose from. r is how many items are selected or arranged. The factorial n! means n multiplied by every whole number down to 1, with permutations counting ordered arrangements and combinations counting unordered selections.
formula.worked_example: Choosing a three-person committee from ten people, where order does not matter: C(10,3) = 10! / (3! x 7!) = 120 possible committees. Arranging three finalists in ranked order instead gives P(10,3) = 720.

misconceptions: Many people think more items means proportionally more arrangements — in reality, arrangements grow factorially, so each added item multiplies the total by a larger factor.
Many people think combinations and permutations are interchangeable labels — in reality, using the ordered count for an unordered problem inflates the answer by the factorial of the selection size.
Many people think a huge count means every arrangement is reachable — in reality, constraints and identical items can rule out most of the counted arrangements in practice.

practice.name: Shrink and verify
practice.instructions: Take four named people and list by hand every two-person committee, then every ordered pair. Check that your lists match C(4,2) = 6 and P(4,2) = 12, and notice exactly where the ordered count double-counts.

practice.name: Password reality check
practice.instructions: Calculate how many four-digit PINs exist, then how many six-character codes can be formed from twenty-six lowercase letters with repetition. Compare the two totals and state in one sentence why length beats cleverness for code strength.

cross_domain: In cryptography, key spaces are permutation-style counts, and security rests on making the count too large to search. In chemistry, combinations of elements and bonds generate molecular diversity that drug researchers screen systematically. In logistics, route permutations explain why delivery sequencing becomes a hard optimisation problem once a driver has even a dozen stops. In sport, league schedulers face permutation counts so large that fixture lists are built by computer optimisation rather than by hand.

name_vi: Cây quyết định
definition: A decision tree maps choices and possible outcomes in branches so you can compare paths before committing resources.
mechanism: Complex decisions hide their structure when kept as a single vague question in your head. A tree forces you to name each choice, each chance event, and what happens after each branch. Once drawn, weak branches become visible, missing options stand out, and you can attach probabilities and values to compare paths fairly. Working backward from end outcomes also prevents a common error, judging a decision only by its first step instead of its full consequences.
classic_example: During the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962, President John F Kennedy and his advisors weighed branching options including blockade, airstrike, and invasion, each with different Soviet responses. The structured comparison of paths and consequences helped them choose the naval quarantine, a middle branch that applied pressure without immediately triggering the most dangerous escalation path.
modern_example: A freelancer considers quitting her job to build a course. She draws a tree with branches for course success, partial sales, and failure, plus a branch for staying employed while testing on weekends. Seeing the full paths, she chooses the weekend test first because it preserves income while still revealing whether the course branch is worth pursuing fully.
failure_mode: Decision trees fail when branches omit the outcome that actually happens or when probabilities are invented to justify a preferred path. They also become useless when drawn in such detail that nobody updates them. A tree is a thinking aid, not a prediction, and it cannot capture emotions, politics, or events outside its branches.
apply_steps: Draw each choice as a separate branch
Add chance outcomes and their probabilities
Write the payoff at each end point
Compare full paths not first steps

situation_notes.considering-job-change: This model reveals the full paths after accepting or rejecting an offer, including fallback options most people forget to map out.
situation_notes.taking-investment-or-not: It shows what happens after each funding path over several years, not just the immediate relief of having cash available now.
situation_notes.career-pivot: It clarifies which pivot steps keep future branches open and which choices quietly close doors you may want later.
situation_notes.big-purchase: It exposes hidden branches like maintenance costs and resale outcomes that the purchase price alone completely hides from view.

case_seeds: Kennedy decision making during Cuban Missile Crisis, 1962
Oil companies using decision trees for drilling choices
origin: Decision trees grew out of twentieth-century operations research and game theory, and were formalised as decision analysis by Stanford professor Ronald A. Howard, who coined that term in the 1960s. Howard's work at Stanford and in consulting turned an intuitive branching sketch into a disciplined method combining probabilities, values, and sequential choices for engineering and business decisions.
mechanism_deep: A tree has two kinds of nodes, and keeping them separate is most of the discipline. Square decision nodes are yours: you pick the branch. Circular chance nodes belong to the world: probabilities, which must sum to one across the branches, decide. Evaluation runs backwards, a procedure called rollback or folding back. At each chance node you replace the branches with their expected value; at each decision node you keep the best expected value and prune the rest. This exposes a quantity novices miss, the value of flexibility: a branch that looks worse on average may win because it preserves a later decision after uncertainty resolves, such as piloting before scaling. Trees also force the end states to be valued in one common currency, which reveals hidden disagreements. The failure boundary is combinatorics: every added stage multiplies branches, so useful trees stay deliberately coarse, modelling only decisions and uncertainties that could change the choice. Intuition fails without the drawing because people evaluate the first step emotionally and never visit the terminal nodes, where bankruptcy, regret, or compounding actually live. A drawn tree cannot fix invented probabilities, but it localises the invention to specific nodes you can research, debate, or test cheaply before committing.
examples_extra: Emergency medicine runs on explicit decision trees. Chest-pain protocols in hospital emergency departments branch on ECG findings, troponin blood results, and patient history to route people toward discharge, observation, or urgent intervention. The tree format matters because the cost of a missed branch, a heart attack sent home, is catastrophic and irreversible.

Pharmaceutical companies manage drug development as staged decision trees: fund a Phase I safety trial, then decide again with that data before paying for larger Phase II and Phase III studies. Most candidate drugs are pruned at early, cheap nodes, which is exactly the tree logic of buying information before committing serious capital.

formula.expression: Value of a chance node = sum over branches of (probability x payoff)
formula.variables: Each branch of a chance node carries a probability, and the branch probabilities must sum to 1. The payoff is the value of the outcome at the end of that branch, expressed in one common unit such as money, time, or utility.
formula.worked_example: A launch branch pays 100 units with probability 0.3 and loses 20 units with probability 0.7. Its value is 0.3 x 100 + 0.7 x (-20) = 30 - 14 = 16 units, so it beats a safe branch worth 10.

misconceptions: Many people think a decision tree predicts the future — in reality, it organises your current beliefs about the future so their consequences can be compared consistently.
Many people think the branch with the best possible outcome is best — in reality, rollback values whole branches by probability-weighted outcomes, including their bad endings.
Many people think more detail always improves a tree — in reality, branches multiply combinatorially, and a tree too detailed to update becomes decoration rather than a decision tool.

practice.name: Three-branch career tree
practice.instructions: Draw one pending decision with exactly three branches. For each, add one chance event with a rough probability and an end-state value in money or satisfaction. Roll the values back and write which assumption, if changed, would flip your choice.

practice.name: Find the missing branch
practice.instructions: Take a plan you already made and list its tree. Deliberately add the two branches people usually omit: the partial-success outcome and the do-nothing outcome. Recompute which path wins once those branches carry honest payoffs.

cross_domain: In computing, machine-learning decision trees split data by questions, a different use of the same branching picture that clinicians also use in diagnostic flowcharts. In chess and game engines, search trees evaluate move branches several plies deep before committing. In public policy, epidemic response plans branch on hospital capacity thresholds decided in advance. In law, litigation strategy trees weigh settlement branches against trial outcomes at each procedural stage before legal costs escalate further.

name_vi: Giá trị kỳ vọng
definition: Expected value averages every possible outcome weighted by its probability to show what a decision is worth overall.
mechanism: A decision can feel attractive because its best outcome is exciting, even when that outcome is unlikely. Expected value corrects this by multiplying each outcome by its probability and adding the results together. This reveals whether a bet, project, or price makes sense across many repetitions. Positive expected value does not guarantee a win this time, and negative expected value can still win once by luck, which is why the model judges decision quality rather than single results.
classic_example: Professional poker players have long used expected value to judge bets rather than single hands. In the 1970s and 1980s, players like Doyle Brunson described in Super System, published in 1979, how calling or folding should depend on pot size and winning probability, not on hope. A mathematically correct call could lose one hand and still be the right decision.
modern_example: A course creator weighs spending two weeks building a bonus module. She estimates a modest chance it lifts sales significantly, a larger chance of a small lift, and some chance of no effect. Multiplying each outcome by its likelihood shows the expected gain exceeds the cost of her time, so she builds a simple version instead of guessing based on optimism alone.
failure_mode: Expected value misleads when a single trial can ruin you, because the average across imaginary repetitions never actually happens. It also fails when probabilities and payoffs are guessed carelessly. For one time decisions with irreversible downside, protecting against the worst case matters more than maximizing the mathematical average of all cases.
apply_steps: List outcomes with honest probability estimates
Multiply each outcome by its probability
Add results to get expected value
Reject positive averages with ruinous downside

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: This model reveals whether a stock is attractive after weighting both upside and downside, not just by its most exciting growth story.
situation_notes.pricing-a-product: It shows which price wins overall by combining conversion chances at each level instead of chasing the highest price tag alone.
situation_notes.taking-investment-or-not: It clarifies the true cost of giving up ownership by averaging future company values instead of focusing only on cash today.

case_seeds: Doyle Brunson Super System on poker decisions, 1979
Insurance pricing built on expected claims
lab_spec: The user builds a simple bet or project by entering up to four outcomes with their probabilities and payoffs. The tool calculates expected value instantly, draws a bar showing each outcome's contribution, and lets the user tweak probabilities to see when the decision flips from positive to negative.
origin: Expected value was born in the same 1654 Pascal and Fermat correspondence that founded probability, in their solution to the problem of points: how to divide stakes fairly when a game is interrupted. Christiaan Huygens gave expectation its first published treatment in 1657, and the concept became the pricing backbone of insurance and gambling mathematics.
mechanism_deep: The mathematics is simple weighted addition, but three subtleties decide whether the number deserves trust. First, expectation is linear, so the expected value of a sum equals the sum of expected values even when outcomes are tangled together; this is what makes portfolio-level and business-level calculations tractable. Second, expected value is a statement about aggregates and repetitions, not about your single draw. A bet can be positive in expectation while losing most of the time, when a rare large payoff carries the average; conversely a negative-expectation purchase like insurance can be rational because the buyer is purchasing survival, not average profit. This is where utility enters: a dollar lost at the edge of ruin costs far more than a dollar gained in comfort, so rational agents maximise expected utility, not raw expected money, and any analysis that ignores the ruin branch is incomplete. Third, the inputs are usually softer than the arithmetic. Probabilities estimated from hope, payoffs estimated from pitch decks, and omitted middle outcomes all flow through the multiplication untouched, producing a precise number built on fog. Sensitivity checking is therefore part of the model: vary each probability until the decision flips, and see whether the flip point is plausible. Human intuition fails because it evaluates outcomes one at a time, overweighting the most exciting and the most frightening, and because outcome bias afterwards rewrites history: a lucky win gets remembered as proof the bet was good, and an unlucky loss as proof it was bad, when the expected value at decision time is the only fair grade. Casinos, insurers, and professional gamblers survive by respecting the aggregate; their customers donate by judging single vivid results. The model's most famous stress test arrived early. In the St Petersburg paradox, published by Daniel Bernoulli in 1738, a coin is flipped until it lands heads, paying two ducats if heads appears on the first flip, four on the second, eight on the third, and so on. The expected value is infinite, yet nobody sensible pays even a modest fortune to play, a contradiction Bernoulli resolved by proposing that money's utility grows logarithmically, so each doubling of wealth matters less than the last. That single move founded expected utility theory and explains real behaviour the raw model cannot: why the same person buys insurance, negative in expected money, and a lottery ticket, also negative, since each protects or buys something utility values beyond cash. Estimation discipline is the other half of mastery. Probabilities should come from base rates and track records rather than from how the pitch made you feel, payoffs should include your time, taxes, and the options you foreclose, and the calculation should be redone after asking what outcome you have quietly left off the list, because omitted outcomes are where positive-looking expectations go to die. Judged this way, expected value is less a formula than an audit: it forces every hope and fear into the same ledger, priced and weighted, where rhetoric loses its power to overweight whichever outcome was described most vividly.
examples_extra: The MIT Blackjack Team, a group of students and former students active from the late 1970s into the 1990s, used card counting to identify moments when the deck's composition gave players a small positive expectation. Their edge per hand was tiny, so the operation only worked through disciplined bankroll management and enormous numbers of hands played by coordinated teammates.

Airlines deliberately sell more tickets than seats, because expected-value arithmetic on no-show rates says the extra revenue usually exceeds the cost of compensating the rare bumped passenger. The calculation occasionally fails publicly when everyone shows up, but across thousands of flights a day the aggregate math keeps load factors and fares where airlines want them.

formula.expression: EV = sum over outcomes of (probability x payoff) = p1x1 + p2x2 + ... + pnxn
formula.variables: Each outcome i has a probability pi, and all probabilities must sum to 1. Each payoff xi is the gain or loss in that outcome, with losses entered as negative numbers, measured in one consistent unit such as dollars or hours.
formula.worked_example: A side project pays 100 dollars with probability 0.4 and costs you 50 dollars with probability 0.6. EV = 0.4 x 100 + 0.6 x (-50) = 40 - 30 = +10 dollars per attempt on average.

misconceptions: Many people think a positive expected value means you will probably win — in reality, skewed payoffs can make most attempts lose while the rare big win carries the average.
Many people think a decision that ended badly was a bad bet — in reality, decision quality is set by the expected value with the information available at the time, not by one realised outcome.
Many people think expected value forbids buying insurance — in reality, insurance trades a small certain loss against a ruinous outcome, which expected utility, not raw expected money, justifies.

practice.name: Price the warranty
practice.instructions: Pick an extended warranty you have been offered. Estimate the chance the product fails in the cover period and the repair cost it would save, compute the expected payout, and compare it with the warranty price before deciding.

practice.name: Flip-point test
practice.instructions: Take a current decision and write its outcomes and rough probabilities. Compute the expected value, then lower your success probability step by step until the value crosses zero, and ask honestly which side of that flip point reality is on.

cross_domain: In public health, vaccination and screening programmes are justified by expected cases prevented across millions of people, even though any individual's expected benefit is small. In climate policy, expected-damage calculations weigh low-probability catastrophic futures against mitigation costs today. In litigation, settlement offers are priced from expected trial outcomes, which is why most civil cases settle. In agriculture, planting decisions weigh expected harvest value across weather outcomes rather than betting the whole farm on the likeliest season.

name_vi: Luật số lớn
definition: The law of large numbers says averages from many repeated trials settle close to the true underlying rate.
mechanism: Single trials are dominated by luck, so early results swing wildly above and below the true rate. As trials accumulate, lucky and unlucky streaks cancel each other out and the average drifts toward the underlying probability. This is why casinos profit predictably despite losing individual hands, and why a handful of customer reviews tells you almost nothing. The model teaches patience with measurement, because reliable conclusions demand volume that most people stop far short of collecting.
classic_example: Jacob Bernoulli proved the law of large numbers in Ars Conjectandi, published in 1713 after his death, showing mathematically that observed frequencies approach true probabilities as trials increase. Casinos later built their entire business on this principle, accepting that individual gamblers sometimes win while knowing the average across millions of bets favors the house.
modern_example: A shop owner tests two homepage designs for one day and declares a winner after thirty visitors. The next week the result reverses completely. Applying the law of large numbers, she waits for several thousand visitors before deciding. The final average is boring but trustworthy, and it stops her from redesigning the site every time random noise produces a dramatic early result.
failure_mode: This law does not help when you only get one trial, such as choosing a cofounder or launching a single career. It also fails when trials are not independent or the underlying rate itself keeps changing. Waiting for more data has a cost too, and sometimes a fast imperfect decision beats a slow statistically perfect one.
apply_steps: Ask how many trials your average uses
Distrust conclusions from tiny trial counts
Wait for volume before redesigning strategy
Check trials are similar and independent

situation_notes.channel-not-growing: This model reveals that five videos cannot prove a channel concept failed, because averages only stabilize after many comparable publishing trials.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: It shows why a tipster with ten winning calls may still be lucky, since reliable skill only appears across hundreds of decisions.
situation_notes.users-but-no-revenue: It clarifies that feedback from a handful of early users is mostly noise until usage volume reveals the stable underlying pattern.

case_seeds: Bernoulli Ars Conjectandi published, 1713
Casino business model built on large bet volumes
origin: Jacob Bernoulli proved the first version, the weak law of large numbers, in his Ars Conjectandi, published in 1713 after his death; he reportedly spent two decades on the proof. Girolamo Cardano had noticed the underlying pattern informally a century earlier in his gambler's manual, but Bernoulli turned the observation into a theorem about frequencies converging to probabilities.
mechanism_deep: The theorem says the average of independent trials with the same underlying probability settles toward that probability as the count grows, with typical deviation shrinking roughly in proportion to one over the square root of the number of trials. That square-root rule explains the model's cruelty: to halve your noise you must quadruple your data, so early samples are wildly misleading and certainty stays expensive forever. Fluctuations do not get corrected by the universe; a run of heads creates no debt that tails must repay. Convergence happens by dilution, as new trials swamp the early imbalance in a growing denominator. Three boundary conditions decide whether the law applies at all. Trials must be independent, or at least not conspiring; they must share a stable underlying rate, which changing markets and learning players violate; and the outcome must have a finite, meaningful average, which extreme power-law payoffs can destroy. Human intuition fails symmetrically in both directions: the hot-hand error reads meaning into short streaks, while the gambler's fallacy expects short-run balancing that the law never promises. Analysts fail when they demand casino-level certainty from a sample of twelve users, or when they keep collecting data long after the rate itself has moved.
examples_extra: South African schoolteacher John Edmund Kerrich, interned in Denmark during the Second World War, tossed a coin 10,000 times and recorded 5,067 heads. His running frequency wandered early on, then settled close to one half, and his experiment, later described by statistician Lancelot Hogben's circle, became a classic teaching demonstration of convergence.

Britain's National Health Service screens and surveys work only because large numbers stabilise rates: a rare side effect invisible in a trial of hundreds becomes measurable when millions receive a vaccine. Pharmacovigilance systems exist precisely to give the law of large numbers enough trials to reveal one-in-a-million events reliably.
misconceptions: Many people think the law makes a loss streak due to reverse — in reality, convergence works by dilution over many future trials, never by compensation for past ones.
Many people think a large sample guarantees the rate is stable — in reality, the law assumes an unchanged underlying process, and a shifting process makes old volume misleading.
Many people think ten trials give a rough but usable rate — in reality, small samples deviate so widely that a fair coin can easily land heads seven times in ten tosses.

practice.name: Running average diary
practice.instructions: Flip a coin one hundred times, recording the running proportion of heads after every ten flips. Plot or list the proportions and note how the swings shrink as the count grows, then state the largest deviation you observed early on.

practice.name: Sample-size interrogation
practice.instructions: Find one statistic quoted in your feed today and hunt down how many observations produced it. Write one sentence on how far the true rate could plausibly sit from the quoted figure given that count, before sharing or acting on it.

cross_domain: In manufacturing, quality engineers rely on large production runs to reveal true defect rates that a single day's output hides. In astronomy, stacking many noisy telescope exposures lets faint signals emerge as random noise cancels. In opinion research, national mood estimates only stabilise once thousands of comparable respondents dilute individual quirks and daily news spikes. In clinical medicine, safe diagnostic thresholds are set only after large patient volumes reveal stable underlying rates of disease and recovery.

name_vi: Hồi quy về trung bình
definition: Regression to the mean is the tendency for extreme results to be followed by more ordinary results afterward.
mechanism: Any single result mixes real skill or quality with random luck. An extreme result usually contains an unusually large dose of luck, good or bad, and luck does not repeat reliably. The next result therefore tends to sit closer to the true average, creating the illusion that praise ruined performance or punishment improved it. Recognizing this pattern stops you from crediting or blaming the wrong cause and from paying peak prices for what was partly a lucky spike.
classic_example: Francis Galton discovered regression while studying the heights of parents and children in the 1880s, publishing his findings in 1886. Very tall parents tended to have children shorter than them, and very short parents had children taller than them. The pattern had nothing to do with biology pulling toward mediocrity and everything to do with chance mixing with inheritance.
modern_example: A sales employee wins top performer of the month after a few large clients happened to close together. Her manager expects the same result next month and is disappointed by a normal performance. Regression explains that the exceptional month mixed her real competence with fortunate timing, so a return to her solid average was predictable rather than a sign of lost motivation.
failure_mode: Regression is not a force and does not guarantee the next result moves toward average, especially when a real change in skill or conditions occurred. Dismissing a genuine improvement or a real decline as mere regression is its own error. The model also says nothing about timing, so the correction may take one trial or many.
apply_steps: Ask how much luck inflated this result
Compare against the long term average
Avoid rewarding or punishing extreme outliers
Wait one more period before concluding

situation_notes.down-30-percent-cut-or-hold: This model reveals that a sharp drop after an unusually strong run may partly be luck reversing rather than the business permanently breaking.
situation_notes.comparing-to-others: It shows a colleague's spectacular month likely mixes skill with fortunate timing, so their next results will probably look more ordinary.
situation_notes.channel-not-growing: It warns that one viral video sets an unfair baseline, because follow up videos naturally return toward your channel's true average performance.
situation_notes.buying-a-stock: It exposes stocks bought after extraordinary years, revealing that exceptional recent returns often drift back toward normal business performance levels.

case_seeds: Galton study of parent and child heights, 1886
Sports Illustrated cover jinx as regression example
origin: Francis Galton discovered the pattern in the 1880s while studying sweet pea seeds and then human height, publishing Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature in 1886. Galton, Charles Darwin's cousin, was measuring inheritance, and the shrinkage of children's heights toward the population average forced him to invent both regression and, soon after, the correlation coefficient.
mechanism_deep: Write any observed result as true level plus noise. Selection is where the trap closes: when you pick out an extreme result, you have mostly selected extreme noise, because true levels rarely sit that far out. Noise, by definition, does not persist, so the next observation re-draws it near zero and the result slides toward the true level, looking exactly like a response to whatever happened in between. The mathematics is precise: with correlation r between two measurements, the best prediction of the second, in standardised units, is r times the first. Only perfect correlation, r equal to one, abolishes regression; every imperfectly reliable measurement, test, season, or market guarantees it. This is why the effect scales with how extreme the selection was and how noisy the measure is. Human intuition fails because minds demand causal stories for changes, and regression supplies change for free, perfectly timed after interventions: hire the consultant after the worst quarter, punish after the worst performance, take the supplement at the peak of the illness. Daniel Kahneman's flight instructors were certain punishment worked and praise backfired, when both patterns were regression wearing a uniform. The boundary condition cuts the other way too: when a real change in the underlying level occurred, a new coach, an injury, a broken business model, results should not be expected to return to the old mean at all. The skill is separating selection on noise from genuine level shifts, which requires knowing the measure's reliability and the group's long-run average before telling any story. Galton himself was briefly confused by a symmetry worth understanding. Tall fathers have sons who average shorter than them, but short sons also have fathers who average taller than them; regression runs in both directions along any imperfect correlation, including backwards in time, which proves it cannot be a biological force pushing generations toward mediocrity. It is simply what imperfect correlation looks like when you condition on an extreme value of one variable. This is why the effect haunts every selection system. Choose the best-performing fund, school, surgeon, or sales region this year and you have selected a bundle of quality and luck; next year's measurement keeps the quality and re-draws the luck, and boards then invent stories about complacency or lost hunger to explain a statistical certainty. The famous Sports Illustrated cover jinx, where athletes supposedly decline after appearing on the magazine's cover, dissolves under this lens: athletes earn covers through peak performances, and peaks, by construction, are followed by ordinary ones. The constructive response is architectural. Evaluate people and programmes on averages across many periods, delay strong conclusions until the second measurement after any extreme, and, where decisions matter, use control groups, because only a comparison group that was equally extreme but untreated can separate an intervention's real effect from the regression that would have happened anyway. Regression is not a counsel of despair about improvement; it is the null hypothesis every improvement claim must beat.
examples_extra: Baseball's sophomore slump is regression's annual ritual: winners of the Rookie of the Year award typically perform worse in their second season. Their rookie campaigns combined real talent with career-best luck, health, and matchups. Scouts who expect the award-year line to repeat mistake a selected extreme for the player's true level, and are disappointed on schedule.

Actively managed mutual funds show the same pattern in finance. Funds ranked at the top over one period routinely slide toward the middle over the next in persistence studies by ratings agencies such as Morningstar. The top ranking selected for luck as well as skill, and only the skill portion, usually the smaller portion, carries into the following period.

formula.expression: Expected z-score next time = r x (z-score this time)
formula.variables: A z-score expresses how many standard deviations a result sits above or below its group's mean. r is the correlation between repeated measurements of the same thing, between 0 and 1 in typical cases; the closer r is to 0, the stronger the regression toward the mean.
formula.worked_example: A student scores two standard deviations above average on test one, z = +2, and test reliability gives r = 0.5. Expected score on test two is z = 0.5 x 2 = +1, one standard deviation above average, with no change in ability.

misconceptions: Many people think regression is a force pulling results toward average — in reality, nothing pulls; extreme selections simply contain extreme luck, which is not redrawn next time.
Many people think regression means everyone converges to the same level — in reality, true differences persist; only the noise component of each result shrinks away.
Many people think a decline after a peak proves complacency — in reality, the decline was statistically scheduled the moment the peak was selected, whatever the person's attitude did.

practice.name: Peak audit
practice.instructions: Pick your best recent result in work, sport, or content. Write its long-run average from at least ten comparable attempts, estimate how much of the peak was timing or luck, and set your next target at the average plus a small real improvement.

practice.name: Intervention diary
practice.instructions: For one month, whenever you intervene after an extreme good or bad day, record the extreme and what happens next with no further changes. Review whether the improvement you credited to the intervention matches what regression alone predicted.

cross_domain: In medicine, patients enrol in trials when symptoms peak, so untreated control groups also improve, which is why placebo arms exist to subtract regression from treatment claims. In education, schools flagged after one terrible year often rebound without any reform, corrupting league-table judgements. In policing, crime crackdowns launched after spike months claim credit for declines that were already statistically likely. In finance, performance fees paid after a single spectacular year systematically overpay managers for what was partly a lucky draw.

name_vi: Phân phối chuẩn — đường cong chuông
definition: The normal distribution describes how many measurements cluster near the average with fewer cases at both extremes.
mechanism: When a measurement results from many small independent influences adding together, the total tends to form a bell shape. Most cases land near the center, and extreme cases become rarer at a predictable rate as you move away. This lets you estimate how unusual a result is and set sensible expectations for variation. Height, measurement errors, and test scores often behave this way because no single factor dominates the final outcome.
classic_example: Carl Friedrich Gauss developed the mathematics of the normal distribution in the early 1800s while studying errors in astronomical measurements. Astronomers found that repeated measurements of the same star position clustered around a central value in a bell pattern, allowing them to estimate the most likely true position and discard the idea that every measurement deserved equal trust.
modern_example: A teacher notices most students in her class score near the middle on a test, with a few very high and very low results. Instead of treating the low scorers as lazy, she checks whether the test was simply hard for everyone. The bell shape helps her set fair grade boundaries and focus extra help on students genuinely far from the group pattern.
failure_mode: Many real world quantities do not follow a bell curve at all, especially wealth, social media reach, and disaster sizes where extremes dominate. Applying normal assumptions there badly underestimates rare events. The model also tempts people to label anyone far from average as abnormal, even when the underlying distribution was never normal to begin with.
apply_steps: Check if many small factors drive it
Expect most cases near the average
Treat extremes as rare not impossible
Confirm the shape before using bell math

situation_notes.comparing-to-others: This model reveals that most people cluster near average performance, so feeling behind often means comparing yourself to the thin extreme tail.
situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: It shows why stories about extreme winners dominate coverage, because ordinary middle outcomes are common but too unremarkable to become headlines.

case_seeds: Gauss work on astronomical measurement errors, early 1800s
Galton quincunx demonstration of the bell curve
origin: Abraham de Moivre first published the bell curve in 1738 as an approximation to the binomial distribution in his Doctrine of Chances. Carl Friedrich Gauss later used it to model astronomical measurement errors, which earned it the name Gaussian distribution, while Adolphe Quetelet in the 1830s controversially extended the curve from errors to human physical and social traits.
mechanism_deep: The deep engine is the central limit theorem: when a quantity is the sum of many small, independent influences, the total drifts toward a bell shape regardless of how the individual influences are distributed. That is why the curve appears for heights and measurement errors, where hundreds of genes and tiny environmental nudges add up, and why it fails for wealth, where effects multiply and feed back instead of adding politely. The curve is fully described by two numbers, the mean locating its centre and the standard deviation setting its width, and its famous proportions follow: about 68 percent within one standard deviation, 95 within two, 99.7 within three. Human intuition fails at the tails and at the centre simultaneously: people treat a result two standard deviations out as impossible rather than merely uncommon, and treat the average as a norm everyone should hit, pathologising the ordinary spread the curve predicts. The boundary condition is distributional shape itself. Before using bell-curve arithmetic, check skewness and tail weight; income, city sizes, and market returns carry fat tails that make six-standard-deviation events arrive far more often than the normal model permits, a mismatch implicated in repeated financial risk failures.
examples_extra: Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet analysed chest measurements of Scottish soldiers in the 1830s and found them distributed almost exactly along a bell curve. His average man concept helped launch social statistics, although critics then and now warn that an average describes a population without prescribing what any individual should be.

Motorola's Six Sigma programme, launched in 1986, built quality management on normal-distribution thinking: engineers measured how many standard deviations fit between a process average and its defect limit. The approach spread through General Electric under Jack Welch in the 1990s and made variation, not just averages, a boardroom topic.

formula.expression: z = (x - mean) / standard deviation ; about 68-95-99.7 percent fall within 1, 2, 3 standard deviations
formula.variables: x is the individual value being judged. The mean is the distribution's centre, and the standard deviation is its typical spread. The z-score states how many standard deviations x sits from the centre, which converts directly into how unusual the value is.
formula.worked_example: A test has mean 70 and standard deviation 10. A score of 85 gives z = (85 - 70) / 10 = 1.5, placing the student around the 93rd percentile, since about 93 percent of a normal distribution falls below z = 1.5.

misconceptions: Many people think most real-world data is normally distributed — in reality, many important quantities, from income to social-media reach, are heavily skewed with dominant extremes.
Many people think the average is the most likely outcome for any distribution — in reality, in skewed distributions the typical case sits far from the mean, which a few extremes drag upward.
Many people think a result beyond three standard deviations cannot happen — in reality, it is expected about three times per thousand observations, and far more often under fat tails.

practice.name: Histogram your life
practice.instructions: Collect thirty comparable numbers you generate, such as daily step counts or commute times. Sketch a quick histogram, mark the mean and one standard deviation each side, and check whether roughly two thirds of your values fall inside that band.

practice.name: Shape before statistics
practice.instructions: Next time someone quotes an average income, price, or wait time, ask whether the underlying quantity adds many small causes or multiplies. Write one sentence justifying bell-curve thinking or rejecting it before using the average.

cross_domain: In manufacturing, process capability indices assume near-normal variation to predict defect rates per million parts. In psychometrics, IQ and standardised test scores are deliberately scaled onto bell-shaped metrics for comparability. In finance, option-pricing models inherited normal assumptions, which is precisely why fat-tailed crashes keep surprising risk systems built on them. In meteorology, forecast errors for temperature are routinely summarised with bell-shaped spreads around the predicted value for each region.

name_vi: Quy luật lũy thừa — thiểu số chiếm đa số
definition: Power laws describe worlds where a small number of cases produce most of the total effect or value.
mechanism: Power laws arise when success feeds on itself, because visibility creates more visibility and advantages accumulate instead of canceling out. Unlike bell curves, there is no typical scale, and the largest cases can dwarf everything else combined. Averages become misleading because a few extremes carry the total. This explains why chasing many average opportunities may matter less than finding or surviving long enough to catch one outsized outcome in domains like publishing, startups, and investing.
classic_example: Vilfredo Pareto observed in 1896 that about twenty percent of Italy's population owned about eighty percent of the land. He found similar skewed patterns in other countries and datasets. The Pareto pattern became a classic early description of power law behavior, where a small minority consistently accounts for a large majority of the total outcome.
modern_example: A video creator reviews a year of uploads and finds three videos generated most of her total views and revenue, while dozens performed modestly. Instead of producing more average content, she studies what those three shared and makes deliberate sequels. Recognizing the power law shifts her strategy from steady volume alone toward hunting repeatable versions of rare breakout formats.
failure_mode: Power law thinking misleads in bell curve domains like height or manufacturing quality, where extremes are genuinely rare and averages work well. It also encourages reckless lottery chasing, funding endless attempts at a breakout while ignoring steady income. Most attempts in a power law world return almost nothing, so survival matters as much as ambition.
apply_steps: Check whether few cases drive totals
Stop trusting the average in skewed domains
Study your biggest winners for patterns
Survive long enough to catch outliers

situation_notes.channel-not-growing: This model reveals that channel growth often comes from a few breakout videos, not from every upload performing slightly better each week.
situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: It shows why some niches reward one dominant creator disproportionately, making second place far less profitable than the winner's results suggest.
situation_notes.buying-a-stock: It explains why a small number of stocks create most long term market wealth, so missing the few winners changes everything.

case_seeds: Pareto observation of land ownership in Italy, 1896
Venture capital returns driven by few startups
origin: Vilfredo Pareto documented the pattern in 1896 while studying income and land ownership in Italy and other countries, finding a consistent skewed formula rather than a bell curve. George Kingsley Zipf later found the same shape in word frequencies and city sizes in the 1930s and 1940s, and twentieth-century physics and network science generalised these observations into power-law distributions.
mechanism_deep: A power law says the frequency or probability of an event falls off as a power of its size, which produces a specific strange geometry: there is no characteristic scale, the tail decays slowly, and events ten times larger are rarer by a constant factor rather than by the vanishing margins of a bell curve. Depending on the exponent, the mean can be dominated by the largest observations or even fail to settle at all, which is why averages from small samples in these domains lie so fluently. Two generative engines recur. Preferential attachment makes the already-visible more visible, so books, cities, and accounts attract growth in proportion to what they have. Multiplicative growth with a floor, random percentage changes that cannot fall below zero, also stretches distributions into the same shape. Human intuition, calibrated on heights and exam scores, expects clustering around a typical value and treats the observed maximum as an anomaly; in power-law domains the maximum is the story, and the median outcome is near failure. The practical boundary is identification: many skewed datasets merely look like power laws on a casual plot, and fitting exponents properly is statistically delicate, as physicist Aaron Clauset and colleagues demonstrated.
examples_extra: Linguist George Kingsley Zipf found that in large English texts, the second most common word appears about half as often as the most common, the third about a third as often, and so on. The word the towers over the vocabulary while thousands of words appear once, a ranking pattern repeated across many languages.

Seismologists Charles Richter and Beno Gutenberg established in the 1940s that earthquake frequency follows a power law: each step up in magnitude is roughly ten times rarer but releases far more energy. The relationship, the Gutenberg-Richter law, still anchors how seismologists estimate the odds of rare destructive quakes from records of small ones.

formula.expression: P(X > x) is proportional to x raised to the power -alpha
formula.variables: X is the size of an event or quantity, and x is a threshold size. Alpha is the scaling exponent, a positive number controlling how heavy the tail is: smaller alpha means extremes dominate more strongly. The proportionality becomes an equality once a minimum size is fixed.
formula.worked_example: Suppose alpha = 1 and the probability of exceeding size 10 is 0.20. Then exceeding size 100, ten times larger, has probability 0.20 / 10 = 0.02, and exceeding 1,000 gives 0.002.

misconceptions: Many people think the 80/20 rule is a law of nature with fixed numbers — in reality, the split varies widely by domain and exponent; sometimes it is 95/5, sometimes a milder 70/30.
Many people think the average describes a typical case in skewed domains — in reality, the mean is dragged by rare giants, so the median participant experiences far less than the average suggests.

Many people think chasing power-law domains guarantees a giant win — in reality, most participants receive almost nothing, and the strategy only works with survival and many attempts or one durable position.

practice.name: Audit your own 80/20
practice.instructions: List your last twenty pieces of work, videos, products, or clients with their results. Sort descending, add up what share the top four produce, and write down whether your totals obey a power law and what that implies for your next month.

practice.name: Median versus mean check
practice.instructions: Find one glamorous average in your field, such as average author earnings or startup valuations. Search for the median figure instead, and note in one sentence how your plans change when the typical case replaces the dragged average.

cross_domain: In linguistics, Zipf's law ranks word frequencies in every large text corpus yet studied. In geophysics, the Gutenberg-Richter relation links countless small tremors to rare great earthquakes on one continuous scale. In economics, firm sizes, city populations, and wealth holdings all show the same long right tail that makes totals hostage to the largest few members. In entertainment, opening weekends and streaming charts show a handful of titles capturing most audience attention in any given week.

name_vi: Ước lượng Fermi — tính nhẩm theo bậc độ lớn
definition: Fermi estimation breaks an unknown quantity into smaller guessable parts and multiplies them for a rough useful answer.
mechanism: Large unknowns feel impossible only because they are asked as a single question. Breaking the problem into factors you can estimate, like population, frequency, and rate, turns one wild guess into several reasonable ones. Individual errors tend to partially cancel, and working in powers of ten keeps the answer at the right scale. The goal is not precision but a fast sanity check that exposes absurd claims and guides whether deeper research is worth doing.
classic_example: Enrico Fermi famously estimated the number of piano tuners in Chicago during the 1930s and 1940s by breaking the problem into population, households, piano ownership, and tuning frequency. His answer landed close to reality despite using no directory. He used the same approach at the Trinity test in 1945, estimating the blast yield by dropping paper scraps and measuring their movement.
modern_example: A manager wonders whether a neighborhood coffee cart could be profitable. She estimates nearby office workers, the share who buy coffee daily, a realistic capture rate, and average spending. The rough product suggests daily revenue in a plausible range, so she runs a one week trial. The estimate did not guarantee success, but it quickly showed the idea was not obviously absurd.
failure_mode: Fermi estimation fails when one factor is unknown by several orders of magnitude or when factors secretly depend on each other. It gives scale, not accuracy, so using it for a final price or safety decision is dangerous. Confident multiplication of bad guesses also creates an illusion of rigor while the answer remains essentially invented.
apply_steps: Break the unknown into estimable factors
Guess each factor within a power of ten
Multiply factors for a rough total
Use result as sanity check only

situation_notes.asking-for-budget: This model reveals a defensible budget size by estimating users, frequency, and unit cost instead of presenting leadership with an unsupported round number.
situation_notes.big-purchase: It shows the true yearly cost of ownership by multiplying small recurring expenses most buyers ignore when focusing on purchase price.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: It exposes whether demand, staff time, and delivery capacity are remotely balanced before you commit to an aggressive growth target.

case_seeds: Fermi estimate of piano tuners in Chicago
Fermi estimate of Trinity test yield, 1945
lab_spec: The user picks a sample question like how many cups of coffee a city drinks daily, then enters estimates for each factor in a guided chain. The tool multiplies the factors, shows the result on a logarithmic scale, and reveals how changing each factor swings the final estimate.
origin: Enrico Fermi, the Italian-American Nobel laureate in physics who worked at the University of Chicago and Los Alamos, became legendary for answering absurd-sounding questions from simple decompositions, estimating everything from piano tuners to the Trinity bomb's yield. Colleagues and students turned his habit into a named estimation method taught across physics, engineering, and consulting.
mechanism_deep: The method works because estimation errors on a logarithmic scale partially cancel: overestimating one factor by a factor of three is often offset by underestimating another, while the final answer inherits the accuracy of your best structural insight, which is the decomposition itself. Choosing factors is therefore the real skill. Good factors are independently guessable, anchored in quantities you have actually observed, such as population, household size, or frequency per week, and each should be stated as a bound as well as a guess: if coffee drinkers are between a fifth and a half of commuters, carry both bounds through and take the geometric middle. Working in orders of magnitude, powers of ten, keeps arithmetic honest and exposes which factor dominates uncertainty; that factor, not the whole estimate, is where research time belongs. Human intuition fails at the two ends: it treats a question with no published answer as unanswerable, and it demands false precision from data that cannot supply it. Its boundary is dependence and ignorance: if two factors secretly move together, or one factor is unknown by a factor of a thousand rather than ten, the tidy multiplication collapses, and the honest output is a wide range plus a plan to measure the wild factor.
examples_extra: Astronomer Frank Drake wrote his famous equation in 1961 to structure a meeting at Green Bank Observatory about searching for extraterrestrial civilisations. It multiplies star formation rates by fractions for planets, life, intelligence, and detectable technology. Nobody knows several factors, but the equation turned an unfalsifiable argument into a map of exactly which unknowns matter.

Hiring interviews at technology firms, famously Microsoft in the 1990s, popularised Fermi questions such as how many golf balls fit inside a Boeing 747. Interviewers scored the decomposition, the stated assumptions, and the sanity checks, not the final number, because the point was watching a candidate reason quantitatively about something nobody has ever counted.

formula.expression: Estimate = factor 1 x factor 2 x ... x factor n
formula.variables: Each factor is one independently estimable component of the unknown quantity, such as population, adoption share, or uses per person per year. The unknown total is the product of the factors, ideally computed with a low and a high bound for each factor.
formula.worked_example: Daily coffee sales in a city of 1,000,000 people: suppose 30 percent buy one coffee out daily. Estimate = 1,000,000 x 0.30 x 1 = about 300,000 cups per day, before refining the weakest factor.

misconceptions: Many people think a Fermi answer is just a guess with extra steps — in reality, decomposition replaces one uncheckable guess with several smaller ones, most anchored in observable quantities.
Many people think the goal is the right number — in reality, the goal is the right order of magnitude and knowing which factor's uncertainty controls the answer.
Many people think more factors always improve accuracy — in reality, each speculative factor multiplies uncertainty, so decompositions stop at factors you can genuinely bound.

practice.name: Piano-tuner warm-up
practice.instructions: Reproduce Fermi's classic yourself: estimate your city's population, households per piano, pianos per household, tunings per year, and jobs per tuner per year. Multiply through, then compare your tuner count with the number of tuning services actually listed locally.

practice.name: Bound, then narrow
practice.instructions: Pick one unknown in your work, such as monthly support tickets next quarter. Write a low and high bound for each factor, multiply both chains, and identify the single factor you could measure this week to narrow the range most.

cross_domain: In astrobiology, the Drake equation is pure Fermi structure, converting one unanswerable question into a chain of estimable unknowns. In venture capital, total addressable market sizing multiplies population, adoption, and spend in the same way. In environmental science, emissions inventories estimate national totals by multiplying activity counts by per-unit emission factors. In logistics, warehouse planners estimate daily pallet movements by multiplying orders, lines per order, and handling rates per line.

name_vi: Tương quan không phải nhân quả
definition: Correlation means two things move together while causation means one thing directly produces a change in the other.
mechanism: Two trends can rise together because one causes the other, because a hidden third factor drives both, or purely by coincidence in noisy data. Correlation alone cannot distinguish these explanations, so the model demands extra work, like checking timing, ruling out confounders, or finding a plausible mechanism. This discipline matters because acting on a false cause wastes resources and sometimes creates harm, while the true cause continues operating untouched in the background.
classic_example: In the nineteenth century, John Snow investigated a cholera outbreak in London in 1854 and mapped cases around the Broad Street water pump. Many explanations circulated at the time, but Snow showed the pattern fit contaminated water rather than bad air. Removing the pump handle is the famous symbol of moving from observed correlation toward an identified cause.
modern_example: A marketing team notices sales rise in weeks when they post more on social media and credits the posts. Checking deeper, they find those weeks also coincide with payday cycles and a seasonal promotion. A simple holdout test, pausing posts in one region, shows little change. The correlation was real, but the promotion calendar was doing most of the actual work.
failure_mode: This model fails when used as a lazy dismissal, rejecting strong evidence just by chanting that correlation is not causation. Sometimes converging correlations, timing, and mechanism make a causal conclusion reasonable. It also offers no alternative explanation by itself, so it starts an investigation rather than ending one with a clever slogan.
apply_steps: Ask what third factor drives both
Check which event came first
Look for a plausible connecting mechanism
Test by changing one variable only

situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: This model reveals when a success story credits a course for results actually driven by market timing, prior skills, or extra effort.
situation_notes.channel-not-growing: It shows that changing thumbnails alongside posting frequency makes it impossible to know which change actually moved your views at all.
situation_notes.users-but-no-revenue: It exposes assumptions that engaged users will naturally pay, when engagement and willingness to pay may share no causal link.

case_seeds: John Snow cholera map of Broad Street, 1854
Smoking and lung cancer research debates
origin: The caution is ancient in philosophy, but it became a formal statistical discipline with Francis Galton's work on correlation in the 1880s and Karl Pearson's mathematical coefficient in the 1890s. Twentieth-century epidemiologists, notably Austin Bradford Hill with his 1965 considerations for inferring causation, turned the slogan into a working checklist for observational evidence.
mechanism_deep: A correlation coefficient compresses co-movement into a number between minus one and one, but it is silent about the graph of causes underneath. Four structures generate identical correlations: A causes B, B causes A, a confounder C drives both, or selection into the sample manufactures the association, as when studying only hospital patients links diseases that never interact in the general public. Time order helps but cannot settle it, and strength helps only weakly, since strong confounders produce strong correlations. The modern toolkit escalates through evidence grades: adjust statistically for measured confounders, exploit natural experiments where exposure changed for unrelated reasons, use instrumental variables or Mendelian randomisation, and, where ethics allow, randomise, which breaks confounding by construction. Human intuition fails because narrative fluency substitutes for structure: a plausible story about A causing B makes the correlation feel explained, and the mind stops generating rival graphs. It also fails in reverse, treating the slogan as a licence to dismiss inconvenient evidence forever. The discipline is comparative: list at least three causal graphs that fit the data, then ask what observation would separate them, and go and get that observation instead of arguing about the correlation itself.
examples_extra: Data analyst Tyler Vigen built a well-known collection of spurious correlations, including the divorce rate in the US state of Maine tracking margarine consumption almost perfectly over a decade. Both series drifted smoothly over time, which manufactures impressive coefficients from pure coincidence, and the example is now a standard warning in statistics teaching.

Hormone replacement therapy shows the serious side. Large observational studies through the 1990s suggested women taking HRT had less heart disease, but the Women's Health Initiative randomised trial, halted in 2002, found increased risks instead. Healthier, wealthier women had been more likely to take HRT, a confounder the observational correlations could not remove.

formula.expression: r = sum of ((x - mean of x) x (y - mean of y)) / square root of (sum of (x - mean of x)^2 x sum of (y - mean of y)^2)
formula.variables: r is Pearson's correlation coefficient, ranging from -1 for perfect opposite movement to +1 for perfect joint movement. x and y are the paired measurements, and each deviation is measured from that variable's own mean.
formula.worked_example: For points (1,2), (2,3), (3,5): means are 2 and 3.33, the numerator is 3, the denominator is about 3.06, so r is about 0.98, a very strong correlation that still says nothing about which variable causes which.

misconceptions: Many people think the slogan refutes any causal claim built on observational data — in reality, converging designs, timing, and mechanisms can justify causal conclusions without a randomised trial.

Many people think a correlation near zero proves no relationship exists — in reality, curved relationships, like anxiety improving then harming performance, can hide inside a near-zero linear coefficient.
Many people think controlling for more variables always helps — in reality, adjusting for a variable caused by both factors, a collider, can manufacture associations that were never there.

practice.name: Three-graph rule
practice.instructions: Take one correlated claim from today's news. Draw three causal structures that fit it: direct cause, reverse cause, and a named confounder. Write the one observation that would distinguish between them, and check whether the article collected it.

practice.name: Confounder hunt
practice.instructions: Pick a correlation from your own work data, such as posting frequency and sales. List the calendar events, campaigns, and selection effects that moved both series, then design the smallest holdout test that isolates one variable.

cross_domain: In genetics, Mendelian randomisation uses randomly inherited gene variants as natural experiments to test whether biomarkers like cholesterol actually cause disease. In economics, rainfall and distance have served as instrumental variables to separate education's effect on earnings from family background. In marketing science, geographic holdout experiments exist precisely to break the correlations that dashboards celebrate. In education research, class-size debates turn on separating the effect of smaller classes from the wealth of districts that can afford them.

name_vi: Lấy mẫu và cỡ mẫu
definition: Sampling means learning about a large group from a smaller part chosen to represent the whole group fairly.
mechanism: A sample works only when it mirrors the population in the ways that matter for the question. Random selection protects against the biases of convenience, because volunteers, friends, and loud customers differ systematically from everyone else. Size matters too, since small samples swing wildly by chance while larger ones stabilize. But size cannot rescue a biased sample, because asking the wrong thousand people still gives a confidently wrong answer about the right population.
