practice.instructions: After any strategy discussion, write one sentence answering: what will concretely be different on Monday, who owns it, and by when? If the sentence cannot be written from the meeting's language, treat the discussion as twaddle and re-run it with those three questions on the table.

practice.name: Translation drill
practice.instructions: Take one paragraph of your own recent professional writing and rewrite it banning your field's ten most common buzzwords. Where the paragraph becomes impossible to write, mark the sentence: that is where content was missing, and either supply evidence or delete the claim.

cross_domain: In consulting and corporate strategy, decks full of synergy and transformation language can be sold for years because no falsifiable claim ever comes due. In academia, fashionable jargon can carry empty papers through peer review, as the Sokal affair demonstrated. In marketing, profound-sounding brand manifestos substitute for product truth, and audiences trained on twaddle reward creators who sound deep over creators who say anything testable.

name_vi: Xu hướng tôn trọng lý do được đưa ra
definition: People cooperate more readily when given a reason, even a weak or meaningless one, than when given none.
mechanism: Humans are explanation hungry: reasons signal respect, make requests feel legitimate, and help the mind file an action as sensible. Because processing every justification deeply is costly, the brain often accepts the form of a reason as a shortcut for its substance. Munger saw the tendency as mostly beneficial for teaching and management, since genuine reasons improve learning, but it also lets manipulators smuggle weak arguments past lazy scrutiny using the word because.
classic_example: Psychologist Ellen Langer demonstrated the effect in 1978 with a photocopier line experiment: a request to cut ahead succeeded far more often when accompanied by a reason, and even the empty reason of needing to make copies performed nearly as well as a genuinely urgent justification for small requests. The structure of an explanation mattered more than its content.
modern_example: Employees accept an unpopular policy far more calmly when leadership explains the reasoning honestly than when it arrives as a bare order. In sales, a simple because clause raises compliance even when the reason is trivial. Conversely, a manager who never explains decisions trains the team to speculate, resist, and eventually stop trusting any instruction at all.
failure_mode: Giving reasons is usually good practice, and demanding them improves decisions, so the tendency is more tool than trap. The failure appears when the mere presence of a plausible sounding reason ends scrutiny of important claims. Overcorrecting by rejecting all explanations leaves you unable to learn from people who genuinely understand their recommendations.
apply_steps: Always give genuine reasons with requests
Ask whether the reason actually supports conclusion
Test reasons on big decisions, not small ones
Explain decisions to teams before speculation starts

situation_notes.persuading-stubborn-person: A sincere reason transforms a demand into a respectable request, dramatically raising cooperation even from someone initially inclined to refuse.
situation_notes.asking-for-budget: Requests with clear, honest reasoning get approved more often because approvers can defend the decision upward using your reasons.
situation_notes.saying-no: A brief genuine reason makes your refusal acceptable, while a bare no invites argument, resentment, and repeated future pressure.

case_seeds: Ellen Langer photocopier line experiment (1978)
origin: Social psychologist Ellen Langer at Harvard formalized the underlying effect with Arthur Blank and Benzion Chanowitz in their 1978 photocopier study of mindless compliance. Charlie Munger named the pattern in his Psychology of Human Misjudgment talk, listing it among his tendencies. It is therefore both a laboratory finding about automatic processing and a practical management observation about why explanations, even thin ones, change how requests are received.
mechanism_deep: Underneath the effect is a division between automatic and deliberate processing. Most daily requests are small, low stakes, and frequent, so the mind handles them with a fast script: a request that sounds complete, polite, and socially normal gets approved without an audit of its logic. A because clause completes the script. It signals that the requester acknowledges your autonomy, has some purpose, and is not issuing a naked command, which lowers social friction independently of the reason's quality. Evolutionarily, this makes sense in cooperative groups where constantly interrogating small requests would poison relationships and waste time. The same shortcut weakens when stakes rise: Langer's own work showed that for larger, costlier requests the empty reason lost much of its power, because higher cost triggers deliberate scrutiny. The tendency is also stronger under distraction, time pressure, and fatigue, when working memory cannot hold both the request and a critique of its justification. Conversely, genuine reasons do extra work that fake ones cannot: they transfer information, let the listener verify the logic later, and build a reputation that makes future requests easier. The bias is therefore not that people love reasons, but that they often grade the packaging of a justification before grading its contents.
examples_extra: In medicine, adherence improves when clinicians explain why a full course of antibiotics matters rather than simply issuing instructions, because patients who understand the reason can reconstruct the plan when doses are missed. The explanation also gives patients questions to ask, turning a bare order into a shared decision they are more likely to complete.

In primary school classrooms, teachers who give a brief reason for a rule, such as keeping voices low so classmates can concentrate, get steadier compliance than teachers who rely on authority alone. Educational researchers describe this as rationale provision within autonomy support: the reason respects the child's judgment, so cooperation feels chosen rather than forced, and the rule survives when the teacher leaves the room.
misconceptions: Many people think any because clause works on any request — in reality, the empty-reason effect largely disappears when the request is large or costly, because higher stakes trigger deliberate scrutiny.

Many people think the tendency proves people are irrational — in reality, accepting the form of a reason is an efficient shortcut for the many small requests where full analysis would cost more than the decision is worth.
Many people think giving reasons is mainly about information — in reality, a reason also signals respect for the listener's autonomy, and that social signal often matters as much as the content.
practice: The reason audit: Before your next three requests, write the because clause in one sentence. If the clause could be attached to any request at all, replace it with the specific fact that actually justifies this one.

The stakes check: When someone gives you a reason for an expensive decision, restate it as evidence and ask what would still be true if the reason were false. This separates a real justification from packaging in under a minute.
cross_domain: In law, judges who give written reasons for sentences face less public backlash than judges who announce identical outcomes without explanation, because the reasoning makes the decision reviewable. In product design, apps that explain why they request a permission, such as location for delivery tracking, get higher opt-in rates than apps showing a bare system prompt. In both fields the stated reason works twice: it justifies the specific ask and it proves the asker can be held accountable later.

name_vi: Hiệu ứng Lollapalooza, nhiều thiên kiến cộng hưởng
definition: When several psychological tendencies act together in the same direction, their combined effect becomes extreme and nonlinear.
mechanism: Individual biases are manageable, but biases reinforce one another: social proof validates authority, incentives reward conformity, envy fuels urgency, and denial blocks correction. Once aligned, the loop feeds itself and produces manias, cults, panics, and catastrophic decisions that no single tendency could explain. Munger considered recognizing these combinations the highest use of his psychology checklist, because the resulting behavior is not additive but explosive, like a critical mass reaction in physics.
classic_example: The Dutch tulip mania of the 1630s combined social proof, envy, incentive caused speculation, and availability of vivid success stories until single bulbs reportedly traded for the price of houses before the February 1637 collapse. Munger used modern equivalents like auction frenzies and cult formation to show the same recipe: multiple tendencies, one direction, and outcomes wildly disproportionate to any single cause.
modern_example: A meme stock frenzy stacks every tendency at once: friends profiting triggers envy, trending posts supply social proof, fear of missing out kills doubt, and sellers of courses profit from the excitement. Participants are not simply greedy; they are inside a reinforcing system where each bias certifies the others, making outside warnings sound like jealousy or ignorance to those caught within it.
failure_mode: Not every strong trend is a lollapalooza; sometimes several signals align because something real is happening, and dismissing genuine movements costs opportunity. The concept can also become a lazy label applied after any crash. Use it as a diagnostic checklist in real time, asking which specific tendencies are visibly reinforcing, not as a dramatic synonym for enthusiasm.
apply_steps: List which biases are active simultaneously
Slow down when three or more align
Seek information from outside the excited group
Precommit exit rules before joining any frenzy

situation_notes.market-panic: Panic stacks stress, social proof, and loss aversion together, producing selling far more extreme than any single fear justifies.
situation_notes.fomo-friends-profit: Envy, social proof, and incentive stories combine into a frenzy where skipping a friend's trade feels like certain loss.
situation_notes.buying-a-stock: When hype, authority endorsements, and rising prices align, your combined biases can overwhelm an otherwise sound investment process completely.
situation_notes.taking-investment-or-not: Founder excitement, investor prestige, and deadline pressure can combine to make a bad funding deal feel irresistibly right momentarily.

case_seeds: Dutch tulip mania collapse (1637)
GameStop meme stock frenzy (2021)
origin: Charlie Munger coined lollapalooza in his 1995 Harvard talk, The Psychology of Human Misjudgment, later published in Poor Charlie's Almanack, to name what his list of separate tendencies missed: their interactions. Munger, a businessman rather than a psychologist, borrowed the logic from physics and chemistry, where systems near a critical threshold change state suddenly. The concept is a practitioner's synthesis built on laboratory biases documented by Kahneman and Tversky.
mechanism_deep: The deep mechanism is feedback between biases that normally check each other. In isolation, most tendencies have natural brakes: doubt slows social proof, self-interest can break conformity, and embarrassment limits envy. A lollapalooza begins when several tendencies align so precisely that each one disables the brake on another. Incentives pay people to conform, which manufactures social proof; social proof silences doubt, which protects the authority figure; admiration for the authority figure makes dissent feel like disloyalty; and envy of early winners supplies a constant stream of new recruits who repeat the cycle at a larger scale. Three properties follow. First, the effect is nonlinear: adding a fourth aligned tendency does not add a quarter more error, it can multiply the error, because each participant's distorted behavior becomes distorted evidence for everyone else. Second, the system becomes self-sealing. Warnings are not merely ignored, they are reinterpreted through the aligned biases, so a critic looks envious, disloyal, or paid to attack, which strengthens the group's conviction that it is right. Third, identity fuses with the position. Once money, status, friendship, and self-image all depend on the same belief, abandoning it means simultaneous financial, social, and psychological loss, so people defend it far past the point where any single bias would have released them. Evolution helps explain why the machinery exists: rapid group coordination around food, danger, and status was often worth more than individual accuracy, so the brain evolved strong conformity, authority, and envy circuits. Those circuits were calibrated for small bands where feedback from reality was fast and personal. Modern markets, media, and social platforms connect millions of people, remove the fast corrective feedback, and let the same circuits run for months at industrial scale. Conditions that strengthen a lollapalooza include rising visible rewards, a charismatic or prestigious leader, a simple story that explains early success, penalties for dissent, and a scoreboard, such as a price or follower count, that updates constantly and appears objective. Conditions that weaken it include independent sources of status, private ballots, pre-committed exit rules, and any institution that rewards people for being the first to report bad news. This is why Munger treated the pattern as the most important item on his checklist: single biases produce ordinary mistakes that experience can correct, but aligned biases produce the extreme outcomes, manias, panics, cults, and institutional collapses, that dominate a lifetime's results, and they are almost impossible to resist from inside once the loop has closed.
examples_extra: Theranos combined nearly every ingredient before its exposure by Wall Street Journal reporting in 2015: a celebrated founder supplied authority and liking, a board of famous statesmen supplied social proof, secrecy suppressed doubt, and investors' envy of earlier backers punished hesitation. Each validator was largely validating the others' confidence rather than the blood-testing technology itself, which is why sophisticated people missed problems that a single independent laboratory check would have exposed.

The run on Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023 showed the panic version at digital speed. Venture firms advised founders to withdraw, founders posted warnings that became social proof, and mobile banking removed the physical friction of a queue, so fear, authority advice, and visible imitation aligned within hours. The bank failed in about two days, not because every depositor independently audited its bond portfolio, but because each withdrawal became evidence justifying the next one.
misconceptions: Many people think a lollapalooza is just a very strong single bias — in reality, it requires several distinct tendencies reinforcing each other, and removing one support can collapse the whole effect.

Many people think only foolish people fall into these episodes — in reality, the alignment specifically disables the checks that intelligence normally provides, which is why sophisticated investors and officials are regularly caught.

Many people think the label can be applied to any boom after it crashes — in reality, Munger's test is diagnostic and prospective: you must be able to name the specific tendencies visibly reinforcing each other in real time.
practice: The tendency inventory: When an opportunity excites you, list which of these are present: social proof, authority, envy, incentives, urgency, and admiration for a leader. If three or more point the same way, delay any irreversible commitment by 48 hours and seek one source with no stake in the outcome.

The brake restoration drill: Write, before investing or joining, the specific evidence that would make you exit, and share it with one person outside the group. Pre-commitment restores the doubt and outside view that the aligned tendencies are designed to switch off.
cross_domain: In public health, vaccine panics can stack parental fear, celebrity authority, social proof from parent groups, and distrust of institutions into a self-sealing refusal that data alone cannot penetrate. In corporate fraud, the same alignment appears as heroic founder narratives, auditor deference, employee incentives tied to growth, and board-level envy of rival valuations. In both domains the visible behavior looks like a single attitude, but intervention only works when it separates the stacked tendencies and addresses each support individually.

name_vi: Thiên kiến xác nhận, chỉ tìm bằng chứng ủng hộ mình
definition: People search for, interpret, and remember information in ways that confirm what they already believe is true.
mechanism: Beliefs are tied to identity, past effort, and social belonging, so contradicting evidence registers as a threat rather than information. The brain economizes by testing ideas with questions designed to produce yes answers, remembering hits and forgetting misses. Algorithms intensify the loop by feeding users content they already engage with. The result is a feeling of overwhelming evidence on your side, manufactured largely by your own selective attention over months and years.
classic_example: Peter Wason's 2 4 6 task, first reported in 1960, showed participants guessing a number rule by proposing sequences that confirmed their hypothesis, rarely testing cases that could falsify it, so most announced wrong rules confidently. Francis Bacon described the same pattern centuries earlier, noting that once the human understanding adopts an opinion, it draws everything else to support and agree with it.
modern_example: An investor who buys a stock then reads only bullish analyses, follows only optimistic accounts, and interprets neutral news as positive, feeling increasingly certain as the position actually deteriorates. In daily life, a manager convinced an employee is lazy notices every late arrival, forgets every late night of work, and builds an airtight case from genuine but selected facts.
failure_mode: Prior beliefs are often right, built from real experience, and treating every conviction as bias leads to paralyzing relativism. Strong priors are how expertise works. The failure is never exposing a belief to a test it could fail, and overcorrection means abandoning sound positions whenever any contrary anecdote appears, however weak or unrepresentative it may be.
apply_steps: Ask what evidence would change my mind
Seek the strongest opposing argument first
Track predictions and score them honestly
Assign someone to argue the other side

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: After buying, you will unconsciously collect bullish evidence and discount warnings, feeling more certain precisely as your information gets worse.
situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: You will judge sources by whether they agree with you, building an information diet that flatters existing beliefs daily.
situation_notes.online-arguments: Debates become evidence hunts for your side, so both parties leave more polarized despite exchanging large amounts of factual material.
situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: Early enthusiasm makes you notice only success stories in a niche, while base rates and failures stay invisible to you.

case_seeds: Wason 2 4 6 task experiments (1960)
Investors holding dotcom stocks through the 2000 crash
origin: Francis Bacon described the pattern in Novum Organum in 1620, but British psychologist Peter Wason formalized it experimentally in the 1960s, with rule-discovery and selection tasks showing people testing hypotheses using confirming cases. The label became standard in cognitive psychology in the following decades, and Raymond Nickerson's 1998 review in Review of General Psychology consolidated evidence across reasoning, memory, and social judgment.
mechanism_deep: Several mechanisms stack to produce the bias, which is why information alone rarely cures it. The first is positive test strategy: when checking a hypothesis, people naturally search the places where the hypothesis predicts something will be found, a reasonable heuristic in a world where target phenomena are rare, but one that almost never generates falsifying evidence. The second is biased interpretation: the same study, statistic, or event is rated rigorous when it agrees and methodologically flawed when it disagrees, so a mixed body of evidence can push two opponents further apart, as Lord, Ross, and Lepper showed with capital punishment studies in 1979. The third is memory: hits are rehearsed in conversation and retelling while misses decay, so over years a person accumulates a personal archive that genuinely feels one-sided. Underneath all three sits motivation. Beliefs are load-bearing for identity, friendships, income, and past decisions, so disconfirmation is processed by the brain partly as social threat, recruiting the same defensive machinery as a personal attack. This explains the bias's boundary conditions. It weakens when the person has no stake in the answer, when accountability to a knowledgeable audience is expected in advance, when the hypothesis is about someone else, and when feedback is fast, unambiguous, and scored, as in weather forecasting, where professionals become well calibrated. It strengthens with intelligence in one uncomfortable way: smarter people are better at constructing counterarguments against unwelcome evidence, so cognitive ability can arm the defense rather than correct the belief. Modern algorithmic feeds industrialize every layer, selecting confirming items, removing the social cost of ignoring opponents, and refreshing the archive daily, so the bias now runs on infrastructure rather than only on individual psychology. The evolutionary account is debated, but one influential view holds that reasoning evolved less for solitary truth-finding than for winning arguments and defending reputation in groups, which would make one-sided evidence search a feature of social cognition that misfires when applied to private forecasting and investing. Ziva Kunda's influential 1990 synthesis of motivated reasoning added an important asymmetry: when people want a particular conclusion, they ask whether they can believe it, searching memory for any supporting reason, but when they dislike a conclusion they ask whether they must believe it, searching just as hard for a flaw that licenses rejection. The two questions have different stopping rules, so identical effort produces opposite verdicts. Relatedly, myside bias in argument production shows people generating more and stronger arguments for their own position even in abstract tasks with no personal stake, suggesting the machinery runs by default rather than only under emotional threat. Interventions that work share one feature: they change the search itself, through consider-the-opposite instructions, assigned devil's advocacy, or adversarial collaboration between opponents who must agree on a test in advance.
examples_extra: The American and British intelligence assessments before the 2003 invasion of Iraq illustrate institutional confirmation bias: ambiguous reports consistent with weapons programs were elevated and circulated, while reports that cut the other way were discounted or stovepiped around. Later official inquiries in both countries documented how an early working assumption organized the reading of fragmentary evidence, so analysts experienced mounting confirmation for a conclusion the underlying data had never securely supported.

In criminal investigation, the 2004 case of Brandon Mayfield showed forensic tunnel vision: the FBI identified the Oregon lawyer's fingerprint as a match after the Madrid train bombings, and examiners who knew of the initial identification and other case details confirmed it, before Spanish authorities matched the print to another man. Knowledge of the expected answer had organized the reading of genuinely ambiguous ridge details, in a laboratory-grade demonstration inside a real, high-stakes investigation.
misconceptions: Many people think confirmation bias means people never change their minds — in reality, people update readily on low-stakes topics; the bias concentrates where beliefs carry identity, money, or past effort.
Many people think more information cures the bias — in reality, mixed information often polarizes people further, because each side audits only the evidence that disagrees with it.
Many people think the bias is a flaw of unintelligent people — in reality, greater cognitive ability can strengthen it, because skilled reasoners build better defenses against unwelcome evidence.
practice: The disconfirmation quota: For any important belief, write the strongest piece of evidence against it and where you found it, before you allow yourself to collect one more supporting item. If you cannot state the opposing evidence fairly, you have not yet researched the question.

The prediction ledger: Record dated, numerical predictions for decisions you care about and score them quarterly. A written record defeats selective memory, because the misses remain on the page instead of quietly dropping out of your personal archive.
cross_domain: In medicine, diagnostic confirmation appears when an early label such as anxiety organizes later test selection, so confirming results are ordered and documented while alternative diagnoses are never tested. In science itself, the file-drawer problem reflects the same pull: journals and researchers favor results confirming a hypothesis, leaving null results unpublished and distorting the literature later reviews rely on. In hiring, an interviewer's first impression quietly scripts the questions asked, manufacturing a transcript that appears to confirm the impression independently.

quote.text: We can be blind to the obvious, and we are also blind to our blindness.
quote.author: Daniel Kahneman

name_vi: Hiệu ứng mỏ neo, bám vào con số đầu tiên
definition: People rely too heavily on the first number or fact they encounter when estimating values and making decisions.
mechanism: The brain estimates by starting somewhere and adjusting, but adjustments are lazy and stop too early, so the starting point drags the final answer toward itself. Anchors work even when obviously random or irrelevant, because the mind also selectively recalls anchor consistent information. Negotiators, retailers, and fundraisers exploit this by naming the first figure. Once an anchor lands, arguing against it still leaves your thinking orbiting around it.
classic_example: In Tversky and Kahneman's famous 1974 experiment, participants watched a rigged wheel of fortune land on 10 or 65, then estimated the percentage of African nations in the United Nations. The median estimates were 25 and 45 percent respectively, dragged dramatically by a number participants knew was random, demonstrating that irrelevant starting points distort serious numerical judgment.
modern_example: A freelancer hears a client mention a tiny budget first and then quotes far below her normal rate, adjusting insufficiently from their number. Shoppers feel a jacket is a bargain at half its listed price although the list price was invented. Founders anchor on a previous funding round's valuation and reject good acquisition offers below that fading figure.
failure_mode: Starting points often carry real information; a first offer, asking price, or expert estimate is rarely arbitrary in practice. Ignoring anchors entirely can mean discarding useful data and insulting counterparts. The failure is unconscious drag, and the cure is generating your own independent estimate before exposure, not pretending numbers can be evaluated in a vacuum afterward.
apply_steps: Write your own estimate before hearing theirs
Generate a counter anchor deliberately
Ask how the anchor was derived
Consider the opposite value and argue it

situation_notes.negotiating-price: The first number named will drag the final deal toward itself, even when both sides know it was arbitrary.
situation_notes.salary-negotiation: Whoever states a salary range first sets the gravitational center, so arriving without your own researched number surrenders that advantage.
situation_notes.buying-a-stock: The price you first saw, or paid, anchors your sense of value long after the company's fundamentals have changed.
situation_notes.pricing-a-product: Your first price anchors customers permanently; later discounts feel like bargains and later increases feel like betrayal to them.

case_seeds: Tversky and Kahneman wheel of fortune experiment (1974)
Real estate listing price effects on appraisals
origin: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman introduced anchoring in their 1974 Science paper, Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, which launched the heuristics-and-biases program. They named the process anchoring and adjustment: people start from an initial value and adjust away from it, but adjustments are typically insufficient. The wheel-of-fortune study remains the canonical demonstration, and the effect has since been replicated across pricing, legal judgment, forecasting, and negotiation.
mechanism_deep: Two distinct mechanisms produce anchoring, and they operate in different situations. The first is effortful adjustment: when people generate their own estimate from a starting value, they move away from the anchor until they reach the edge of the plausible range and then stop, because further adjustment requires effort and a justification they do not have. This is why self-generated anchors, such as a previous salary or a first budget figure, bind so tightly to deliberate decisions. The second mechanism is selective accessibility: merely considering whether a value is higher or lower than an anchor activates anchor-consistent knowledge. Asked whether a river is longer or shorter than an anchor number, people retrieve facts supporting the anchor's neighborhood, and that primed evidence then drives the estimate. This second route explains why even obviously random, externally supplied anchors work, and why warning people about anchoring barely helps, since the bias lives in which facts come to mind rather than in conscious deference to the number. Anchoring strengthens when the judge is uncertain, when the domain lacks precise feedback, when the anchor is extreme but still discussable, and when the same person must both hear the anchor and produce the estimate under time pressure. It weakens, though rarely disappears, when people generate an independent estimate in writing before exposure, consider the opposite range explicitly, or work from a memorized reference class. Evolutionarily, the machinery is sensible: in natural environments, the first information encountered about a quantity, such as the size of a rival group or a food source, usually is informative, and updating conservatively around it beats restarting from nothing. The modern vulnerability is that commercial environments deliberately manufacture first numbers, list prices, opening demands, and suggested donations, precisely because the ancient update rule can be steered by whoever chooses the starting point. Negotiation research shows the practical stakes: Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler reported in 2001 that the party making the first offer captures a systematic advantage, because the offer anchors the bargaining range and forces the counterpart to adjust from it, while also revealing information. Anchors also propagate socially. In committees and markets, one member's opening figure becomes the group's reference even when everyone knows it was a guess, and subsequent speakers anchor on the previous speaker, so a meeting can ratchet around a number nobody ever defended. Price anchors exploit a further subtlety: buyers treat the distance between anchor and price, the perceived discount, as itself a benefit, experiencing transaction pleasure from the gap rather than evaluating the final price alone. This is why experienced buyers and procurement rules increasingly require independent written estimates, sealed bids, and reference prices gathered before any vendor number is heard: the only reliable protection is controlling which number arrives first, since once an anchor lands, even deliberate resistance mostly reorganizes thought around it.
examples_extra: In a widely cited study by Gregory Northcraft and Margaret Neale in 1987, professional real estate agents toured a house, received full information, and still produced valuations pulled substantially toward the listing price they had been given, while insisting the list price had not influenced them. Different groups received different listing prices for the same property, and their appraisals followed the anchor, demonstrating the effect among experienced professionals pricing the asset they knew best.

German judges were the subjects of experiments by Birte Englich, Thomas Mussweiler, and Fritz Strack published in 2006: experienced legal professionals read case files and then rolled dice or received a prosecutor's demand before sentencing. Their sentences shifted measurably toward the suggested number, including when the suggestion came from a throw of dice they knew was irrelevant, showing that even high-stakes, expert, accountable judgment remains anchored by numbers encountered first.
misconceptions: Many people think anchoring only affects novices or the uninformed — in reality, real estate agents, judges, and physicians show the effect in their own domains, because it works through selective memory rather than ignorance.

Many people think being warned about the anchor removes it — in reality, warnings and incentives for accuracy reduce the effect only slightly; generating an independent estimate before exposure works far better.

Many people think anchors must be plausible to work — in reality, numbers people know are random still shift estimates, although extremely absurd anchors lose power once they leave the range anyone will discuss.
practice: The sealed estimate: Before any negotiation, appraisal, or purchase discussion, write your own number and the reasoning behind it, and keep it visible during the meeting. An estimate recorded before exposure is the strongest known personal defense against drag.

The opposite anchor drill: When a first number is presented, deliberately argue for a specific number far on the other side and list facts supporting it for two minutes. This activates anchor-inconsistent knowledge and widens the range your final judgment can reach.
cross_domain: In medicine, an early working diagnosis or a triage number such as an initial pain score anchors later clinicians, who adjust around the first figure in the chart rather than reassessing from the examination alone. In public policy, last year's budget anchors this year's appropriation in legislatures worldwide, so programs grow or shrink by percentages of the inherited figure instead of being re-estimated from need. In both domains the starting number survives not because anyone defends it, but because every later discussion is organized around departing from it.

name_vi: Hiệu ứng đóng khung, cách trình bày đổi quyết định
definition: People choose differently depending on whether identical options are presented as gains or losses, risks or safety.
mechanism: The brain evaluates outcomes relative to a reference point and codes them as gains or losses, and losses trigger risk seeking while gains trigger caution. Presentation controls the reference point: survival rates versus mortality rates, discounts versus surcharges, and ninety percent lean versus ten percent fat all describe identical facts with opposite emotional coding. Because the feeling arrives before analysis, even trained professionals reverse preferences when only the wording changes.
classic_example: Tversky and Kahneman's Asian disease problem, published in 1981, gave participants a choice between a certain outcome and a gamble for a disease outbreak expected to kill 600 people. Framed as lives saved, most chose certainty; framed as lives lost, most chose the gamble, although the options were mathematically identical in both versions of the question.
modern_example: A subscription described as costing less than a coffee a day converts better than the honest yearly total, while a medical treatment pitched with success rates feels safer than the same treatment pitched with failure rates. Managers frame layoffs as restructuring to capture savings, and employees accept or resist the identical plan depending on the story wrapped around the numbers.
failure_mode: Framing is unavoidable; every description chooses some emphasis, and communicators who refuse to frame simply frame badly by accident. Some frames also highlight genuinely important aspects. The failure is being moved by frames unknowingly, and the defense is reframing choices both ways yourself, not searching for a mythical neutral presentation that does not exist.
apply_steps: Restate the choice in opposite frame
Convert percentages into absolute numbers
Ask what facts both frames share
Decide using totals, not descriptions

situation_notes.writing-sales-copy: Your framing decides whether customers feel gain or loss from identical facts, making wording a genuine product feature itself.
situation_notes.big-purchase: Sellers frame monthly payments instead of total cost, making expensive purchases feel painless until the full commitment becomes clear.
situation_notes.presenting-to-leadership: The same results framed as market share defended versus growth missed will produce opposite reactions from identical leadership audiences.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: Advisers frame returns without risk or inflation, making mediocre products sound impressive until you restate them in complete terms.

case_seeds: Asian disease problem by Tversky and Kahneman (1981)
Ground beef labeling studies on lean versus fat framing
origin: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman formalized it in their 1981 Science paper, The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice, which presented the Asian disease problem and connected preference reversals to the prospect theory they had published in 1979. The work showed that choices violate the invariance principle of rational choice theory. Kahneman received the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics partly for this program.
mechanism_deep: The mechanism runs through reference dependence and the editing phase of choice. Before evaluating options, the brain recodes outcomes relative to a reference point set by the wording: lives saved codes the certain option as a gain, lives lost codes the identical option as a loss. Prospect theory then predicts the reversal, because people are risk averse among gains and risk seeking among losses. The frame also steers attention: a survival frame brings recoveries and successes to mind, while a mortality frame summons images of death, and those accessible images do emotional work before any arithmetic begins. Framing is stronger when outcomes are emotional, when the chooser is a bystander to precise probabilities, and when the frame arrives from a trusted source. It weakens when people must justify choices, when both frames are shown side by side, or when outcomes are expressed as natural frequencies with visual aids. The deeper point is that there is no unframed presentation: every description selects a reference point, a denominator, and a vocabulary, so the choice is never between framing and neutrality, only between deliberate and accidental framing.
examples_extra: Barbara McNeil, Stephen Pauker, Harold Sox, and Amos Tversky reported in 1982 that patients, referring physicians, and graduate students all shifted between surgery and radiation therapy for lung cancer depending on whether outcomes were stated as survival or mortality probabilities. The statistics were identical; only the frame changed. That trained physicians reversed alongside laypeople made the study a landmark demonstration that framing penetrates professional medical judgment, not just consumer choice.

In a 1988 study by Irwin Levin and Gary Gaeth, shoppers tasted ground beef described as 75 percent lean or 25 percent fat. The lean frame produced more favorable ratings of taste and quality, even though the meat was the same, and the advantage persisted, though reduced, after tasting. Modern food labeling rules in several countries, standardizing fat and sugar presentation, built partly on this result.
misconceptions: Many people think framing is just marketing spin that fools careless shoppers — in reality, physicians, judges, and experienced managers reverse preferences under reframing in controlled studies.

Many people think there exists a neutral way to present any choice — in reality, every presentation selects a reference point and vocabulary, so the practical skill is choosing frames deliberately and checking both versions.

Many people think the effect disappears once the equivalence is pointed out — in reality, people often keep their framed preference even after acknowledging the two descriptions are identical, because the emotional coding persists.
practice: The double-frame rewrite: For any major decision presented to you, rewrite the key numbers in the opposite frame, converting survival to mortality, discounts to totals, and percentages to absolute numbers. Decide only after both versions are on the page.

The denominator check: Whenever you see a percentage in a pitch, ask out of how many, over what period, compared with what. Restoring the missing denominator dismantles most manipulative frames in seconds.
cross_domain: In criminal justice, presenting a forensic match as a one-in-millions error rate versus as a near-certain identification changes how jurors weigh identical laboratory evidence. In climate communication, describing policy costs as investment losses today versus avoided losses tomorrow recruits opposite risk attitudes toward the same projected figures. In each domain the facts survive translation intact, while the willingness to act flips with the reference point the wording installs.

name_vi: Ngụy biện chi phí chìm, tiếc công đã bỏ
definition: People keep investing in failing efforts because of what they have already spent, rather than future value.
mechanism: Abandoning a project forces the brain to record the earlier spending as pure loss, which loss aversion makes intensely painful, while continuing keeps hope of redemption alive. Self justification adds pressure, since quitting admits the original decision was wrong. The effect strengthens with personal responsibility and public commitment. Rational choice depends only on future costs and benefits, but emotion keeps billing the future for debts the past has already paid.
classic_example: The Concorde supersonic airliner became the textbook case: Britain and France continued funding the program long after its commercial prospects collapsed, partly because so much had already been invested, and the aircraft retired in 2003 having never justified its development costs. Psychologists Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer demonstrated the same effect experimentally in 1985 with theater ticket pricing studies.
modern_example: A founder keeps paying for a feature nobody uses because six months of development would feel wasted if she cut it now. Individuals finish bad degrees, bad books, and bad relationships for the same reason, and investors hold losing stocks until they can get even, although the market does not know or care what anyone originally paid.
failure_mode: Persistence is often the right call; many valuable things look like failures midway, and quitting at every dip guarantees mediocrity. Past investment sometimes signals information about quality too. The distinction is whether you would start the project today with fresh eyes. Overcorrecting into instant abandonment wastes the genuine option value of staying power.
apply_steps: Ask if I would start this today
Evaluate only future costs and benefits
Set kill criteria before investing more
Let someone uninvolved review the decision

situation_notes.down-30-percent-cut-or-hold: Your purchase price is gone either way, yet the urge to get even keeps you holding a deteriorating company indefinitely.
situation_notes.users-but-no-revenue: Months of building make shutting down feel like waste, so you keep serving users whose behavior already answered the question.
situation_notes.channel-not-growing: Hundreds of published videos argue for continuing a dead format, although future effort deserves allocation by future returns only.
situation_notes.career-pivot: Years invested in a career feel too large to abandon, trapping you in work you would never choose starting today.

case_seeds: Concorde program continued despite poor economics
Arkes and Blumer sunk cost experiments (1985)
origin: Richard Thaler gave the pattern its modern name in a 1980 paper, Toward a Positive Theory of Consumer Choice, describing how paying for the right to use something increases its use. Organizational psychologist Barry Staw documented the workplace twin in 1976, in research on escalation of commitment showing that decision-makers who initiated a failing course invested most to continue it. Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer established the effect in 1985.
mechanism_deep: The fallacy is powered by at least three interlocking mechanisms. The first is loss realization: while a project continues, its losses remain paper losses that might still be redeemed, but abandoning it converts them into a certain, recorded failure, and loss aversion makes that conversion feel far worse than an equivalent future waste. The second is self-justification. The person who authorized the original spending experiences quitting as a public verdict on their competence, which is why escalation is consistently stronger when the same decision-maker controls both the initial and the continuation decision, and why new managers kill inherited projects with an ease that horrifies their predecessors. The third is waste aversion, a quasi-moral rule learned early, finish what you paid for, that treats unused purchases as a character flaw rather than as irrelevant history. Boundary conditions follow directly. The effect grows with the size and visibility of prior investment, with personal responsibility, and with the closeness of apparent completion, since a project that feels ninety percent done recruits the goal-gradient pull as well. It shrinks when future costs are made vivid and itemized, when stopping rules are set in advance, when the decision is handed to someone without authorship of the original choice, and when organizations publicly reward early termination of failing projects. Evolutionarily, some persistence heuristic was valuable: ancestors who abandoned hunts, shelters, or alliances at the first setback would have starved, and many real endeavors do reward those who push through a discouraging middle. The fallacy is the miscalibration of that useful grit to situations where the prior spending carries no information about future returns, and where each additional unit of persistence is purchased at full price to protect an ego rather than a prospect. Payment structure matters as well. Research on payment depreciation shows that the felt cost of a purchase fades as time passes and as payment recedes into the past, which is why a prepaid failing subscription feels easier to keep using wastefully than an identical pay-as-you-go one feels to cancel: the pain that would discipline the decision has already been absorbed and written off. Groups add a further amplifier, because each member's advocacy becomes evidence for the others and responsibility for the original decision diffuses, letting organizations escalate long after every individual privately doubts the project. De-escalation research therefore targets structure rather than willpower: rotating in decision-makers without authorship, separating continuation budgets from original budgets so new money must win its own approval, publishing kill criteria in advance, and creating face-saving exits, such as redefining the project as a completed experiment, all reduce the ego and accounting costs that keep failing courses alive.
examples_extra: In professional basketball, Barry Staw and Ha Hoang reported in 1995 that NBA teams gave more playing time, kept players longer, and traded them less readily when the player had been a higher draft pick, even after controlling for actual on-court performance. The draft position is a pure sunk cost once the season begins, yet it purchased minutes that performance alone would not have earned, at the direct expense of better players sitting on the bench.

Barry Staw's original 1976 escalation research used the Vietnam War as its framing case, noting that American administrations repeatedly justified expanded commitment by the sacrifices already made, arguing that withdrawal would render previous losses meaningless. The logic inverted sound strategy: past casualties, which could not be recovered by any future policy, were treated as a reason to risk future casualties, and each escalation raised the psychological price of the eventual withdrawal.
misconceptions: Many people think sunk cost reasoning is simply stupidity about money — in reality, it is driven by loss realization and self-justification, which is why it intensifies for the person who made the original decision.

Many people think the cure is to quit failing projects quickly — in reality, the correct test is forward-looking: whether you would start the project today at its remaining cost, which sometimes still favors continuing.

Many people think the effect only involves money — in reality, time, effort, and public commitment bind just as strongly, which is why unpaid personal projects and announced goals are so hard to abandon.
practice: The fresh-eyes test: Write one sentence answering whether you would start this project today, at today's remaining cost, knowing what you now know, if you had spent nothing so far. If the answer is no, the only thing keeping it alive is history, and that is the fallacy speaking.

The pre-set kill criteria: At a project's start, record the results and dates that will trigger termination, and give a copy to someone who did not propose the project. Deciding the exit before ego and spending accumulate removes the two strongest fuels of escalation.
cross_domain: In medicine, sunk costs appear as continued aggressive treatment justified by how much intervention a patient has already endured, where each prior procedure becomes an argument for one more rather than a datum about prognosis. In software, teams keep maintaining legacy systems whose migration was postponed for a decade, citing the accumulated customization as the reason replacement is impossible. In both fields the prior investment is real, but it answers a question nobody should be asking: the relevant comparison is always between futures, not between a future and a past that no option can change.

name_vi: Ác cảm mất mát, sợ mất hơn ham được
definition: Losses feel roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains feel pleasurable, skewing choices toward avoiding loss over seeking gain.
mechanism: Protecting existing resources mattered more for survival than chasing extra gains, so the brain wired loss as an alarm and gain as a mild pleasure. Kahneman and Tversky formalized this in prospect theory in 1979, showing value is judged relative to a reference point with a curve far steeper for losses. The asymmetry explains risk seeking when losing, excessive caution when winning, and why people reject fair bets with slightly favorable odds.
classic_example: In prospect theory experiments reported by Kahneman and Tversky in 1979, participants rejected gambles most people would profit from over repeated plays, such as a coin flip offering a larger win against a smaller loss, because the pain of losing loomed disproportionately large. The finding reshaped economics by contradicting the assumption that people evaluate final wealth rationally and consistently.
modern_example: An investor checks her portfolio daily and feels each dip sharply, so she sells solid funds during corrections to stop the pain, locking in losses. Employees refuse a higher paying job with slightly less security, and customers keep unwanted subscriptions because canceling feels like losing a possession, although the money saved would buy something they value more.
failure_mode: Loss aversion is partly rational: some losses are irreversible, threaten survival, or carry consequences beyond their size, and margin of safety thinking depends on respecting them. The bias is the unexamined two to one emotional exchange rate applied everywhere. Overcorrecting into loss blindness produces gamblers who treat real downside as mere statistics until ruin arrives.
apply_steps: Judge outcomes from zero, not current position
Decide review intervals in advance, check less
Compare loss pain against long term totals
Ask what a fresh buyer would do

situation_notes.down-30-percent-cut-or-hold: The pain of realizing a loss will push you to gamble on recovery instead of calmly comparing future prospects rationally.
situation_notes.market-panic: Loss pain compounds with each price check, making selling at the bottom feel like relief rather than the mistake it is.
situation_notes.idle-cash-decision: Fear of any loss keeps cash idle for years, quietly guaranteeing the slow loss to inflation you were avoiding dramatically.
situation_notes.saying-no: Refusing a request feels like losing goodwill, so you accept harmful commitments to avoid a small, imagined social loss.

case_seeds: Prospect theory experiments by Kahneman and Tversky (1979)
Equity premium puzzle research on investor behavior
origin: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky formalized loss aversion in prospect theory, published in Econometrica in 1979, and refined it in their 1992 prospect theory paper. The theory replaced expected utility's focus on final wealth with value defined over gains and losses relative to a reference point, with a value function steeper for losses. Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011) popularized the two-to-one ratio as an approximation.
mechanism_deep: The asymmetry begins in how the brain codes outcomes. A gain is evaluated as improvement, a pleasant signal, while an equivalent loss is coded as damage to the current state, closer to pain, and neuroimaging work shows losses engage threat and salience circuitry more strongly than comparable gains engage reward circuitry. The reference point does the quiet work: because value is computed as change rather than level, the same salary feels like progress or insult depending on what a person expected, earned before, or watches peers receive, and expectations themselves become reference points so that an anticipated bonus, once mentally spent, registers as a loss when it shrinks. Several boundary conditions matter. Loss aversion weakens for small, routine stakes handled by experienced traders who reframe single outcomes as one draw in a long series, a technique Samson and colleagues documented among professional market participants. It strengthens when the loss threatens identity, status, or survival resources, when it is framed as caused by one's own action rather than by circumstance, and when the person must actively accept the loss, as in selling a holding, rather than passively watch it expire. The disposition effect, holding losers and selling winners, is the portfolio signature of that acceptance problem. Evolutionarily the asymmetry is defensible: for an organism near subsistence, a loss of food, warmth, or status could be fatal while an equal gain was merely pleasant, so a nervous system that guards the current endowment more fiercely than it chases improvements would out-survive a symmetric one. The modern misfire is scope. The alarm calibrated for survival threats now fires on paper fluctuations, expiring coupons, and minor perks, and institutions exploit it through trial periods, free returns, and default enrollments that convert a product into a possession before payment, knowing that giving something up will hurt roughly twice as much as acquiring it pleased. The frequency of evaluation interacts powerfully with the asymmetry. Shlomo Benartzi and Richard Thaler proposed in 1995 that myopic loss aversion, checking results often while weighing losses heavily, explains the equity premium puzzle, the historically large gap between stock and bond returns: investors who evaluate frequently experience the market's many short-term losses at full emotional price and demand high compensation for enduring them. The same mathematics governs everyday behavior: the more often a person checks a portfolio, a weight, or a sales dashboard, the more losses they will register relative to gains, and the more conservative or reactive their choices become, even when the underlying process is unchanged. Reducing evaluation frequency, widening the accounting window, and judging outcomes in batches are therefore not denial strategies but direct treatments of the mechanism, since they change how many losses the reference-dependent system gets to count.
examples_extra: Professional golf provided a clean field test: Devin Pope and Maurice Schweitzer reported in 2011 that PGA Tour players putted noticeably more accurately for par, where a miss costs a stroke relative to par, than for birdie, where a miss merely forgoes a gain of the same size. The players were elite experts competing for prizes with millions of observed putts, yet the reference point of par still bent their performance, showing loss aversion operating inside highly practiced motor skill, not only in financial deliberation.

In the endowment experiments reported by Kahneman, Jack Knetsch, and Richard Thaler in 1990, students randomly given a Cornell mug demanded roughly twice as much to sell it as other students offered to buy the identical mug minutes later. Random assignment ruled out taste differences: mere possession moved the reference point, so parting with the mug registered as a loss and acquiring it as a gain, and the gap between the two prices measured the asymmetry directly.
misconceptions: Many people think losses always hurt exactly twice as much as gains feel good — in reality, the ratio is an average that varies widely with stake size, experience, and what the loss threatens.

Many people think loss aversion is the same as risk aversion — in reality, loss-averse people often gamble desperately when already losing, because a gamble offers the only chance to erase a loss; the pattern is about reference points, not timidity.

Many people think loss aversion is always a bias to eliminate — in reality, some losses are genuinely irreversible or ruinous, and respecting them asymmetrically is the foundation of margin-of-safety thinking.
practice: The series reframe: Before reacting to a single loss, write down the last twenty comparable outcomes and this one's place in the series. Judging the portfolio of outcomes instead of the single painful draw measurably reduces the urge to overcorrect.

The neutral redescription: Restate any pending loss as a price, for example the cost of information, an exit fee, or rent paid for an option that expired. Naming what the loss buys, in advance of feeling it, weakens the coding of the event as pure damage.
cross_domain: In negotiation, parties fight harder to avoid concessions from their current position than to win equivalent improvements, which is why mediators reframe exchanges so each side codes its movement as protecting something rather than surrendering it. In public policy, reforms that remove an existing benefit provoke far more resistance than reforms that merely withhold a new one, so governments grandfather existing recipients to bypass the asymmetry. In both domains the objective change is the same size in either direction, while the political cost differs by the direction of travel from the reference point.

quote.text: Losses loom larger than gains.
quote.author: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky
quote.source: Prospect theory, summarized in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)

name_vi: Hiệu ứng Dunning-Kruger, càng kém càng tự tin
definition: People with low skill in a domain overestimate their ability because the same skill is needed to judge performance.
mechanism: Competence and self evaluation run on the same knowledge: without knowing what good performance looks like, a beginner cannot see the gaps in their own work, producing the double burden of being unskilled and unaware. Early learning also brings quick wins that inflate confidence before complexity appears. Meanwhile genuine experts, knowing the domain's depth, rate themselves more cautiously and assume tasks are easier for others than they really are.
classic_example: David Dunning and Justin Kruger published their studies in 1999, showing that Cornell students scoring lowest on tests of humor, grammar, and logic consistently estimated their performance near the top of the class. Their work was partly inspired by the case of McArthur Wheeler, who robbed banks in 1995 believing lemon juice made his face invisible to cameras.
modern_example: A beginner trader wins during a rising market and concludes he has a gift, increasing position sizes just before his first real downturn. A new manager who watched leadership videos rates herself ready to run a company, while experienced operators around her discuss risks she cannot yet perceive, let alone manage, because her mental model of the job is still a cartoon.
failure_mode: The effect is often overstated in popular culture, and statistical regression explains part of the pattern. Low confidence is not proof of competence either, and some beginners really do have unusual talent. The failure is using confidence, yours or others, as evidence of skill at all, instead of checking scored track records on comparable tasks.
apply_steps: Test skills with scored, objective exercises
Ask experts what good actually looks like
Predict outcomes numerically, then compare results
Treat early confidence as a warning sign

situation_notes.learning-from-zero: Your confidence will peak dangerously early, right after basic concepts click, before the domain's real difficulty becomes visible to you.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: The loudest, most confident voices in markets are often the least skilled, because genuine expertise sounds cautious and conditional by comparison.
situation_notes.stronger-colleague-threat: You may misjudge a stronger colleague as merely lucky or political because your current skill cannot yet perceive their skill.

case_seeds: Dunning and Kruger Cornell studies (1999)
McArthur Wheeler lemon juice bank robberies (1995)
origin: The effect is named for Cornell psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger, whose 1999 paper, Unskilled and Unaware of It, reported the humor, grammar, and logic studies. Dunning has said the work was prompted by reports of the 1995 McArthur Wheeler bank robberies. The paper named a metacognitive mechanism: the knowledge needed to produce correct answers is the same knowledge needed to recognize them.
mechanism_deep: The core mechanism is metacognitive: evaluating a performance requires the same mental model that producing it does. A weak chess player cannot see why a move fails, a weak writer cannot hear the clumsiness of a sentence, and a weak reasoner cannot detect the gap in an argument, because detection is itself the missing skill. Layered on this is a statistical and social mixture. Beginners experience rapid early progress and frequent praise for effort, both of which supply genuine evidence of improvement that gets extrapolated too far. Experts show the mirror distortion, the false consensus about ease: they assume peers share more of their knowledge than they do, and so rate themselves only modestly above average. The effect is strongest where feedback is delayed, ambiguous, or social rather than scored, and weakest where outcomes are immediate and public, such as timed races. It also varies within a person: the same individual can be calibrated in a practiced trade and wildly overconfident in an adjacent one, because the mechanism is local knowledge, not global arrogance. Training shrinks it efficiently: even modest instruction gives learners the missing criteria, which is why teaching logic improved the worst performers' self-assessment as much as their scores.
examples_extra: A review by David Davis and colleagues published in JAMA in 2006 compared physicians' self-assessments with observed competence measures and found self-assessment accuracy was limited, with some of the worst accuracy among those who were least skilled and most confident. The finding matters because medicine relies on practitioners judging when they need consultation or training, a judgment the review showed cannot be left to unaided self-perception.

In workplace safety, new equipment operators routinely rate themselves ready for solo work after a short supervised period, while trainers' checklists show they still miss hazard scanning steps they do not know exist. The gap closes fastest not through warnings about confidence but through scored simulations with immediate feedback, which give novices the missing criteria for judging a good performance, exactly as the metacognitive account predicts.
misconceptions: Many people think the effect means confident people are usually incompetent — in reality, confidence and skill are only weakly related, and many confident people are genuinely expert; the claim is about calibration within a domain, not a personality type.

Many people think the famous curve showing a peak of beginner confidence is the original finding — in reality, that graph is a later popular stylization; the 1999 studies measured percentile self rankings against test scores.

Many people think the effect is just arrogance — in reality, part of the pattern is statistical regression plus a real metacognitive deficit, and it partly dissolves once people are given criteria and feedback.
practice: The scored rep: Pick one skill you rate yourself highly on and take a scored, timed test or submit work for blind grading this week. Calibration requires an external number; reflection alone rehearses the same model that produced the overestimate.

The criteria-first review: Before judging your own draft, performance, or analysis, write the checklist an expert would grade it against, then score each line separately. Supplying the missing criteria is the fastest way to see gaps you could not see before.
cross_domain: In investing forums, the effect appears as fluent commentary from traders who cannot state their own past returns, where vocabulary substitutes for the accounting that would reveal performance. In management, it appears when leaders who have never run a hiring or firing process rate their people judgment highly, because every outcome can be explained away without a scorecard. In both settings the tell is identical: strong self ratings coexist with an absence of recorded, comparable results.

name_vi: Lỗi quy kết cơ bản, đổ tại người thay vì hoàn cảnh
definition: People explain others' behavior by personality while underweighting circumstances, yet excuse their own behavior by those same circumstances.
mechanism: An observer sees the actor prominently and the situation faintly, so character becomes the default explanation. Correcting for constraints requires effortful second stage thinking that busy brains skip. For ourselves, we feel the constraints from inside, so our excuses seem like facts. The asymmetry poisons management, politics, and relationships: others are lazy or dishonest, while we are tired, rushed, or poorly supported by broken systems nobody fixed.
classic_example: In the Jones and Harris study of 1967, participants read essays about Fidel Castro that writers had been assigned to compose for or against him, yet still concluded the essays revealed the writers' true opinions. Even knowing the position was forced by a coin flip style assignment, observers could not fully discount the situational pressure shaping the behavior they judged.
modern_example: A manager labels a quiet employee unmotivated without noticing the employee's briefs are contradictory and deadlines impossible. When her own project slips, she cites those exact kinds of circumstances fluently. Drivers do it hourly: the other motorist is a reckless idiot, while their own swerve was a necessary response to conditions only they could see.
failure_mode: Character explanations are sometimes correct; repeat behavior across many situations does reveal personality, and excusing everything as circumstance enables bad actors. Managers who attribute nothing to individuals cannot coach or hire well. The failure is skipping the situational check, not eventually concluding, after checking, that the person really is the problem.
apply_steps: List situational causes before personal ones
Ask how I would act in their position
Check behavior across different situations
Fix systems before blaming people

situation_notes.team-conflict: You will read a colleague's difficult behavior as character while your own identical behavior feels like a reasonable response to pressure.
situation_notes.stronger-colleague-threat: Attributing a colleague's success to talent alone hides the systems and support behind it that you could copy or request.
situation_notes.reading-a-new-partner: One bad meeting makes you label a partner unreliable, ignoring the circumstances that might fully explain their unusual behavior that day.

case_seeds: Jones and Harris Castro essay study (1967)
Milgram participants blamed by observers ignoring situational pressure
origin: Stanford social psychologist Lee Ross coined the term in 1977, building on the 1967 essay study by Edward Jones and Victor Harris at Duke University. Ross called it fundamental because the overuse of dispositional explanation appeared to underlie many other judgment biases. Daniel Gilbert later popularized the near-synonym correspondence bias, while attribution theory itself traced back to Fritz Heider's foundational work on explaining behavior, published in 1958.
mechanism_deep: Attribution happens in stages, and the error is a shortcut through them. The first stage is automatic characterization: seeing a behavior, the mind immediately tags the actor with a matching trait, rude, lazy, generous, because behavior is perceptually vivid and the actor fills the visual field. The second stage, adjusting for the situation, is optional and effortful: it requires noticing constraints that are often invisible, such as orders received, incentives in place, or information the actor lacked. Busyness, distraction, and cognitive load therefore widen the error, while prompting people to consider the situation shrinks it. Culture moderates the pattern too: studies comparing American and East Asian participants, including work by Incheol Choi and Richard Nisbett in the late 1990s, found more situational sensitivity in collectivist settings, suggesting the error is a default of individualist interpretation rather than a universal constant. For the self, the geometry reverses: we experience our own constraints from inside and our behavior from the receiving end, so situational explanations feel immediate and character explanations feel like excuses when applied by others. The actor-observer gap is thus partly an information gap, which is why learning what pressures someone faced is the most reliable debiasing step.
examples_extra: Lee Ross, Teresa Amabile, and Julia Steinmetz demonstrated the role effect in 1977 with a quiz game: participants assigned as questioners invented hard questions, contestants missed many, and observers rated the questioners as more knowledgeable, despite knowing the roles were assigned by chance and the questioners' advantage was built into the game. The study isolates the error: the situation fully explains the performance gap observers converted into a trait difference.

In debates about poverty, the error appears when low income is attributed primarily to individual laziness or poor choices while wages, rents, health shocks, and local job availability, the situational machinery, receive little weight. The same observers explain their own financial setbacks fluently in situational terms, citing layoffs and costs, revealing the asymmetry: character is the explanation reserved for other people's outcomes, circumstance for one's own.
misconceptions: Many people think the error means personality never explains behavior — in reality, behavior repeated across varied situations is informative about character; the error is skipping the situational check, not reaching a dispositional conclusion after one.

Many people think only judgmental people make this error — in reality, it is the automatic first stage of attribution in everyone, widened by distraction and narrowed by deliberately considering constraints.
Many people think the bias applies equally everywhere — in reality, cultural norms shift it, with more collectivist settings showing greater routine sensitivity to situational causes.
practice: The constraint inventory: When someone's behavior angers you this week, list three situational pressures that could produce the same behavior from a good person before you say anything. If one plausible constraint exists, ask about it first; the question costs nothing and often rewrites the whole interpretation.

The role swap: Re-describe a conflict with the roles exchanged, including your own behavior explained as a trait by the other side. The discomfort of hearing your circumstances ignored is the fastest calibration of how your own explanations sound.
cross_domain: In medicine, the error appears as blaming patients for non-adherence while underweighting shift work, medication cost, and confusing regimens that the system designed. In customer operations, firms discipline frontline staff for rudeness spikes that track understaffing and queue length, punishing individuals for a scheduling decision. In both domains the fix that works is situational first: change rosters, prices, and instructions, and the supposedly defective personalities improve at rates no character campaign ever produced.

name_vi: Hiệu ứng hào quang, một điểm tốt che mờ tất cả
definition: One admired trait, like attractiveness or past success, spills over and colors judgments of a person's unrelated qualities.
mechanism: The brain prefers coherent stories about people, so a single strong impression organizes all later judgments to match it. Attractive, confident, or previously successful individuals get credited with intelligence, honesty, and competence they may not possess, while one negative trait casts the reverse shadow. Because the spillover feels like intuition built from many observations, evaluators are surprised to learn their supposedly independent ratings all came from one initial glow.
classic_example: Psychologist Edward Thorndike named the effect in 1920 after finding that commanding officers' ratings of soldiers' physique correlated suspiciously with ratings of intelligence and character. A modern business version is the halo around Steve Jobs era Apple, where admiration for breakthrough products led many observers to assume every operational and strategic choice the company made was equally brilliant.
modern_example: A startup with a famous founder raises money on the assumption that past success guarantees judgment in an unrelated market. In hiring, a polished, good looking candidate is rated more competent on identical answers. Customers similarly assume a brand excellent at phones must make excellent laptops, transferring trust across categories without evidence either way.
failure_mode: Traits genuinely correlate in places: conscientious people often are more reliable across tasks, and strong brands usually do maintain standards. Treating every impression as halo makes evaluation paranoid and slow. The failure is unexamined spillover, and the practical cure is scoring separate traits separately, with evidence attached to each, before forming an overall view.
apply_steps: Rate separate qualities on separate evidence
Review work samples blind when possible
Ask what this person has actually done here
Beware first impressions in high stakes hiring

situation_notes.choosing-cofounder: One dazzling strength, like fundraising charisma, will make you assume competence in operations and honesty that you never verified separately.
situation_notes.reading-a-new-partner: A partner's prestige creates a glow that makes their vague promises feel like guarantees backed by an impeccable record.
situation_notes.big-purchase: A beloved brand's halo makes its weaker products feel reliably excellent, so you skip the comparison research you normally do.

case_seeds: Thorndike officer rating studies (1920)
Investor halo around celebrated founders in new markets
origin: American psychologist Edward Thorndike named the effect in his 1920 paper, A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings, after analyzing how commanding officers rated soldiers across unrelated traits. Ratings of physique, intelligence, and character moved together far more than the traits plausibly did. Solomon Asch extended the construct in 1946, and Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson showed in 1977 that people explain halo-driven judgments with reasons they cannot access.
mechanism_deep: The engine is global evaluation: the mind forms one overall affective verdict about a person and then generates trait ratings to be consistent with it, rather than building the verdict from independent trait evidence. This is cognitively cheap and socially useful, since real traits do correlate weakly and a coherent impression supports fast decisions about trust. The distortion enters through three channels. First, ambiguous behavior gets interpreted in the halo's direction, so the same directness reads as leadership in an admired person and abrasiveness in a disliked one. Second, memory retrieval is guided by the verdict, surfacing confirming episodes. Third, the horns effect runs the process in reverse from a single negative cue. Halo is strongest in domains with subjective criteria, long evaluation forms, and a salient cue such as attractiveness, fame, or a prestigious employer appearing early. It weakens when traits are scored separately, in randomized order, against written behavioral anchors, and when evaluators must cite observable evidence per trait. Notably, awareness does little: Nisbett and Wilson's participants denied the influence of the cue that demonstrably moved their ratings, insisting on plausible alternative reasons, which is why structural fixes outperform intentions.
examples_extra: Karen Dion, Ellen Berscheid, and Elaine Walster reported in 1972 that participants rated photographs of attractive people as possessing more desirable personalities and better life prospects, in the study summarized as what is beautiful is good.
