classic_example: Garrett Hardin published The Tragedy of the Commons in Science in 1968, using herders adding cattle to shared pasture until the land was destroyed. Real fisheries echoed it: Newfoundland northern cod stocks collapsed and Canada imposed a fishing moratorium in 1992, ending a five hundred year fishery.
modern_example: A shared team drive or group chat becomes useless when everyone dumps files and messages without organizing. Each person saves a minute by not labeling or summarizing, while everyone loses hours searching. Clear ownership, quotas, and cleanup norms are the small scale version of fisheries regulation.
failure_mode: Commons are not doomed. Elinor Ostrom documented communities governing shared resources successfully for centuries through local rules and monitoring, winning a Nobel Prize in 2009. The model fails when it assumes only privatization or central control can work, ignoring proven community governance.
apply_steps: Identify the shared resource being silently depleted
Show how private gain creates shared damage here
Propose clear rules, limits, or ownership for use
Add monitoring and consequences people actually respect

situation_notes.team-conflict: This model reveals shared resources like meeting time collapse when each person adds just one more agenda item unchecked.
situation_notes.channel-not-growing: This model explains attention commons on platforms degrade as creators flood feeds, making each individual post less discoverable for everyone.
situation_notes.online-arguments: This model shows comment sections collapse when each person gains status from dunking while collective conversation quality pays the price.

case_seeds: Hardin essay in Science 1968
Newfoundland cod fishery moratorium 1992
origin: Garrett Hardin, a biologist at the University of California, published The Tragedy of the Commons in Science in 1968, reviving an argument the English economist William Forster Lloyd had made about shared pasture in 1833. Hardin wrote amid rising concern about population growth and pollution, and his herder parable became one of the most cited social science articles of the century.
mechanism_deep: The arithmetic is brutal because it is asymmetric at the level of the individual decision. A herder who adds one animal captures nearly the full value of that animal when it is sold, while the grazing cost is divided among every herder using the pasture. As long as the private share of the benefit exceeds the private share of the cost, adding animals is the rational move, and it stays rational at every level of crowding until the resource fails. Note what this implies: the tragedy does not require greed, ignorance, or short-sightedness. Fully informed, public-spirited people can still destroy a commons if each knows that personal restraint, unmatched by others, merely leaves more grass for someone else's cattle while impoverishing only the restrainer. The structure, not the character of the users, produces the outcome. Three variables decide how fast collapse arrives. First, whether the resource renews and how quickly use exceeds that renewal rate. Second, whether users can observe each other's behaviour and communicate, since invisible extraction invites worst-case assumptions. Third, whether the group is stable and bounded, because transient users discount the resource's future entirely. Elinor Ostrom's field research, recognised with the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2009, showed that communities which set clear boundaries, monitor use, apply graduated sanctions, and let users write their own rules routinely escape the tragedy without privatisation or central command. Hardin's model is therefore best read as a description of open access, where no governance exists at all, rather than of all shared ownership. Wherever access is open, benefits are private, and costs are shared, the same signature appears, from fisheries to shared attention, regardless of how enlightened the participants consider themselves to be. Technology and discounting quietly steer the outcome as well. Cheap monitoring, from satellite tracking of fishing vessels to sensors on irrigation wells, lowers the cost of the observation on which every successful commons regime depends, turning previously invisible extraction into behaviour that can be priced or punished. Conversely, when users heavily discount the future, because they are poor, insecure, or expect to lose access anyway, even a renewable resource is mined as if it were exhaustible, which is why secure tenure often conserves resources better than lectures about sustainability. Scale compounds the difficulty: small groups can rely on reputation and face-to-face sanction, but as membership grows into the thousands or millions, anonymity dissolves those tools and formal rules, metering, and enforceable rights must replace them. The atmosphere and the high seas remain the hardest cases precisely because no authority exists that can impose the boundary, monitoring, and sanction package Ostrom's successful communities all possessed in some local form.
examples_extra: California's groundwater basins were pumped for decades under rules that let landowners extract freely, so farmers drilled deeper wells as water tables fell, raising costs for everyone and causing land subsidence in parts of the Central Valley. California passed the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act in 2014, requiring local agencies to bring basins into balance, a century after pumping began. The Act's long timelines, with full sustainability required over roughly two decades, show how slowly governance arrives once overuse is deeply established.

The atmosphere functions as a global commons for carbon emissions: each country captures the full economic benefit of burning fossil fuel while the climate cost is spread across all nations and future generations. This structure, identical to Hardin's pasture at planetary scale, explains why voluntary national pledges repeatedly fall short of the reductions their own signatories agree are necessary. The same logic explains why international climate agreements focus on monitoring and reporting rules, since commitments without observation invite quiet non-compliance.
misconceptions: Many people think the tragedy means shared resources always fail — in reality, open access without any rules fails, while many communities govern commons successfully for centuries with boundaries and monitoring.
Many people think the problem is greedy individuals — in reality, the incentive structure makes overuse rational even for restrained, well-informed people acting in good faith.
Many people think privatisation is the only cure — in reality, Ostrom documented durable community governance, and quotas, norms, and shared ownership also change the underlying payoffs.

practice.name: Audit one commons you use
practice.instructions: Name a shared resource you draw on, such as a team channel, shared kitchen, or local park. Write who benefits from extra use and who pays the cost, then propose one visible rule, limit, or rotation that changes that payoff. Suggest it to the group this week.

practice.name: Design Ostrom rules in miniature
practice.instructions: For the same commons, draft three elements: a clear boundary for who may use it, a simple way members can see usage, and a mild first consequence for overuse. Keep each element to one sentence so the system stays enforceable.

cross_domain: In medicine, antibiotic resistance follows the same structure in hospital wards and farms worldwide: each course of antibiotics benefits one patient while eroding drug effectiveness shared by all future patients. In computing, shared networks suffer when every application grabs maximum bandwidth, so engineers build throttling and priority rules into protocols, effectively fencing a digital pasture that open access would quickly render unusable for everyone connected to it. In fisheries science, individual transferable quotas convert an open-access race into allocated rights, and several fisheries managed this way have stabilised stocks that open competition was steadily depleting.

name_vi: Vấn đề người uỷ quyền – người đại diện
definition: When one person hires another to act for them, the agent goals and information differ, so the agent may serve themselves instead.
mechanism: The principal cannot watch everything or judge expert work perfectly, giving the agent room to shirk, overspend, or chase personal rewards like status and easy targets. Contracts help by tying pay to outcomes the principal cares about, but every metric can be gamed. The problem persists wherever trust meets asymmetric knowledge: shareholders and managers, patients and doctors, voters and officials, clients and contractors.
classic_example: The Enron collapse of 2001 showed executives, as agents of shareholders, enriching themselves through off balance sheet entities while hiding debt. Auditors who should have policed them were paid by Enron itself. Shareholders and employees lost billions when the hidden misalignment finally surfaced and the firm collapsed.
modern_example: A salaried marketer rewarded only for report metrics may buy cheap traffic that looks good in dashboards but never converts. The company wants profit, the agent wants an easy green chart. Tying evaluation to revenue and retention, reviewed over longer periods, narrows that gap between reported success and real success.
failure_mode: Not every gap is betrayal; agents often know more precisely because principals hired their judgment. Excessive monitoring destroys trust, speed, and initiative. The model can also make you cynical about genuine loyalty and craftsmanship, which do exist and which heavy incentives sometimes crowd out.
apply_steps: Name who acts for whom in this relationship
List what each side actually gets rewarded for
Find where information is hidden from the principal
Redesign incentives or checks around real outcomes

situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: This model reveals advisors earn from products sold or assets gathered, so their recommendation may optimize their income before your returns.
situation_notes.taking-investment-or-not: This model shows investors as principals will demand controls because they cannot watch daily decisions, and founders should expect that.
situation_notes.presenting-to-leadership: This model explains leaders ask probing questions because they must trust reports they cannot verify line by line themselves.

case_seeds: Enron collapse 2001
origin: Michael Jensen and William Meckling gave the problem its modern formal treatment in their 1976 paper on the theory of the firm, defining agency costs as monitoring, bonding, and residual loss. The underlying dilemma is older, discussed by Adam Smith in 1776, who doubted managers of other people's money would watch it with the same vigilance as their own.
mechanism_deep: Agency problems combine two ingredients: divergent goals and asymmetric information about effort or quality. Because the principal cannot observe effort directly, pay tied to easily measured outcomes invites the agent to optimise the measure rather than the mission, a distortion that grows with the gap between the metric and the true goal. Contracts therefore trade off three imperfect tools. Monitoring reduces hidden action but costs money and trust. Outcome-based pay aligns incentives but forces risk-averse agents to bear risks they do not control, for which they demand compensation. Selection and reputation work slowly but cheaply, which is why long relationships and repeat dealings often outperform elaborate contracts. The problem intensifies with each layer of delegation, since shareholders delegate to boards, boards to executives, and executives to managers, and each link adds its own divergence. Agency costs can be itemised, which makes them manageable: monitoring expenditure by the principal, bonding expenditure by the agent to prove trustworthiness, and the residual loss that remains because perfect alignment is impossible. Total agency cost is minimised, not eliminated, and mature institutions accept some residual loss as cheaper than total surveillance.
examples_extra: Real estate agents illustrate the gap measurably: a widely discussed analysis in Freakonomics, published in 2005 by Steven Levitt and Stephen Dubner, reported that agents' own homes stayed on the market longer and sold for higher prices than comparable client homes, because an agent keeps only a small commission share of any extra client price while bearing the full cost of extra weeks of work.

Mechanics diagnosing car problems act as agents for owners who cannot verify whether a recommended repair is necessary. Because the mechanic profits from the repair itself, owners rationally seek second opinions on expensive work. Warranties, itemised quotes, and returning replaced parts are all institutional attempts to narrow this information gap.
misconceptions: Many people think agency problems mean agents are dishonest — in reality, honest people respond to the incentives and information they are given, and badly designed rewards mislead even the well-intentioned.
Many people think tighter monitoring always helps — in reality, surveillance costs money, slows work, and can destroy the trust and initiative the principal hired the agent for.
Many people think paying on results solves everything — in reality, agents then game the measured result and neglect valuable outcomes that are hard to count.

practice.name: Rewrite one reward
practice.instructions: Pick a relationship where you are the principal, such as a contractor, tutor, or service provider. Write what they are actually rewarded for today in one sentence, then rewrite the arrangement so part of the reward depends on the outcome you truly care about.

cross_domain: In medicine, doctors act as agents for patients who cannot judge treatment quality, which is why second opinions, clinical guidelines, and malpractice law all exist as partial correctives. In politics, voters are principals and elected officials their agents, but elections are blunt monitoring tools held years apart, so officials enjoy wide discretion between moments of accountability, exactly as agency theory predicts for weakly monitored delegates.

name_vi: Rủi ro đạo đức / ỷ lại vì được bảo vệ
definition: People take greater risks when someone else bears the cost of failure, because protection weakens their personal reason to be careful.
mechanism: Insurance, bailouts, and guarantees change behavior after the deal is signed. When downside is transferred, the protected party rationally spends less on prevention and attempts riskier moves, since gains stay private while losses are shared. The effect is not about bad character but altered payoffs. Deductibles, partial coverage, and skin in the game exist specifically to restore some personal cost to careless choices.
classic_example: Before the 2008 financial crisis, large banks made risky mortgage bets believing governments would rescue systemically important firms. The phrase too big to fail captured this hazard. When Lehman Brothers was allowed to fail in September 2008, panic showed how deeply markets had priced in rescue.
modern_example: An employee who knows the company absorbs all mistakes may skip careful checks before sending a campaign live. A freelancer spending their own money double checks. Smart teams use review budgets and shared accountability, not blame, so the person deciding also feels a meaningful share of any failure cost.
failure_mode: Insurance also enables valuable risk taking that fear would otherwise block, like surgery or starting firms. Calling every protected risk moral hazard ignores that purpose. The model struggles to separate changed behavior from the fact that risky people seek protection more in the first place.
apply_steps: Ask who pays if this decision goes wrong
Check whether decision maker shares that downside personally
Add deductibles, reviews, or skin in the game
Reassess risk once protection changes the incentives

situation_notes.taking-investment-or-not: Moral hazard reveals easy investor money can tempt founders to spend carelessly because losses fall mostly on someone else capital.
situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Moral hazard explains why guaranteed bailouts encourage bank shareholders to cheer risky lending they would otherwise fear and avoid.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: Moral hazard shows advisors recommending risky products risk only reputation while you bear the actual financial loss if wrong.

case_seeds: Global financial crisis and bank bailouts 2008
Lehman Brothers failure September 2008
origin: The term originated in the insurance industry in the nineteenth century, describing how coverage might change an insured person's behaviour. Kenneth Arrow brought it into formal economics in a 1963 paper on uncertainty and medical care, and economists later applied it widely to banking, employment contracts, and any setting where protection separates decisions from their consequences.
mechanism_deep: Moral hazard is specifically a problem of hidden action after a contract is signed, which distinguishes it from hidden information before signing. The insured party chooses how much care to take, and the insurer cannot observe that care cheaply, so full coverage pushes prevention below the level both sides would choose if care were visible. Contract design responds by restoring marginal cost to the decision maker: deductibles make the insured pay the first portion of any loss, co-insurance shares a percentage, and experience-rated premiums punish past claims. Each tool trades protection against incentives, since a deductible large enough to fully discipline behaviour would also destroy the insurance's purpose. In finance the same logic scales dangerously, because a firm whose creditors expect a public rescue borrows as if its downside were capped, and that expectation itself increases the chance rescue becomes necessary. The concept extends quietly into everyday organisations through soft budget constraints, a term economist Janos Kornai developed for state firms that expected rescue: any team that learns overruns will always be covered stops treating budgets as real limits. The cure is credibility, not severity.
examples_extra: Flood insurance in the United States has repeatedly covered rebuilding homes in high-risk flood zones, and some properties have been rebuilt multiple times after successive floods. When premiums do not fully reflect location risk, owners have weak financial reason to relocate or elevate structures, so public programmes absorb losses that private pricing would have discouraged building into in the first place.

Deposit insurance, introduced in the United States in 1933 with the creation of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, stopped bank runs by guaranteeing depositors their money. Economists note it also removed depositors' incentive to monitor bank risk, which is why deposit insurance is paired with bank regulation and supervision rather than left to discipline banks alone.
misconceptions: Many people think moral hazard means insured people become immoral — in reality, the term describes a rational response to changed payoffs, not a character defect or deliberate fraud.

Many people think moral hazard and adverse selection are the same — in reality, adverse selection is hidden information before a deal, while moral hazard is changed behaviour after protection is in place.
Many people think eliminating protection is the answer — in reality, insurance enables valuable risk taking, and the goal is sharing costs so care remains worthwhile, not removing cover.

practice.name: Find your free downside
practice.instructions: List one activity where someone else absorbs most of the cost if you fail, such as a guaranteed refund, a backup colleague, or insurance. Ask honestly whether your level of care dropped because of it. Add one small personal stake, like a checklist or deposit, to restore it.

cross_domain: In workplace safety, when a company absorbs all accident costs through insurance while workers face no consequences for skipping protective steps, compliance tends to slip unless supervisors monitor directly. In sport, guaranteed long-term contracts show a mild version: some athletes' performance measurably dips after signing, because the financial downside of a poor season has been transferred entirely to the team that must pay regardless of output.

name_vi: Lựa chọn bất lợi / chọn ngược
definition: When one side knows more about quality than the other, bad options drive out good ones because buyers price for average quality.
mechanism: Sellers know if their car is a lemon, borrowers know their true risk, and applicants know their work ethic. Buyers, unable to distinguish, offer a price based on average quality. Owners of genuinely good items refuse that low price and exit, leaving a worse pool, which lowers prices further. Markets unravel unless signals, warranties, reputation, or screening restore trust in quality differences.
classic_example: George Akerlof published The Market for Lemons in 1970, explaining how used car markets collapse when buyers cannot tell good cars from defective ones. Good sellers withdraw, only lemons remain, and trust dies. The paper initially faced rejection but later earned Akerlof a Nobel Prize in 2001.
modern_example: On freelance platforms, the most desperate low bidders flood proposals while strong professionals leave for referral networks. Clients picking mainly by price repeatedly hire poor work and conclude the whole platform is bad. Portfolios, paid trials, and verified reviews are screening tools fighting exactly this selection spiral.
failure_mode: Reputation systems, guarantees, and repeat relationships often solve selection problems well enough that markets function fine. The model also assumes quality is fixed and hidden, while in many services quality is created during the work. Overusing it breeds suspicion toward every stranger and bargain.
apply_steps: Ask who knows more about quality here, and what
Expect average pricing to push good options away
Look for warranties, trials, reputation, or verifiable signals
Design screening that bad types cannot fake cheaply

situation_notes.choosing-cofounder: Adverse selection warns the people most eager to join any startup may be those with fewest alternatives elsewhere available.
situation_notes.reading-a-new-partner: Adverse selection reveals a partner hiding quality details benefits from your average assumptions, so verification matters most before commitment deepens.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: Adverse selection explains free advice channels attract product sellers disproportionately because genuine experts rarely need to give expertise away.

case_seeds: Akerlof Market for Lemons paper 1970
origin: George Akerlof introduced the modern analysis in The Market for Lemons, published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 1970, using used cars to show how hidden quality can unravel a market. The paper shared in shaping information economics, and Akerlof received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2001 alongside Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz for work on asymmetric information.
mechanism_deep: The unravelling logic is iterative. Buyers who cannot observe quality offer a price reflecting average expected quality. Sellers of above-average items find that price insulting and withdraw or sell elsewhere. Their exit lowers the average quality of what remains, so rational buyers lower their offers again, driving out the next tier of good sellers. The process can end with only the worst items trading, or no market at all, even though mutually beneficial trades existed at full information. Whether collapse actually happens depends on how large the quality spread is, how easily buyers can learn, and whether institutions like certification, warranties, reputation, or mandatory disclosure restore enough confidence. Insurance markets show a second form: at a single pooled premium, the healthiest customers judge coverage overpriced and leave, concentrating risk until premiums must rise again. Mandatory participation is the bluntest institutional answer, which is why employer-based insurance pools and compulsory motor insurance exist: forcing low risks into the pool keeps average cost low enough for the market to survive. Voluntary markets must instead invest in classification, separating buyers into risk groups with different prices, which restores viability but raises fairness questions when the classification tracks poverty, illness, or other traits buyers cannot change.
examples_extra: Health insurance markets before the Affordable Care Act in the United States showed the spiral clearly in several states' individual markets: insurers priced for a sicker-than-average pool, healthy people declined coverage, and the remaining pool grew sicker and more expensive. Policy responses such as subsidies, standardised plans, and open-enrolment windows were designed specifically to keep healthier buyers inside the pool.

In online marketplaces for freelance services, clients unable to judge skill in advance often anchor on low bids, and experienced professionals with full order books quietly leave for referral work. The visible pool then skews toward beginners and desperate sellers, confirming clients' belief that the platform is low quality, even though excellent providers once listed there.
misconceptions: Many people think adverse selection means buyers get cheated by fraud — in reality, no fraud is required; honest sellers of good items simply exit when pooled prices undervalue them.
Many people think it is the same as moral hazard — in reality, adverse selection concerns hidden type before a contract, while moral hazard concerns hidden behaviour after it.
Many people think low prices always benefit buyers — in reality, pricing for average quality can destroy the supply of high quality entirely, leaving buyers worse off.

practice.name: Spot the pooled price
practice.instructions: Think of a purchase where you paid an average price without being able to judge quality, such as a course, repair, or hire. Write what signal, warranty, or trial would have separated good from bad before you paid. Use that test first in your next similar purchase.

cross_domain: In biology, mate selection faces the same information problem: individuals advertise quality with costly displays precisely because cheap claims cannot separate strong from weak partners. In banking, borrowers most eager to accept high interest rates are often the riskiest, so a bank that simply raises rates can worsen its own loan pool, a selection effect that explains why lenders ration credit instead of always clearing the market by price.

name_vi: Lý thuyết trò chơi
definition: Game theory studies decisions where your best move depends on what others will do, and their best move depends on yours.
mechanism: Players, strategies, and payoffs are mapped explicitly, then each side reasons about the others likely response, including responses to responses. This reveals traps like arms races and price wars where everyone acting sensibly produces a bad outcome for all. It also shows how rules, repetition, reputation, and credible commitments change behavior. The framework works whenever outcomes are interdependent rather than controlled by one decision maker alone.
classic_example: The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 became a classic game theory case. The United States and Soviet Union each weighed escalation against humiliation, signaling resolve through a naval quarantine while secretly negotiating. Thomas Schelling work on strategic conflict, published in 1960, directly informed thinking about such standoffs.
modern_example: Two rival creators copying each other content daily both lose originality and burn out, yet neither dares stop first. Recognizing the game, one changes format and posts less often but distinctly, escaping the trap. In pricing, salary talks, and platform strategy, naming the game usually reveals a move outside it.
failure_mode: Real people are not perfectly rational payoff calculators. Emotion, honor, misperception, and incomplete information regularly break model predictions. Simple games also strip away context that actually decides outcomes, so treating a payoff matrix as truth instead of a thinking aid leads to elegant but wrong strategies.
apply_steps: Name the players and what each wants
List moves each side can realistically make
Predict responses to your move, then counter responses
Look for rule changes or commitments altering the game

situation_notes.competitor-price-war: Game theory reveals cutting price only helps if rivals cannot match, otherwise everyone ends poorer with same market shares.
situation_notes.salary-negotiation: Game theory shows your offer strength depends on alternatives both sides believe exist, not just your actual performance alone.
situation_notes.team-conflict: Game theory explains repeated team games reward cooperation and reputation, so one selfish win can cost many future collaborations.
situation_notes.negotiating-price: Game theory clarifies each concession signals how you will react next, teaching the other side to push harder later.

case_seeds: Cuban Missile Crisis 1962
Cold War nuclear deterrence standoff
origin: John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern founded modern game theory with Theory of Games and Economic Behavior in 1944, formalising strategic interaction mathematically. John Nash extended it in 1950 to non-cooperative games where players cannot make binding agreements, and Thomas Schelling added the analysis of commitment and focal points in The Strategy of Conflict in 1960, shaping Cold War strategic thinking.
mechanism_deep: The discipline begins by specifying a game precisely: who the players are, what strategies each can choose, what each combination pays every player, and what each player knows when moving. That discipline alone exposes most strategic confusion, because arguments about the right move usually turn out to be disagreements about the payoffs or about whether the game is played once or repeatedly. A dominant strategy is best whatever others do; where none exists, players must forecast rivals, which creates the regress of I think that you think that I think, resolved in equilibrium concepts rather than by deeper guessing. Repetition transforms results. In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, defection dominates, but in an indefinitely repeated game, strategies like tit-for-tat can sustain cooperation because today's betrayal is punished tomorrow, which is why reputation and ongoing relationships civilise markets that anonymous one-off encounters leave brutal. Information structure matters as much as payoffs: moving first can be an advantage when commitment is credible, as when a firm builds capacity rivals cannot ignore, or a disadvantage when the second mover can copy the pioneer's revealed plan. Mixed strategies, deliberately randomising choices, explain behaviour from penalty kicks to audit selection, where predictability itself is exploitable. The framework is strongest where players are few, moves are observable, and stakes are clear, and weakest where crowds, emotion, identity, and rule-changing dominate, though even there it usefully predicts which pressures will push behaviour over time. Its most practical lesson is meta-strategic: when every available move loses, the winning response is often to change the game itself, its players, its timing, its information, or its payoffs, rather than to optimise harder inside a losing structure. Zero-sum and non-zero-sum structures deserve separate attention because confusing them produces needless conflict. In a zero-sum game one side's gain is exactly the other's loss, so pure distribution is the whole contest, as in dividing a fixed bonus pool. Most economic and organisational games are non-zero-sum: both sides can gain together or lose together, and the strategic problem is coordinating on the jointly good outcome and dividing it acceptably, not defeating the opponent outright. Mechanism design, the reverse branch of the field recognised by the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2007, starts from a desired outcome and engineers rules, such as spectrum auctions or kidney exchange systems, so that self-interested play produces it. Bounded rationality research adds a final correction: real players use heuristics, care about fairness enough to reject insulting offers in ultimatum experiments, and sometimes cooperate unconditionally, so applied game theory works best as a map of pressures rather than a literal script of behaviour.
examples_extra: Penalty kicks in professional football are a genuine mixed-strategy game studied by economists using match data: kickers and goalkeepers must randomise left, centre, and right choices because any predictable pattern gets exploited. Research published in the early 2000s on league penalty data found professionals randomise remarkably close to the proportions game theory prescribes for keeping opponents indifferent. The finding matters because it shows the theory describing real expert behaviour under pressure, not merely prescribing how perfectly rational players ought to behave.

OPEC members repeatedly face a cartel game: each country gains if all restrict output and prices stay high, yet each individually profits by quietly selling more than its quota at that high price. The recurring pattern of agreed cuts followed by partial cheating, visible across decades of oil markets, is the prisoner's dilemma structure operating at the scale of national economies. Attempts to enforce quotas through monitoring and sanctions are attempts to rewrite the game's payoffs so that restraint becomes individually rewarding rather than naive.
misconceptions: Many people think game theory assumes people are selfish calculators — in reality, payoffs can include fairness, loyalty, or reputation; the framework models interdependence, not a fixed view of human nature.
Many people think it predicts one perfect move — in reality, many games have multiple equilibria or require deliberate randomness, so it often narrows options rather than naming a winner.
Many people think cooperation means ignoring game theory — in reality, repeated-game analysis explains exactly when cooperation is the rational strategy and what sustains it.

practice.name: Draw the two-by-two
practice.instructions: Take a live rivalry, such as a price dispute or a workload conflict, and draw a two-by-two grid of your two main moves against theirs. Fill each cell with the outcome for both sides. Look for a dominant strategy and for the cell both sides are drifting toward by default.

practice.name: Change the game, not the move
practice.instructions: For the same situation, list one change to each element: the players involved, the order of moves, the information shared, and the payoffs. Choose the single change that most improves your position and test whether you can implement it this week.

cross_domain: In evolutionary biology, game theory predicts stable mixtures of behaviours such as hawks and doves competing for resources, formalised as evolutionarily stable strategies where no mutant approach can invade. In computer science, network protocols and auction systems are designed as games, with mechanisms engineered so that self-interested software agents, advertisers, or bidders produce orderly outcomes, from search advertising auctions to how packets are routed across competing networks. In biology, the same mixed-strategy logic explains why some prey animals vary their escape patterns unpredictably, since a predictable routine would be learned and exploited by predators.

name_vi: Cân bằng Nash
definition: A Nash equilibrium is an outcome where no player can improve their result by changing strategy alone, given what others are doing.
mechanism: Each player best responds to the others current choices, and those choices mutually lock in. The result is stable not because it is good but because unilateral change hurts the changer. The famous prisoners dilemma shows two suspects both confessing, the equilibrium, leaves both worse than mutual silence. John Nash proved in 1950 that such an equilibrium exists in every finite game, giving strategy a universal anchor.
classic_example: John Nash published his equilibrium concept in 1950 while a Princeton graduate student, work that eventually earned the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1994. The prisoners dilemma, formalized at RAND around 1950 by Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher, became its most famous illustration in textbooks worldwide.
modern_example: Every driver in a city drives because everyone else drives, even though all would prefer reliable transit and emptier roads. No single driver improves life by switching alone to a slow bus. Only coordinated investment changes the equilibrium, which explains why traffic habits persist despite universal complaints about congestion.
failure_mode: Games often have multiple equilibria, and the model cannot say which one people will land on. Real players communicate, learn, and change rules, escaping supposedly stable outcomes. Equilibrium also describes stability, not fairness or efficiency, so treating it as the right outcome confuses description with endorsement.
apply_steps: Find what each player does given others behavior
Test whether anyone gains by changing alone
Distinguish stable outcome from best collective outcome
Change payoffs or coordination to shift equilibrium

situation_notes.competitor-price-war: Nash equilibrium explains price wars persist because undercutting alone feels necessary even though all firms prefer higher stable prices.
situation_notes.team-conflict: Nash equilibrium shows defensive team behavior locks in when nobody trusts others to cooperate first without getting exploited themselves.
situation_notes.online-arguments: Nash equilibrium reveals outrage becomes stable online because moderate voices gain nothing by staying calm while extremes dominate attention.

case_seeds: Nash equilibrium paper 1950
Prisoners dilemma experiments at RAND 1950
origin: John Nash introduced the concept in his 1950 Princeton doctoral dissertation and a short paper the same year, proving that every finite game has at least one equilibrium when players may randomise strategies. The work transformed economics and strategy, and Nash shared the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1994 for his pioneering analysis of equilibria in non-cooperative game theory.
mechanism_deep: An equilibrium is found by checking best responses: for each player, is the chosen strategy the most rewarding reply to everyone else's strategy? Where every player's answer is yes simultaneously, nobody gains by deviating alone, so the outcome persists without any enforcement. The concept's power is its modesty: it predicts stability, not desirability, and the prisoner's dilemma shows a stable outcome can be strictly worse for every player than an unstable one. Real games often contain several equilibria, some good and some bad, and which one a group lands on depends on history, focal points, and communication, none of which the bare concept selects. Refinements and learning dynamics were developed later precisely to address that selection problem. Mixed-strategy equilibria add that stability can require deliberate unpredictability, as in inspection games or sports, where any pure pattern would invite exploitation by an attentive opponent. Coordination games show the concept's gentler side. When drivers all keep to the same side of the road, or firms adopt the same technical standard, the equilibrium is genuinely good, and its stability is a social achievement rather than a trap. The practical skill is distinguishing trap equilibria, where everyone would gain from coordinated escape, from coordination equilibria worth defending.
examples_extra: At concerts and sporting events, audiences drift into a standing equilibrium: once some fans stand, those behind must stand to see, until everyone stands though most would prefer all sitting. No individual can fix it by sitting down, since that only blocks their own view, so the worse outcome locks in without anyone choosing it directly.

Competing farmers planting the same fashionable crop illustrate a market version: each grower rationally follows high recent prices, but the collective harvest then floods the market and crashes the price for all. Individually sensible planting decisions, each a best response to last season's signals, combine into an equilibrium harvest nobody would have chosen together.
misconceptions: Many people think a Nash equilibrium is the best outcome for everyone — in reality, it is only stable; the prisoner's dilemma equilibrium leaves all players worse off than mutual cooperation would.
Many people think there is always exactly one equilibrium — in reality, many games have several, and history and expectations decide which one a group actually reaches.
Many people think equilibrium requires players to reason like mathematicians — in reality, habits, imitation, and trial and error can push groups into equilibria nobody consciously calculated.

practice.name: Test the solo deviation
practice.instructions: Describe a frustrating stable pattern in your team or market in one sentence. For each party, ask whether they would gain by changing alone. If nobody would, stop blaming individuals and identify one payoff or rule change that could move the whole pattern.

cross_domain: In traffic engineering, the user equilibrium named after John Wardrop, published in 1952, mirrors Nash's idea: each driver chooses a personally fastest route until no driver can improve by switching alone, even though total congestion is worse than a coordinated optimum. In ecology, an evolutionarily stable strategy is the biological analogue, a behaviour pattern that, once common in a population, cannot be invaded by any rare alternative strategy. In language, spelling and grammar conventions persist as coordination equilibria: individually switching to a more logical spelling gains nothing unless the whole community moves together.

name_vi: Phát tín hiệu và sàng lọc
definition: Signaling lets informed people prove quality through costly actions, while screening lets uninformed people design tests that reveal hidden quality.
mechanism: Cheap claims cannot separate good types from bad because anyone can copy words. A signal works only when it costs low quality types more than high quality types: degrees, warranties, portfolios, or money back guarantees. Screening flips the process, offering menus or trials where people reveal themselves by choosing. Michael Spence formalized job market signaling in 1973, explaining why credentials persist even when coursework itself adds little skill.
classic_example: Michael Spence published his job market signaling model in 1973, arguing university degrees signal ability and persistence to employers who cannot observe talent directly. The degree is valuable partly because weaker candidates find completing it costlier, making the credential a credible filter rather than pure knowledge proof.
modern_example: A consultant offering a small paid pilot with a performance guarantee signals confidence that weak competitors cannot safely imitate. Clients screen agencies by assigning the same test project and comparing thinking, not pitches. In dating, hiring, and investing, costly consistent actions reveal what polished self descriptions deliberately conceal.
failure_mode: Signals inflate into wasteful arms races, like degrees required for jobs that never needed them. Once a signal becomes cheap to fake, it stops separating anyone. Screening can also discriminate unfairly, using proxies that punish capable people lacking money, polish, or conventional backgrounds.
apply_steps: Ask what claim needs proof beyond words
Find proof that is costly for fakers
Design a small test revealing real quality
Update the signal as fakers learn to copy it

situation_notes.salary-negotiation: Signaling reveals documented outside offers and scarce results persuade employers far more than claiming you deserve higher pay.
situation_notes.reading-a-new-partner: Signaling shows consistent costly actions over time reveal a partner character better than charming promises made when stakes are low.
situation_notes.presenting-to-leadership: Signaling explains leaders trust presenters who volunteer risks and numbers because hiding weaknesses would be cheaper for weak proposals.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: Signaling separates credible advisors who show audited track records from promoters relying on lifestyle images and confident predictions alone.

case_seeds: Spence job market signaling model 1973
origin: Michael Spence formalised signaling in Job Market Signaling, published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 1973, showing how education can sort workers even apart from skills taught. Joseph Stiglitz developed screening theory in the mid-1970s, examining how uninformed parties design choices that reveal information. Both shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Economics with George Akerlof for analysing markets with asymmetric information.
mechanism_deep: A signal separates types only under a strict condition economists call single-crossing: the signal must be cheaper, in money, effort, or risk, for the high-quality type to produce than for the low-quality type to fake. A degree works as a signal insofar as capable students complete it at lower personal cost; a warranty works because a maker of reliable products expects fewer claims than a maker of fragile ones, so offering it is cheap for the good firm and ruinous for the bad one. When technology or fashion lowers the cost of faking, separation collapses into a pooling equilibrium where everyone displays the signal and it certifies nothing, triggering demand for a costlier replacement. Screening inverts the initiative: the uninformed side offers a menu, such as insurance plans with different premiums and deductibles, designed so each type voluntarily picks the option intended for it, revealing its risk without ever being asked directly. Signal inflation follows a predictable cycle worth recognising early. Once employers require a degree, more people obtain one, its separating power weakens, and employers quietly demand a postgraduate qualification or a prestigious institution instead, restarting the race at a higher cost to everyone. The information gained may barely change while the resources burned in the contest multiply.
examples_extra: Peacocks' extravagant tails are biology's classic costly signal, explained by Amotz Zahavi's handicap principle proposed in 1975: only a genuinely healthy bird can afford such a burden, so the tail honestly advertises fitness precisely because it is expensive to carry. Economists cite it because the same cost-asymmetry logic governs human credentials and guarantees.

In hiring for software roles, public portfolios of working code and open-source contributions function as signals that are cheap for genuinely skilled developers to produce from their normal work and painfully expensive for weak candidates to fabricate convincingly. Employers increasingly screen with small paid work trials, which reveal ability directly instead of relying on interview performance.
misconceptions: Many people think any impressive credential is a valid signal — in reality, a signal informs only when faking it costs low-quality types more than it costs genuine ones.

Many people think signaling and screening are identical — in reality, signaling is initiated by the informed side proving itself, while screening is designed by the uninformed side to extract the truth.
Many people think stronger signals are always socially useful — in reality, signaling races can burn real resources, as when jobs demand degrees whose content the work never uses.

practice.name: Design a costly proof
practice.instructions: Identify one claim you need others to believe, such as reliability or expertise. Design a proof that would be easy for you if the claim is true and hard to fake if it were false, such as a small guaranteed trial. Offer that proof instead of repeating the claim.

cross_domain: In law, posting bail and offering collateral signal that a party expects to comply or win, because forfeiting the stake is a real cost only the confident accept. In marketing, heavy advertising expenditure itself can signal a firm's confidence in repeat purchases, since a company selling a poor product could never recover the campaign cost from one-time buyers who never return to buy again. In nature, flowers invest in nectar and vivid colour as costly advertisements that reliably indicate a real reward, separating genuine food sources from empty imitations insects learn to ignore.

name_vi: Độ co giãn của cầu theo giá
definition: Price elasticity measures how strongly buyers change how much they purchase when the price changes by a small amount.
mechanism: Demand is elastic when buyers have substitutes, low urgency, or treat the good as optional, so small price rises cause large drops in volume. Demand is inelastic for necessities without alternatives, like insulin or fuel for commuters, where buyers pay despite increases. Businesses live or die by this difference: raising prices grows revenue only when elasticity is low enough that lost customers do not erase the gain.
classic_example: When OPEC raised oil prices sharply in 1973, fuel demand barely fell in the short run because drivers had no alternatives, proving highly inelastic. Over years, efficient cars and new supply made demand far more elastic. The contrast taught economists that elasticity grows with time and available substitutes.
modern_example: A streaming service raising prices slightly may lose few subscribers if its shows are exclusive and habits are strong. A generic online course raising prices loses many buyers instantly because free alternatives abound. Before pricing, smart sellers test how volume actually moves instead of guessing from their own attachment.
failure_mode: Elasticity is not fixed. It shifts with income, fashion, competitors, and time horizon, so last year measurement misleads today. It also averages buyers together, hiding segments with opposite sensitivity. Treating one number as a law leads to confident pricing errors in changing markets.
apply_steps: Identify substitutes buyers can switch to quickly
Judge urgency and necessity of the purchase
Test small price changes and measure volume response
Price differently for sensitive and insensitive customer segments

situation_notes.pricing-a-product: Price elasticity reveals raising price grows revenue only when buyers lack substitutes and still need your product urgently enough.
situation_notes.negotiating-price: Price elasticity shows the side with more alternatives concedes less because their demand for this specific deal is elastic.
situation_notes.competitor-price-war: Price elasticity explains price cuts steal share dramatically in elastic markets but mostly burn margin where demand barely responds.

case_seeds: OPEC oil price shock short run inelastic demand 1973
origin: Alfred Marshall gave elasticity its formal definition in Principles of Economics in 1890, expressing responsiveness as a ratio of percentage changes so it could be compared across goods and currencies. Cournot had explored related demand responsiveness earlier in the nineteenth century, but Marshall's formulation, complete with the distinction between elastic and inelastic demand, became the standard taught today.
mechanism_deep: Elasticity is a ratio of percentage changes, which makes it unit-free and comparable between a litre of fuel and a concert ticket. Four determinants dominate. Substitutes: the more and closer they are, the higher the elasticity, which is why demand for one brand of cereal is elastic while demand for food in general is not. Necessity: essentials tolerate price rises that luxuries cannot. Budget share: items consuming a large share of income get scrutinised, raising elasticity. Time: elasticity almost always grows with the adjustment horizon, because buyers eventually replace equipment, move house, or form new habits. Revenue logic follows directly: when demand is inelastic, a price rise increases total revenue because volume barely falls; when elastic, the same rise destroys revenue, and firms instead profit from cutting price to expand volume faster than margin shrinks. Cross-price elasticity completes the picture by measuring how demand for one good responds to the price of another: positive for substitutes like butter and margarine, negative for complements like printers and ink cartridges. Firms use it to predict whether a rival's discount will steal their customers or expand the whole category.
examples_extra: Airlines price the same cabin differently because elasticity differs by traveller: business passengers booking late for a necessary trip tolerate high fares, while leisure travellers comparing destinations weeks ahead abandon expensive flights quickly. Revenue management systems exploit exactly this split, holding some seats for inelastic late demand while discounting early seats to fill the aircraft.

Cigarette demand is famously price inelastic among addicted smokers, which is why governments use tobacco taxes both to raise reliable revenue and, gradually, to discourage use. Studies across many countries consistently find that a sustained ten percent price increase reduces consumption by a smaller percentage, with stronger responses among teenagers and new smokers than among long-term users.

formula.expression: E = %ΔQd / %ΔP
formula.variables: E is price elasticity of demand, %ΔQd is the percentage change in quantity demanded, and %ΔP is the percentage change in price. Values are usually reported as absolute numbers.
formula.worked_example: A cafe raises coffee from 4 dollars to 5 dollars, a 25 percent increase, and daily sales fall from 200 cups to 170, a 15 percent decrease. Elasticity is 15 divided by 25, or 0.6, so demand is inelastic, and daily revenue rises from 800 to 850 dollars.

misconceptions: Many people think elasticity is a property of a product alone — in reality, it depends on the buyer segment, the time horizon, and the available substitutes, so one product has many elasticities.
Many people think a steep demand curve discussion is about slope — in reality, elasticity varies along a straight-line demand curve, being high at high prices and low at low prices.

Many people think inelastic demand means price rises are always wise — in reality, reputation, regulation, and long-run substitution can punish firms that exploit short-run inelasticity too aggressively.

practice.name: Run a ten percent test
practice.instructions: Choose one offer and change its price by about ten percent for a limited group or period, keeping everything else constant. Compare quantity sold and total revenue, not just sales feelings. Compute the implied elasticity from the two percentage changes before deciding the permanent price.

cross_domain: In medicine, demand for essential prescription drugs is highly inelastic, which shapes debates about pharmaceutical pricing and insurance design worldwide. In energy policy, short-run electricity demand is inelastic because appliances are fixed, so regulators rely on long-run efficiency standards and building codes, knowing price signals alone change usage only slowly until households can replace the equipment that consumes the power. In transport planning, congestion charges work only modestly in the short run for the same reason, since commuters cannot quickly change jobs or homes, so cities pair charges with better public transit options.

name_vi: Hào kinh tế / lợi thế phòng thủ bền vững
definition: An economic moat is a durable advantage that protects a business from competitors trying to steal its customers and profits.
mechanism: Strong businesses earn more than their cost of capital, which attracts rivals eager to copy them. A moat blocks that erosion through sources competitors cannot easily replicate, such as trusted brands, patents, low production costs, network effects, or painful switching costs. The wider and more durable the moat, the longer excess profits compound before competition pushes returns toward average. Investors therefore study moat durability as carefully as current profitability itself.
classic_example: Warren Buffett bought a major stake in Coca-Cola in 1988, arguing its global brand, distribution reach, and habitual consumption formed a moat rivals could not cross with money alone. Pepsi could spend heavily on advertising, yet Coke still owned shelf space, fountain contracts, and a place in everyday routines built over a century.
modern_example: A small accounting software firm serving Vietnamese pharmacies may look ordinary, yet deep integrations with local invoicing rules, trained staff habits, and years of stored records can protect it. A cheaper foreign rival must overcome trust, migration risk, and retraining before price even matters, giving the incumbent time to improve.
failure_mode: Moats erode quietly when technology, regulation, or tastes change. Leaders mistake past protection for permanent safety, stop investing, and discover too late that customers have found a new route around the castle walls.
apply_steps: Name the exact source of your advantage
Test whether rivals can copy it cheaply
Measure how long the advantage should last
Reinvest profits into widening the moat

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: This model reveals whether high profits are defensible for years or just a temporary gap competitors will quickly close.
situation_notes.competitor-price-war: This model reveals whether you can survive discounting because customers value something rivals cannot match at lower prices.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: This model reveals whether growth will strengthen your defenses or simply expose a weak advantage to much larger competitors.

case_seeds: Buffett investing in Coca-Cola, 1988
Microsoft defending Windows and Office in the 1990s
origin: Warren Buffett popularised the moat metaphor in Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters and annual meetings from the 1990s onward, picturing a good business as an economic castle that competitors constantly try to storm. Charlie Munger sharpened the test by asking whether the castle would still stand in ten years. Morningstar analyst Pat Dorsey systematised the sources of moats for ordinary investors in The Little Book That Builds Wealth, published in 2008.
mechanism_deep: A moat deepens when each year of operation makes the next year harder to attack. A trusted brand lowers the customer's perceived risk, which supports premium prices, which funds better service and wider distribution, which exposes the brand to still more customers. Scale works the same way: volume spreads fixed costs, cheaper unit costs fund either lower prices or higher margins, and both attract more volume. Knowledge compounds too, because an incumbent serving millions of transactions learns failure patterns, supplier behaviour, and customer preferences that a newcomer cannot download. Rivals therefore rarely attack a moat head-on. They try to go around it by serving a neglected niche the leader finds too small, by bundling the product free inside a larger platform, by persuading regulators to mandate access or interoperability, or by riding a technology shift that makes the old asset irrelevant, as online search did to printed directories. Moats also erode from inside when managers harvest the advantage instead of reinvesting, letting quality slip while prices rise. The critical judgement is direction, not snapshot: a wide but narrowing moat, where each defence is quietly weakening, can be worth less than a narrow moat that widens every year. Durability also depends on the industry's pace of change. Slow-changing industries such as soft drinks, confectionery, and rating services let advantages persist for decades, while fast-moving software categories can dissolve a strong position within one product cycle. Finally, a moat protects profits, not revenue. A firm can keep growing sales while its moat drains away, because growth bought with discounts and advertising looks healthy until pricing power and returns on capital are examined honestly. Analysts who rate moats professionally, following the system Morningstar built from Dorsey's work, sort firms into wide, narrow, and no-moat categories, and the wide label demands confidence that excess returns will persist for decades, not merely years. That persistence test exposes a common error: confusing a good year, a good product cycle, or a good manager with a structural advantage. Managers retire and products age, while a moat lives in assets and positions that keep working under average leadership. Return on invested capital is the scoreboard that reveals which story is true, because a genuine moat shows up as returns held above the cost of capital across a full business cycle, including the downturn when weak advantages vanish. Capital allocation then decides the ending. Excess profit reinvested into the source of the advantage widens the moat, while excess profit spent on unrelated acquisitions usually dilutes it, which is why so many celebrated franchises fade under empire-building successors who inherited the castle but never understood its walls.
examples_extra: Moody's illustrates an intangible and regulatory moat in credit ratings. Large bond issuers seek ratings from agencies that investors already recognise and that regulations and investment mandates already reference, so a new rating agency faces a credibility problem money alone cannot quickly solve, even if its analysis is technically sound. An issuer that chose an unknown agency would pay for that obscurity in harder bond sales and sceptical investors, so issuers keep returning to the recognised names.

Deere and Company shows a service-network moat in farm machinery. Farmers buy tractors partly for the nearby dealer who stocks parts and can repair a machine quickly during planting or harvest, when a breakdown is most costly. A rival tractor maker must build that dense local service coverage, relationship by relationship, before its machines feel equally safe to own.
misconceptions: Many people think a famous brand is automatically a moat — in reality, fame without pricing power or repeat purchase is just awareness that fades.
Many people think a moat is permanent once established — in reality, every moat narrows or widens each year depending on reinvestment and industry change.
Many people think high current profit proves a moat — in reality, high profit without a moat is exactly what attracts the competition that destroys it.

practice.name: Four-question moat audit
practice.instructions: Pick a company you know well. Answer in writing: What exactly stops a well-funded rival copying it within two years? Could customers switch without pain? Has it raised prices without losing volume? Is the advantage stronger than five years ago? Any vague answer marks a weak moat.

practice.name: Moat direction check
practice.instructions: For the same company, list one force widening the advantage and one force narrowing it this year. Decide which force is stronger and what evidence would change your mind within twelve months.

cross_domain: The same logic appears in biology, where an established species with deep roots, stored reserves, and symbiotic partners resists invasive newcomers, and in geopolitics, where geography such as mountain ranges or island positions historically protected states the way brands protect firms. In academia, a researcher's citation record and laboratory infrastructure form a comparable moat: newcomers compete against accumulated reputation and equipment, not just against current ideas. The castle metaphor survives translation into each of these settings because accumulated, hard-to-copy position, rather than current performance, is what does the protecting in every case.

name_vi: Hiệu ứng mạng lưới
definition: Network effects occur when a product becomes more valuable for everyone as more people start using it regularly together.
mechanism: Each new user adds value for existing users by expanding reach, liquidity, content, or compatibility. Early growth is slow because a sparse network offers little benefit, but past a threshold adoption can accelerate as joining becomes the obvious choice. The same dynamic defends leaders, because a challenger must recreate the whole network, not just the product features. This explains why technically superior products often lose to incumbents with far denser, more active user bases.
classic_example: The telephone showed the pattern early: a single phone was useless, while each additional subscriber made owning one more worthwhile. In the twentieth century, fax machines and later Microsoft Windows followed the same logic, as users chose the system most other people and software makers already supported.
modern_example: A marketplace for freelance translators stays empty until both clients and translators arrive together. A solo creator building a community faces the same problem: members join for other members, not for features. Seeding one focused group and making early interactions succeed matters more than launching to everyone at once.
failure_mode: Network effects are not automatic and can reverse. Spam, low-quality users, or congestion make growth harmful, while multi-homing lets users switch easily. Counting registered users instead of active, valuable connections overstates the strength of the network.
apply_steps: Identify who makes the product valuable for whom
Start with one dense, narrow group
Make the first interaction succeed quickly
Track active connections, not signups

situation_notes.scaling-decision: This model reveals whether each new user strengthens the offer or simply adds cost, noise, and support burden.
situation_notes.channel-not-growing: This model reveals whether your audience stays isolated or actively brings, answers, and creates value for other members.
situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: This model reveals which narrow community can reach critical density first instead of spreading early users too thin.

case_seeds: Facebook overtaking MySpace in social networking, 2008
Visa building its payments network from the 1970s
origin: The idea grew out of telephony in the early twentieth century, when telephone executives argued that a network's usefulness rose with every subscriber it connected. Robert Metcalfe later gave the intuition a quantitative form for computer networks, and economists Carl Shapiro and Hal Varian popularised network effects for business strategy in Information Rules, published in 1998, just as internet platforms were making the pattern impossible for managers to ignore.
mechanism_deep: Network effects come in distinct forms that behave differently. Direct effects arise when users value other users of the same kind, as in messaging. Indirect effects link two groups, so more drivers shorten passenger waits and more passengers raise driver earnings. Local effects matter when only a user's immediate cluster counts, which is why a social product can feel alive in one school and dead in another. Growth is hardest below critical mass, the cold-start zone where the network is too sparse to deliver its core promise, so early strategy is about density in one narrow group rather than breadth. Past the threshold, adoption can become self-reinforcing, but the same mechanism can run in reverse: spam, fraud, congestion, and low-quality participants are negative network effects that make each addition harmful. Multi-homing is the main solvent. If users can cheaply belong to several networks at once, as with ride-hailing apps installed side by side, no single network captures the full value and leadership stays contestable. Switching costs and exclusive content are the usual counterweights. Rivals attack strong networks asymmetrically: they serve a niche the leader neglects, offer a tool so good that users bring their network with them, subsidise one side of the market, or exploit openness, as email did against closed messaging systems. Data effects are often mislabelled as network effects; more data only creates a true network advantage when it visibly improves the product for other users and keeps improving rather than plateauing. Judging a network therefore means measuring active connections, retention of connected users, and the cost of serving both sides, not celebrating raw registration totals that include dormant accounts. The structure of the network decides how defensible it really is. Global networks, where every user values every other user, concentrate into a single worldwide winner, while local networks, where a rider in one city gains nothing from drivers in another, fragment into city-by-city contests that better-funded challengers can still enter one market at a time. Clustering cuts both ways: dense clusters make the product sticky inside a community, yet they also give a rival a beachhead strategy, winning one cluster completely instead of fighting the whole network at once. Platform envelopment is the heavyweight attack, where an adjacent platform with its own large user base bundles the network's function into its existing product and imports its users overnight. Defenders answer by deepening identity, reputation history, and stored content inside the network, so leaving means abandoning an accumulated public self, not just changing an app. The mature strategic question is therefore not whether network effects exist, but which kind, at what geographic scope, with what multi-homing cost, and against which enveloping neighbour. Counting only registered accounts hides all of this, which is why serious operators report active, connected users instead of headline signups.
examples_extra: eBay built an indirect network effect between buyers and sellers of unusual second-hand goods. More sellers meant a buyer could find almost anything, and more buyers meant auctions reached fair prices, so both sides had reason to stay. A rival auction site with better software still struggled, because the listings and bidders themselves were the product.

WhatsApp spread through a direct network effect tied to phone contacts. Each person who installed it made it more useful for their existing friends and family, and groups locked whole circles in together. Competing messengers could copy features quickly, yet they could not copy the fact that a user's actual contacts were already reachable inside WhatsApp.

formula.expression: V is proportional to n x (n - 1), approximately n squared
formula.variables: V = potential value of the network; n = number of active users; n x (n - 1) = number of possible one-to-one connections
formula.worked_example: A network of 10 active users allows 10 x 9 = 90 possible connections. Growing to 100 active users allows 100 x 99 = 9,900 connections, roughly 110 times more, even though the user count grew only tenfold. This is Metcalfe's law as an approximation, not a valuation guarantee.

misconceptions: Many people think more users always strengthen a network — in reality, spam, congestion, and low-quality users can make growth actively harmful.
Many people think viral growth proves network effects — in reality, a product can spread fast yet retain nobody if users add no value to each other.
Many people think Metcalfe's law values a company — in reality, it only approximates possible connections and ignores activity, revenue, and connection quality.

practice.name: Map who creates value for whom
practice.instructions: Draw your product's user groups as circles and arrows showing which group makes the product better for which other group. If no arrow exists, you have an audience, not a network. Redesign one feature so users genuinely improve the experience of other users.

practice.name: Density before breadth test
practice.instructions: Choose one narrow community you could fully serve this month. Define the density you need, such as thirty active members interacting weekly, and list the seeding actions that reach it before any wider launch.

cross_domain: Languages show the pattern in education and travel: English is valuable to learn largely because so many others already speak it, which reinforces its position against objectively simpler constructed languages. Technical standards behave similarly in manufacturing, where a connector or file format wins because tools, spare parts, and trained technicians already surround it, making the standard's installed base its main competitive defence. In both settings the installed base itself becomes the argument for joining, so the leader's advantage grows simply by being chosen more often.

name_vi: Chi phí chuyển đổi
definition: Switching costs are the money, time, risk, and effort customers lose when moving from one provider to another.
mechanism: Customers stay not only because they like a product, but because leaving means migrating data, retraining people, rebuilding integrations, or risking downtime. These frictions raise retention and pricing power even when rivals look similar on paper. The strongest switching costs come from genuine workflow value, not deliberate lock-in tricks that breed resentment. Buyers effectively compare total lifetime cost and disruption, not headline price alone, when deciding whether to stay or leave.
classic_example: Enterprise software illustrated this for decades, as banks and manufacturers built processes, records, and staff training around systems from providers such as IBM and later SAP. Replacing the software was rarely just a purchase decision; it meant months of migration, testing, and operational risk across the whole organization.
modern_example: A freelancer who stores client files, automations, and templates in Notion may dislike a price rise yet stay, because rebuilding everything elsewhere costs a full week. Small teams feel the same pull with their accounting, email, and project tools once history and habits accumulate inside them.
failure_mode: High switching costs can hide a decaying product until a rival makes migration effortless. They also invite complacency and customer resentment, and regulators or open standards can suddenly lower the barriers that protected the incumbent.
apply_steps: List what customers would lose by leaving
Deepen useful integrations, not artificial lock-in
Reduce onboarding friction for incoming switchers
Watch for rivals offering free migration

situation_notes.pricing-a-product: This model reveals how much price increase customers will tolerate before the pain finally exceeds the cost of leaving.
situation_notes.users-but-no-revenue: This model reveals whether users stay from real embedded value or merely because they have not bothered to leave.
situation_notes.competitor-copied-you: This model reveals whether copied features matter when your customers face real migration risk moving to the imitator.

case_seeds: Banks retaining core systems from IBM for decades
Salesforce embedding into sales workflows in the 2000s
origin: Michael Porter placed switching costs among the barriers protecting industries in Competitive Strategy, published in 1980. Economist Paul Klemperer then formalised the concept in academic work during the mid-1980s, modelling how markets with locked-in customers differ from ordinary competition. The idea moved from strategy textbooks into software and subscription businesses, where data, integrations, and learned habits made leaving visibly expensive.
mechanism_deep: Switching costs stack in layers. Procedural costs cover searching, learning a new system, and rebuilding habits. Financial costs include exit fees, lost loyalty rewards, and buying replacements for accessories or integrations. Relational costs mean abandoning trusted contacts, support relationships, and communities stored inside the old product. These layers accumulate quietly: every imported record, trained employee, connected tool, and customised workflow raises the exit toll, which is why retention often strengthens with tenure even when satisfaction stays flat. The same accumulation hands the incumbent pricing room, because a rival must not merely match the price but compensate the customer for the whole disruption. Erosion usually arrives as a tool rather than an argument. Migration software, open file standards, data-portability rules, and artificial intelligence that converts formats automatically all lower the toll without the rival being better. Incumbents defend ethically by deepening genuine usefulness, such as richer history and better integrations, rather than by hiding export buttons, which converts protection into resentment and invites regulation.
examples_extra: Hospitals running a large electronic health record system such as Epic face a switching cost measured in retraining thousands of staff and migrating years of patient records safely. Even dissatisfied administrators renew, because a failed migration risks daily clinical operations, not just inconvenience, so the vendor's position survives complaints that would sink a simpler tool.

A family deep in Apple's ecosystem owns purchased apps, shared photo libraries, message history, and accessories that work best together. Moving one member to another platform is easy, but moving the whole household means friction at every shared service, which is why the ecosystem, rather than any single device, holds the customer.
misconceptions: Many people think locked-in customers are loyal customers — in reality, many stay resentfully and leave the moment migration becomes easy.
Many people think switching costs are mainly exit fees — in reality, time, retraining, data loss, and operational risk usually matter far more.
Many people think higher switching costs are always good strategy — in reality, obvious lock-in tricks deter new customers from joining at all.

practice.name: Exit toll inventory
practice.instructions: List everything a customer of yours would lose, redo, or risk by leaving: data, training, integrations, relationships, downtime. Score each item honestly. Then mark which items are genuine value you created and which are artificial friction you should remove before a regulator or rival does.

cross_domain: Education shows the pattern when a student changes schools and loses credits, friendships, and familiarity with a curriculum, so families tolerate a mediocre school longer than course quality alone would predict. In logistics, a warehouse built around one carrier's labels, software, and pickup routines faces the same toll, making a cheaper carrier unattractive until volumes justify retooling the whole operation.

name_vi: Tài sản thương hiệu
definition: Brand equity is the extra value a trusted name adds beyond what the product alone would otherwise be worth.
mechanism: Repeated good experiences compress into a mental shortcut: buyers pay more, choose faster, and forgive occasional mistakes because the name reduces perceived risk. Strong brands also lower marketing costs, since each new message builds on existing associations. Equity accumulates slowly through consistent delivery, distinctive symbols, and stories customers repeat to each other.
