cross_domain: Ecology runs on the same law: biodiverse grasslands survive droughts that kill monoculture fields, because different species draw water and nutrients at different depths and times. Agriculture learned it through catastrophe — reliance on a single potato variety turned blight into the Irish famine of the 1840s. Careers show it too: a worker with skills valued by several industries survives the collapse of one employer or sector, while a single-skill specialist shares the Enron employees' fate in slower motion.

name_vi: Nguy cơ cháy túi / mất trắng
definition: Risk of ruin is the chance that a loss becomes so large you can never recover or play again.
mechanism: Returns compound multiplicatively, so a fifty percent loss requires a one hundred percent gain just to break even, and a total loss ends the game permanently. Even a strategy with positive expected value can ruin you if bet sizes are too large and a normal losing streak arrives early. Survival therefore outranks maximizing average returns, because only survivors get to collect the long-run odds that make strategies profitable.
classic_example: Long-Term Capital Management collapsed in 1998 despite Nobel Prize-winning founders and historically profitable trades. The fund used extreme leverage, so a rare market move during the Russian debt crisis erased its capital within weeks and forced a Federal Reserve-brokered rescue, proving brilliance offers no protection once ruin becomes mathematically possible.
modern_example: A crypto trader risking forty percent of savings on each leveraged trade wins four times and feels invincible, then two ordinary losses leave him nearly broke despite a winning record. A friend risking two percent per trade survives the identical losing streak with capital and confidence intact to keep trading.
failure_mode: Obsession with ruin can make investors so timid they never take enough risk to grow, quietly losing to inflation instead. The model also depends on honest estimates of worst cases, and people routinely underestimate how bad correlated losses, leverage, and personal emergencies can combine.
apply_steps: Identify the loss that ends your game
Cap each bet well below that threshold
Avoid leverage that can force total loss
Keep emergency cash outside all investments

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Risk of ruin reveals whether being wrong on this one stock merely hurts or permanently removes you from future opportunities.
situation_notes.deciding-under-stress: Under stress, it reveals the one decision rule that matters most: never accept any outcome that ends your ability to recover.
situation_notes.down-30-percent-cut-or-hold: Down thirty percent, it reveals whether holding risks a compounding hole too deep to climb out of if losses continue.

case_seeds: Collapse of Long-Term Capital Management, 1998
origin: The mathematics comes from the classic gambler's ruin problem, analysed in the Pascal–Fermat correspondence of the 1650s and in Christiaan Huygens's work of 1657: a gambler with finite capital playing against a richer opponent is eventually ruined even in a fair game. Finance inherited the logic through Kelly sizing and the hard experience of leveraged funds.
mechanism_deep: Ruin risk is governed by multiplication, not addition. Each loss shrinks the base from which recovery must be earned, so drawdowns are asymmetric: lose half and you need a double, lose ninety percent and you need a tenfold gain, lose everything and no future edge matters. Leverage and oversized bets convert ordinary losing streaks — which are guaranteed to occur eventually in any probabilistic activity — into terminal events, because the probability of a bad sequence is never zero and time keeps dealing new hands. Survival also has a behavioural layer: capital kept intact preserves the option to act when rare, wonderful opportunities appear in crises, while the ruined investor can only watch. The model breaks when caution becomes paralysis — cash eroded by inflation is a slow ruin of its own — and when worst cases are estimated from calm recent history, understating how leverage, correlation, and personal emergencies stack.
examples_extra: Barings Bank, founded in 1762, collapsed in February 1995 after trader Nick Leeson's unauthorised derivatives losses in Singapore exceeded the bank's capital. A single desk's escalating bets, hidden in an error account, destroyed a 233-year-old institution, which was sold to ING for a nominal one pound — ruin arriving through size and concealment, not a bad year.

Archegos Capital Management imploded in March 2021 when concentrated, leveraged stock positions built through total-return swaps moved against it and margin calls cascaded. Banks that had extended the leverage lost billions of dollars, and a fortune estimated in the billions evaporated within days — a modern ruin driven by leverage plus concentration.
misconceptions: Many people think a strategy with positive expected value cannot ruin them — in reality, bet size and leverage can make ruin likely even when the average outcome is favourable.
Many people think ruin requires a freak event — in reality, an ordinary losing streak at oversized stakes is usually sufficient.
Many people think avoiding ruin means avoiding risk — in reality, it means sizing risk so no single outcome, or plausible sequence, can end the game.

practice.name: Worst-streak simulation
practice.instructions: Take your riskiest activity and write down a losing streak that is plausible, not apocalyptic — say five losses in a row. Multiply the damage at your current stake size. If the result ends or cripples the activity, cut the stake until the same streak is merely painful.

cross_domain: Aviation treats ruin as the outcome to engineer away: aircraft carry redundant hydraulics, multiple engines, and fuel reserves because a single failure at altitude is unrecoverable, so cost is accepted to make the fatal path nearly unreachable. Public health does the same with herd immunity thresholds and hospital surge capacity — systems sized for the plausible worst week, not the average one, because collapse, once started, feeds on itself in both domains.

quote.text: Rule No. 1: Never lose money. Rule No. 2: Never forget Rule No. 1.
quote.author: Warren Buffett
quote.source: Widely attributed to Buffett and repeated in Berkshire Hathaway shareholder tradition

name_vi: Tiêu chuẩn Kelly — công thức cỡ cược tối ưu
definition: The Kelly criterion is a formula that sizes bets to grow wealth fastest without risking everything on uncertain outcomes.
mechanism: The formula balances edge against odds, betting more when your advantage is large and nothing when you have no advantage at all. Betting far above the Kelly amount paradoxically lowers long-term growth because deep losses take disproportionate gains to recover, while betting below it grows more slowly but far more smoothly. Because real-world edges are estimates, many practitioners use half Kelly, trading some theoretical growth for protection against their own overconfidence.
classic_example: John Kelly Jr published his formula in a 1956 paper on information theory at Bell Labs, originally aimed at gambling on noisy telephone signals. Gambler and investor Edward Thorp later applied Kelly sizing to blackjack and markets, demonstrating in practice that disciplined bet sizing could turn a small edge into substantial compounded wealth.
modern_example: An investor who estimates a sixty percent chance of a stock gaining fifty percent or losing thirty percent uses Kelly math to find a modest suggested position. Instead of going all in on conviction, she invests roughly half the suggested size, acknowledging her probability estimate could easily be optimistic or simply wrong.
failure_mode: Kelly is only as good as the probabilities fed into it, and investors routinely overestimate their edge, producing dangerously large suggested bets. It also assumes you can tolerate brutal drawdowns along the optimal path, which most people's emotions and financial obligations simply cannot withstand.
apply_steps: Estimate your edge and odds honestly
Calculate the full Kelly suggested fraction
Invest half Kelly or less in practice
Resize when evidence changes your edge

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Kelly reveals that even a genuinely good stock deserves only a sized position, because your estimated edge is itself uncertain.
situation_notes.big-purchase: For a big speculative purchase, it reveals the fraction of your wealth the odds actually justify, not the amount excitement suggests.
situation_notes.deciding-under-stress: Under stress, it reveals a precomputed sizing rule to follow, replacing improvised all-in decisions made while fear or greed peaks.

case_seeds: Kelly's paper on information theory and gambling, 1956
Edward Thorp applying Kelly sizing in Beat the Market, 1967
origin: John L. Kelly Jr., a Bell Labs physicist, published the formula in 1956 in a paper titled A New Interpretation of Information Rate, extending Claude Shannon's information theory to a gambler receiving tips over a noisy channel. Kelly showed the growth-optimal strategy was to bet the fraction of capital equal to your information advantage — mathematics born from telephones, not casinos.
mechanism_deep: Kelly's insight is that wealth grows multiplicatively, so the right target is not average profit per bet but the long-run growth rate of the whole bankroll — the geometric mean, which punishes large losses far more than arithmetic averages suggest. Betting a fixed fraction proportional to your edge balances two failure modes: bet too little and the edge is wasted, compounding slowly; bet too much and volatility itself destroys growth, because a fifty percent loss needs a one hundred percent gain to repair, so an overbettor with a genuine edge can still go broke. The formula's peak is surprisingly flat on the cautious side and a cliff on the aggressive side — betting half the Kelly fraction keeps most of the growth while cutting drawdowns dramatically, whereas betting double Kelly can produce zero or negative growth despite a real advantage. This asymmetry is why practitioners favour fractional Kelly. The deeper problem is epistemic: the formula demands the true probability and payoff, but investors feed it estimates, and estimates are usually optimistic precisely when enthusiasm is highest. An overstated edge produces an oversized bet, and because the bettor believes the size is mathematically blessed, the error is amplified rather than checked. Kelly also assumes many repeated, roughly independent bets with known odds — conditions that markets violate when positions correlate, odds shift mid-game, or a single event (fraud, default) takes a position to zero rather than to the modelled loss. It further assumes the bettor can psychologically survive the optimal path, which includes drawdowns that would break most people's discipline and trigger abandonment at the bottom. In practice the criterion's greatest value is therefore negative and disciplinary: it gives a hard ceiling. Whenever excitement suggests committing more than Kelly allows, the formula exposes the urge as gambling. Kelly also reframes what a losing streak means. At the growth-optimal fraction, deep drawdowns are not a sign the system has failed; they are a mathematical certainty built into the path, and the bettor who does not pre-accept them will abandon a working system at its worst moment, converting a temporary drawdown into a permanent one. This is why the criterion pairs naturally with written rules and automatic resizing after losses: as capital falls, the same fraction automatically stakes fewer dollars, which throttles exposure exactly when the edge may have vanished. In markets there is a further complication — payoffs are continuous rather than win-or-lose, and several positions usually share the same hidden driver, so a portfolio of individually correct Kelly bets can secretly be one enormous Kelly bet on a single factor. Practitioners therefore haircut the formula for estimation error, correlation, and the chance their model of the game is simply the wrong game. And when it returns zero or a negative number, it states the most useful sentence in speculation — you have no edge, so the correct bet is nothing at all.
examples_extra: In 1961 Claude Shannon and Edward Thorp built one of the first wearable computers to time a roulette wheel in Las Vegas, applying information-theory thinking from Kelly's intellectual circle to size bets only when their device gave them a measurable edge. The episode, an early marriage of computing, probability, and disciplined staking, is documented in Thorp's memoir A Man for All Markets, published in 2017.

Bill Benter's Hong Kong horse-racing syndicate, built from the 1980s onward and profiled by Bloomberg in 2018, combined statistical win-probability models with disciplined Kelly-style staking across thousands of races. The operation reportedly won close to a billion Hong Kong dollars over its run, showing Kelly logic working where probabilities could be estimated from enormous data sets.

formula.expression: f* = (bp − q) ÷ b
formula.variables: f* = fraction of bankroll to bet; b = net odds received (profit per unit staked); p = probability of winning; q = probability of losing (1 − p)
formula.worked_example: An even-money bet (b = 1) that you win 55 percent of the time: f* = (1×0.55 − 0.45) ÷ 1 = 0.10, so full Kelly stakes 10 percent of bankroll; a half-Kelly practitioner stakes 5 percent.

misconceptions: Many people think Kelly tells you which bets are good — in reality, it only sizes bets; a negative Kelly result means your supposed edge does not exist.
Many people think full Kelly is the safe optimal choice — in reality, it maximises growth while permitting savage drawdowns, so most practitioners use half Kelly or less.
Many people think the formula removes judgement — in reality, its inputs are probability estimates, and overconfident estimates turn Kelly into a machine for oversizing.

practice.name: Coin-flip Kelly by hand
practice.instructions: Take a coin weighted in your favour: you judge a 60 percent win chance, even-money payoff. Compute f* = (0.60 − 0.40) ÷ 1 = 20 percent, then halve it for estimation error. Write down what drawdown a run of four losses would cause at both sizes before risking anything.

practice.name: Edge honesty test
practice.instructions: For an investment you like, state your win probability and payoff ratio in numbers, then ask what evidence would justify them. If you cannot defend the inputs to a sceptical friend, treat your Kelly fraction as zero until you can.

cross_domain: Venture capital quietly runs a Kelly-like logic: funds spread capital across many startups because payoffs follow power laws, sizing each cheque so that the many expected failures cannot end the fund while one outlier can return it several times over. Ecology shows a version in bet-hedging — desert plants produce seeds that germinate in different years, staking fractions of their reproductive capital across uncertain seasons rather than committing everything to one rainfall. In both fields, survival-weighted sizing beats maximising any single attempt.

name_vi: Định cỡ vị thế — mỗi khoản đầu tư bao nhiêu tiền
definition: Position sizing means deciding how much money each investment gets based on its risk, not just your enthusiasm for it.
mechanism: Two investors can pick identical stocks and get opposite results depending on how much each position represents, because sizing determines how much any single outcome moves total wealth. Sizing by risk, such as limiting the loss if a thesis fails, keeps inevitable mistakes survivable and roughly equal in impact. It also enforces honesty: a position sized tiny reveals low conviction, while oversized positions reveal gambling disguised as research.
classic_example: George Soros reportedly bet an enormous share of his Quantum Fund against the British pound in 1992, sizing the position to match his conviction and analysis. The trade earned the fund around one billion dollars when Britain left the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, illustrating how sizing, not selection alone, creates outsized outcomes.
modern_example: A beginner splits her portfolio so no single stock exceeds five percent and newer, riskier ideas start at two percent. When one small company collapses after an accounting scandal, she loses one percent overall, learns the lesson cheaply, and continues investing instead of swearing off markets forever in disgust.
failure_mode: Mechanical sizing rules can strangle genuinely exceptional opportunities if applied without judgment, and equal percentages ignore real differences in quality and certainty. Sizing also cannot rescue a portfolio of bad picks; it only controls how much damage each bad pick is allowed to inflict.
apply_steps: Set a maximum percentage per position
Start smaller when uncertainty is higher
Add only when evidence strengthens thesis
Define acceptable loss before buying anything

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Position sizing reveals your true conviction in numbers, forcing the amount invested to match evidence rather than storytelling or excitement.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: When scaling up, it reveals whether growth in position size follows growing proof or simply follows a rising price and confidence.
situation_notes.deciding-under-stress: Under stress, it reveals that positions sized beforehand let you endure volatility calmly instead of panic-selling at the worst moment.

case_seeds: Soros and the Quantum Fund betting against the British pound, 1992
origin: The discipline grew up in gambling bankroll management and was formalised for markets by the Turtle Traders experiment of 1983, where Richard Dennis and William Eckhardt taught novices to size trades by market volatility. Author Van K. Tharp later popularised the very term position sizing in his 1998 book Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom.
mechanism_deep: Sizing works because portfolio outcomes are the product of selection and stake: the same idea at two percent and at forty percent of capital is effectively two different investments, one survivable and one existential. Risk-based sizing equalises the damage each position can do by accounting for how far it could plausibly fall, not just how much cash it absorbs — a volatile small-cap and a utility stock at equal dollar amounts carry wildly unequal risk. Sizing also manages correlated danger: several positions that share one driver act as a single oversized bet. The model breaks when gaps and fraud make planned exit losses fictional, when volatility is estimated from calm periods, and when rigid rules are applied so mechanically that a rare, genuinely exceptional opportunity is capped to homeopathic size. Sizing also interacts with information flow: starting small buys the right to learn from real exposure — filings read differently when money is at stake — and lets the investor add as evidence, rather than hope, accumulates. The position grows up with the thesis instead of arriving fully formed on day one.
examples_extra: The Turtle Traders, recruited through newspaper advertisements in 1983 by Richard Dennis, were taught to risk a small, fixed percentage per trade and to scale unit size by each market's volatility (its Average True Range). Novices following those sizing rules reportedly earned large aggregate profits, suggesting the money-management system, not stock-picking genius, carried much of the result.

Bridgewater's All Weather strategy, developed under Ray Dalio in the mid-1990s, sizes asset classes by their risk contribution rather than by dollars, deliberately holding far more in bonds than equities so each environment — growth rising or falling, inflation rising or falling — carries roughly balanced weight. It is position sizing applied to entire economic regimes.

formula.expression: Position Size = (Account × Risk %) ÷ Distance to Exit Price
formula.variables: Account = total capital; Risk % = fraction you accept losing if wrong; Distance to Exit Price = entry price minus the price at which the thesis is abandoned, per share
formula.worked_example: With a $100,000 account risking 1 percent ($1,000) and an exit $5 per share below entry, position size = 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200 shares, so being wrong costs exactly the planned $1,000.

misconceptions: Many people think equal dollar amounts mean equal risk — in reality, a volatile stock risks far more per dollar than a stable one, so sizing must adjust for movement.
Many people think sizing is a detail after the real work of picking — in reality, sizing often decides whether a good picker survives long enough for skill to show.
Many people think bigger conviction should always mean a much bigger position — in reality, conviction is least reliable exactly when it feels strongest, so caps exist for emotional peaks.

practice.name: One-percent rule trial
practice.instructions: For your next three investment decisions, calculate the position so that a thesis failure costs no more than one percent of total capital. Write the exit condition before buying. Review after three months whether the constraint changed which ideas you chose.

cross_domain: Medicine doses by exposure, not enthusiasm: chemotherapy and paediatric drugs are scaled to body weight and tolerance because the same fixed dose that cures one patient can poison another — the treatment is identical, the sizing decides the outcome. Fire services do the same, committing crews and water in proportion to the structure and fire load rather than sending everything to every call, preserving capacity for the next emergency.

name_vi: Chu kỳ thị trường
definition: Market cycles are recurring swings between optimism and pessimism that push prices far above and below underlying business value.
mechanism: Success breeds confidence, easy credit, and copycat investing, which inflate prices until disappointment reverses psychology and lenders retreat, driving prices below value until fear exhausts itself and recovery quietly begins. Each phase changes what behavior gets rewarded, so yesterday's winning strategy often fails in the next phase. Recognizing the current phase helps investors calibrate aggression, buying carefully when optimism peaks and acting boldly when pessimism offers bargains.
classic_example: Howard Marks built his reputation at Oaktree Capital partly on cycle awareness, famously urging caution before the 2007 credit bubble and buying aggressively during the 2008 financial crisis. His memos, later collected in Mastering the Market Cycle in 2018, argue investors cannot predict cycles but can recognize extremes and position accordingly.
modern_example: A retail investor notices friends who mocked stocks in the crash now borrowing to trade meme coins and quit their jobs for day trading. Reading that euphoria as a late-cycle signal, she stops adding risk, builds cash gradually, and writes a shopping list of quality companies to buy if pessimism returns.
failure_mode: Cycles have no fixed schedule, so acting on a phase call too early can mean years of missed gains or premature buying. Many investors also see cycles everywhere, using the model as a story to justify market timing they cannot actually perform consistently.
apply_steps: Gauge crowd mood from behavior, not headlines
Reduce risk when euphoria and leverage spread
Prepare shopping lists during calm periods
Buy in stages when pessimism peaks

situation_notes.market-panic: In a panic, market cycles reveal that widespread despair historically sits near the phase where future returns improve, not worsen permanently.
situation_notes.fomo-friends-profit: When friends profit effortlessly, cycles reveal you are likely watching a late optimistic phase where risk quietly builds underneath gains.
situation_notes.comparing-to-others: Cycles reveal that outperformers you envy may simply hold assets favored by this phase, which will punish them in the next.

case_seeds: Howard Marks buying distressed debt during the 2008 financial crisis
The dot-com bubble peaking in 2000
source_ref: Howard Marks — Mastering the Market Cycle
origin: Cycle thinking runs from Charles Dow's market writings around 1900 through Hyman Minsky's financial instability hypothesis, developed in the 1970s, which argued stability itself breeds the leverage that causes the next crisis. Howard Marks brought the framework to a wide investing audience with Mastering the Market Cycle (2018), built on memos he had written for Oaktree Capital since 1990.
mechanism_deep: Cycles are powered by a reflexive loop between results and behaviour. Good times raise collateral values and lender confidence, credit expands, asset prices rise, and the rising prices are then cited as proof the risk was justified — Minsky's progression from prudent to speculative to Ponzi finance. The loop guarantees overshoot because the variable being measured, price, is changed by the behaviour it encourages. On the way down the same loop reverses through margin calls, covenant breaches, and vanished refinancing. Different cycles run at different speeds — credit, inventory, property, and sentiment cycles overlap rather than synchronise — which is why no calendar predicts turning points. The model breaks when treated as a timing device: regimes can stay extreme for years, policy intervention can extend or truncate phases, and structural change can make the last cycle a poor map of the next. The practical output of cycle awareness is therefore a posture dial, not a prediction: leverage, cash reserves, purchase standards, and willingness to act boldly all turn gradually as evidence of excess or despair accumulates, long before any peak or trough can be identified with confidence by anyone honestly watching.
examples_extra: Japan's asset bubble peaked when the Nikkei 225 closed at its all-time high on 29 December 1989, after years of soaring land and share prices fuelled by easy credit. The index then fell for years and did not regain that level for more than three decades — a full cycle from euphoria to a generation of caution.

In the United States housing cycle, home prices peaked around 2006 on loose lending that assumed prices could not fall nationally. When they did, defaults cascaded through mortgage securities into the 2008 financial crisis, and the pessimism that followed made credit scarce even for sound borrowers — the cycle's two extremes feeding each other.
misconceptions: Many people think cycles run on a predictable schedule — in reality, they recur in pattern but not in timing, and acting early can be as costly as acting late.
Many people think recognising a cycle phase guarantees profit — in reality, it only adjusts the odds and the appropriate level of caution or aggression.
Many people think this cycle is abolished by new technology or policy — in reality, the instruments change while the human loop of greed, leverage, and fear repeats.

practice.name: Cycle thermometer
practice.instructions: Score your market on five observable signs: how easily unprofitable ventures raise money, how much friends discuss investing, credit availability, media tone, and how sceptics are treated. Write the score and date in a journal; repeat quarterly and compare your behaviour against the reading.

cross_domain: Fashion obeys the same loop: a style spreads because it signals novelty, saturation destroys the signal, rejection becomes the fashion, and revival follows once a new generation forgets the embarrassment — hemlines and logos cycling without any change in clothing's function. Technology adoption shows it in the hype pattern of inflated expectations, disillusionment, and eventual productive plateau, where the technology's real capability changes far less than the crowd's emotional valuation of it.

name_vi: Lãi suất như trọng lực của giá tài sản
definition: Interest rates act like gravity on asset prices, pulling valuations down when they rise and lifting them when they fall.
mechanism: Every investment competes with the return available from safe government bonds, so when those yields rise, future business cash becomes less attractive by comparison and prices adjust downward, especially for companies whose profits lie far in the future. Falling rates reverse the pull, making distant earnings worth more today. The metaphor explains why the same company, unchanged operationally, can deserve very different prices in different rate environments.
classic_example: Warren Buffett popularized the gravity metaphor, explaining that interest rates affect financial valuations the way gravity affects physical matter. The early 1980s illustrated it brutally: with United States Treasury yields in double digits under Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker, stock valuations stayed depressed despite solid businesses, then expanded for years as rates steadily declined.
modern_example: In 2022, a saver watched profitable technology stocks and unprofitable growth names fall sharply as central banks raised rates rapidly, even though many companies kept growing revenue. Her boring dividend stocks fell less, teaching her that distant promised profits lose value fastest when safe bonds finally pay meaningful interest again.
failure_mode: The gravity metaphor can oversimplify, because strong earnings growth can overpower rising rates and weak companies can fall even when rates decline. Investors also cannot reliably forecast rates, so using the model to time markets often fails; it explains valuation pressure better than it predicts timing.
apply_steps: Check what safe bonds currently yield
Ask how distant the company profits are
Demand higher returns when rates rise
Revalue holdings when rate regime changes

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Interest rates reveal what return you must beat, since the stock competes directly with the yield on safe government bonds today.
situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: It reveals whether a guru's past returns came from skill or from decades of falling rates lifting nearly every asset price.
situation_notes.idle-cash-decision: For idle cash, it reveals that higher rates finally pay you to wait, raising the bar any risky purchase must clear.

case_seeds: Volcker-era double-digit Treasury yields depressing stock valuations in the early 1980s
The 2022 rate-hiking cycle repricing growth stocks
origin: The underlying mathematics is Fisher's present-value logic from The Theory of Interest (1930): every asset competes with the return on waiting. Warren Buffett popularised the gravity metaphor in Berkshire Hathaway letters and interviews, saying interest rates act on financial valuations the way gravity acts on matter — a force that is invisible day to day but inescapable over distance.
mechanism_deep: The mechanism is the discount rate applied to every future cash flow. A stock is a claim on cash arriving over decades, so it behaves like a very long-duration bond: when the risk-free rate rises, each distant payment is worth less today, and the effect compounds with distance, which is why unprofitable growth companies fall hardest and near-cash businesses least. Rates also work through the real economy — mortgage costs, corporate refinancing, and the hurdle rate for new projects — so earnings themselves eventually bend. The model breaks as a timing tool because earnings growth, inflation pass-through, and risk premiums move at the same time; the 1970s showed rates and prices falling together, but strong growers have also outrun rising rates for years. It explains pressure and relative vulnerability, never the date of repricing. There is also a second channel through corporate behaviour itself: high rates make buybacks funded by cheap debt and speculative expansion less attractive, while low rates push companies and households alike toward leverage and longer, riskier projects — so gravity changes not only what cash flows are worth, but which cash flows get created in the first place.
examples_extra: In the 2013 taper tantrum, after Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke suggested in May 2013 that bond purchases might slow, the US ten-year Treasury yield rose from under two percent to about three percent by year-end. Emerging-market currencies and bonds sold off sharply as the global discount rate reset — gravity reasserting itself far from Washington.

Britain's September 2022 gilt crisis showed the violent end of the mechanism: after the Truss government's mini-budget, long-dated gilt yields spiked within days, pension funds using liability-driven strategies faced margin calls, and the Bank of England intervened to buy gilts. Asset values built for a low-rate world failed within a week of rates jumping.

formula.expression: Approx. % Change in Price ≈ −Duration × Change in Yield
formula.variables: Duration = weighted average time until an asset's cash flows arrive, in years; Change in Yield = rise or fall in the discount rate, as a decimal
formula.worked_example: A growth asset with an effective duration of 15 years faces a one-point rise in yields (0.01): approximate price change = −15 × 0.01 = −0.15, a fall of about 15 percent before any change in earnings.

misconceptions: Many people think rising rates always crush all stocks equally — in reality, companies with near-term cash and pricing power can grow through rate rises, while distant-promise assets suffer most.
Many people think the metaphor predicts when to sell — in reality, rates can stay high or low far longer than expected; gravity explains vulnerability, not timing.
Many people think low rates make any price safe — in reality, low gravity inflates valuations, so assets bought then carry the most risk if rates normalise.

practice.name: Duration ranking
practice.instructions: List five holdings or watchlist stocks and rank them by how distant their profits are: cash today, profits in five years, or profits promised in fifteen. For the two longest-duration names, write what return you would demand if safe bonds paid two points more.

cross_domain: Real estate runs on the identical mechanism through capitalisation rates: when borrowing costs rise, buyers pay less for the same rental stream, so buildings lose value without a single tenant leaving. Infrastructure and toll roads behave the same way, which is why pension funds model them like bonds. Even career choices bend to it — in a high-rate, high-wage present, a qualification paying off only after a decade of study must clear a much higher bar than when safe returns are near zero.

name_vi: Ăn chênh lệch nhờ tầm nhìn dài hạn hơn đám đông
definition: Time horizon arbitrage means profiting by staying focused on long term value while most investors obsess over short term results.
mechanism: Most market participants are judged quarterly or chase immediate price moves, so they overpay for near-term certainty and underprice businesses whose payoff arrives in three to five years. An investor who can wait calmly captures that gap simply by holding through periods when short-term holders panic or lose interest. The edge requires no secret information, only a horizon longer than the crowd and finances structured to avoid forced selling.
classic_example: Warren Buffett has repeatedly described Berkshire Hathaway's advantage as a longer time horizon than competitors, buying businesses like See's Candies in 1972 and holding them for decades. While traders rotated constantly, Berkshire collected growing cash flows year after year, compounding value that short-term holders of the same assets never stayed long enough to receive.
modern_example: A salaried investor buys a broad index fund monthly and ignores financial news for weeks at a time. During a two-month market dip, colleagues day-trading the same funds lock in losses switching strategies, while her unchanged plan buys more shares cheaply and recovers fully when the temporary panic eventually fades.
failure_mode: A long horizon is not an excuse to hold a deteriorating business forever, because time amplifies decline as reliably as it amplifies quality. The strategy also fails if life forces you to sell early, so money needed soon never belongs in long-horizon investments regardless of expected payoff.
apply_steps: Match investment horizon to real financial needs
Evaluate businesses on three to five years
Ignore quarterly noise unless thesis breaks
Keep living expenses outside invested money

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Time horizon arbitrage reveals mispricing created by sellers who need results this quarter while the business payoff arrives over years.
situation_notes.market-panic: In a panic, it reveals your structural advantage: you can simply wait out sellers who are forced to act immediately.
situation_notes.chronic-procrastination: For procrastinators, it reveals that starting a boring automatic plan now beats endlessly researching while waiting for a perfect entry point.

case_seeds: Buffett holding See's Candies for decades after buying in 1972
origin: The practice is as old as Buffett's partnership, but the concept was named and studied in the long-term-capitalism debate of the 2010s: McKinsey director Dominic Barton argued in his 2011 Harvard Business Review article Capitalism for the Long Term that short quarterly pressure was mispricing patient capital, and the Focusing Capital on the Long Term initiative followed in 2013 to institutionalise the idea.
mechanism_deep: The arbitrage exists because most capital is rented, not owned: fund managers are graded quarterly, executives are paid on annual targets, and media reward immediacy, so the market's effective discount rate for payoffs beyond two or three years is far higher than any individual's need be. Businesses whose value arrives slowly — brands being built, networks reaching scale, research maturing — are therefore systematically cheap relative to businesses with certain near-term earnings. The patient investor's edge is structural, not informational, which makes it durable but slow, and it demands an equally structural defence: no leverage, no money needed soon, and a temperament or mandate that survives looking wrong for years. It breaks when the long term is used to subsidise a deteriorating business — time amplifies decay as faithfully as quality — and when the holder's own horizon secretly shortens through job loss, divorce, or margin debt. The edge is also self-limiting in an interesting way: it cannot be crowded away as easily as an informational edge, because exploiting it requires enduring years of social and emotional discomfort that most institutions are structurally unable to copy, however well they understand the idea in theory.
examples_extra: Paul Polman, becoming chief executive of Unilever in 2009, stopped giving quarterly profit guidance and short-term forecasts, explicitly to free the company for long-term brand and sustainability investment. The move was controversial with short-horizon shareholders at the time and became a reference case in the long-term capitalism debate that followed.

Amazon's early public years tested holders severely: after the dot-com peak, its shares fell by more than ninety percent into 2001 even as revenue kept growing and the logistics network kept expanding. Investors whose horizon matched the build-out, and who could survive the quotation, participated in one of the great compounding runs that followed; those graded quarterly were forced out near the bottom.
misconceptions: Many people think a long horizon excuses holding any loser — in reality, time helps only sound businesses; it deepens losses in deteriorating ones.
Many people think the edge requires predicting the future better — in reality, it requires only out-waiting participants whose incentives force them to sell or chase early.

Many people think patience alone is the strategy — in reality, without finances structured to avoid forced selling, the first emergency converts the long-term investor into a forced short-term seller.

practice.name: Horizon matching audit
practice.instructions: Write next to each investment the year you genuinely will not need the money. Sell or move to cash anything whose payoff horizon is longer than that date, and write a three-to-five-year thesis sentence for everything that remains.

cross_domain: Forestry is the purest physical version: an oak planted for timber is worthless to a farmer who needs this year's crop and valuable to a family trust thinking in generations, so the same tree changes price with the holder's horizon. Preventive health works identically — exercise and screening look like poor trades on a quarterly view of effort, and like the best bargains available on a thirty-year view, which is why systems that reward immediate metrics chronically underfund both.

name_vi: Hệ số định giá (P/E, P/S…)
definition: Valuation multiples compare a company price to a measure like earnings or sales, showing how much investors pay per unit.
mechanism: A multiple compresses a valuation into one comparable number, letting investors quickly judge whether a stock is cheap or expensive relative to its own history and to similar businesses. High multiples embed high expectations for growth and durability, while low multiples signal expected trouble or neglect. The shortcut works because earnings and sales eventually anchor value, but it only compares; it never explains whether the underlying measure is sustainable.
classic_example: During the dot-com bubble peaking in 2000, many internet companies traded at extreme price-to-sales multiples despite having no earnings at all. When growth failed to match those embedded expectations, prices collapsed even at companies that survived, demonstrating how multiples quietly record the hopes a buyer has already paid for in advance.
modern_example: A new investor compares two bank stocks, one trading at eight times earnings and another at eighteen, and initially assumes the cheaper is better. Reading further, she finds the expensive bank earns far higher returns on equity with cleaner loans, while the cheap bank's earnings are inflated by one-off gains this year.
failure_mode: Multiples ignore differences in growth, debt, accounting quality, and competitive position, so the lowest multiple is often cheap for good reason. They also mislead at cycle peaks, when temporarily swollen earnings make dangerous stocks look statistically cheap just before earnings collapse.
apply_steps: Compare multiples only among similar businesses
Check whether earnings are normal or temporary
Pair multiples with growth and debt analysis
Ask what expectations the multiple implies

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Valuation multiples reveal how much optimism is already priced in per dollar of earnings compared with similar businesses you could own.
situation_notes.negotiating-price: In negotiation, multiples reveal a shared reference point for price, shifting argument from feelings toward comparable transactions and measurable fundamentals.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: They reveal whether a recommendation compares the stock fairly with peers or cherry-picks the one multiple that looks most flattering.

case_seeds: Dot-com stocks trading at extreme price-to-sales multiples in 2000
origin: Graham and Dodd systematised earnings-based comparison in Security Analysis (1934), teaching analysts to ask what a business earned relative to its price rather than trading on tips. The price-to-earnings ratio became Wall Street's everyday shorthand through the twentieth century, later joined by price-to-sales in the 1980s and enterprise-value multiples as leverage grew more complex.
mechanism_deep: A multiple is a compressed DCF: price divided by earnings silently bundles assumptions about growth, durability, capital needs, and interest rates into one number, which is why comparing multiples is really comparing bundles of expectations. The mechanism fails through the denominator as often as the numerator — earnings at a cyclical peak, flattered by one-off gains, buybacks, or aggressive accounting, make a dangerous stock look cheap, while temporarily depressed earnings make a recovering business look expensive. Leverage distorts equity multiples too, since debt magnifies earnings per share while adding ruin risk that P/E never displays; enterprise-value ratios exist partly to correct that blindness. Multiples also inherit the crowd's mood: in euphoric phases entire sectors re-rate upward together, so a stock can look fairly priced against peers while the whole comparison group is overpriced — relative cheapness inside a bubble is still a bubble. Multiples are therefore best used as a first screen and a lie detector: they flag where expectations are extreme, where denominators look suspiciously swollen, and where a full cash-flow valuation is worth the hours it takes, rather than serving as the valuation itself.
examples_extra: Cisco Systems became briefly the world's most valuable company in March 2000, trading at an earnings multiple well above one hundred at the dot-com peak. Its earnings continued growing for years, yet the share price fell by more than four-fifths from the peak and stayed below it for decades — the multiple, not the business, had been the bubble.

The Nifty Fifty stocks of the early 1970s — celebrated American growth names such as Polaroid and Avon — traded at earnings multiples of forty, fifty, or more on the theory that quality justified any price. In the 1973–74 bear market many fell seventy percent or more, teaching a generation that expectations embedded in a multiple can matter more than business quality.

formula.expression: P/E = Price per Share ÷ Earnings per Share
formula.variables: P/E = price-to-earnings multiple; Price per Share = current market price; Earnings per Share = net earnings attributable to each share over the past or forecast year
formula.worked_example: A stock trades at $50 with earnings per share of $2.50: P/E = 50 ÷ 2.50 = 20, meaning buyers pay twenty dollars for each dollar of current annual earnings.

misconceptions: Many people think a low multiple always means cheap — in reality, it often means the market expects earnings to fall, and the denominator may be about to collapse.
Many people think multiples can be compared across any companies — in reality, growth, debt, accounting, and cyclicality differences make cross-industry comparisons meaningless.
Many people think a high multiple means a bad investment — in reality, durable fast growth can justify it; the question is whether the implied expectations are achievable.

practice.name: Normalise before you compare
practice.instructions: Take two rival companies and compute each one's P/E twice: on last year's earnings and on the average earnings of the last seven years. Note any ranking that flips between the two calculations — that stock's multiple was a cycle artefact, not a valuation.

cross_domain: Property buyers use the identical shortcut as price per square metre: indispensable for comparing similar flats on one street, and dangerously misleading across neighbourhoods, building quality, or legal status — exactly the peer-group discipline multiples demand. Hiring does it too when firms compare candidates by salary multiples of expected output, and software businesses are bought on revenue multiples, where the same trap applies: the denominator says nothing about whether the revenue is profitable, recurring, or about to churn away.

name_vi: Doanh nghiệp chất lượng sinh lãi kép
definition: Quality compounders are strong businesses that reinvest profits at high returns for years, growing owner wealth steadily without constant trading.
mechanism: A business earning high returns on capital with room to reinvest can grow its earnings internally year after year, so value compounds inside the company while the owner simply holds. Durable competitive advantages, honest management, and pricing power protect those returns from competition. Because the growth is generated by operations rather than multiple expansion, owners depend less on finding a greater fool to sell to at a higher price.
classic_example: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger shifted Berkshire Hathaway toward quality with See's Candies in 1972, paying up for a brand that raised prices yearly with little new capital. Buffett later said See's taught them to pay fair prices for wonderful businesses instead of hunting only for statistically cheap mediocre ones.
modern_example: An investor holds a dominant payments company and a beloved software subscription business through several market scares, watching both reinvest profits into products customers keep renewing. Over a decade of doing almost nothing, their growing earnings carry her portfolio further than her earlier years of frequent trading ever managed to achieve.
failure_mode: Quality is now fashionable, so famous compounders often trade at prices that already assume decades of flawless execution, leaving no margin for disappointment. Advantages also erode: technology shifts, regulation, or complacent management can quietly turn yesterday's compounder into a melting business still priced like a champion.
apply_steps: Verify high returns on invested capital
Check the moat protecting those returns
Confirm room to reinvest profits profitably
Pay a fair, not euphoric, price

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Quality compounders reveal that a fair price for durable high returns often beats a bargain price for a business slowly decaying.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: When scaling, it reveals whether profits can be reinvested at the same high returns or whether growth will dilute what worked.
situation_notes.what-to-learn-next: It reveals the skill worth learning deeply: judging business durability and management quality, which compounds in value across every future decision.

case_seeds: Buffett's purchase of See's Candies, 1972
origin: The approach crystallised at Berkshire Hathaway after the 1972 See's Candies purchase, when Munger persuaded Buffett that a wonderful business at a fair price beats a fair business at a wonderful price. It was later codified for a wider audience by fund managers such as Terry Smith, who founded Fundsmith in 2010 around buying good companies, not overpaying, and doing nothing.
mechanism_deep: The engine has two cylinders that must fire together: a high return on capital already earned, and a long runway to reinvest new capital at similar returns. Return without reinvestment produces a cash cow whose growth stalls; reinvestment without return destroys value faster the more it grows. Durability is supplied by the moat — brand trust, network effects, switching costs, or cost advantages — which delays the competitive mean reversion that normally grinds high returns down. Management quality enters through capital allocation: the compounder's chief executive must keep reinvesting in the core advantage rather than diversifying into empire. The model breaks at the purchase price first — when a compounder is priced for perfection, a decade of good execution can still yield poor shareholder returns — and at the moat second, when technology or regulation quietly drains the advantage while reported returns still look healthy. The holding discipline matters as much as the selection: because compounding needs uninterrupted years, the compounder investor's main job after buying well is resisting the urge to trim a winner into mediocrity or to trade a durable franchise for a cheaper, weaker one.
examples_extra: Berkshire Hathaway bought shares in Moody's Corporation in 2000, attracted by the rating agency's asset-light economics: dominant market position, pricing power, and almost no capital required to grow. Moody's compounded earnings for years afterward on tiny incremental investment, becoming a canonical example of a business that grows richer without growing heavier.

Microsoft under Satya Nadella, chief executive from 2014, redirected a mature software giant's profits into Azure cloud infrastructure and subscription products customers renew automatically. Earnings compounded through the following decade not from a single hit product but from reinvesting a protected franchise's cash flows into adjacent high-return services — the compounder pattern at enormous scale.

formula.expression: CAGR = (Ending Value ÷ Beginning Value)^(1÷n) − 1
formula.variables: CAGR = compound annual growth rate; Ending Value = earnings or value at the end; Beginning Value = earnings or value at the start; n = number of years
formula.worked_example: A compounder grows earnings per share from $1.00 to $2.60 over ten years: CAGR = (2.60 ÷ 1.00)^(1÷10) − 1 ≈ 0.10, roughly 10 percent growth compounded every year for a decade.

misconceptions: Many people think quality justifies any price — in reality, even a superb compounder bought at a euphoric valuation can deliver a decade of poor returns.
Many people think a famous brand guarantees a compounder — in reality, the test is numerical: sustained high returns on capital plus room to reinvest at those returns.
Many people think compounders are safe and steady — in reality, their shares can halve in panics like any stock; the compounding happens in the business, not the quotation.

practice.name: Ten-year compounder check
practice.instructions: For a company you admire, pull ten years of return on invested capital and earnings per share from annual reports. Confirm returns stayed high while earnings grew; if returns slid as growth rose, the business is buying growth, not compounding it.

cross_domain: Skill acquisition compounds the same way when each year's learning is reinvested on a protected base — a musician whose technique frees practice time for interpretation, or a writer whose backlist keeps selling while new work is written. Ecosystems show it in keystone species: a beaver colony's dams create ponds that support more life each year, the habitat itself appreciating like retained earnings. In each case the pattern is identical — returns generated by the asset are fed back into the asset, protected from erosion long enough for multiplication to dominate.

name_vi: Đầu tư theo chỉ số
definition: Indexing means owning the whole market through a cheap diversified fund instead of trying to pick individual winning stocks yourself.
mechanism: Most active investors underperform the market average after fees because winners are few, costs compound, and timing mistakes are common. An index fund captures the average return of the whole market at minimal cost and with automatic diversification, so the investor's return depends on business progress broadly rather than on picking skill. The small annual fee advantage compounds into a large gap over decades of holding.
classic_example: John Bogle launched the first retail index fund at Vanguard in 1976, initially mocked on Wall Street as Bogle's folly for settling for average returns. The fund and its successors grew into trillions of dollars as evidence accumulated that low-cost indexing beat most professionally managed funds over long periods after fees.
modern_example: A busy office worker automates a monthly purchase of a broad index fund inside her retirement account and spends investing time on her career instead. Colleagues swapping hot stock tips each lunch break mostly trail her boring results once their trading fees, taxes, and panic-driven mistakes are honestly counted over several years.
failure_mode: Indexing guarantees the market's return, including its crashes, and offers no protection when the overall market itself is wildly overvalued. It also requires the discipline to keep buying through frightening declines; investors who abandon the index at bottoms end up with worse results than the fund they left.
apply_steps: Choose a broad, low-cost index fund
Automate regular contributions every month
Ignore tips and short-term market forecasts
Review allocation once a year only

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Indexing reveals the honest alternative every stock pick must beat after fees and effort, which most individual selections historically fail to do.
situation_notes.idle-cash-decision: For idle cash, it reveals a default destination requiring no forecast, putting money to work whenever no special opportunity clearly exists.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: It reveals the benchmark any advisor must clear: if their picks cannot beat a cheap index, the advice destroys value.

case_seeds: Bogle launching the first retail index fund at Vanguard, 1976
source_ref: Bogle — The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
origin: Burton Malkiel argued in A Random Walk Down Wall Street (1973) that most investors would do better owning the whole market, and economist Paul Samuelson publicly challenged the industry in 1974 to create such a fund. John Bogle answered at Vanguard, launching the First Index Investment Trust in 1976 — initially ridiculed on Wall Street as Bogle's folly and as un-American for accepting average returns.
mechanism_deep: Indexing rests on arithmetic, not prophecy. William Sharpe showed in The Arithmetic of Active Management (1991) that, before costs, the average actively managed dollar must earn the market return — because active investors collectively are the market — and after fees, taxes, and trading costs it must earn less. Costs are therefore the most predictable variable in investing: a one or two percent annual fee gap, compounded over a working life, reliably transfers a large share of the investor's ending wealth to intermediaries. The index also automates diversification and a crude momentum discipline, since winners grow in weight and losers shrink without any decision. The model breaks at the extremes: cap-weighted indexes concentrate in whatever is already huge, so at bubble peaks the index investor's largest holdings are the most overpriced assets, and the strategy offers no exit from a broadly overvalued market — it guarantees the market's return, including its worst decades.
examples_extra: In 2007 Warren Buffett bet one million dollars for charity that a simple S&P 500 index fund would beat a basket of hedge funds chosen by Protégé Partners over ten years. When the bet ended in 2017, the index fund had won decisively: the hedge funds' fees and complexity failed to clear the market's average, exactly as the arithmetic of indexing predicts.

The long-running SPIVA scorecards, published by S&P Dow Jones Indices since the early 2000s, compare active funds with their benchmarks across many countries and periods. Their persistent finding — that a majority of active large-cap funds underperform over fifteen-year horizons — turned indexing from a theory into the documented default for most savers.

formula.expression: Future Value = Principal × (1 + Return − Fee)ⁿ
formula.variables: Principal = starting amount; Return = yearly market return before fees; Fee = yearly fund fee; n = years invested
formula.worked_example: Invest $10,000 at a 7 percent market return for 30 years. With a 0.1 percent index fee the net 6.9 percent grows to about $74,000; with a 1.1 percent active fee the net 5.9 percent reaches only about $56,000 — fees quietly consume roughly $18,000.

misconceptions: Many people think indexing means settling for mediocre results — in reality, after fees the average active fund underperforms it, so the index beats most professionals over long periods.
Many people think index funds are risk-free because they are diversified — in reality, they deliver the full market crash along with the full market return.
Many people think indexing requires no discipline — in reality, its results belong only to investors who keep contributing through declines instead of abandoning the plan.

practice.name: Fee drag calculation
practice.instructions: Take your current savings amount and expected yearly contribution. Run the indexing formula twice, once with your actual funds' total fees and once with a broad index fee under 0.2 percent. Write down the thirty-year difference and decide whether your funds' performance justifies it.

cross_domain: Defaults in public policy exploit the same insight: pension auto-enrolment, as in Britain's scheme launched in 2012, raised participation dramatically because doing nothing became the sensible option rather than the negligent one. Evolution offers a parallel — the average organism in a stable environment is remarkably fit, and exotic mutations usually do worse than the proven default, which is why beating the average consistently is rare in both markets and nature. In each domain, a cheap, broad default quietly defeats most expensive attempts to be clever.

name_vi: Sức mạnh lợi nhuận bền vững
definition: Earnings power is the level of profit a business can sustain in normal conditions, stripped of temporary booms and one-off events.
mechanism: Reported profits swing with cycles, accounting choices, and unusual gains, so valuing a business on a single year's number invites serious error. Estimating normalized earning power, what the business can earn across a full cycle with its competitive position intact, gives a steadier base for valuation. A price that looks cheap against peak earnings may be expensive against true earnings power, and the reverse holds in recessions.
classic_example: Benjamin Graham and David Dodd emphasized normalized earnings in Security Analysis in 1934, urging analysts to average results across years rather than trusting one prosperous period. Their approach helped investors avoid overpaying for cyclical companies whose Depression-era collapses revealed how quickly boom profits could vanish when conditions normalized downward.
modern_example: A homebuyer-turned-investor examines a shipping company whose profits tripled during a freight shortage and refuses to value it on those earnings. She averages ten years of results instead, discovers the stock is actually expensive relative to normal earning power, and watches later as freight rates normalize and the share price follows earnings down.
failure_mode: Normal is hard to define when an industry is genuinely transforming, and averaging the past can anchor investors to earning levels that will never return. The method also smooths away real deterioration if each weak year is excused as temporary instead of evidence of decline.
apply_steps: Average earnings across a full cycle
Remove one-off gains and losses carefully
Judge whether competitive position remains intact
Value the business on normalized earnings

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Earnings power reveals the sustainable profit you are actually buying, hidden beneath this year's unusually flattering or frightening reported numbers.
situation_notes.users-but-no-revenue: For a product with users but no revenue, it reveals the missing question: what normalized profit could this attention eventually sustain?
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: It reveals whether a recommendation leans on peak or one-off earnings that make a fragile business look deceptively cheap and safe.

case_seeds: Graham and Dodd's normalized earnings approach in Security Analysis, 1934
origin: Graham and Dodd made normalised earnings the analyst's base unit in Security Analysis (1934), insisting profits be averaged across a cycle rather than taken from a single flattering year. Columbia professor Bruce Greenwald later formalised the approach as Earnings Power Value in Value Investing (2001), and Buffett's 1986 shareholder letter supplied its cash-based cousin, owner earnings.
mechanism_deep: Reported profit is a mixture of signal and weather: cycle position, commodity prices, one-off gains, accounting choices, and management's incentive to flatter the current year all distort it. Earnings power estimation strips those layers by averaging across a full cycle, removing non-recurring items, and deducting the maintenance capital spending needed merely to hold competitive position — the step reported earnings most often hide. The result is the profit stream a buyer can actually capitalise. The model breaks when normal itself moves: a structurally declining industry makes historical averages a fantasy ceiling, while a business crossing into a genuinely larger market makes them a misleading floor. Judgement about competitive position is therefore not decoration on the calculation — it is the calculation's most important input. This is why two honest analysts can produce different earnings-power figures from the same accounts: they disagree about which years were normal, which costs are truly maintenance, and whether the franchise survived the cycle intact — and those disagreements, surfaced explicitly, are the real research product the method exists to create.
examples_extra: ExxonMobil's reported results show why single years mislead: the company recorded an annual loss in 2020 as oil prices collapsed during the pandemic, then a record profit in 2022 as prices surged. Neither year represented its earnings power; an investor capitalising either figure alone would have wildly mispriced one of the world's most cyclical businesses.

Airlines demonstrated the same distortion in mirror image: US carriers that earned solid profits through the late 2010s posted enormous losses in 2020 when travel stopped. Buyers who valued them on 2020 earnings saw worthlessness, while buyers using 2019 earnings saw a bargain — earnings-power analysis, averaging across the shock, was the only route between the two errors.

formula.expression: Earnings Power Value = Normalised EBIT × (1 − Tax Rate) ÷ Cost of Capital
formula.variables: Normalised EBIT = operating profit averaged across a full cycle, cleaned of one-offs; Tax Rate = expected cash tax rate; Cost of Capital = required yearly return
formula.worked_example: A business with normalised EBIT of $100 million, a 25 percent tax rate, and a 10 percent cost of capital: EPV = 100 × 0.75 ÷ 0.10 = $750 million — the value of its current earning power with no growth assumed.

misconceptions: Many people think last year's reported profit is the earnings power — in reality, one year mixes cycle, luck, and accounting into a number that may be double or half the sustainable level.
Many people think averaging the past is always conservative — in reality, for a business in structural decline the historical average flatters the future badly.
Many people think earnings power ignores growth entirely — in reality, it deliberately values growth separately, so the buyer can see exactly how much of the price pays for hope.

practice.name: Cycle-average a cyclical stock
practice.instructions: Take a shipping, mining, or airline company and average its operating profit over the last ten years, including the worst year. Compare a valuation built on that average with one built on its best year, and write down which assumptions each price secretly requires.

cross_domain: Sport uses the same normalisation instinct: a footballer's value is judged on performance across several seasons, not on one hat-trick or one injury-ruined year, because single samples mix form, luck, and opposition. Climate science formalises it — weather is a single hot week, climate is the thirty-year average — and policy built on one extreme season fails the same way valuations built on one extreme earnings year do. Both fields learned to price the average, not the anecdote.

name_vi: Lỗ vĩnh viễn khác dao động giá tạm thời
definition: A quotation fluctuation is a temporary price swing, while permanent loss means the underlying value or your capital is truly destroyed.
mechanism: Prices move daily for reasons unrelated to business health, including forced selling, fashion, and macroeconomic fear, so a falling quote alone does not reduce what a sound business will earn. Permanent loss happens when earning power is impaired, debt forces a sale at the bottom, or the purchase price was so high that even good performance cannot rescue returns. Separating the two tells investors when to hold calmly and when to actually act.
classic_example: During the 2008 financial crisis, many bank stocks suffered permanent losses as their earning power and capital were genuinely destroyed, while strong consumer companies saw quotations halve and later fully recover. Investors who treated both situations identically either sold future compounders in panic or held impaired banks hoping a price recovery that fundamentals no longer supported.
modern_example: A teacher's retirement fund drops twenty percent in a month and headlines declare investors wiped out. She checks her broad index holdings, confirms the underlying companies still earn and pay dividends, recognizes a quotation fluctuation, and continues contributions, while separately selling one individual stock whose business model a new competitor genuinely broke.
failure_mode: The distinction is clear only afterward, and investors abuse it by labeling every loss temporary to avoid admitting mistakes. Some fluctuations become permanent precisely because leverage, margin calls, or personal cash needs force selling before any recovery has time to arrive.
apply_steps: Ask whether earning power actually changed
Check debt that could force selling
Hold sound assets through price storms
Exit quickly when impairment is real

situation_notes.down-30-percent-cut-or-hold: Down thirty percent, it reveals the decisive question: is earning power impaired permanently, or only the quotation suffering temporarily?
situation_notes.market-panic: In a panic, it reveals that most quoted losses are provisional and become real only when you sell or fundamentals break.
situation_notes.deciding-under-stress: Under stress, it reveals a sorting task instead of a single sell decision: separate broken businesses from merely unpopular ones.

case_seeds: The 2008 financial crisis separating impaired banks from temporarily depressed quality companies
origin: The distinction is Graham's core teaching in The Intelligent Investor (1949): price quotations are conveniences, while real loss is the impairment of earning power or of the investor's capital. Howard Marks restated it for modern risk management in The Most Important Thing (2011), defining investment risk primarily as the probability of permanent loss rather than temporary volatility.
mechanism_deep: The two outcomes differ in mechanism, not just size. A fluctuation is a change in other people's offers caused by liquidity, mood, or macro fear, while the business's cash-generating machinery stays intact — nothing has been destroyed except a quotation. Permanent loss arrives through specific channels: earning power is impaired by competition or technology, the balance sheet forces dilution or default, fraud reveals the earnings never existed, or the purchase price was so extreme that even good performance cannot produce a decent return. A reflexive middle case makes the distinction hard: for banks, developers, and any firm needing market confidence or refinancing, a collapsing quotation can itself cause the impairment, so yesterday's fluctuation becomes tomorrow's permanent loss. Leverage performs the same conversion inside a portfolio, turning a survivable dip into a forced sale. The model breaks as a comfort device when investors label every decline temporary to protect their ego — the test must be evidence about earning power and solvency, gathered precisely when it is most unpleasant to look.
examples_extra: General Electric's decline after 2016 began as a falling quotation but became permanent loss: earnings deteriorated, debt taken on in earlier expansion pressed in, GE Capital shrank, and the company cut its dividend in 2017 and again in 2018. Investors who treated the fall as mere mood were holding a business whose earning power had genuinely been impaired.

Johnson & Johnson's 1982 Tylenol crisis shows the opposite pattern: after cyanide-laced capsules killed seven people in the Chicago area, the shares fell sharply and the product was recalled nationwide. The underlying franchise, cash flows, and management response proved intact, the brand recovered, and the quotation loss turned out to be temporary — impairment had been feared, but never actually occurred.
misconceptions: Many people think an unrealised loss is not a real loss — in reality, if earning power is impaired or the price paid was absurd, the loss is already real whether or not you sell.
Many people think every big fall is a buying opportunity — in reality, some falls are the market correctly detecting permanent impairment before the reports confirm it.
Many people think holding forever converts losses into fluctuations — in reality, time heals only intact businesses; for impaired ones it compounds the damage.

practice.name: Two-column impairment test
practice.instructions: For any holding down sharply, draw two columns: evidence earning power is impaired, and evidence only the quotation moved. Demand filings, results, and debt dates — not opinions. Act on the column with evidence; if both are empty, the honest position is a smaller one.

cross_domain: Medicine draws the same line between a fever, which is a temporary signal that usually resolves while the body stays intact, and organ damage, which permanently reduces what the body can do — and treatment differs completely depending on which one the falling numbers represent. Relationships show it too: an argument is a quotation fluctuation in a sound partnership, while broken trust through betrayal is impairment, and confusing the two leads people to either panic over noise or tolerate destruction as if it were weather.

name_vi: Quyết định luận địa lý
definition: Geographic determinism says climate, land, rivers, and resources strongly shape how societies develop, what they produce, and how powerful they become.
mechanism: Geography sets the starting costs of farming, travel, trade, and defense before any leader makes a decision. Fertile soil, navigable rivers, and natural harbors lower the price of growth, while mountains, deserts, and disease raise it. Over centuries these small cost differences compound into large gaps in wealth and technology. The model does not claim geography is destiny, only that it loads the dice heavily and persistently.
classic_example: Jared Diamond argued in Guns, Germs, and Steel, published in 1997, that Eurasia spread farming and technology faster because its east west axis kept climates similar across long distances. Crops and livestock moved easily along that axis, while the north south axes of Africa and the Americas forced adaptation to new climates at every step.
modern_example: A retail business on a busy walking street inherits foot traffic that an identical shop two blocks away must buy through advertising. Location quietly decides margins before skill enters the picture. The same applies to careers: living near an industry cluster gives casual access to jobs, mentors, and information that remote effort struggles to replicate.
failure_mode: Taken too far, the model becomes an excuse that erases human choice, policy, and culture, and history shows similar geographies producing very different outcomes. North and South Korea share a peninsula yet diverged completely. Geography explains starting conditions and costs, not final results. Use it to read constraints honestly, never to declare outcomes inevitable or peoples incapable.
apply_steps: List the fixed geographic facts shaping this situation
Calculate what those facts make cheap or expensive
Position yourself where geography works for you
Invest effort where geography can be overcome

situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: Geographic determinism reveals that where your audience, suppliers, and competitors sit physically shapes a niche more than enthusiasm does.
situation_notes.big-purchase: A big purchase like property is mostly a geography decision, since location costs and benefits compound for decades afterward.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: Scaling succeeds when geography supports distribution and hiring, and stalls when distance quietly taxes every new unit added.

case_seeds: Diamond explaining Eurasian advantage through its east west axis in 1997
origin: Geographic explanation has older roots in Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748), but its modern form comes from Jared Diamond, a UCLA geography professor whose Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997) won the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction in 1998. Diamond framed the book as an answer to Yali's question from Papua New Guinea about unequal cargo.
mechanism_deep: The causal chain starts before politics: the local stock of domesticable plants and large mammals determines whether farming can produce storable surpluses. Surpluses support denser populations, full-time specialists, states and writing, while close contact with livestock generates crowd diseases that later become a devastating advantage in conquest. Latitude matters because crops spread fastest along similar day lengths and temperatures. Critics accept much of this biogeography but dispute its reach. James Blaut accused Diamond of Eurocentric environmental determinism, while Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson argued in Why Nations Fail (2012) that institutions, not geography, better explain cases such as the two Koreas or the two halves of Nogales on the United States-Mexico border. The model works best for very long-run, continental-scale differences in starting conditions, and weakens sharply when used to explain a single country's policy success or failure within one generation. Used at the right scale, geography is a distribution of costs and probabilities. Used at the wrong scale, it becomes post hoc storytelling that can rationalise almost any outcome after it happens.
examples_extra: Across a broad belt of central Africa, the tsetse fly transmitted trypanosomiasis, or sleeping sickness, to humans and lethal nagana to cattle and horses well into the twentieth century. Without reliable draft animals, farmers could not use heavy ploughs or wheeled transport at Eurasian scale, and states found cavalry and bulk haulage far harder to sustain over long distances.

Bolivia illustrates the modern cost of losing coastline. Chile seized Bolivia's Litoral department during the War of the Pacific (1879-1884), and the 1904 treaty left Bolivia landlocked. Its trade still depends on Chilean and Peruvian ports and on transit politics with neighbours, a permanent geographic tax even though the original loss came from war and diplomacy, not terrain alone.
misconceptions: Many people think geographic determinism says tropical peoples are inherently less capable — in reality, Diamond's argument explicitly rejects biological differences and points instead to environments, crops and animals.
Many people think a rich location guarantees success — in reality, geography shifts probabilities and costs, and institutions or policy can waste or amplify the same endowment.
Many people think the model explains every income gap today — in reality, its strongest claims concern pre-industrial starting conditions over millennia, not quarterly growth or individual careers.

practice.name: Map the cost gradient
practice.instructions: Pick one business or career decision and list the geographic facts you cannot change this year. For each fact, write what it makes cheap and what it makes expensive. Then choose one move that places you on the cheap side of the gradient instead of fighting it.

practice.name: The two Koreas check
practice.instructions: Take any outcome you are tempted to explain by geography alone and find a paired case with similar geography but a different outcome.
