Write down what institutions, policy or timing explain the difference. If you cannot find the pair, your geographic explanation is probably too strong.

cross_domain: The same loading of the dice appears outside history. In ecology, a species' range is set first by climate, soil and barriers before competition refines it. In business, a shop, port or factory inherits foot traffic, supplier distance and energy costs from its site. In technology, a startup inside a dense cluster gains hiring and information spillovers that a remote rival must buy deliberately.

quote.text: History followed different courses for different peoples because of differences among peoples' environments, not because of biological differences among peoples themselves.
quote.author: Jared Diamond

name_vi: Phụ thuộc vào lối đi đã chọn
definition: Path dependence means early choices, even accidental ones, lock in later options because switching costs grow as people build around the original path.
mechanism: Once a standard, skill, or system gains users, everyone adapts to it: training, tools, and habits all align around the existing choice. Each adaptation raises the cost of switching, even if a better alternative appears later. Small early advantages therefore snowball into durable dominance. The present is constrained less by what is best now than by the sequence of decisions that made the current arrangement expensive to undo.
classic_example: The QWERTY keyboard layout, designed in the 1870s for early typewriters, still dominates modern keyboards despite the Dvorak layout being promoted as faster since the 1930s. Typists, teachers, and manufacturers all built around QWERTY, so switching would require retraining millions of people. The layout persists through accumulated habit rather than proven superiority.
modern_example: Choosing a career specialty early quietly locks in your network, reputation, and skill stack, making later pivots increasingly expensive with each year invested. The same happens with software: a team that picks one platform builds templates, integrations, and habits around it, so a genuinely better tool two years later still loses to switching costs.
failure_mode: Path dependence can become fatalism, as if change were impossible, yet paths do break when switching benefits overwhelm costs or a shock resets the field. It also gets overused to defend bad systems just because they are old. The model explains resistance to change; it does not prove the locked in option deserves to survive.
apply_steps: Treat early standard choices as long commitments
Ask what switching will cost in three years
Keep exit options open where uncertainty is high
Revisit lock in when a genuine shock occurs

situation_notes.career-pivot: Path dependence reveals that career pivots get more expensive each year, so earlier exploration is worth far more than later regret.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: Scaling locks in tools, hires, and processes, meaning early sloppy choices become very expensive structural problems later on.
situation_notes.buying-a-stock: A stock purchase creates path dependence through taxes, attention, and emotional attachment, so entry decisions deserve more care than exits.

case_seeds: QWERTY keyboard layout persisting since the 1870s despite alternatives
origin: The modern economics of path dependence was crystallised by Stanford economic historian Paul David in 'Clio and the Economics of QWERTY' (American Economic Review, 1985) and by W. Brian Arthur at the Santa Fe Institute in papers from 1989 on increasing returns and lock-in. David supplied the historical cases; Arthur supplied the formal mechanism that explained them.
mechanism_deep: Arthur identified four self-reinforcing mechanisms that make early leads grow. Large setup costs spread over more users make the incumbent cheaper per person. Learning effects mean people get better at using the established option, so its real performance improves with adoption. Coordination effects reward choosing what everyone else chooses, because compatibility itself is valuable. Adaptive expectations complete the loop: if people believe a standard will win, they invest in it, and their investment makes the belief true. Together these produce a non-ergodic process, one where small, even random early events are not averaged away but amplified, so history cannot be treated as noise around an inevitable efficient outcome. The strongest scholarly pushback came from Stan Liebowitz and Stephen Margolis, whose 1990 paper 'The Fable of the Keys' re-examined David's QWERTY case and argued that the United States Navy study used to prove Dvorak's superiority was flawed, that typists could switch layouts at modest cost, and that markets often do correct inferior standards. They usefully distinguished weak path dependence, where history matters but the outcome is still about as good as available alternatives, from strong claims that a clearly inferior standard is permanently locked in despite everyone knowing better. The strong version is rare and needs proof; the weak version is everywhere. Paul Pierson extended the argument to politics in 2000, noting that laws create constituencies, agencies and expectations that make policy reversal far harder than adoption. The model applies best in the early, fluid phase of a technology, institution or career, before complements accumulate, and it weakens when a shock, a collapsing incumbent or a large performance gap suddenly makes coordinated switching worthwhile for many actors at once. Douglass North carried the idea into institutional economics in Institutions, Institutional Change and Economic Performance (1990), arguing that the incentives built into laws and organisations reward activities that reinforce the existing path, which is why inefficient institutions can persist for centuries. Gregory Unruh named a contemporary version carbon lock-in in 2000: power stations, grids, suburbs and fuel supply chains were built to support each other, so fossil energy persists as a system rather than as a series of separate choices anyone can reverse alone. The same interlocking explains why precedent in common law is sticky: each judgment becomes an input to the next, and departing from it imposes costs on every contract written in reliance on the old rule. These cases also mark the model's boundary conditions. Path dependence is strongest where network effects and complementary investments are large, where early choices are public and hard to reverse, and where users must coordinate any switch. It is weakest for cheap, modular choices a single user can change alone, which is why fashions and phone apps turn over quickly while gauges, grids and legal codes endure. Knowing which situation you face tells you how much weight an early decision actually deserves.
examples_extra: Railway gauges show lock-in measured in steel. George Stephenson's 4 feet 8.5 inches became Britain's standard gauge after the Gauge Act of 1846, while the Australian colonies chose different gauges, New South Wales standard, Victoria broad and Queensland narrow, forcing passengers and freight to change trains at border towns such as Albury well into the twentieth century, long after federation in 1901 made the costs obvious to everyone involved.

Nuclear power locked in early around light-water reactors because the United States Navy, under Admiral Hyman Rickover, proved pressurised water reactors in submarines in the 1950s, starting with USS Nautilus in 1955. Utilities then bought the design with trained crews, regulators and suppliers already aligned to it. Alternatives such as molten-salt reactors, tested at Oak Ridge in the 1960s, were not necessarily worse, but they arrived after the civilian path had already hardened.
misconceptions: Many people think path dependence means the first option always wins forever — in reality, lock-in breaks when a shock or a large performance gap makes coordinated switching worthwhile.
Many people think a locked-in standard must be inferior — in reality, many locked-in standards are perfectly good; the model explains persistence, not necessarily inefficiency.

Many people think sunk cost and path dependence are the same — in reality, sunk cost is a psychological bias about past spending, while path dependence is a structural fact about complements and switching costs.

practice.name: Trace one personal lock-in
practice.instructions: Choose one habit, tool or commitment in your own life and list everything that has been built around it: skills, files, relationships, routines. Estimate honestly what switching would cost in money and weeks. Then ask whether you would choose it again today at that switching price.

practice.name: Pre-commit the exit test
practice.instructions: Before adopting a new platform, format or supplier, write down the condition that would make you switch and the export or migration step you will keep tested. Review that note after ninety days. Path dependence is cheapest to manage before the complements pile up around your first choice.

cross_domain: Lock-in appears wherever complements accumulate. In law, precedent makes early rulings cheaper to follow than to overturn, so legal systems inherit their own past reasoning. In biology, evolved body plans constrain later anatomy, which is why vertebrates solve new problems by modifying old structures. In software, an early database or file format gathers integrations and training around it until replacing the format costs more than tolerating its flaws.

name_vi: Chu kỳ văn minh (hưng thịnh – suy tàn)
definition: Civilizational cycles describe how societies tend to rise through discipline and unity, peak in wealth, then decline through comfort, division, and decay.
mechanism: Success changes the conditions that produced it. Hardship forges cooperation and thrift, prosperity relaxes discipline, inequality and faction grow, and institutions built for an earlier phase struggle under new pressures. Thinkers from Ibn Khaldun to modern historians describe similar arcs because the feedback is real: each generation inherits outcomes, not the experiences that created them, so lessons must be relearned painfully.
classic_example: Ibn Khaldun, writing the Muqaddimah in 1377, argued that dynasties rise on strong group solidarity, then decay within a few generations as luxury and taxation erode that solidarity. He watched North African dynasties repeat the pattern of conquest, consolidation, decadence, and collapse. His cycle theory is still cited as an early foundation of historical sociology.
modern_example: Family companies often follow the same arc: a founder builds through sacrifice, the second generation professionalizes, and the third spends without understanding how the money was made. Nations, brands, and online communities show softer versions of this rhythm. Recognizing which phase an organization is in helps you predict whether its problems are growing pains or decay.
failure_mode: Cycle theories are seductive but vague: they fit almost any story after the fact and rarely predict timing. Societies also renew themselves, borrow ideas, and break the pattern entirely. Treating decline as inevitable breeds cynicism and missed chances to reform. Use cycles as a checklist of risks that accumulate with success, not as a prophecy.
apply_steps: Identify which phase this organization is in
Watch for comfort eroding founding discipline
Reinvest success into renewal, not just display
Teach the hard lessons, not just the results

situation_notes.comparing-to-others: Civilizational cycles reveal that comparing your rising phase to anothers peak misleads, because every success carries hidden decay risks.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: Scaling during the decadent phase amplifies waste and faction, while scaling during the disciplined phase compounds strength instead.
situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: News narratives about inevitable national decline often recycle cycle storytelling, so check specific evidence before accepting the arc.

case_seeds: Ibn Khaldun describing dynastic cycles in the Muqaddimah in 1377
origin: The foundational statement is Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah, written in 1377 in present-day Algeria, which explained dynastic rise and decay through asabiyyah, or group solidarity. The idea returned for a mass European readership in Oswald Spengler's The Decline of the West (1918, 1922) and Arnold Toynbee's twelve-volume A Study of History (1934-1961), both shaped by civilisational crisis and world war.
mechanism_deep: Khaldun's mechanism was fiscal as well as moral. A conquering group with strong solidarity taxes lightly and spends little, but sedentary luxury raises court expenditure, so rulers raise tax rates, farm out collection and hire mercenaries, weakening both the economy and the original solidarity that made rule cheap. Peter Turchin's structural-demographic theory gives a modern version: population growth, elite overproduction and state fiscal distress combine into secular cycles that he tested against the Seshat historical database. The scholarly criticism is severe, however. Spengler and Toynbee selected and periodised their civilisations so flexibly that almost any event could be fitted after the fact, and neither produced dates that could fail. Long-lived cases also resist the scheme: the Ottoman Empire lasted over six centuries and China repeatedly reunified under new dynasties rather than dying once. Renewal is the standing counterexample, from Meiji Japan after 1868 to market reform in China after 1978. The model is therefore best used as a checklist of stresses that accumulate with success, applied to specific institutions with evidence, not as a timetable for whole societies.
examples_extra: China's dynastic cycle gave the pattern a name. Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming dynasty in 1368 after rebellion against Mongol Yuan rule, redistributed land and rebuilt administration. By the early seventeenth century, court factionalism, tax-exempt elite estates and fiscal strain had hollowed the state out, and Beijing fell in 1644 first to rebel Li Zicheng and then to the Manchu Qing.

The Ottoman Empire complicates any short cycle, lasting from about 1299 to 1922. Its classical system rested on timar cavalry grants and devshirme recruitment, but from the late sixteenth century price inflation, tax farming and military change eroded both. Ottoman reformers repeatedly adapted, which is why the empire declined, recovered and transformed over centuries rather than collapsing on a tidy generational schedule.
misconceptions: Many people think a cycle model can date a collapse in advance — in reality, no cycle theorist has produced reliable timing, and the patterns are fitted retrospectively.
Many people think decline is caused by moral softness alone — in reality, fiscal strain, elite competition and institutional mismatch do most of the documented work.
Many people think every old society must be in decay — in reality, age alone predicts little, because states and companies sometimes renew themselves for centuries.

practice.name: Phase audit of one organisation
practice.instructions: Pick a company, team or institution you know well and score it on founding discipline, spending habits, elite competition and willingness to reform. Support each score with one observable fact, not a feeling. Then name the single decay risk that evidence supports most strongly.

cross_domain: Cyclical rise and decay recur in other systems. In ecology, succession moves from fast-growing pioneers to a mature forest that becomes vulnerable to fire and pests. In business, the product life cycle runs from growth through maturity to decline unless a new curve is started. In sport, championship dynasties age together, overpay veterans and draft late, recreating decline through success itself.

quote.text: Dynasties have a natural life span like individuals.
quote.author: Ibn Khaldun

name_vi: Chu kỳ thế hệ
definition: Generational cycles say each generation reacts against how it was raised, creating repeating swings in values, risk appetite, and social mood.
mechanism: Children experience the world their parents built as normal, so they optimize for its problems and ignore the problems it solved. A generation raised in crisis values security, their children raised in stability value freedom, and their grandchildren may rediscover risk the hard way. Because memory lives in people, not institutions, societies forget lessons on a roughly human lifespan schedule and repeat them.
classic_example: William Strauss and Neil Howe published Generations in 1991, arguing that Anglo American history moves in repeating generational turnings of roughly twenty years. Their framework described alternating eras of crisis, rebuilding, awakening, and unraveling. While historians debate its precision, the book strongly influenced how marketers and commentators discuss generational differences like those of millennials and boomers.
modern_example: In workplaces, managers who endured harsh early careers may preach endurance to younger staff who prioritize balance and meaning. Neither side is simply wrong; each is reacting to a different formative economy. Understanding the cycle turns generational complaints into information about what each cohort experienced when its habits and expectations were permanently formed.
failure_mode: Generational labels are blunt averages that hide huge differences of class, region, and individual temperament. Treating every member of a cohort as identical produces bad hiring, marketing, and family judgments. The cycle timing is also loose enough to be stretched to fit anything. Use it to generate empathy and hypotheses, then verify with the actual person in front of you.
apply_steps: Ask what shaped this cohorts formative years
Expect reaction against the previous generations excess
Translate complaints into unmet formative needs
Verify with individuals before applying labels

situation_notes.team-conflict: Generational cycles reveal that workplace friction often reflects different formative economies, not laziness or entitlement on either side.
situation_notes.reading-a-new-partner: A partners attitudes toward money and risk usually trace back to the economic weather of their formative years.
situation_notes.persuading-stubborn-person: Persuading across generations works when you frame change in values their cohort trusts, not values yours assumes.

case_seeds: Strauss and Howe publishing Generations in 1991
origin: Karl Mannheim laid the sociological foundation in his 1928 essay 'The Problem of Generations', arguing that shared formative experience creates a generational location. William Strauss and Neil Howe popularised the cyclical version in Generations (1991) and The Fourth Turning (1997), proposing roughly eighty- to one-hundred-year saecula divided into four turnings, a scheme built on Anglo-American history rather than a universal law.
mechanism_deep: The defensible core is the impressionable-years finding: attitudes formed in late adolescence and early adulthood, when people first meet the economy and public events, tend to persist, as shown in work by Alvin Krosnick and Duane Alwin in 1989 and in later political socialisation research. That core is much weaker than the full cycle. Demographers face the age-period-cohort identification problem: age, calendar period and birth cohort are linearly dependent, so their effects cannot all be separated from the same data without extra assumptions, a difficulty formalised by Norval Glenn in the 1970s. Strauss and Howe added a stronger claim, that turnings recur in a fixed sequence, but historians criticise the scheme as unfalsifiable, since eras can be re-dated and exceptions reclassified until the pattern survives. Cohort averages also hide class, regional and ethnic differences that often exceed the generation gap itself. The model works best for documented shared shocks, such as depression, war or a sudden policy regime, and worst as a horoscope for individual personalities or precise future crises. Treat cohort as a prior to be updated by the person in front of you.
examples_extra: Americans who were children during the Great Depression (1929-1939) carried distinctive financial caution into adulthood. Economists Ulrike Malmendier and Stefan Nagel showed in 2011 that people who lived through low stock-market returns in their formative years participated less in equities decades later, an effect they called Depression babies, even after controlling for wealth and later experience.

China's one-child policy generation shows a policy-made cohort. Born under the policy introduced in 1979 and relaxed only in 2015, many urban children grew up without siblings, concentrated family investment in education and housing, and now face the so-called 4-2-1 structure of supporting two parents and four grandparents, shaping savings, marriage timing and care expectations in ways their parents never experienced.
misconceptions: Many people think everyone in a generation shares the same values — in reality, cohort averages conceal differences of class, region and temperament that are often larger than the average generation gap.
Many people think the four turnings predict the next crisis on schedule — in reality, the sequence has no verified forecasting record and its dates are routinely adjusted after events.
Many people think generational traits are fixed for life — in reality, later shocks and life stages also reshape attitudes, so formative influence is a tendency, not a life sentence.

practice.name: Formative-years interview
practice.instructions: Interview one older and one younger person about the economic and public events of their late teens and early twenties. Ask what those years taught them about money, security and authority. Compare their answers with your own cohort's lessons before you use any generational label at work.

cross_domain: Cohort effects appear wherever entry timing shapes a lifetime path. In labour economics, graduating in a recession depresses earnings for years, a finding documented for Canadian graduates by Philip Oreopoulos and co-authors in 2012. In technology, each cohort of users treats the interface it learned first as natural. In literature, successive movements define themselves against the style of the generation they were taught at school.

name_vi: Sóng dài Kondratieff
definition: Kondratieff waves are long economic cycles of roughly fifty years driven by clusters of major technologies that rise, mature, and eventually exhaust themselves.
mechanism: A breakthrough technology like steam, electricity, or computing opens decades of investment as industries rebuild around it. Early years bring rapid growth and optimism, then overinvestment, debt, and saturation slow the wave until a new technology cluster restarts the process. Capital spending, infrastructure lifetimes, and generational memory all stretch the rhythm far beyond ordinary business cycles, making booms and stagnation feel like permanent conditions while they last.
classic_example: Nikolai Kondratieff, a Soviet economist, published his long wave research in the 1920s after studying prices, production, and trade across capitalist economies. He identified repeating waves of about fifty years tied to major innovations. His conclusions were politically unwelcome in the Soviet Union, and he was executed in 1938, but economists still debate his waves today.
modern_example: An investor who understands long waves treats a technology boom as a phase, not a permanent state, and asks whether the industry is in early buildout or late overinvestment. Careers follow the same logic: joining a field early in its wave offers decades of tailwind, while joining at saturation means fighting for a shrinking share of mature demand.
failure_mode: The evidence for neat fifty year waves is contested, and the timing is too imprecise to trade or plan by directly. Economists disagree on wave dates and causes, and hindsight makes patterns look cleaner than they were. Use the idea to think in decades about technology and debt, never as a calendar that predicts turning points.
apply_steps: Place your industry on a decades long timeline
Ask whether this technology is building or saturating
Avoid debts sized for permanent boom conditions
Watch for the next technology cluster forming

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Kondratieff thinking reveals that a great company in a saturating wave faces headwinds no management quality can fully overcome.
situation_notes.what-to-learn-next: Learning skills early in a long technology wave gives decades of compounding demand, unlike skills tied to maturing platforms.
situation_notes.career-pivot: A career pivot succeeds more easily when it rides a rising long wave rather than defending a declining one.

case_seeds: Nikolai Kondratieff publishing long wave research in the 1920s
origin: Nikolai Kondratieff, director of Moscow's Institute for the Study of Business Cycles, published his long-wave findings in the 1920s, notably a 1925 paper on long cycles in economic life. Joseph Schumpeter named the waves after him in Business Cycles (1939) and tied them to clusters of innovation. Kondratieff himself was arrested in 1930 and executed in the Great Terror in 1938.
mechanism_deep: Schumpeter supplied the mechanism Kondratieff lacked: innovations arrive in swarms, because one breakthrough lowers the cost of many related experiments, and entrepreneurs and credit expand together until the new industries mature and returns fall. Carlota Perez later recast this as installation and deployment phases of techno-economic paradigms, separated by a financial bubble and crash. The evidence problem is fundamental. Kondratieff's original series were mostly prices, wages and production from Britain, France and the United States before the First World War, an era of the gold standard, major wars and commodity discoveries that can bend a fifty-year series without any technology wave. Statistical re-examinations by Angus Maddison and by Solomos Solomou in Phases of Economic Growth (1987) found long swings in growth but much weaker support for regular, clock-like waves, especially after 1945. Proponents also disagree by decades about when each wave starts, which destroys the theory's value as a calendar. The model survives best as a discipline of horizon: major infrastructures really do take decades to build and exhaust, debts really do accumulate across a working life, and careers really are helped or hurt by entering a technology early or late.
examples_extra: Proponents count a first wave around steam and textiles in Britain from the 1780s to the 1840s. Mechanised cotton spinning, Watt steam engines and canals cut transport and power costs together, drew labour into factory towns such as Manchester, and left a capital stock of mills and canals that later railway builders could extend rather than invent from nothing at all.

The information technology wave is the clearest recent candidate. Intel released the 4004 microprocessor in 1971, personal computers spread in the 1980s, and commercial internet buildout in the 1990s triggered enormous investment in fibre, software and data centres. The dot-com crash of 2000 then looked, to long-wave theorists, like the familiar overinvestment phase before the surviving infrastructure supported cheaper growth.
misconceptions: Many people think Kondratieff waves run exactly fifty years and can be traded on schedule — in reality, scholars cannot even agree on the waves' start dates, so no tradable calendar exists.
Many people think a long wave means the whole economy rises or falls together — in reality, old and new industries overlap, and a declining wave for one sector is a rising wave for another.
Many people think Kondratieff proved his waves beyond dispute — in reality, later statistical studies found, at best, irregular long swings rather than a regular cycle.

practice.name: Date your industry's buildout
practice.instructions: For your own industry, list the foundational technology, the year commercial buildout began, and the year investment clearly outran demand. Estimate whether you are in installation, saturation or replacement. Use the answer to size career bets in decades, not to predict next year's turning point.

cross_domain: Long waves have analogues in slower systems. In forestry, a stand planted in one decade matures and is harvested together, creating price gluts and shortages a generation later. In higher education, buildings and tenured hiring from an expansion era constrain budgets for forty years. In energy, power stations and grids built in one investment surge age together and demand a replacement surge two generations later.

name_vi: Chu kỳ bá quyền
definition: Hegemonic cycles describe how one dominant power sets global rules, enriches itself, then declines as rivals copy its methods and free ride on its order.
mechanism: A rising power builds the trade routes, currency, and rules that others adopt because the system benefits them too. Dominance is expensive to maintain, however, while challengers can focus resources on catching up without paying for global order. Over time the gap closes, the hegemon overextends, and a transition period of rivalry begins until a new order settles. Leadership therefore contains the seeds of its own erosion.
classic_example: Britain dominated global trade and finance in the 1800s with its navy, empire, and the pound sterling. Two world wars exhausted its finances, and by 1945 the United States had replaced it, designing the Bretton Woods system and making the dollar central. The transition showed how hegemony passes when the old leader can no longer pay its costs.
modern_example: A dominant platform or market leader faces the same pattern: it pays to educate the market, build infrastructure, and set standards, while smaller rivals copy what works and attack profitable corners without the overhead. Leaders who assume permanent dominance overspend on defense and miss the moment when focus should shift from control to adaptation.
failure_mode: Hegemonic theory can make every rivalry look like an inevitable changing of the guard, yet transitions are not automatic and old leaders can renew themselves. It also operates on timescales too long for most personal decisions. Applying it loosely to any market leader and challenger produces dramatic stories with little predictive value for timing or outcomes.
apply_steps: Identify who pays for maintaining this order
Watch challengers who free ride and specialize
Avoid overextension defending every position equally
Renew the source of advantage before it erodes

situation_notes.competitor-copied-you: Hegemonic cycles reveal that being copied is the normal tax on leadership, so renewal speed matters more than secrecy.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: Scaling like a hegemon, defending every market at once, overextends resources and invites focused challengers to win local battles.
situation_notes.competitor-price-war: Price wars often mark a leadership transition, where the challenger can afford losses the incumbent structure cannot sustain.

case_seeds: Britain yielding financial leadership to the United States by 1945
origin: Modern statements include Robert Gilpin's War and Change in World Politics (1981), George Modelski's long-cycle work in the 1980s, and Paul Kennedy's bestseller The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers (1987), which warned of imperial overstretch. Charles Kindleberger's account of the 1930s, The World in Depression (1973), supplied the related theory of hegemonic stability and leadership.
mechanism_deep: Hegemonic stability theory holds that a leading power supplies public goods others will not: open markets, a reserve currency, sea-lane security and a lender of last resort. Kindleberger argued the crisis of 1929-1939 became catastrophic because Britain could no longer lead and the United States would not yet lead, leaving nobody to perform those functions. Power-transition theory, from A. F. K. Organski in 1958, adds that danger peaks when a dissatisfied challenger approaches parity. The critics qualify both claims. Robert Keohane's After Hegemony (1984) showed that institutions built under hegemony can sustain cooperation after the hegemon's relative decline, because regimes lower transaction costs for everyone. Joseph Nye's soft power and the sheer cost of modern war, especially under nuclear deterrence, also make old-style succession by decisive hegemonic war less automatic than Gilpin's historical pattern suggested. The Britain-to-America transition, the case optimists cite, was eased by shared language and institutions and by two shared wars. The model therefore predicts strain and bargaining during relative decline far better than it predicts war, collapse or a specific successor.
examples_extra: The Dutch Republic was the seventeenth century's commercial hegemon. Amsterdam founded its Wisselbank in 1609, the Dutch East India Company had been chartered in 1602, and Dutch finance priced credit for much of Europe. A small state could not also pay indefinitely for land war against France and naval war against England, and after 1672 its relative lead narrowed as rivals copied Dutch finance.

Venice lost Mediterranean primacy as oceanic routes bypassed it. After Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498, Portuguese carracks brought pepper directly to Lisbon, undercutting the Venetian and Mamluk overland spice chain that had enriched Venice for centuries. Venice remained rich and adaptive, shifting into manufactures and mainland estates, but the route change ended its chokepoint rent without any single decisive battle.
misconceptions: Many people think hegemonic decline always ends in a great war — in reality, the Dutch and British cases included long negotiated adjustments, and institutions can outlive the hegemon's peak.

Many people think the hegemon profits from everything it provides — in reality, public goods such as open markets and sea security are costly, and free-riding by allies and rivals is built into the model.
Many people think any rising challenger is already the next hegemon — in reality, most challengers stall, and supplying global public goods is a far higher bar than growing quickly.

practice.name: Who pays for the order?
practice.instructions: Pick one market, platform or workplace order you rely on and list who pays to maintain it and who benefits without paying. Note which maintainer cost is rising fastest. That imbalance, not headline rivalry, is where hegemonic-cycle thinking predicts the first visible strain will appear.

cross_domain: The pattern repeats at smaller scales. In technology, a platform owner pays for standards, developer tools and moderation while smaller firms free-ride on the ecosystem and attack its most profitable niches. In sport, a dominant league sets calendars and rules that rival competitions copy without bearing the development cost. In ecosystems, a keystone species maintains conditions many others exploit until its decline reorganises the whole community.

name_vi: Anh hùng cá nhân hay thời thế
definition: This model asks whether history is driven mainly by exceptional individuals or by broad conditions that would have produced similar outcomes through someone else.
mechanism: Conditions create openings: technology, crisis, and public mood determine what is possible at a moment. Individuals decide how fully and how fast an opening is used, and their talent or failure can bend timing and details. The model works as a dial, not a switch. Weighing both ends prevents two errors: crediting a leader for a wave anyone would have ridden, and ignoring the rare person who genuinely changes direction.
classic_example: The debate sharpened in the 1800s between Thomas Carlyle, who argued history is the biography of great men, and thinkers who stressed social forces. The computer industry offers a test case: personal computing was clearly coming in the 1970s, yet specific choices by founders at Apple and Microsoft shaped which designs and business models won.
modern_example: When a company succeeds, ask how much was the founders brilliance and how much was a rising market lifting every competitor. Investors and hiring managers who separate the person from the wave make fewer expensive hero bets. The same question improves self judgment: your wins and losses both contain a personal part and a timing part worth separating honestly.
failure_mode: The model gives no formula for splitting credit, so people bend it toward their biases, worshipping leaders they like and dismissing those they dislike as lucky. Survivorship makes it worse because we only study winners. Without comparing similar people in similar conditions, the debate stays philosophical and cannot settle individual cases.
apply_steps: Describe the conditions before judging the person
Ask who else could have filled this role
Compare peers facing the same conditions
Credit the person only for the difference

situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: Great man thinking reveals that a famous investors record may reflect a favorable era more than repeatable personal skill.
situation_notes.stronger-colleague-threat: A stronger colleagues rise may ride a favorable project wave, so compare conditions before concluding you are simply outmatched.
situation_notes.comparing-to-others: Comparing outcomes without comparing conditions credits heroes for timing and blames strugglers for storms they did not create.

case_seeds: Thomas Carlyle arguing the great man theory in the 1800s
origin: Thomas Carlyle set out the heroic pole in lectures published as On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and The Heroic in History (1841). Herbert Spencer answered that great men are products of their societies, Leo Tolstoy attacked commander-centred history in the second epilogue to War and Peace (1869), and Sidney Hook refined the debate in The Hero in History (1943), distinguishing eventful from event-making people.
mechanism_deep: The strongest evidence for the zeitgeist side is simultaneous invention. Sociologist Robert Merton documented 'multiples', cases where the same discovery is made independently at the same time, which is hard to explain unless the prior state of knowledge made the discovery ripe. The strongest evidence for the individual side is variance: occupants of the same role, facing the same conditions, regularly produce very different outcomes, and Hook's event-making person is precisely someone whose choices redirect, not merely accelerate, events when genuine alternatives are open. Individual leverage is therefore not constant. It is highest at critical junctures, in young institutions and in crises, where rules are unsettled and one decision selects among very different paths, and lowest inside mature bureaucracies designed to produce similar outputs regardless of who is in charge. Georgi Plekhanov made a version of this point in 1898, arguing that individuals can change the individual features and timing of events but not their general direction when social relations drive them. The practical method is the replaceability test: describe the conditions first, name the plausible replacement person, and credit the individual only with the difference that replacement would probably have made. Anything more is storytelling dressed as analysis.
examples_extra: Simultaneous invention is the zeitgeist's best evidence. Alexander Graham Bell and Elisha Gray filed telephone patent documents in Washington on the same day, 14 February 1876, working independently on similar harmonic telegraph research. Bell won the patent and built the company, shaping who profited and whose design standardised, but the telephone itself was clearly ready to be invented by more than one mind.

Martin Luther shows timing changing a reformer's fate. Jan Hus made similar criticisms of the Catholic Church and was burned at Constance in 1415. Luther posted his Ninety-five Theses in 1517, after Gutenberg's printing system, developed around 1440, could multiply his pamphlets across German towns within weeks and after German princes had political reasons to shield him. Similar dissent, different media and protection, radically different outcome.
misconceptions: Many people think the model forces a choice between heroes and conditions — in reality, it is a dial for apportioning credit, and most serious answers assign weight to both.
Many people think a simultaneous invention proves individuals never matter — in reality, it proves the invention was ripe, while individuals still decided its form, timing and ownership.

Many people think successful leaders must have caused their era's success — in reality, survivorship and hindsight inflate personal credit, because failed leaders in identical conditions are rarely studied.

practice.name: Run the replaceability test
practice.instructions: Take one celebrated success and write down the conditions that existed before the leader acted. Name the most plausible replacement person and estimate what would still have happened without the hero. Credit the individual only with the remaining difference, and notice how much smaller, and more believable, the claim becomes.

cross_domain: The same attribution problem runs through other fields. In science, the Matthew effect gives famous researchers credit for work their laboratories and era made likely. In sport, a star player's value depends on the system, teammates and rule changes of the period. In investing, a manager's record in a long bull market must be separated from the market itself before skill can be claimed.

quote.text: The history of the world is but the biography of great men.
quote.author: Thomas Carlyle
quote.source: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and The Heroic in History (1841)

name_vi: Lịch sử phản thực (nếu… thì sao)
definition: Counterfactual history explores what might have happened if one key event had gone differently, to test how much that event really mattered.
mechanism: By changing one variable and reasoning carefully about consequences, you expose hidden assumptions about cause and effect. If a small change produces a wildly different world, the original event was a true hinge. If outcomes converge anyway, deeper forces were in charge. The discipline lies in changing only one thing and respecting what people at the time could actually know and do.
classic_example: In July 1944, German officers led by Claus von Stauffenberg tried to kill Adolf Hitler with a bomb at the Wolf Lair headquarters. Hitler survived, the coup collapsed, and the war continued into 1945. Historians use the near miss to examine how much of the wars final year depended on one man surviving one explosion.
modern_example: After a failed product launch, run the counterfactual: if the price had been lower, would it really have succeeded, or were distribution and timing the true causes? This prevents fixing the wrong variable next time. Investors use the same tool after losses to separate bad luck from bad process, which decides what actually needs changing.
failure_mode: Counterfactuals are unfalsifiable stories, and each imagined step multiplies uncertainty until confidence becomes pure fiction. People also smuggle in hindsight, giving past actors knowledge they never had. One changed variable is analysis; five changed variables is a novel. Keep counterfactuals short, single change, and clearly labeled as reasoning tools rather than evidence.
apply_steps: Change exactly one variable, nothing else
Respect what actors knew at the time
Trace only two or three consequences deep
Ask whether outcomes converge anyway

situation_notes.idea-rejected-by-boss: Counterfactual thinking reveals whether your rejected idea failed on merit, or whether timing and audience were the real blockers.
situation_notes.down-30-percent-cut-or-hold: Asking what would have to be true for recovery exposes whether holding rests on evidence or on hope alone.
situation_notes.deciding-under-stress: A quick counterfactual under stress, asking what happens if you do nothing, often clarifies the real stakes instantly.

case_seeds: Stauffenberg assassination attempt on Hitler in July 1944
origin: The genre has a name from Charles Renouvier, who coined 'uchronie' in Uchronie, drafted in 1857 and published in 1876. E. H. Carr dismissed counterfactuals as a parlour game in What Is History? (1961). Niall Ferguson revived academic interest with Virtual History (1997), insisting that plausible alternatives must be ones contemporaries actually considered, evidenced in documents from the time itself.
mechanism_deep: Methodologists Philip Tetlock and Aaron Belkin set out criteria in 1996 for disciplined counterfactuals: clarity about what is changed, logical consistency, consistency with established historical facts, and the minimal-rewrite rule, changing as little as possible to produce the alternative. Ferguson added that the alternative should be one contemporaries demonstrably contemplated, which anchors speculation in letters, memoranda and war plans rather than in the historian's imagination. Two failure patterns dominate undisciplined work. The first is the long chain, where each imagined consequence multiplies uncertainty until the final scene is fiction. The second is hindsight smuggling, quietly giving past actors information available only later. Richard Evans pressed the critical case in Altered Pasts (2013), arguing that many popular counterfactuals mainly express the author's politics about the present. The defence is modesty about purpose: a good counterfactual does not claim to know what would have happened, it tests a causal claim about what did happen, by asking whether removing one factor plausibly changes the outcome or whether deeper forces would have produced something similar by another route. Short horizons, single changes and documented alternatives keep that test honest.
examples_extra: On 27 October 1962, at the height of the Cuban Missile Crisis, United States destroyers dropped signalling depth charges on Soviet submarine B-59, whose captain believed war might have begun and proposed firing a nuclear torpedo. Flotilla chief of staff Vasili Arkhipov refused the consent required aboard, and the submarine surfaced instead. Historians treat his dissent as a genuine hinge, not a colourful detail in a settled story.

Before Antietam, a lost document tested contingency. Confederate general Robert E. Lee's Special Orders No. 191, detailing his divided Maryland campaign, was found wrapped around cigars by Union soldiers on 13 September 1862 and reached George McClellan. The windfall helped push the armies toward battle on 17 September 1862, and historians still debate how much faster or bolder McClellan actually became because of it.
misconceptions: Many people think a vivid counterfactual is evidence for what would have happened — in reality, it is only a test of a causal claim, and its confidence should fall with every extra imagined step.
Many people think changing more variables makes the analysis richer — in reality, each added change destroys the comparison, because you can no longer tell which change produced the imagined result.

Many people think counterfactual history is just fiction — in reality, disciplined versions are restricted to documented alternatives and minimal rewrites, which is what separates analysis from alternate-history novels.

practice.name: One-change post-mortem
practice.instructions: Take a recent failure and state one variable you will change in the counterfactual, and only one. Trace two consequences, then ask whether the outcome plausibly converges back to the same result through other causes. Write the single lesson that survives that convergence test and act on it next time.

cross_domain: Counterfactual reasoning is routine outside history. In law, the but-for test asks whether the harm would have occurred but for the defendant's act, making causation itself a counterfactual. In engineering, fault-tree analysis and pre-mortems imagine single component failures to find which ones are true hinges. In medicine, clinicians reason counterfactually when they ask whether a patient would have recovered without a given treatment.

name_vi: Điểm nghẽn và tuyến thương mại
definition: Chokepoints are narrow places where trade or movement must pass, giving whoever controls or disrupts them power far beyond their size.
mechanism: When many routes converge into one strait, canal, or platform, the flow through that point becomes a dependency for everyone using it. Control brings tolls, intelligence, and leverage, while blockage forces expensive detours or total stops. Value concentrates at bottlenecks because alternatives are slow, costly, or nonexistent. Mapping any system to find its narrowest passage reveals where power and fragility actually live.
classic_example: In March 2021 the container ship Ever Given ran aground and blocked the Suez Canal for six days. Hundreds of ships waited at both ends while global supply chains absorbed delays and costs. A single vessel in a single narrow waterway demonstrated how much of world trade depends on a handful of passages.
modern_example: In a business, the chokepoint might be one payment platform, one app store, one star employee who approves everything, or one supplier with no substitute. Profits and risk both concentrate there. Smart operators map their chokepoints early, negotiate from awareness rather than panic, and quietly build alternative routes before a blockage forces the issue.
failure_mode: Not every narrow point is a true chokepoint; if users can switch routes cheaply, the supposed leverage is imaginary. Chokepoints also shift as technology and behavior change, so yesterdays bottleneck can become irrelevant. Overinvesting in controlling or avoiding a weak chokepoint wastes resources that belong on the constraint that actually binds.
apply_steps: Map where flow narrows to one passage
Ask who controls that passage and their incentives
Measure the cost if it closes tomorrow
Build one alternative route before you need it

situation_notes.scaling-decision: Scaling reveals the chokepoint that will break first, usually approvals, supply, or support, long before demand becomes the problem.
situation_notes.users-but-no-revenue: Users without revenue often mean the flow stops at one chokepoint, usually payment trust or a missing paid tier.
situation_notes.channel-not-growing: A channel chokepoint is often one platform algorithm deciding all reach, making diversification a survival issue, not vanity.

case_seeds: Ever Given blocking the Suez Canal in March 2021
origin: The strategic logic descends from Alfred Thayer Mahan's The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890) and Halford Mackinder's heartland paper of 1904, which made narrow seas and land corridors central to state power. The modern term is maintained by agencies such as the United States Energy Information Administration, which tracks world oil transit chokepoints including Hormuz, Malacca and Bab el-Mandeb.
mechanism_deep: Network theory explains why small places hold large power: a chokepoint has high betweenness, meaning many shortest paths pass through it, so its controller sees the flow, can tax it and can credibly threaten to interrupt it. Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman called the modern version weaponised interdependence in 2019, showing how states exploit central nodes in finance and information networks for surveillance and coercion. The leverage has hard limits, however. Its strength depends on substitution cost: Saudi and Emirati pipelines bypass part of the Strait of Hormuz, and when Houthi attacks made the Red Sea dangerous from late 2023, many container lines rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope, accepting roughly ten extra days rather than stopping trade altogether. That episode proved both halves of the model at once: the chokepoint's disruption raised freight and insurance costs worldwide, yet the flow adapted, so control was expensive to use and impossible to make absolute. Control also need not mean ownership, since a weak actor with missiles, mines or a grounded ship can close a passage it could never administer. The practical question is therefore never just where the narrows are, but what bypassing them costs, in money and in time, for each user.
examples_extra: The Strait of Malacca, between Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore, is the shortest sea route between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. Tankers and container ships bound for China, Japan and South Korea crowd a channel that narrows near Singapore, which is why Chinese strategists discuss a 'Malacca dilemma', a concern publicly associated with President Hu Jintao in 2003, about energy imports depending on a passage others could interdict.

The Panama Canal showed that weather can close a chokepoint without an enemy. The canal depends on freshwater from Gatun Lake to work its locks, and drought in 2023 forced the Panama Canal Authority to cut daily transits from the usual high thirties toward twenty-four slots by January 2024, delaying bulk and container traffic and pushing some shippers back toward Suez or overland alternatives.
misconceptions: Many people think whoever holds a chokepoint can dictate any price — in reality, leverage is capped by the cost of the bypass, and pushing too hard accelerates investment in alternative routes.
Many people think chokepoints are permanent features of geography — in reality, canals, pipelines, ice melt and new platforms create and destroy chokepoints within a generation.
Many people think only states can close a chokepoint — in reality, an accident, a drought or a non-state armed group can interrupt a passage none of them could ever govern.

practice.name: Draw your own chokepoint map
practice.instructions: Sketch the flow of money, customers or approvals in one system you depend on and mark every place it narrows to a single passage. For the narrowest point, write the bypass cost in money and days if it closed tomorrow. Build the cheapest alternative route now, while you do not need it.

cross_domain: Chokepoints structure many non-geographic systems. In computing, a single authentication service or payment processor can halt hundreds of dependent products at once. In biology, a keystone enzyme or a narrow genetic bottleneck decides the fate of a whole population. In organisations, one approver through whom every decision passes becomes a human strait, collecting both power and blame. In supply chains, one specialised factory making a single component can hold up carmakers and electronics firms on three continents, as the semiconductor shortage of 2021 demonstrated.

name_vi: Thiên lệch lưu trữ (ai được ghi lại)
definition: Archival bias means the historical record overrepresents the powerful and literate, because they created and preserved most of the documents that survive.
mechanism: Records are not a neutral sample of the past. Governments, churches, and wealthy families wrote things down, stored them safely, and decided what was worth keeping, while ordinary peoples lives left few traces. Later historians can only work with what survived, so the archive silently shapes every conclusion. The same filtering happens in any data system where what gets recorded follows power, convenience, and survival.
classic_example: Much of what is known about ancient Rome comes from elite male authors like senators and historians, while the experiences of slaves, women, and the rural poor survive mainly in fragments, graffiti, and archaeology. Reading Roman history through its texts alone produces a Rome that looks far more senatorial and urban than the empire most people actually lived in.
modern_example: Company dashboards suffer archival bias: they record what was easy to measure, like clicks and ticket counts, while unrecorded conversations and quiet churn stay invisible. Decisions made only from the dashboard inherit its blind spots. Asking what the system never records, and who never appears in the data, often matters more than refining the numbers already present.
failure_mode: Archival bias does not mean surviving records are useless or that the undocumented past can be invented freely to fill gaps. Guessing what silenced people thought is its own distortion. The model also becomes an excuse to dismiss solid evidence merely because it comes from official sources. The correction is humility and triangulation with other evidence types, not rejection.
apply_steps: Ask who created this record and why
Identify whose experience never gets recorded
Triangulate with a different evidence type
Mark conclusions drawn from one sided sources

situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: Archival bias reveals that news and courses preserve success stories systematically, while the far larger record of failures stays unpublished.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: Investment advice archives winners prominently, so the track record you see excludes the advisors and funds that quietly disappeared.
situation_notes.reading-a-hard-book: A hard history book reflects its archive, so asking whose documents survived clarifies why certain viewpoints dominate the narrative.

case_seeds: Roman history surviving mainly through elite male authors
origin: Haitian historian Michel-Rolph Trouillot gave the model its sharpest form in Silencing the Past: Power and the Production of History (1995), arguing that silences enter history at four moments, from fact creation to retrospective significance. Ann Laura Stoler's Along the Archival Grain (2009) extended the approach to colonial archives, reading them as instruments of rule rather than neutral storehouses.
mechanism_deep: Trouillot's four moments show how many chances power gets to edit the past. Silences enter when facts are created, because only some events get recorded at all; when archives are assembled, because only some records are kept; when archives are retrieved, because only some are catalogued and funded; and when retrospective significance is assigned, because only some stories become 'history'. Material survival adds a second filter that has nothing to do with importance: clay, stone and dry tombs preserve, while palm leaf, bark and damp paper rot. Digitisation now adds a third filter, favouring records that are already catalogued, in major languages and in formats scanners and funders prioritise. The corrective tradition is older than the theory. Jan Vansina's methodology for oral tradition, developed from the 1960s, showed how to test transmitted testimony, and Carlo Ginzburg's The Cheese and the Worms (1976) read Inquisition records against the grain to recover the cosmology of a sixteenth-century miller. The scholarly warning runs both ways, however: an absence in the archive is a reason for humility and triangulation, not a licence to invent the missing voices in whatever form suits the present.
examples_extra: The Haitian Revolution (1791-1804) was long marginal in Western textbooks although it created the first state founded by formerly enslaved people and ended French rule in Saint-Domingue, France's richest sugar colony. Trouillot argued the revolution was 'unthinkable' within contemporary racial categories, so it was minimised in archives and narratives alike, even though French, Spanish and American records of it are extensive when historians choose to read them.

Material survival can be pure accident. The library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, assembled in the seventh century BCE, survives because clay tablets were baked hard when the palace burned during Nineveh's fall in 612 BCE. Literatures written on papyrus, leather or palm leaves in damper climates mostly rotted away, so the ancient record overrepresents Mesopotamian clay cultures partly because their medium could survive fire.
misconceptions: Many people think archival bias means official records are simply lies — in reality, biased records still contain hard evidence, especially when read against the grain and checked against other sources.
Many people think missing records prove a group did nothing important — in reality, absence usually proves only that recording and preservation followed power, literacy and durable materials.

Many people think digitising archives removes the bias — in reality, digitisation adds a new filter, because what gets scanned first is what was already catalogued, funded and written in major languages.

practice.name: Audit one dashboard for silence
practice.instructions: Take a report or dashboard you trust and list three things it never records and one group of people who never appear in it. Find one alternative source, a conversation, a physical count or an outside record, that covers one of those silences. Mark which of your recent conclusions rested on the silent data alone.

cross_domain: The same filter distorts other evidence systems. In machine learning, training data overrepresents whoever was online, literate and photographed, so models inherit an archival bias at scale. In palaeontology, the fossil record favours hard-bodied species in sediment, warping the apparent tree of life. In finance, databases of surviving funds and listed companies quietly delete the failures, flattering every historical average built on them.

name_vi: Phức tạp và sụp đổ (Tainter)
definition: Tainter argues societies collapse when growing complexity costs more than it returns, making simplification the rational response to unsustainable overhead.
mechanism: Societies solve problems by adding layers: more officials, rules, infrastructure, and specialists. Each layer works at first, but returns diminish while coordination costs keep rising, funded by taxing the productive base. Eventually the system spends so much maintaining itself that a shock it once could absorb becomes fatal. Collapse, in this view, is not irrational failure but an economizing move when complexity stops paying.
classic_example: Joseph Tainter examined the fall of the Western Roman Empire in The Collapse of Complex Societies, published in 1988. Rome kept adding administration, military commitments, and currency debasement to fund them, while returns from new conquest disappeared. When pressures mounted, many ordinary people experienced imperial collapse as relief from taxes and bureaucracy rather than pure catastrophe.
modern_example: A growing small business hits the same pattern when every new problem gets a new manager, meeting, tool, and approval step. Coordination quietly eats the margin that growth was supposed to create. Founders who periodically delete processes, not just add them, keep complexity paying. Individuals feel it too when productivity systems become heavier than the work they organize.
failure_mode: Complexity is not automatically bad; some layers genuinely protect health, safety, and scale, and cutting them causes real harm. Tainter model also explains collapse better than it predicts it, since societies can run diminishing returns for a long time. Using it to justify reckless simplification of systems you merely dislike misreads an analytical tool as a slogan.
apply_steps: List what each layer of complexity costs
Ask what return the newest layers actually deliver
Delete one process before adding another
Keep reserves instead of funding permanent overhead

situation_notes.scaling-decision: Tainter reveals that scaling fails when coordination overhead grows faster than revenue, making the larger organization poorer per person.
situation_notes.chronic-procrastination: Personal procrastination often follows complexity collapse, when your task system costs more energy to maintain than the work itself.
situation_notes.asking-for-budget: Budget requests should show whether new spending removes complexity or funds another layer with diminishing returns attached.

case_seeds: Tainter analyzing the Western Roman Empire collapse in 1988
source_ref: Tainter — The Collapse of Complex Societies
origin: Joseph Tainter, an archaeologist and historian, published The Collapse of Complex Societies with Cambridge University Press in 1988, synthesising cases from Rome to the Maya and the Chacoans. He wrote against romantic views of collapse as mere failure or moral decay, arguing instead from diminishing returns to complexity, and later extended the argument to energy costs and the problem of sustaining innovation.
mechanism_deep: Tainter's curve is the heart of the model. Early investments in complexity, a professional army, roads, a civil service, pay handsomely, but each later layer solves a harder remaining problem at higher cost, so marginal returns fall while the population's dependence on the whole structure rises. Energy makes the trap physical: Rome funded expansion from conquest, then had to fund defence of the same territory from taxation once expansion stopped, a transition Tainter generalised into a warning about any system whose complexity is subsidised by a one-time surplus. Critics in the volume Questioning Collapse (2010), edited by Patricia McAnany and Norman Yoffee, object that 'collapse' bundles together political fragmentation, population movement and cultural change, and that many supposed collapses were reorganisations in which ordinary people did well. Climate research has also complicated single-cause versions: Maya droughts are now documented in lake sediments and cave deposits, yet cities responded very differently to similar rainfall stress. Tainter himself noted the Byzantine counter-case, where simplification restored solvency. The model therefore explains vulnerability, a rising cost of staying the same, better than it predicts any date, and it applies only where leaders cannot or will not shed functions whose returns have turned negative.
examples_extra: The Byzantine Empire survived by simplifying where Rome had not. After Arab conquests in the 630s and 640s stripped away Syria and Egypt, Constantinople reorganised much of Anatolia into theme districts where soldiers were supported by land rather than a costly central payroll. The empire that remained was poorer and smaller, but its reduced complexity matched its revenues, and it endured for centuries afterward.

Classic Maya collapse was regional, not total. Many southern lowland cities such as Tikal lost population and stopped erecting dated monuments during the eighth and ninth centuries, amid drought episodes and intensifying warfare, while northern centres such as Chichen Itza flourished longer and Maya peoples and languages never disappeared. Tainter's frame explains stressed southern polities better than any story of a whole civilisation vanishing overnight.
misconceptions: Many people think Tainter says complexity is bad — in reality, he argues complexity is a problem-solving strategy whose returns diminish, so the danger is paying peak prices for layers that no longer pay back.
Many people think collapse means everyone dies — in reality, collapse is rapid loss of political complexity, and Tainter notes populations often experienced it as lower taxes and less bureaucracy.

Many people think the model predicts when a modern state will fall — in reality, it diagnoses rising maintenance costs, and societies can run diminishing returns, or reform them, for a very long time.

practice.name: Complexity ledger for one system
practice.instructions: List every recurring process, meeting, tool and approval in one system you run, with its monthly cost in hours or money. For each, write the problem it was added to solve and whether that problem still exists. Delete or merge the one layer whose original problem has vanished, and bank the saved hours.

cross_domain: Diminishing returns to complexity recur across domains. In software, legacy platforms accumulate patches and integrations until maintenance consumes the budget meant for new features, and a rewrite becomes rational. In biology, overspecialised species thrive in stable conditions but cannot absorb environmental change. In personal life, productivity systems can grow so elaborate that maintaining the system displaces the work it was built to organise.

name_vi: Thiên lệch sống sót trong lịch sử
definition: Survivorship in history means we learn mainly from the societies, texts, and leaders that endured, while the many that failed left little evidence behind.
mechanism: Survival filters the sample before analysis begins. Winning nations wrote the histories, successful institutions preserved their records, and failed experiments vanished without documenting why. Studying only survivors makes their traits look like recipes for success, even when identical traits existed among the vanished. The missing failures hold the comparison data that would show which traits actually mattered and which were decoration.
classic_example: During the Second World War, statistician Abraham Wald studied returning bombers to decide where to add armor. Commanders wanted armor where bullet holes clustered, but Wald argued the holes showed where a plane could be hit and survive. The missing planes, hit elsewhere, never returned to be counted. His insight became the classic survivorship bias demonstration.
modern_example: Business advice built only from famous winners suffers the same flaw: thousands of companies copied the same habits and died unrecorded. Before imitating a winners routine, ask how many failures did the same thing. The same applies to investment legends and study tips from top students; the invisible majority who used identical methods with ordinary results never get interviewed.
failure_mode: Survivorship thinking can paralyze learning if taken as proof that success stories teach nothing at all. Survivors still contain real information, especially about what did not kill them. The error is treating survivor traits as sufficient causes. The fix is comparison: actively hunt for failures that shared the trait before crediting it with the win.
apply_steps: Ask who is missing from this sample
Search for failures that shared the winning trait
Separate necessary traits from decorative ones
Weight base rates above inspiring stories

situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Survivorship reveals that famous winning stocks hide thousands of similar picks that failed, so story quality is not evidence.
situation_notes.comparing-to-others: Comparing yourself only to visible winners compares you to a filtered sample that excludes everyone who tried and stalled.
situation_notes.evaluating-investment-advice: Advice from surviving funds excludes closed and merged failures, inflating the apparent skill behind the strategies being sold.

case_seeds: Abraham Wald analyzing returning bomber damage during the Second World War
origin: The canonical analysis came from statistician Abraham Wald at Columbia University's Statistical Research Group, whose 1943 memorandum on estimating aircraft vulnerability from the damage visible on survivors formalised the missing-data logic during the Second World War. Later statisticians, notably Marc Mangel and Francisco Samaniego in 1984, revisited Wald's work and generalised it as a named statistical phenomenon.
mechanism_deep: Formally, survivorship is a missing-data problem in which the chance of being observed depends on the outcome itself, what statisticians call data missing not at random. Any average computed on the observed cases is then biased, and the bias grows with the failure rate, which is why winner-only samples are most misleading in exactly the fields, war, business and investing, where failure is commonest. Philip Rosenzweig's The Halo Effect (2007) traced the business version: studies such as In Search of Excellence (1982) selected firms on current performance, attributed their traits as causes, and then watched many celebrated firms stumble within a few years, because performance itself had selected the sample. Elton, Gruber and Blake demonstrated the same deletion mechanically in mutual fund data in the 1990s. The correction is not to ignore survivors, who are excellent evidence for existence proofs and for necessary conditions, since whatever killed the missing cases is absent or survived in them. The correction is to reconstruct the denominator: count everyone who started, hunt for the failures that shared the celebrated trait, and ask whether the trait separated winners from losers or merely decorated both. Where the dead cannot be counted, conclusions should be stated as hypotheses, not recipes.
examples_extra: Mutual fund databases quietly delete the dead. When a fund performs badly, its sponsor often merges or liquidates it, and its record disappears from the averages investors later inspect. Studies by Edwin Elton, Martin Gruber and Christopher Blake in the 1990s showed this survivorship effect materially inflated reported United States mutual fund performance, meaning the average fund an investor could actually have held did worse than the surviving database suggested.

Ancient literature is a survivor sample in the most literal sense. Sophocles is credited with writing more than 120 plays in the fifth century BCE, yet only seven tragedies survive complete, including Oedipus Rex and Antigone. Judgements about Greek theatre therefore rest on a tiny, school- and monastery-filtered fraction of what audiences actually watched, and the lost majority included celebrated works by rivals who were famous in their own lifetimes.
misconceptions: Many people think survivorship bias means success stories teach nothing — in reality, survivors prove what is possible and reveal necessary conditions; they just cannot prove which traits were sufficient.
Many people think the bias only affects ancient history — in reality, it is strongest in modern data, where failed funds, startups and products are deleted from databases every year.
Many people think spotting one missing group fixes the sample — in reality, the bias is corrected only by reconstructing the full starting population, including failures nobody recorded at all.

practice.name: Find the missing failures
practice.instructions: Take one success story you admire and write down its three most praised traits. Then search deliberately for two failures that shared at least two of those traits and note what actually differed. Downgrade any trait the failures also had from 'cause of success' to 'background condition' in your notes.

cross_domain: Selection by survival warps many fields at once. In medicine, the healthy worker effect makes employed populations look healthier than the general public because the seriously ill have already left work. In evolution, the living species available for study are the lineages that escaped extinction, biasing reconstructions of the past. In aviation safety, incident databases overrepresent flights that returned, which is why near-miss reporting systems were created to capture the missing cases.

name_vi: Vòng OODA (Quan sát – Định hướng – Quyết định – Hành động)
definition: The OODA loop says whoever observes, orients, decides, and acts fastest with good judgment disrupts rivals who are still reacting to outdated situations.
mechanism: Fighter pilot John Boyd studied air combat and found winners were not just faster but better oriented: they read the situation accurately and acted before opponents finished processing the last change. Each fast, apt action creates a new situation the rival must reprocess, compounding their confusion. Speed without orientation is just flailing, so the loop rewards the combination of fresh observation, honest interpretation, decisive choice, and immediate action.
classic_example: During the Korean War, American F-86 Sabre pilots achieved a strong record against MiG-15 fighters despite similar aircraft performance. Boyd later attributed much of the edge to the Sabres better visibility and faster responding controls, which let pilots cycle through observe and act faster. He developed the OODA loop from studying these engagements and his own flying career.
modern_example: A small business that checks sales data weekly and adjusts prices, offers, and stock in days beats a larger rival whose reports take a quarter to approve. The advantage is not brilliance but cycle speed with decent judgment. Job seekers iterating applications based on real responses each week likewise outlearn those who plan perfectly for months.
failure_mode: Speed is not the goal by itself; cycling fast on bad observation produces confident, rapid mistakes. Some decisions are irreversible and deserve slow orientation, like contracts and safety. The loop also degrades under exhaustion and overload. Use OODA to shorten honest feedback cycles, not to justify impulsive action on every important call.
apply_steps: Shorten the time between action and feedback
Observe fresh data, not last months assumptions
Decide with the orientation you have now
Act, then immediately observe the new situation

situation_notes.decision-under-time-pressure: The OODA loop reveals that under time pressure, a good decision now usually beats a perfect decision after conditions change.
situation_notes.competitor-copied-you: When copied, faster iteration cycles create new advantages before rivals finish copying your previous move properly.
situation_notes.deciding-under-stress: Under stress the loop narrows to observing one fresh fact and taking one reversible action, restoring momentum.

case_seeds: F-86 Sabre versus MiG-15 engagements in the Korean War
John Boyd developing OODA from air combat studies
origin: United States Air Force colonel John Boyd developed the idea from the 1950s onward, first as a fighter pilot and instructor, then in briefings during the 1970s and 1980s. He never published a finished book; the loop survives through his briefing slides, especially The Essence of Winning and Losing in 1995, and through students who carried it into Marine Corps doctrine and business strategy.
mechanism_deep: The decisive part of the loop is orientation, not raw speed. Orientation is the stock of mental models, cultural habits, prior experience, and information flows through which raw observation becomes meaning. Two competitors can receive the same data and orient completely differently: one sees a price cut as desperation, the other as a funded land grab, and they will choose opposite actions from identical facts. Boyd called orientation the Schwerpunkt, the focal point, because it shapes what you notice, what you ignore, and which options even occur to you. This is why a faster loop beats a slower one in an adversarial setting rather than merely finishing sooner. Every action you take changes the situation your opponent is still orienting to, so their next decision is built on a picture that is already obsolete. Repeated often enough, the lag compounds: they are not just behind on facts, they lose confidence in their own picture, hesitate, and then rush, which degrades their orientation further. Boyd described the end state as opponents folding inward, unable to cooperate or adapt, long before they are physically destroyed. Opponents are not passive, however, and a sophisticated rival attacks your loop directly. They feed false or noisy observations through deception and overload, they slow the contest into committees and negotiations where your tempo cannot be used, and they force you onto irreversible decisions where a fast cycle is a liability rather than an asset. They may also simply refuse to react, absorbing small provocations while preparing one large, well-oriented move, which is the correct counter to an opponent who mistakes activity for advantage.
