The honest business translation is therefore not move fast and break things. It is building a shorter, cleaner path from signal to action than your rival has: sales staff who can report a lost deal the same day and see pricing change within the week, a product team whose release cycle lets it test a feature before a competitor's planning cycle even approves one, a founder who talks to customers weekly instead of commissioning quarterly research. In each case the advantage is that the rival is forced to respond to your previous position while you are already testing the next one, and their strategy process, tuned for stability, starts producing confident plans for a market that no longer exists. The loop also explains why copying a fast rival fails: imitators copy the visible action, which is the last step, without the observation channels and orientation that produced it, so they arrive quickly at the wrong move. Protecting the loop therefore means protecting the quality of orientation above all: diverse information sources, permission to report bad news quickly, and enough rest and slack that decision makers can actually think. Tempo built on corrupted orientation is just a faster route to a larger mistake, which is why Boyd paired speed with harmony, initiative, and variety rather than with haste alone.
examples_extra: In May and June 1940, German forces defeated France despite broadly comparable tank numbers, partly through faster decision cycles. German commanders used mission-style orders and radios fitted in tanks to adapt locally, while French command often relied on slower, centralised orders. German tempo repeatedly made French plans obsolete before they were executed, turning local breakthroughs into a campaign-level collapse within about six weeks.

Spanish retailer Zara, part of Inditex, founded by Amancio Ortega in 1975, built its advantage on cycle speed rather than prediction. Stores reported what was actually selling, designers revised garments quickly, and nearby factories produced small batches that reached shops within weeks. Rivals planning collections many months ahead had to guess demand; Zara observed real demand and acted while the season was still alive.
misconceptions: Many people think the OODA loop means acting as fast as possible — in reality, orientation is the decisive stage, and fast action on a wrong reading only produces faster mistakes.
Many people think OODA is only a military concept — in reality, Boyd himself applied it to any competitive situation where opponents adapt to each other's moves.

Many people think getting inside a rival's loop means confusing them with chaos — in reality, it means presenting them with a changing situation they must reprocess while you already act on the new one.
practice: Run one real OODA sprint: Pick a live competitive decision, such as a rival's new offer. Spend one day only observing fresh evidence, write your orientation in five lines, decide one reversible response, act within the week, and record what changed. Repeat the cycle and measure whether your observe-to-act time shrinks.

Shorten one feedback path: Choose a recurring decision you make monthly, list every hand-off between signal and action, and remove or delegate one step so fresh information reaches the decision maker days sooner. Track for a month whether decision quality, not just speed, improves.
cross_domain: Emergency medicine runs the same loop when a triage team repeatedly reassesses a deteriorating patient, adjusts treatment, and watches the response, because a treatment plan built on the first examination becomes dangerous as physiology changes. Wildland firefighting shows it too: incident commanders who re-read wind, fuel, and fire behaviour faster than the fire changes keep crews positioned ahead of it, while a slow cycle leaves firefighters reacting to where the fire was, not where it is going.

name_vi: Sương mù chiến tranh (mù mờ thông tin)
definition: Fog of war means decisions must be made with incomplete, delayed, and often wrong information, because the situation never reveals itself fully in time.
mechanism: Reports arrive late, sensors miss things, people exaggerate or hide bad news, and the opponent actively deceives. Even honest information conflicts, so commanders act on probabilities rather than facts. Clausewitz noted that friction and uncertainty make simple plans hard in practice. The model does not excuse guessing; it demands plans that remain workable across several possible realities instead of one predicted future.
classic_example: At the Battle of Gettysburg in July 1863, Confederate general Robert E Lee operated with poor information because his cavalry under J E B Stuart was absent and out of contact. Lee attacked without a clear picture of Union positions and strength. The three day battle ended in a major Confederate defeat that shifted the American Civil Wars momentum.
modern_example: Launching a product happens in fog: real demand, competitor moves, and costs are estimates until money is spent. Managers who demand certainty before acting usually act last. Better practice is small reversible probes that buy information cheaply, reserves for surprises, and explicit statements of what is assumed versus what is actually known.
failure_mode: Fog becomes an excuse for laziness when people skip homework they could easily have done, or ignore clear signals because uncertainty feels safer. It also cuts the other way: some facts are knowable and decisive, and hiding behind fog to avoid them is negligence. The model applies to genuine irreducible uncertainty, not to homework left undone.
apply_steps: Separate what is known, assumed, and unknown
Prefer reversible moves while fog is thick
Send cheap probes to buy real information
Keep reserves for the surprise you cannot name

situation_notes.deciding-under-stress: Fog of war reveals that stress often comes from demanding certainty that the situation structurally cannot provide in time.
situation_notes.buying-a-stock: Buying a stock happens in permanent fog, so position size should reflect how much of your thesis is assumption.
situation_notes.decision-under-time-pressure: Under time pressure, naming your single biggest unknown prevents the whole fog from feeling equally threatening and paralyzing.

case_seeds: Lee fighting at Gettysburg without Stuart cavalry in July 1863
origin: Prussian theorist Carl von Clausewitz analysed uncertainty throughout On War, published posthumously in 1832 by his wife Marie von Clausewitz after his death in 1831. He wrote that war is the realm of uncertainty and that most information in war is contradictory, false, or uncertain. The exact phrase fog of war became common later, as shorthand for his account of friction, chance, and incomplete knowledge.
mechanism_deep: Fog is not a single missing fact but a system that manufactures error. Sensors and scouts sample only fragments, reports are delayed and compressed as they pass up a hierarchy, each layer quietly removing doubt to sound competent, and an intelligent opponent deliberately injects false signals into the same channels. The result is that confidence often rises as information travels, even as accuracy falls, which is fog's most dangerous property. The correct response is not to wait for fog to lift, because in competitive settings it rarely does, and waiting hands the initiative to the opponent. Capable commanders instead design for several possible worlds at once, keep a reserve useful in all of them, prefer moves that remain acceptable if the main assumption is wrong, and spend resources on cheap probes whose only job is to buy information before the expensive commitment. A rival exploits your fog by forcing early commitment, presenting a tempting picture that fits your expectations, or attacking the assumption your whole plan silently rests on. In business the identical structure appears as forecast theatre: polished dashboards, a competitor's intentions actively concealed, and advantage going to the firm that treats its plan as explicit, testable assumptions updated on a schedule.
examples_extra: At the Battle of Midway in June 1942, both fleets fought inside deep fog. American codebreakers had partly read Japanese intentions, yet Admiral Nagumo still had to decide about rearming aircraft with incomplete reports about American carriers. Delayed and conflicting scout information left Japanese decks crowded with fuelled aircraft when American dive-bombers arrived, and Japan lost four aircraft carriers in the battle.

Quibi, the short-video streaming service founded by Jeffrey Katzenberg and Meg Whitman, launched in April 2020 after raising about 1.75 billion dollars, then announced its shutdown that October. Its core assumption, that commuters would pay for premium short episodes on phones, collided with pandemic lockdowns and free rivals. The episode shows commercial fog: enormous resources could not substitute for testing the demand assumption cheaply first.
misconceptions: Many people think fog of war means nothing can be known — in reality, much is knowable with effort; fog describes the irreducible remainder after homework is done.
Many people think more information always reduces fog — in reality, unreliable or contradictory information can increase false confidence and deepen the fog.
Many people think fog is mainly a battlefield problem — in reality, any launch, hire, or investment made against an adapting opponent happens inside the same uncertainty.
practice: Known-assumed-unknown audit: For a current decision, draw three columns labelled known, assumed, and unknown, and force every key claim into one column in writing. Circle the single assumption whose failure would hurt most, then design the cheapest test that could check it this week.

Design one cheap probe: Before your next expensive commitment, define a small reversible action whose only purpose is to buy information, such as a limited release or a paid pilot, and write in advance what result would make you proceed, change course, or stop.
cross_domain: Medicine works in fog whenever a doctor treats from symptoms and partial test results, which is why good clinicians keep a differential diagnosis rather than marrying the first explanation, and order the test that best separates the dangerous possibilities. Weather forecasting institutionalises the same humility: ensemble models run many slightly different futures and report probabilities, so decisions are built around ranges and worst cases instead of one confident predicted line on a map.

quote.text: No plan survives first contact with the enemy.
quote.author: Helmuth von Moltke the Elder
quote.source: Popular shortened form of the argument in Moltke's 1871 essay 'On Strategy', where he held that no plan extends with certainty beyond the first encounter with the enemy's main force.

name_vi: Chiến tranh bất đối xứng
definition: Asymmetric warfare is when the weaker side wins by refusing the stronger sides preferred contest and attacking where strength does not apply.
mechanism: Superior size, budget, and technology only matter inside the contest they were built for. The weaker side changes the arena: speed instead of mass, niche instead of breadth, patience instead of direct battle. This forces the strong side to defend everywhere while the weak concentrate anywhere. Costs invert too, because the strong spend heavily maintaining dominance while the weak spend little imposing those costs.
classic_example: During the American Revolutionary War, colonial forces could not match British regulars in conventional European style battle. George Washington preserved his army, struck selectively, and relied on local knowledge and French support, winning at Yorktown in 1781. Avoiding decisive battle on British terms turned inferior numbers into a winning strategy over time.
modern_example: A solo creator competes asymmetrically against a media company by being faster, more personal, and focused on one narrow audience the giant ignores. She cannot win on production budget, so she wins on intimacy and speed. Small software teams do the same, serving one painful niche deeply instead of cloning the market leaders full feature list.
failure_mode: Asymmetry is not magic: if the strong side adapts, copies the tactic, or simply outlasts you, the edge disappears. Refusing the main contest also means giving up its prizes, which fails if you actually needed scale or legitimacy. And some gaps are real; no clever angle lets the hopelessly under resourced win every time.
apply_steps: Name the contest the stronger rival wants
Refuse it, choose ground favoring your strengths
Attack where their size becomes a burden
Keep costs low while raising theirs

situation_notes.stronger-colleague-threat: Asymmetric thinking reveals you beat a stronger colleague by owning a different valued skill, not by outworking their specialty.
situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: A niche is asymmetric ground where a giants broad focus becomes weakness and your narrow depth becomes strength.
situation_notes.competitor-price-war: Refusing a giants price war and competing on service or specificity is asymmetry applied to a losing contest.

case_seeds: Washington preserving his army and winning at Yorktown in 1781
source_ref: Sun Tzu — The Art of War
origin: The practice is ancient and is implicit in Sun Tzu's Art of War, traditionally dated to the fifth century BCE in China, which advises avoiding strength and striking emptiness. The modern analytical term was popularised by political scientist Andrew J. R. Mack in his 1975 article Why Big Nations Lose Small Wars, which asked why powerful states kept failing against far weaker opponents in the twentieth century.
mechanism_deep: Asymmetry works because power is specific, not general. A large army, budget, or brand is a bundle of capabilities optimised for one kind of contest, and much of that bundle becomes dead weight when the contest changes shape. Heavy forces need supply lines worth attacking, large firms need mass markets, and prestigious rivals must protect a reputation a small challenger does not have to defend. The weaker side therefore chooses metrics the strong cannot adopt without harming themselves: a guerrilla's patience is unusable by a government facing elections, and a free product is impossible for a rival whose shareholders expect margins. The strong side's adaptation problem is structural, not stupid: copying the weak side's method usually means cannibalising the assets that made it strong, so responses arrive late and half-hearted. But asymmetry decays. Once the weak side's arena matters, the strong side will invest, buy the challenger, or change the rules, and the refuge closes. The weaker side must therefore convert temporary asymmetry into something durable, such as loyal community, specialised knowledge, or an unmatched cost base. In business this means serving an overlooked segment so specifically that a generalist's broader offer feels clumsy, while refusing the incumbent's advertising, pricing, or feature war.
examples_extra: In the Winter War of 1939 to 1940, Finland faced a Soviet invasion with far fewer men and almost no tanks or aircraft by comparison. Finnish ski troops used forests, snow, and local knowledge to cut Soviet columns into isolated pockets, called motti, and destroyed them piecemeal. Finland inflicted disproportionate losses and preserved its independence, although it still ceded territory in the March 1940 peace settlement.

Dollar Shave Club, launched in the United States in 2012, attacked Gillette's retail razor model asymmetrically with a cheap subscription, direct shipping, and a single low-budget viral video featuring founder Michael Dubin. It refused the shelf-space and advertising contest Procter and Gamble was built to win. The challenge grew large enough that Unilever acquired Dollar Shave Club in 2016 for a reported one billion dollars.
misconceptions: Many people think asymmetric warfare means any clever trick by an underdog — in reality, it means systematically refusing the strong side's preferred contest and changing the arena itself.
Many people think the weaker side wins because it is braver — in reality, it wins by making the strong side's advantages irrelevant or expensive to use.
Many people think asymmetry is a permanent shield — in reality, it erodes as soon as the strong side adapts, buys in, or changes the rules of the arena.
practice: Arena audit: Write down the contest your strongest rival wants you to fight, in one sentence, then list three properties of that contest that favour them. Choose one property to invert this month, for example speed instead of scale or depth in one niche instead of breadth, and define what success there would look like.

Cost inversion check: List what your rival must spend to respond to your next move, and what the same move costs you. Prefer, for the next quarter, only moves where their response costs at least several times yours, and write down why the gap exists.
cross_domain: Open-source software competes asymmetrically when volunteer projects such as Linux, first released in 1991, give away what commercial rivals must sell, turning the rival's revenue model into a constraint. Retail shows the same shape when a single-product direct-to-consumer brand undercuts a department store not by matching its range, but by removing rent, intermediaries, and inventory breadth that the store cannot shed without ceasing to be itself.

name_vi: Địa thế cao và địa hình
definition: High ground and terrain mean the physical or structural setting of a contest shapes the outcome as much as the strength of the competitors.
mechanism: Elevation gives visibility, easier defense, and gravity assisted attack, while the defender below spends extra energy on every move. Terrain channels movement, creates choke points, and decides which weapons and tactics even function. Skilled commanders therefore choose or shape ground before fighting. In broader terms, distribution channels, timing, regulations, and platform rules are terrain that quietly decide whose effort counts double and whose counts half.
classic_example: At the Battle of Agincourt in 1415, English forces under Henry V chose a narrow muddy field bordered by woods. French knights, crowded and slowed by mud, could not use their superior numbers, and English longbowmen shot into the compressed mass. Terrain and weather neutralized a much larger army and produced a famous English victory.
modern_example: A job candidate who applies through a warm referral fights from high ground compared with identical resumes arriving through a crowded portal. In business, owning the channel customers already trust, like a top search position or a retailers shelf, gives the same structural lift. Choosing where you compete often matters more than trying harder where you stand.
failure_mode: Terrain advantages are real but not permanent: opponents can refuse battle, go around, or wait for conditions to change, and technology regularly flattens old high ground. Overvaluing a position also breeds complacency, as many dominant firms learned when digital distribution erased their shelf space edge. Never confuse favorable ground with guaranteed victory or skip improving actual capability.
apply_steps: Assess the terrain before committing effort
Choose channels where your strengths count double
Avoid attacking entrenched rivals uphill directly
Reassess terrain when technology or rules change

situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: Terrain thinking reveals that some niches are uphill fights against entrenched distribution, while others give newcomers natural elevation.
situation_notes.salary-negotiation: Negotiating after delivering visible results and holding another offer is high ground that raises pay without harder arguing.
situation_notes.presenting-to-leadership: Presenting on leaderships home terrain, their metrics and current priorities, makes the same proposal land far more easily.

case_seeds: Henry V using muddy narrow ground at Agincourt in 1415
source_ref: Sun Tzu — The Art of War
origin: Sun Tzu's Art of War, traditionally dated to the fifth century BCE in China, devotes sustained attention to ground, classifying terrain types and arguing that a commander must study them before battle rather than discover them during it. Later military writers from Vegetius in Roman times onward repeated the principle, and modern strategists extended terrain to include channels, regulations, and platform rules that shape a contest before it begins.
mechanism_deep: Terrain multiplies or divides effort before skill enters the picture, so it is often misread as a difference in talent. A defender on a slope spends less energy, sees further, and forces the attacker to arrive tired and disordered, so the same soldier is worth more in one position than another. Choke points cap how much of a larger force can engage at once, quietly deleting a numerical advantage without defeating it. Terrain is also partly chosen and partly made: commanders choose where to offer battle, and businesses spend years building distribution, search rankings, default settings, and relationships that function as elevated ground long before any single campaign starts. Opponents counter in three standard ways: they refuse to attack and wait, they move around the strong position and make it irrelevant, or technology changes the value of the ground itself, as aircraft devalued hilltop fortresses and e-commerce devalued premium retail frontage. That third counter is the one incumbents miss, because ground that has paid them for decades feels permanent rather than temporary. The model therefore asks two questions: where does my existing strength count double, and is that ground rising or eroding? Modest effort occupying rising ground compounds quietly; heroic effort defending eroding ground is usually wasted.
examples_extra: At Thermopylae in 480 BCE, a Greek force led by the Spartan king Leonidas held a narrow pass against the larger invading army of the Persian king Xerxes. The confined ground prevented the Persians from deploying their numbers and let Greek hoplites fight on equal terms for days. The position fell only after a local path over the hills was revealed, letting Persian troops attack from the rear.

Sam Walton opened the first Walmart store in Rogers, Arkansas, in 1962 and deliberately built in small rural towns that large discount rivals considered too small to bother with. That neglected terrain gave Walmart loyal customers, cheap land, and little direct competition while it refined its logistics system. By the time rivals contested the same towns, Walmart's distribution network had turned its early ground into a durable advantage.
misconceptions: Many people think high ground guarantees victory — in reality, it only multiplies effort; a careless or outnumbered defender can still lose it, and opponents can refuse to attack it.
Many people think terrain is only physical geography — in reality, distribution, defaults, regulations, and trusted channels are terrain that decide whose effort counts in modern contests.
Many people think good ground lasts forever — in reality, technology and rule changes regularly flatten old high ground, as e-commerce did to premium shop frontage.
practice: Terrain map: For your main goal, list the five arenas where you could compete, and score each on how much it multiplies your specific strengths and how crowded the top already is. Move one concrete activity this month from your lowest-scoring arena to your highest-scoring one.

Ground erosion check: Name the one positional advantage you rely on most, then write what technology or rule change would make it worthless and when that could plausibly happen. Decide one small investment that would still pay off if that ground disappeared.
cross_domain: Retail location economics is terrain theory in civilian dress: a shop on the natural walking route between a station and offices receives demand it did not create, while an identical shop one street away must buy every visit with advertising. Search and platform markets behave identically, where the first result or the default app collects a disproportionate share of attention regardless of small quality differences further down the list.

name_vi: Hậu cần
definition: Logistics is the unglamorous work of supplying food, fuel, equipment, and people to the right place in time for plans to actually happen.
mechanism: Armies and organizations consume resources continuously, so capability at the front is capped by supply behind it. Distance multiplies cost, stockouts stop operations regardless of courage or talent, and excess stock wastes money and mobility. Good logistics is invisible when it works, which is why amateurs celebrate strategy while professionals study supply. The model generalizes: any ambitions ceiling is set by the support system feeding it.
classic_example: Napoleons invasion of Russia in 1812 collapsed largely through logistics rather than battle. His Grande Armee advanced faster than its food, fodder, and supply wagons could follow across vast distances, and Russian forces retreated while destroying supplies. Hunger, disease, and the winter retreat destroyed most of the army before decisive combat did.
modern_example: A creators output collapses without logistics: ideas captured, footage organized, editing time protected, and publishing scheduled. Talent is visible in the video, but the supply chain behind it decides whether videos appear weekly or randomly. Similarly, a students exam result depends on sleep, materials ready, and revision scheduled, not only intelligence on the day.
failure_mode: Logistics thinking becomes a trap when preparation expands endlessly and substitutes for action; stockpiling tools, courses, and systems can feel like progress while nothing ships. It also has diminishing returns once supply is reliably sufficient. The model warns against ignoring support systems, not against ever accepting a calculated shortage for the sake of speed.
apply_steps: List what your plan consumes daily
Find which supply runs out first
Build boring systems before ambitious pushes
Check logistics before blaming talent or strategy

situation_notes.scaling-decision: Logistics reveals that scaling breaks supply systems first, so support capacity must grow ahead of demand, not behind it.
situation_notes.chronic-procrastination: Procrastination often has a logistics cause, like missing materials or unclear next steps, rather than a motivation failure.
situation_notes.users-but-no-revenue: Users without revenue frequently trace to broken logistics of payment, onboarding, or support rather than lack of demand.

case_seeds: Napoleons Grande Armee collapsing in Russia in 1812 through supply failure
origin: Swiss-born theorist Antoine-Henri Jomini, who served under Napoleon and later in Russian service, gave logistics its modern military definition in his Summary of the Art of War, published in French in 1838. Jomini treated logistics as the practical art of moving armies, arranging marches, camps, and supply. The word itself derives from the French logis, lodging, reflecting its roots in quartering and provisioning troops.
mechanism_deep: Logistics governs outcomes through rates and distances rather than dramatic events. An army consumes food, fuel, and ammunition every day whether it fights or not, so its effective strength is a flow problem: what arrives per day minus what is consumed per day, stretched over the length of the supply line. Each extra mile taxes that flow, because transport consumes fuel and breaks down, which is why offensives culminate rather than simply stop: the spearhead outruns its support until it must halt within reach of the enemy. Strategy is discussed in terms of intentions, but logistics quietly decides, months before the famous battle, which intentions are physically available. Opponents therefore attack logistics rather than strength, targeting bridges, depots, ports, and repair capacity, because destroying supply destroys every unit it feeds at once. Organisations have identical physics with different nouns: cash is supply, staff time is transport capacity, and every new commitment lengthens the line. Growth is a logistics event before it is a triumph, since doubling output roughly doubles consumption of support, coordination, and working capital. The discipline is sequencing: build the depot before the offensive, hire support before the sales push, and find the supply that runs out first, because that constraint sets the plan's real ceiling.
examples_extra: During the Berlin Airlift of 1948 to 1949, Western Allies supplied West Berlin by air after the Soviet Union blockaded road, rail, and canal access in June 1948. American and British aircraft flew hundreds of flights a day at peak, delivering food and coal, more than two million tons in total according to commonly cited figures. Logistics, organised as an industrial system, defeated a blockade without a battle.

Amazon launched its Prime membership in 2005 with fast shipping as the promise, which forced the company to build fulfilment centres, inventory placement, and delivery systems years ahead of demand. Rivals could copy the visible offer of quick delivery only by first copying the invisible supply network behind it. The episode shows logistics as strategy: the customer-facing advantage was simply the surface of a supply system competitors lacked.
misconceptions: Many people think logistics is a support detail beneath strategy — in reality, supply rates and distances decide which strategies are physically possible at all.
Many people think logistics failure means running out completely — in reality, operations usually fail earlier, when supply arrives too slowly, in the wrong place, or in the wrong mix.
Many people think more stock is always safer — in reality, excess stock consumes cash, space, and mobility, and can hide problems until they become expensive.
practice: Find your first empty supply: Take a current project and list everything it consumes weekly, including money, your hours, other people's hours, and materials. Identify which item runs out first if the project doubled, and write one concrete action that extends that specific supply before you expand anything else.

Audit one supply line end to end: Pick a recurring output, such as a weekly post or report, and trace every input it needs from first idea to delivery, noting where delays actually occur. Remove or pre-position the single input that caused the most recent delay.
cross_domain: Hospital care runs on logistics when operating theatres sit idle waiting for sterile instruments, blood, or a free recovery bed, so a surgeon's skill is capped by supply systems most patients never see. Restaurants show the same structure in miniature: preparation done before service, the mise en place, decides whether a kitchen survives a busy night, and no amount of cooking talent rescues a station whose ingredients were never delivered or prepared.

name_vi: Răn đe và hủy diệt lẫn nhau (MAD)
definition: Deterrence stops an attack by making its cost unacceptable, and mutually assured destruction is deterrence where both sides can destroy each other even after being hit.
mechanism: Deterrence works on the opponents decision, not their capability: they must believe you can retaliate, will retaliate, and that the damage outweighs any gain. A survivable second strike force makes the threat credible even after a first attack. Communication matters as much as weapons, because an unknown deterrent deters nothing. The logic creates stability through fear, provided both sides are rational and control their forces.
classic_example: During the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union each built nuclear forces large and dispersed enough to survive a first strike and retaliate massively. The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 brought the logic to its most dangerous test, yet both sides stepped back. No direct war between the superpowers followed despite decades of rivalry.
modern_example: In everyday life, clear consequences deter bad behavior better than vague warnings: a contract with real penalties, a freelancer who stops work when invoices go unpaid, a platform that bans repeat abusers. The threat only works if the other side believes you will actually enforce it, which is why bluffing repeatedly destroys deterrence faster than having no policy.
failure_mode: Deterrence fails with irrational, desperate, or misinformed opponents, and through accidents or false alarms that trigger the very destruction it prevents. It also fails when threats are not believed or when punishment would hurt the punisher too much to be credible. In personal disputes, heavy deterrence talk escalates conflict and poisons relationships that cooperation would serve better.
apply_steps: Define the behavior you want to prevent
Make the consequence clear before it happens
Ensure your threat is credible and proportionate
Leave the opponent a face saving exit

situation_notes.saying-no: Deterrence reveals that a clear, calm consequence stated once prevents more boundary violations than repeated emotional refusals later.
situation_notes.negotiating-price: Price deterrence works when walking away is genuinely possible, because the other side prices against your credible alternative.
situation_notes.team-conflict: In team conflict, proportionate stated consequences deter repeated bad behavior better than silent resentment or sudden explosions.

case_seeds: Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962
United States and Soviet Union nuclear standoff during the Cold War
origin: American strategist Bernard Brodie argued in The Absolute Weapon, published in 1946, that after nuclear weapons the chief purpose of military establishments must shift from winning wars to averting them. During the 1960s, United States Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara formalised assured destruction as doctrine, and the label mutually assured destruction, with its acronym MAD, became the popular name for a balance based on survivable retaliation.
mechanism_deep: Deterrence operates entirely inside the opponent's calculation, making it a psychological and communicative system wearing a military costume. Three conditions must hold simultaneously: the capability to inflict the threatened cost, the credibility that you would actually do so, and clear communication of both, since a threat the opponent has not understood deters nothing. Credibility is usually the fragile condition, because carrying out the threat often damages the threatener too, and a rational opponent knows it. Survivable second-strike forces solve part of this problem by removing the temptation of a disarming first strike: if retaliation is guaranteed even after absorbing an attack, striking first buys nothing, and stability emerges from both sides being unable to escape punishment. Yet the same logic creates characteristic pathologies. Stability at the top can license aggression at lower levels, as each side probes where the threshold really is. Opponents also adapt by working around the deterrent, using proxies, cyber operations, and gradual steps each too small to justify the threatened response, a salami pattern formal deterrence handles badly. In commercial life the same conditions explain why some boundaries are theatre: a late-payment clause deters only when the supplier has stopped work before, can survive losing the client, and states the consequence in advance.
examples_extra: India and Pakistan both conducted nuclear tests in May 1998, and fought the limited Kargil War in the Kargil district of Kashmir in 1999. India restricted its counteroffensive largely to its own side of the Line of Control, and international pressure for restraint was intense. Scholars still debate how far nuclear deterrence limited the war, but Kargil is the standard case of fighting conducted in the shadow of possible escalation.

The smartphone patent wars that began with Apple's lawsuit against Samsung in the United States in 2011 spread across many countries, with countersuits by Samsung and other manufacturers. Large patent portfolios functioned partly as deterrents, since suing a rival invited retaliation against your own products. The Apple and Samsung dispute was settled in 2018, after years in which mutual legal exposure shaped behaviour as much as any single verdict.
misconceptions: Many people think deterrence is about being stronger — in reality, it is about the opponent believing that retaliation is capable, credible, and clearly communicated; unperceived strength deters nothing.
Many people think mutually assured destruction means nobody is ever attacked at any level — in reality, stability at the top can encourage limited probes and proxy conflict underneath the threshold.
Many people think a threat works better if it is vague and frightening — in reality, deterrence needs a specific behaviour, a proportionate consequence, and a believable willingness to carry it out.
practice: Credibility audit: Take one boundary you rely on, such as a payment term or a deadline, and score it honestly on capability, credibility, and communication. Fix the weakest of the three this week, usually by stating the consequence in writing before the situation arises, not during a dispute.

Threshold rehearsal: For a recurring conflict, write down in advance the exact behaviour that triggers your response, the proportionate response itself, and the exit you will leave the other side. Compare this written version with how you actually reacted last time and note the gaps.
cross_domain: Cybersecurity uses deterrence when organisations publicise attribution capability, prosecution referrals, and rapid recovery, aiming to convince attackers that an intrusion will be costly and unprofitable rather than merely difficult. Contract law runs on the same machinery: liquidated damages clauses rarely exist to be collected, they exist so that both parties can predict the cost of breach in advance and quietly choose to perform instead.

name_vi: Chia để trị
definition: Divide and conquer wins by splitting a larger opponent or problem into smaller parts that can be defeated or solved one at a time.
mechanism: A united opponent pools strength, information, and morale, while a divided one cannot coordinate or support its parts. Splitting works through geography, timing, conflicting interests, or simply sequencing: handle one segment while others cannot interfere. In problem solving, the same logic applies because subproblems are simpler, testable, and reusable. The gains compound when each solved part weakens resistance in the next.
classic_example: Julius Caesar conquered Gaul between 58 and 50 BC partly by exploiting divisions among Gallic tribes, allying with some against others and defeating them in sequence. When Vercingetorix finally united many tribes against Rome, Caesar still prevailed at Alesia in 52 BC, but the earlier years show how disunity let a smaller force absorb a large region piece by piece.
modern_example: A huge intimidating project becomes manageable when divided into a first deliverable, a second milestone, and a cleanup phase, each finishable in days. Negotiators use the same principle constructively by settling easy issues first, shrinking the contested remainder. Conversely, teams that let stakeholders negotiate separately without a shared picture get divided by whoever controls the sequence.
failure_mode: Some problems cannot be split without destroying what matters: relationships, ecosystems, and tightly integrated systems break when carved naively. Dividing people also has ethical and practical costs, breeding distrust that outlasts the victory. And an opponent who notices the strategy can reunite with greater urgency. Check the seams are real before assuming division helps.
apply_steps: Find the natural seams in this problem
Sequence parts so early wins help later ones
Prevent solved parts from recombining into trouble
Keep a map of the whole while dividing

situation_notes.learning-from-zero: Divide and conquer reveals that learning from zero works by mastering one subskill fully before combining it with others.
situation_notes.team-conflict: Team conflict shrinks when you separate the people, issues, and timing, instead of fighting one merged emotional battle.
situation_notes.decision-under-time-pressure: Under time pressure, splitting the decision into urgent and deferrable parts prevents the whole problem feeling equally immediate.

case_seeds: Caesar exploiting Gallic tribal divisions from 58 to 50 BC
source_ref: Sun Tzu — The Art of War
origin: The maxim divide et impera, divide and rule, is traditionally associated with Philip II of Macedon in the fourth century BCE, who kept Greek city-states divided while Macedonian power grew, and it later described Roman practice in Italy and beyond. The attribution of the exact Latin phrase is debated by historians, but the policy it names, profiting from a rival coalition's divisions, is documented throughout ancient and colonial history.
mechanism_deep: Division works because a coalition's strength is not the sum of its parts but the product of their coordination. United opponents share information, reinforce each other's weak points, and present a single negotiating position; divided opponents must watch each other as well as you and cannot agree who sacrifices first. The mechanism targets relationships, not just numbers: sequencing, separate negotiations, and selective alliances raise the other side's cost of coordinating while lowering your cost of dealing with one piece at a time. Division also has a built-in expiry date, because a visible pattern of divide and rule teaches the remaining parts to unite urgently against you. In problem solving the same structure appears without an adversary: a large problem resists direct attack because its parts interact, so you cut along seams where interaction is weakest, solve subproblems that can be tested independently, and recombine results you can check piece by piece. The failure mode is symmetric in both worlds: cut along a false seam and the pieces either cannot be solved alone or cannot be put back together, and with people the recombination cost is paid in lasting distrust. In business the constructive version is honest segmentation: serve one customer group completely before the next.
examples_extra: At the Battle of Plassey on 23 June 1757, Robert Clive of the British East India Company faced the much larger army of Siraj ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal. Clive had secretly allied with Mir Jafar, a senior commander in the Nawab's army, whose troops largely held back during the battle. Bengal's divided leadership turned a risky engagement into a victory that opened India to expanding Company rule.

Amazon, founded by Jeff Bezos in 1994, divided the problem of retail by conquering one category first: books, chosen because they were easy to catalogue, ship, and compare. Only after mastering inventory data, reviews, and fulfilment on books did Amazon expand category by category into the general store it later became. Sequencing the problem let a small company absorb a huge market in pieces it could actually finish.
misconceptions: Many people think divide and conquer just means splitting anything into pieces — in reality, it only works when you cut along real seams where the parts interact weakly.
Many people think dividing opponents is always clever — in reality, once the pattern is noticed it gives the other side an urgent reason to unite against you.
Many people think solving the parts solves the whole — in reality, tightly integrated problems can be destroyed by naive division, and recombination has its own cost.
practice: Seam-finding exercise: Take your largest current project and draw its parts as boxes, marking which parts genuinely depend on each other. Choose the box with the fewest dependencies, define what finished means for it in one sentence, and complete only that box this week before touching the rest.

Coalition check: Before a negotiation involving several stakeholders, write what each party wants, what each fears, and where their interests conflict without you. Use that map to sequence conversations so early agreements make later ones easier, rather than letting others sequence you.
cross_domain: Software engineering institutionalises the principle in modular design and debugging: a failing system is bisected until the faulty component is isolated, because a defect that resists whole-system inspection surrenders quickly to systematic halving. Medicine uses the same cut in differential diagnosis, separating possible causes by body system and testing them in sequence, so a frightening symptom becomes a series of smaller questions each with a decisive test.

name_vi: Chiến lược Fabian (tránh giao chiến, làm mòn đối thủ)
definition: The Fabian strategy avoids decisive battle against a stronger enemy, instead harassing, delaying, and exhausting them until the balance of strength shifts.
mechanism: A stronger opponent needs a quick decisive win to justify the cost of their campaign, while the weaker side needs only to survive and keep imposing costs. Refusing battle denies the enemy their advantage, stretches their supplies, and lets time, distance, and public patience work against them. The strategy demands discipline, because your own side constantly demands a heroic fight you would probably lose.
classic_example: Roman general Quintus Fabius Maximus faced Hannibal after devastating Roman defeats in the Second Punic War. Fabius shadowed the Carthaginian army, cut off foragers, and refused pitched battle, earning the nickname Cunctator, the Delayer. Romans initially mocked the caution, but after reckless aggression failed at Cannae in 216 BC, his approach became Romes long term path to outlasting Hannibal.
modern_example: A small brand competing against a funded rival uses Fabian logic by refusing a discount war it cannot afford, serving loyal customers profitably, and waiting while the rival burns cash on growth. Endurance is the weapon. Individuals do the same by declining every provocative argument at work, conserving energy and reputation while an aggressive colleague exhausts credibility.
failure_mode: Delay looks like cowardice or drift, and morale, funding, or political support may collapse before the enemy tires. Fabian strategy also surrenders initiative, so if time actually favors the opponent, waiting is suicide in slow motion. It requires an honest judgment that time is on your side, plus visible small wins to sustain your own sides patience.
apply_steps: Confirm time genuinely favors your side
Refuse the decisive contest you would lose
Impose small steady costs on the rival
Show your side small wins to sustain patience

situation_notes.competitor-price-war: Fabian strategy reveals that outlasting a price war profitably beats winning it, when the rivals burn rate exceeds yours.
situation_notes.down-30-percent-cut-or-hold: Holding through a decline is Fabian only when time genuinely heals the asset, not when delay avoids admitting error.
situation_notes.stronger-colleague-threat: Against a stronger colleague, refusing direct contests and accumulating quiet wins shifts standing without a battle you would lose.

case_seeds: Fabius delaying Hannibal during the Second Punic War
Cannae disaster in 216 BC vindicating Fabius caution
origin: Roman statesman Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus was appointed dictator in 217 BCE, after Hannibal destroyed Roman armies in the Second Punic War, and chose shadowing and delay over pitched battle. His nickname Cunctator, the Delayer, began as an insult and became an honour; the poet Ennius later wrote that one man, by delaying, restored the state to the Romans, a line quoted by Virgil and Cicero.
mechanism_deep: Fabian strategy is a bet about which side time taxes more heavily. The invader or market leader usually operates far from home, spends heavily to stay in the field, and needs a visible decisive result to justify the campaign. The delayer needs only to remain intact and keep collecting small advantages and forcing the stronger side to pay full price for every day without a decisive result. Morale is the real battlefield, and it cuts both ways: your own side experiences delay as humiliation and demands the glorious battle that would probably destroy it, so a Fabian commander must manufacture visible evidence of progress to buy political patience. The opponent adapts predictably, trying to provoke battle and attacking your legitimacy by calling delay cowardice. The strategy fails completely when its core bet is wrong, when the opponent's supply, funding, or patience is actually deeper than yours, because then delay is just a slower form of losing, and it also fails when endurance is never converted into a later offensive or settlement. In commercial life it fits refusing a subsidised rival's price war while keeping a profitable loyal core, but only when your burn rate is lower and your customers stay, checked in numbers rather than hoped.
examples_extra: After the British victory at the Battle of Long Island in August 1776, George Washington preserved the Continental Army through retreats across New Jersey rather than risking it in a decisive battle it would likely lose. His surprise counterstroke at Trenton on 26 December 1776 delivered the small, morale-saving victory Fabian logic requires. British commanders and later historians frequently described Washington's approach as Fabian in character.

In-N-Out Burger, founded in California in 1948 by Harry and Esther Snyder, expanded slowly, stayed privately owned, and refused the rapid franchising that built its fast-food rivals. While competitors funded fast growth and often took on debt and inconsistent franchise quality, In-N-Out protected a simple menu, company-owned stores, and loyal regional demand. Its patience turned endurance and consistency into a durable regional advantage rather than a quick national footprint.
misconceptions: Many people think Fabian strategy is just avoiding conflict — in reality, it is active delay combined with constant small costs imposed on the enemy and small wins shown to your own side.
Many people think delay always favours the defender — in reality, it only works when time genuinely taxes the opponent more than you, which must be checked rather than assumed.
Many people think Fabius was simply cautious by temperament — in reality, his delay was a calculated response to Hannibal's superiority in open battle after repeated Roman disasters.
practice: Time-favours-whom test: For a contest you are tempted to delay, write two columns listing what time costs your opponent each month and what it costs you, in money, morale, and options. Commit to the Fabian course only if their column is clearly heavier, and set a date to re-run the test.

Small-win schedule: If you choose delay, plan one visible, low-risk win every few weeks, such as a retained client, a published result, or a cost imposed on the rival, and record them in one place. If you cannot produce such wins, treat that as evidence the strategy is drift, not delay.
cross_domain: Investing shows Fabian logic when a patient holder keeps cash during an expensive market, refusing to compete for overpriced assets while leveraged buyers exhaust themselves, then buys when prices fall. Sport produced a famous version at the 1974 Rumble in the Jungle in Kinshasa, where Muhammad Ali absorbed George Foreman's punches on the ropes for rounds, letting the stronger puncher tire, before knocking him out in the eighth round.

name_vi: Tập trung lực lượng
definition: Concentration of force means massing your limited resources at one decisive point instead of spreading them evenly across every possible front.
mechanism: Outcomes at the point of contact depend on local superiority, not total resources. A smaller force concentrated beats a larger force dispersed, because each engagement happens where you are strongest and they are thinnest. Concentration also creates momentum: a breakthrough at one point unbalances the whole defense. The cost is deliberate weakness elsewhere, accepted as a calculated risk rather than spread thin failure everywhere.
classic_example: At the Battle of Austerlitz in December 1805, Napoleon deliberately weakened his right flank to lure Austrian and Russian forces south, then smashed their thinned center with concentrated troops. The allied army split in two and collapsed. The battle is still taught as a model of deception combined with massing force at the decisive point.
modern_example: A marketer with a small budget wins by dominating one channel and one audience instead of posting thinly everywhere. A student near exams concentrates on the highest weight topics rather than rereading everything equally. In both cases local superiority at the chosen point produces visible results that fund motivation and credibility for the next push.
failure_mode: Concentration gambles: if you pick the wrong point, you are maximally committed to an irrelevant target while real threats develop elsewhere. It also fails when the neglected fronts collapse before your breakthrough pays off. The model demands honest reconnaissance and a reserve, not just motivational advice to focus. Spreading is sometimes correct for defense, exploration, or learning.
apply_steps: Choose the one point that decides the outcome
Move resources there from lower value fronts
Accept calculated weakness elsewhere consciously
Keep a small reserve for surprises

situation_notes.scaling-decision: Concentration reveals that scaling everything at once dilutes force, while sequencing one decisive market creates momentum and proof.
situation_notes.what-to-learn-next: Learning next should concentrate on the single skill blocking your current goal, not spread across fashionable topics equally.
situation_notes.channel-not-growing: A channel grows when effort concentrates on one format and audience until breakthrough, instead of scattering across every trend.

case_seeds: Napoleon concentrating against the allied center at Austerlitz in 1805
origin: Clausewitz argued in On War, published in 1832, that superiority of numbers at the decisive point is the most common factor in victory, and Napoleon had built a career on the same practice a generation earlier. British engineer Frederick W. Lanchester gave the principle a mathematical form during the First World War in Aircraft in Warfare, published in 1916, where his equations modelled how concentrated aimed fire multiplies combat power.
mechanism_deep: Concentration exploits the fact that contests are decided locally and sequentially, not globally and simultaneously. A force spread evenly can be beaten in detail by an opponent who is weaker overall but stronger at each successive point of contact, because the dispersed side's unused strength elsewhere never participates in the engagements that decide the outcome. Momentum then converts one local win into systemic collapse: a breakthrough forces the defender to abandon prepared positions, commit reserves early, and defend a broken line, so later engagements start from worse odds than the numbers alone predict. The opponent's counters all refuse local inferiority: trading space for time until your force outruns its supply, attacking the weak fronts you deliberately stripped, or dispersing into targets too numerous and small for concentration to pay. Concentration is therefore inseparable from intelligence and timing: you must know which point is truly decisive, arrive before the opponent reinforces it, and accept that weakened fronts are real risks with real deadlines. In business the same geometry explains why a small firm dominating one town, segment, or use case can defeat a larger rival's thin presence there and fund the next concentration from the profits, while the identical budget spread across five fronts produces five respectable defeats.
examples_extra: At the Battle of Trafalgar on 21 October 1805, Admiral Horatio Nelson abandoned the parallel line of battle and sailed two British columns at the Franco-Spanish fleet. The plan concentrated British ships against part of the enemy line, breaking it into segments that could be fought separately at close range. Britain lost no ships and Nelson was killed, while the combined fleet lost many vessels and its freedom of action.

Apple concentrated extraordinary resources on the original iPhone, announced in January 2007, assigning top engineers and delaying other work to finish a single flagship product. Larger rivals such as Nokia and Microsoft spread effort across many models, operating systems, and carrier variants. Apple's local superiority in design, software, and marketing at one decisive point let it redefine the smartphone market from a position of initially small market share.
misconceptions: Many people think concentration of force just means working harder — in reality, it means deliberately weakening other fronts so one chosen point has overwhelming local superiority.

Many people think the side with more total resources wins — in reality, outcomes depend on superiority at the point and moment of contact, where a smaller concentrated force beats a larger dispersed one.
Many people think focus is always correct — in reality, concentration is a gamble that fails badly when the chosen point turns out not to be decisive or neglected fronts collapse first.
practice: Front inventory: List every project, channel, or commitment currently drawing your resources, then mark the single one whose success would most change your position this quarter. Move a named block of time or money from the two weakest fronts to that one, and write down what you are consciously accepting might fail.

Decisive-point test: Before your next push, write one sentence naming the exact customer, segment, or metric where you intend to be locally superior, and the evidence that this point decides the larger outcome. If you cannot write the sentence, spend a day on reconnaissance instead of spending resources.
cross_domain: Scientific research concentrates force when a field funds one flagship instrument, such as a major telescope or particle accelerator, instead of dividing the same money among dozens of underpowered projects, because some discoveries are only reachable above a threshold of capability. Firefighting applies the identical rule at a building fire, where commanders mass water and crews on the seat of the fire or on protecting one exposure, knowing that a little water everywhere saves nothing anywhere.

formula.expression: dA/dt = -beta * B,  dB/dt = -alpha * A
formula.variables: A and B are the sizes of two opposing forces; alpha is the effectiveness of force A against B, and beta is the effectiveness of force B against A, under aimed fire where every unit can engage. Under these conditions, fighting strength scales with effectiveness multiplied by the square of numbers.
formula.worked_example: Assume equal per-soldier effectiveness, so alpha = beta. A concentrated force of 100 has relative strength 100² = 10,000, while an opposing force of 50 has 50² = 2,500. The larger force has four times the fighting strength, not merely twice, illustrating why local concentration matters.

name_vi: Nghi binh / đánh lừa đối thủ
definition: Deception shapes what an opponent believes about your strength, position, or intentions so they prepare for the wrong contest and misplace their resources.
mechanism: Opponents act on their picture of reality, not reality itself, so corrupting that picture redirects their effort cheaply. Effective deception confirms what the target already suspects, uses consistent supporting details, and hides the real move behind the expected one. It buys disproportionate results because a fooled enemy concentrates in the wrong place voluntarily. The cost is complexity and the risk that your own side confuses the story with the truth.
classic_example: Before the Normandy landings of June 1944, Allied Operation Fortitude convinced German commanders that the main invasion would strike the Pas de Calais. A fictitious army group in Scotland and southeast England, fake radio traffic, and double agents sustained the story. German forces stayed positioned away from Normandy even after the real landings began, buying the Allies crucial time.
modern_example: In negotiation, revealing your true deadline and desperation invites the other side to wait you out, while calm pacing and a genuine alternative change their calculation. Companies hold back launch dates and roadmap details for the same reason. The ethical everyday version is privacy and misdirection about plans, not lying to partners who depend on your word.
failure_mode: Deception collapses when discovered, destroying trust far beyond the single contest, and it is inappropriate with allies, customers, and anyone owed honesty. Complex deceptions also fail internally when teams forget which story is false. Finally, smart opponents price in deception and verify, so tricks have a short shelf life and should never substitute for real capability.
apply_steps: Ask what your opponent currently believes
Protect information about your real intentions
Keep any misdirection simple and consistent
Never deceive partners who rely on your word

situation_notes.salary-negotiation: Deception awareness reveals that concealing desperation and deadlines protects your price, since employers negotiate against your perceived alternatives.
situation_notes.negotiating-price: Price negotiation rewards controlling information about your limits, while false claims discovered mid deal destroy trust and leverage.
situation_notes.online-arguments: Online arguments often involve staged provocations, so checking what reaction the poster wants prevents you playing their script.

case_seeds: Operation Fortitude deceiving Germany before Normandy in June 1944
source_ref: Sun Tzu — The Art of War
origin: Sun Tzu's Art of War, traditionally dated to the fifth century BCE in China, opens its first chapter, Laying Plans, with the claim that all warfare is based on deception, and then advises appearing weak when strong and inactive when ready to act. Deception is therefore not a late refinement of the text but its starting assumption: because opponents act on appearances, shaping appearances is a primary weapon.
mechanism_deep: Deception works because opponents cannot act on your reality, only on their estimate of it, and that estimate is built from signals you partly control. The most effective false picture is rarely a pure invention: it confirms what the target already believes, arrives through several apparently independent channels, and lets the target feel clever for believing it. Deception and self-deception are therefore partners; the target's own hopes and doctrines do most of the persuading, and the deceiver mainly supplies the evidence those hopes were waiting for. Every deception also has a logistics of its own: the story must stay consistent across visible preparations, communications, and human sources, often for months. Opponents counter with verification discipline, demanding physical evidence over reports, keeping reserves uncommitted until the real move reveals itself, and asking what they would do in your place. Once real action begins, deception's value decays within hours or days, so it must be timed to buy one specific advantage. In legitimate business the usable core is narrower: controlling the timing and framing of what you reveal, protecting negotiating information and launch plans, and remembering that careless transparency about deadlines or desperation is free intelligence for the other side.
examples_extra: In Operation Mincemeat in 1943, British intelligence placed a corpse, dressed as a Royal Marines officer called Major William Martin, off the coast of Spain carrying letters suggesting the Allies would invade Greece and Sardinia rather than Sicily. Spanish and German channels passed the documents upward, and German forces were redeployed accordingly. The real invasion of Sicily followed in July 1943 against a defender whose expectations had been deliberately misdirected.

Apple's first iPhone demonstration in January 2007 was a carefully controlled presentation rather than a free exploration of a finished product. As later reporting, notably by Fred Vogelstein, documented, the prototype was fragile and the demonstration followed a fixed sequence of actions, sometimes called the golden path, to avoid known crashes. The audience concluded the phone was nearly complete, shaping competitor and press expectations months before the June 2007 launch.
misconceptions: Many people think deception means telling one big lie — in reality, effective deception usually confirms what the target already suspects and supports it with many small, consistent details.
Many people think deception is a substitute for real strength — in reality, it only redirects the opponent's response; you still need real capability at the point where the truth is revealed.
Many people think being deceptive with everyone is smart — in reality, deceiving partners, customers, or your own team destroys the trust and coordination that future success depends on.
practice: Signal audit: List what a rival could learn about your next move from your public posts, job adverts, pricing pages, and deadlines this month. Remove or delay the one disclosure that gives away the most, and note which of your own conclusions about rivals rest on signals they could easily have staged.

Red-team your picture: Take a belief you hold about a competitor and write what evidence would exist if it were a deliberate false picture designed to attract you. Check one independent, preferably physical or financial, source before acting on the belief.
cross_domain: Cybersecurity builds deception into defence through honeypots, decoy servers and credentials that look valuable but are isolated and monitored, so an intruder reveals their tools and targets while touching nothing real. Nature arrived first: harmless species such as hoverflies carry the warning colours of wasps, borrowing a predator's learned caution, and anglerfish turn a lure into a false signal of food, each exploiting the same gap between signal and reality.

quote.text: All warfare is based on deception.
quote.author: Sun Tzu
quote.source: The Art of War, Chapter 1, Laying Plans

name_vi: Đánh vu hồi và bao vây
definition: Flanking attacks an opponent from the side or rear where they are weakest, while encirclement surrounds them so escape and supply become impossible.
mechanism: Defenses face one direction, so force arriving from an unexpected angle meets thinner resistance and creates panic disproportionate to its size. Encirclement compounds this by cutting supply and retreat, turning a strong position into a trap as resources run out. Both maneuvers require mobility, timing, and fixing the enemy frontally so they cannot turn. The principle generalizes: attack the unguarded assumption, channel, or customer segment rather than the fortified front.
classic_example: At Cannae in 216 BC, Hannibal arranged a deliberately yielding center and strong flanks that closed behind the advancing Roman army. The Romans, packed tightly and surrounded on all sides, could not use their numbers and suffered one of the worst defeats in their history. Cannae remains the most studied encirclement battle in military education worldwide.
modern_example: A startup flanks an incumbent by serving the overlooked segment the leader considers too small, building loyalty there, then expanding into the main market from a secured base. Attacking the leaders flagship customers head on would meet their full strength. Job seekers flank by entering through a contract project or adjacent role instead of the guarded front door of open applications.
failure_mode: Flanking forces can themselves be cut off if timing or communication fails, and encirclements demand more troops and coordination than most attackers actually have. In business, the overlooked flank is sometimes overlooked because it is genuinely unprofitable. Verify the weak side is weak because of neglect, not because there is nothing worth taking there.
apply_steps: Identify where the rivals defense faces away
Fix their attention on the expected front
Enter through the neglected segment or channel
Consolidate the flank before expanding further

situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: Flanking reveals that the best niche is often the incumbents neglected rear, valuable but undefended because their attention faces elsewhere.
situation_notes.considering-job-change: Changing jobs through an adjacent role or project flanks the guarded application process where hundreds compete head on.
situation_notes.competitor-copied-you: When copied at the front, flanking into a new segment or channel restores advantage instead of fighting over copied ground.

case_seeds: Hannibal encircling the Roman army at Cannae in 216 BC
source_ref: Sun Tzu — The Art of War
origin: Theban general Epaminondas pioneered oblique tactics at the Battle of Leuctra in 371 BCE, massing his best troops on one wing to crush the strongest Spartan flank before the rest of the line decided the battle. Encirclement as an ideal was later perfected in practice by Hannibal at Cannae in 216 BCE, and modern German doctrine in the twentieth century formalised the encirclement battle as the Kesselschlacht, the cauldron battle.
mechanism_deep: A defence is an argument made in one direction: weapons, attention, reserves, and morale are arranged to meet the expected attack, so force arriving from the flank finds defenders whose entire preparation points the wrong way. Turning to face it takes time and creates disorder, so the psychological effect is out of proportion to the attacking force. Encirclement adds a clock to that shock: a surrounded force may still be strong, but its food, ammunition, and medical capacity deplete on a fixed schedule while the attacker's supply continues, so time itself becomes a weapon. The manoeuvre's demands explain its rarity: the flanking force needs mobility, concealment, and precise timing, the frontal force must fix the enemy without being destroyed, and a failed encirclement leaves the attacker split into parts that can be defeated in detail. Opponents counter by refusing a fixed front, keeping mobile reserves behind the flanks, and breaking out early before the ring hardens. In markets the translation is segment geometry: an incumbent's sales force, pricing, and product design face its largest customers, so a challenger entering through the segment the incumbent literally does not look at gains time to grow strong before heavier, slower machinery can turn around.
examples_extra: In Operation Bagration, launched on 22 June 1944, Soviet forces attacked Germany's Army Group Centre in Belarus behind extensive deception about where the main blow would fall. Coordinated breakthroughs on multiple axes produced deep advances and large encirclements around Vitebsk, Bobruisk, and Minsk. Within weeks Army Group Centre had effectively been destroyed as a coherent formation, in one of the most complete encirclement campaigns of the Second World War.

Nintendo launched the Wii console in November 2006 against Sony's PlayStation 3 and Microsoft's Xbox 360, which were fighting frontally over graphics power and high-definition specifications. Nintendo flanked that contest with motion controls and simple games aimed at families and casual players who had been ignored by the power race. The Wii sold over one hundred million units, proving the neglected flank was a mass market, not a leftover.
misconceptions: Many people think flanking just means attacking from the side — in reality, it requires fixing the enemy's attention frontally and arriving where their preparation, reserves, and morale are pointed the wrong way.
Many people think encirclement wins by immediate destruction — in reality, it often wins by cutting supply and escape so time and depletion defeat a force that is still strong on paper.

Many people think an overlooked market segment is automatically a good flank — in reality, some segments are neglected because they are genuinely unprofitable, so the flank must be verified, not assumed.
practice: Flank map: Draw your strongest rival as an arrow and write which customers, channels, and assumptions their organisation faces toward. List what sits behind that arrow, the segments and needs they monitor least, and pick one to test with a small offer this month.

Encirclement risk check: For your own position, list your supply lines in business form: cash, key supplier, key platform, and key person. Mark any line a rival or platform change could cut alone, and build one alternative for the most exposed line this quarter.
cross_domain: Retail strategy shows flanking when hard discounters such as Aldi, which expanded internationally from its German base after the Second World War, attacked supermarkets not on range or experience but on a narrow front of limited assortment and very low prices that full-range stores could not match without breaking their model. Chess teaches the same geometry at small scale, where an attack on a weak square behind a pawn chain can decide a game whose centre looks completely solid.

name_vi: Chiến tranh du kích
definition: Guerrilla warfare uses small mobile groups, ambush, and local support to wear down a stronger occupier who cannot find a decisive battle to win.
mechanism: Guerrillas trade territory for time, striking supply lines and isolated posts, then dispersing into terrain and populations the enemy cannot easily search. The occupier must defend everywhere, spends heavily, and often alienates locals through heavy handed responses, which recruits more guerrillas. Victory comes politically, when the stronger sides cost and patience run out, not from destroying its army in open combat.
classic_example: During the Vietnam War, Viet Cong and North Vietnamese forces used tunnels, jungle terrain, ambushes, and extensive supply trails to offset American firepower. Despite heavy losses, they sustained the conflict until United States political will ended, and Saigon fell in 1975. The war became the defining modern case study of guerrilla strategy against a superpower.
modern_example: Independent creators and tiny brands compete guerrilla style: quick experiments, community intimacy, rapid replies, and niche ambushes of trending topics that big slow organizations cannot match. They win attention without buying it, retreating from any format that stops working. The method suits anyone whose advantages are speed, authenticity, and local knowledge rather than budget.
failure_mode: Guerrilla methods rarely deliver quick decisive results and can drag on for years, exhausting your own side. They also struggle to hold gains: taking a market or position still requires conventional strength eventually. If the stronger opponent wins local support or simply refuses to leave, the strategy stalls. It is a survival and harassment system, not a complete growth plan.
apply_steps: Stay mobile, avoid the rivals strongest ground
Strike small winnable targets for momentum
Build local support as your supply base
Convert endurance into negotiation or expansion later

situation_notes.channel-not-growing: Guerrilla thinking reveals that small channels win through rapid experiments and community closeness, not by imitating big channels production scale.
situation_notes.competitor-price-war: In a price war, guerrilla tactics shift competition to speed, service, and community where the giants cost advantage cannot follow.
situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: A guerrilla niche strategy picks terrain you know intimately and giants cannot patrol, making local knowledge your supply line.

case_seeds: Viet Cong guerrilla campaign culminating in the fall of Saigon in 1975
origin: The word guerrilla, Spanish for little war, entered wide use during the Peninsular War of 1808 to 1814, when Spanish irregular bands harassed Napoleon Bonaparte's occupying armies in Spain. The method was later systematised in writing by Mao Zedong, whose On Guerrilla Warfare appeared in 1937 during China's war with Japan, arguing that guerrilla forces must root themselves in the population to survive against a stronger enemy.
mechanism_deep: Guerrilla warfare converts the occupier's strength into a coverage problem. Regular forces concentrate around cities, roads, and their own bases, leaving the countryside, the night, and the intervals between patrols ungoverned, and the guerrilla lives in those gaps. Each ambush is militarily small but politically expensive, because the occupier must respond everywhere, spend heavily on protection, and govern a population whose cooperation it needs, while its own heavy responses keep damaging that cooperation. This recruitment loop is the model's engine: repression intended to end resistance manufactures the grievances and information networks that sustain it, so the stronger side can win most engagements and still lose the campaign. Time is therefore the guerrilla's main weapon and main cost; survival itself is progress, because every year raises the occupier's financial and political bill. Modern states counter with population protection, local allies, intelligence penetration, and reforms that separate guerrillas from their support, confirming that the decisive terrain is allegiance, not ground. For a small business or creator the honest translation keeps the structure and drops the romance: stay too mobile and community-embedded for a large rival to target profitably, strike only at niches you can actually win, treat community trust as your supply line, and plan how endurance converts into a durable position.
examples_extra: During the Second World War, Yugoslav Partisans under Josip Broz Tito fought German, Italian, and collaborationist forces from 1941 onward, using mountains, forests, and mobile brigades to survive far stronger occupiers. They liberated and held territory, built a parallel political organisation, and by 1945 emerged as the dominant force in Yugoslavia. Their campaign is a standard case of guerrilla survival converting, unusually, into state power.

Craigslist, launched by Craig Newmark in San Francisco in the mid-1990s and expanded city by city from 2000, waged a guerrilla-style campaign against newspaper classified advertising. A famously small team, a plain text site, and free listings for most categories undercut the newspapers' expensive classified departments without ever matching their newsrooms. Over the following decade, classified revenue, once a foundation of local newspaper economics, migrated massively to the lean challenger.
misconceptions: Many people think guerrilla warfare is just small-scale regular warfare — in reality, its centre of gravity is political: population support, endurance, and the occupier's costs, not battlefield totals.
Many people think guerrillas win by destroying the enemy army — in reality, they usually win by outlasting political will, then converting survival into negotiation or power.
Many people think any small competitor is automatically a guerrilla — in reality, the method requires mobility, local support as a supply base, and discipline to refuse unwinnable contests for years.
