practice: Supply-base exercise: Name the community, audience, or customer group that functions as your support base, and list what it supplies you: trust, referrals, information, revenue. Choose one concrete action this week that strengthens that base, and one action you will stop because it spends the base's goodwill for short-term gain.

Winnable-target list: Write down five small targets you could realistically win in the next month, a niche topic, a single location, one underserved customer type, and rank them by cost to you versus embarrassment or cost to a larger rival. Commit to the top target only, and define in advance what converting that win into a durable position would require.
cross_domain: Food businesses show the pattern when food trucks use mobility, low rent, and social media to serve shifting crowds that a fixed restaurant, paying for premises on quiet and busy days alike, cannot chase profitably. Activism and open-source communities use the same structure too, where small, distributed groups sustain a campaign or a project for years at costs a centralised opponent cannot match without changing its own nature.

name_vi: Kiểm soát và cân bằng quyền lực
definition: Power stays safer when different branches of government can limit, review, and block each other from acting alone.
mechanism: Ambition is made to counter ambition. By giving legislatures, executives, and courts separate powers and overlapping veto points, no single faction can capture the whole system quickly. Each branch defends its own authority, and that selfish defense protects public freedom as a side effect. Montesquieu articulated the separation logic in 1748, and the American founders built it into a constitution of explicit mutual restraints.
classic_example: In United States versus Nixon in 1974, the Supreme Court unanimously ordered President Richard Nixon to release Watergate tapes despite his claim of executive privilege. Nixon complied and resigned sixteen days later. The ruling showed courts could check a sitting president even during a national political crisis.
modern_example: Inside a company, separating who requests spending, who approves it, and who audits it prevents one manager from quietly approving personal expenses. Startups that skip these checks for speed often discover fraud or reckless commitments only after cash is gone and trust inside the team collapses.
failure_mode: Too many veto points create gridlock where urgent problems go unsolved and voters blame everyone and no one. Checks also fail when one party controls all branches and loyalty overrides institutional pride. Formal separation on paper means little without people willing to enforce it.
apply_steps: Map who can decide, block, and review this decision
Ensure no single person controls all three powers
Give reviewers independent information, not just summaries
Protect people who raise legitimate blocks from retaliation

situation_notes.team-conflict: Checks and balances reveal healthy teams need someone empowered to block a dominant leader decision before it becomes irreversible damage.
situation_notes.asking-for-budget: Checks and balances explain budget approvals feel slow because separate approvers exist specifically to catch what requesters cannot see themselves.
situation_notes.presenting-to-leadership: Checks and balances show strong proposals anticipate reviewer objections and build evidence for each independent gatekeeper in the room.

case_seeds: United States versus Nixon Supreme Court ruling 1974
Watergate scandal and Nixon resignation 1974
source_ref: Montesquieu — The Spirit of the Laws (1748)
origin: Charles-Louis de Secondat, baron de Montesquieu, set out the separation logic in The Spirit of the Laws in 1748, drawing partly on his reading of English government. James Madison then turned the idea into overlapping checks in The Federalist in 1788, arguing each branch needed constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachment by the others.
mechanism_deep: The deeper engine is not goodwill but institutional self-interest attached to different bases of power. Legislators depend on elections and committee standing, executives on administration and public blame for results, and judges in many systems on tenure and professional reputation. Because their careers, time horizons, and constituencies differ, an action that benefits one branch often threatens another, so resistance emerges even without civic virtue. Veto points, confirmation hearings, budget control, judicial review, and impeachment each raise the cost and time needed to concentrate power, creating space for evidence, opposition, and public reaction to surface. The system self-reinforces when a branch successfully defends a prerogative and sets a precedent others later cite. It weakens when party loyalty cuts across branches, when executives rule through emergency powers or decrees that bypass legislatures, when courts are packed or intimidated, or when voters punish obstruction more than overreach. Polarisation also changes the calculation: officials may calculate that defending their own party helps re-election more than defending their branch. Checks therefore depend on both formal rules and the informal norm that losing an institutional fight is acceptable, while destroying the referee is not.
examples_extra: In the United Kingdom in 2019, the Supreme Court ruled in the Miller case that Prime Minister Boris Johnson's advice to suspend Parliament for five weeks during the Brexit debate was unlawful. Parliament resumed sitting the next day. The judgment showed a court without a written United States style constitution could still check an executive act it found to have an extreme effect on democratic scrutiny.

In South Korea, the Constitutional Court unanimously upheld the impeachment of President Park Geun-hye in March 2017, removing her from office after the National Assembly had voted to impeach in December 2016. A presidential election followed in May 2017. The sequence showed legislative accusation, judicial decision, and electoral replacement operating as separate steps rather than as a single political act.
misconceptions: Many people think checks and balances mean the three branches are completely separate — in reality, effective systems deliberately overlap them through vetoes, appointments, budgets, and review.
Many people think checks guarantee good decisions — in reality, they mainly slow and expose power; they can also produce gridlock, delay, and blurred accountability.
Many people think written rules enforce themselves — in reality, checks fail when officials refuse to use their powers or voters reward loyalty over institutional defence.

practice.title: Map the veto points
practice.instructions: Pick a recent decision in your organisation or city. Draw three columns for who proposes, who can block, and who reviews afterwards. Then note what information each reviewer sees independently, and identify any point where one person controls two columns.

practice.title: Stress-test a rule
practice.instructions: Take one safeguard you rely on and ask what happens if the same party, manager, or family controls every step. Write down which norm or precedent would have to break first. That first break is the weak point to protect.

cross_domain: In companies, the same structure appears as segregation of duties: one person requests a payment, another approves it, and internal audit reviews it, so fraud needs collusion rather than one signature. In nonprofits, an independent board, a treasurer, and external auditors play the separate branches. In online communities, elected moderators, an appeals process, and published logs reproduce the pattern: proposal, enforcement, and review sit in different hands, which makes arbitrary bans harder and legitimate enforcement easier to defend.

quote.text: If men were angels, no government would be necessary.
quote.author: James Madison

name_vi: Thượng tôn pháp luật / Nhà nước pháp quyền
definition: Everyone, including rulers, is bound by known laws applied equally, rather than by the personal whims of whoever holds power.
mechanism: Predictable rules let strangers cooperate, invest, and plan because they know disputes will be settled by process, not connections or force. When officials themselves obey courts and procedures, citizens trust the system enough to comply voluntarily, lowering enforcement costs. The mechanism depends on independent judges, public laws, and consistent application. Without those, law becomes merely a weapon rulers use selectively against opponents.
classic_example: In 1215, English barons forced King John to accept Magna Carta at Runnymede, establishing that even the king was not above the law and that free men deserved lawful judgment. Though limited at first, the document became a lasting symbol and legal foundation for constitutional limits on power.
modern_example: A creator earning income online benefits when platform rules and tax law are stable and applied evenly. If enforcement depends on who you know, planning becomes gambling. Countries and companies that honor contracts predictably attract long term investment because partners price in lower political and legal risk.
failure_mode: Laws themselves can be unjust, and strict legality once protected slavery and segregation. Rule of law guarantees process, not wisdom or morality. It also decays into rule by law when rulers write the rules, control the judges, and merely legalize their own arbitrary power.
apply_steps: Ask whether a written rule governs this situation
Check if the rule is applied equally to everyone
Demand process and evidence, not personal discretion
Appeal through established channels before seeking exceptions

situation_notes.reading-a-new-partner: Rule of law reveals a partner who respects contracts when inconvenient is far safer than one who honors agreements only willingly.
situation_notes.negotiating-price: Rule of law shows written terms protect both sides once memories fade and incentives change after the handshake deal ends.
situation_notes.team-conflict: Rule of law suggests team conflicts resolve better through agreed procedures applied equally than through a leader personal preferences shifting daily.

case_seeds: Magna Carta at Runnymede 1215
origin: British jurist A. V. Dicey popularised the modern phrase in Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution in 1885, stressing supremacy of regular law, equality before the law, and rights protected by courts. His account built on much older roots, including Magna Carta in 1215 and Aristotle's argument that law should govern rather than individual rulers.
mechanism_deep: The mechanism runs on predictability and credible commitment. When rules are public, stable, and applied by judges who do not take instructions from the ruler of the day, people can sign contracts, lend money, and invest effort without pricing in arbitrary confiscation or favouritism. Officials gain too: a government bound by its own procedures can make promises that others believe, from repaying debt to honouring election results. Compliance then becomes partly voluntary, because most people accept an adverse ruling they see as procedurally fair more readily than a favourable whim they expect to be reversed. The loop reinforces itself as courts build precedent, precedent guides behaviour, and stable behaviour reduces the caseload of disputes. It weakens through selective enforcement, retroactive laws, emergency decrees that never expire, and courts dependent on executives for budgets or careers. A subtler decay is complexity: when law becomes so dense that only the wealthy can navigate it, formal equality survives while practical equality erodes, and citizens begin to experience the system as rule by lawyers rather than rule of law.
examples_extra: In Entick v Carrington in England in 1765, the court ruled against government agents who had searched John Entick's home and seized papers without specific legal authority. Lord Camden held that state action needed a basis in law, not merely official instruction. The case is still cited in common law countries as an early statement that executive power is limited by law.

In State v Makwanyane in 1995, South Africa's new Constitutional Court unanimously abolished the death penalty, holding it inconsistent with the interim constitution's rights protections. The decision applied constitutional limits in a politically sensitive criminal justice question during the country's transition to democracy, and Parliament did not restore capital punishment afterwards.
misconceptions: Many people think rule of law means having many laws — in reality, a state can pass endless laws and still rule arbitrarily if officials apply them selectively.
Many people think rule of law guarantees just outcomes — in reality, it guarantees known process and equal application; unjust laws can still be enforced lawfully until changed.
Many people think rule of law is the same as rule by law — in reality, rule by law means rulers use law as a tool while staying above it themselves.

practice.title: Government of laws test
practice.instructions: Take a recent disputed decision at work or in public life. Ask three questions: was there a written rule beforehand, was it applied the same way to a similar case, and could the loser appeal to an independent reviewer? Score each yes or no and note which element failed.

cross_domain: In business, franchising works on the same logic: a manual applied equally to every outlet lets strangers invest with confidence, while ad hoc exceptions destroy trust in the brand. In sport, published rules and independent referees let losing teams accept results and return next season. In online platforms, transparent moderation rules with a real appeals route produce the same effect: users invest effort in building accounts because they expect process, not a moderator's mood, to decide disputes.

quote.text: a government of laws, and not of men
quote.author: John Adams
quote.source: Massachusetts Constitution (1780), Part the First, Article XXX

name_vi: Lý thuyết lựa chọn công
definition: Public choice applies economics to politics, assuming officials and voters pursue their own interests just like people in markets do.
mechanism: Instead of imagining benevolent rulers, the theory asks what politicians, bureaucrats, and voters are rewarded for. Politicians chase reelection, agencies chase budgets, and voters stay rationally ignorant because one vote rarely decides outcomes. Concentrated groups with much at stake organize effectively, while diffuse taxpayers each lose little and stay silent. James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock developed this framework, notably in The Calculus of Consent in 1962.
classic_example: James Buchanan received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1986 for public choice work begun decades earlier with Gordon Tullock. Their 1962 book The Calculus of Consent analyzed voting rules and bureaucracy with the same self interest assumptions economists applied to consumers, transforming how scholars studied government failure alongside market failure.
modern_example: A city subsidy for a stadium wins political support because a team owner and construction firms gain hugely and lobby hard, while each taxpayer pays a small hidden share. The same logic explains why reforming any perk is difficult: beneficiaries organize fiercely, losers of reform barely notice their savings.
failure_mode: Assuming pure selfishness everywhere misses genuine public service, civic duty, and ideological commitment that do motivate many officials. The theory can become lazy cynicism that treats every policy as corrupt dealing. Some collective action through government solves problems markets demonstrably cannot handle alone.
apply_steps: Ask what each political actor personally gains
Identify concentrated winners and diffuse cost bearers
Expect organized minorities to out lobby silent majorities
Design rules assuming self interest, not benevolence

situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: Public choice reveals commentators and officials promote policies that grow their audience, budget, or reelection chances, not only public welfare.
situation_notes.asking-for-budget: Public choice shows budget holders approve requests that protect their status and headcount, so frame proposals around their incentives too.
situation_notes.online-arguments: Public choice explains political arguments online reward tribal signaling for likes more than persuading opponents or solving the stated problem.

case_seeds: Buchanan and Tullock The Calculus of Consent 1962
origin: James M. Buchanan and Gordon Tullock founded the approach in The Calculus of Consent in 1962, building the Virginia school of political economy. Anthony Downs had applied similar reasoning to voters and parties in An Economic Theory of Democracy in 1957. Buchanan received the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences in 1986 for this work on contractual and constitutional foundations of decision-making.
mechanism_deep: Start from the voter. Learning the details of a policy costs time, while one vote almost never changes the result, so staying uninformed is individually rational even when collective ignorance is costly. Politicians facing elections therefore optimise for visible, concentrated benefits delivered before polling day and for costs that are hidden, deferred, or spread thinly. Bureaucrats, who cannot keep profits, are modelled by William Niskanen in 1971 as maximising budgets, staff, and discretion, which are the bureaucratic equivalents of income and status. Organised groups exploit this structure through logrolling, where legislators trade support for each other's local projects, and through long-term relationships with the agencies that regulate them. The pattern self-reinforces because every successful organised claim funds more lobbying capacity, while diffuse losers never learn what each policy cost them. The model weakens where professional norms, transparency, competitive media, or strong party programmes make reputation a real asset, and where voters do punish rent extraction. It also underplays expressive voting: people often vote to affirm identity rather than to buy outcomes, which can push politics away from material self-interest in either direction.
examples_extra: The United States sugar programme has restricted imports through quotas since the early 1980s, supporting domestic prices above world levels. The benefit concentrates on a relatively small number of growers and processors, while the cost spreads across millions of consumers in slightly higher food prices. Economists across the spectrum cite it as a textbook case of concentrated benefits and diffuse costs sustaining a policy.

The European Union's Common Agricultural Policy, created in 1962, long guaranteed prices and payments that benefited organised farm producers, who were well placed to lobby in Brussels and national capitals. Food consumers and taxpayers paid diffusely. Successive reforms from the 1990s onward shifted support from price guarantees toward direct payments, partly in response to budget costs and international trade pressure.
misconceptions: Many people think public choice says all officials are corrupt — in reality, it says ordinary incentives shape behaviour even for honest people inside badly designed rules.
Many people think voters are stupid for ignoring policy detail — in reality, rational ignorance follows from one vote rarely deciding an outcome, not from low intelligence.
Many people think markets always beat government — in reality, public choice compares imperfect institutions; it also identifies cases where collective provision solves real coordination problems.

practice.title: Who gains, who pays audit
practice.instructions: Choose one current public policy and list its winners and losers in two columns, estimating how much each person gains or loses per year. Then ask which group is more likely to organise, donate, or protest. Compare that prediction with the lobbying and coverage you can actually observe.

practice.title: Follow the bureaucrat's reward
practice.instructions: Pick an agency decision you dislike. Write down what its leaders are rewarded for: budget size, avoiding scandal, cases processed, or problems solved. Rewrite the decision as the rational output of those rewards before assuming bad faith.

cross_domain: Inside companies, department heads behave like bureaus: they defend headcount at budget time, spend remaining funds before year end, and propose projects that raise their unit's visibility. In universities, committees multiply concentrated benefits for organised departments while costs fall on the general budget. In online platforms, a small group of highly active users shapes rules and moderation priorities because they show up consistently, while the diffuse majority who are mildly affected never organise a counterweight.

name_vi: Cơ quan quản lý bị chi phối / bắt giữ
definition: Regulatory capture happens when an agency meant to oversee an industry ends up serving that industry interests instead of the public.
mechanism: Regulators depend on industry for expertise, data, and future jobs, while the industry gains enormously from favorable rules and lobbies constantly. The public, harmed diffusely, pays little attention. Over time appointments, revolving doors, and shared worldviews align the referee with one team. George Stigler formalized this theory in 1971, arguing regulation is often acquired by industries to block competition and secure profits.
classic_example: The United States Interstate Commerce Commission, created in 1887 to regulate railroads, came over decades to protect railroads from truck competition and stabilize their profits instead. Economists widely cite it as a classic capture case, and the agency was eventually abolished in 1995 after deregulation exposed its failures.
modern_example: When a dominant social platform helps write the rules for smaller rivals, compliance costs it can easily afford become barriers crushing new entrants. Founders should notice that regulation praised by incumbents often protects incumbents. Reading who benefits from a rule reveals more than reading its stated public purpose.
failure_mode: Industry input is sometimes genuinely needed because regulators lack technical knowledge, and cooperation is not proof of capture. Some agencies do resist industry pressure for decades. The model becomes conspiratorial when every unfavorable ruling is called capture without evidence of mechanisms like revolving doors or lobbying.
apply_steps: Ask who benefits most from this specific rule
Trace career paths between regulator and industry
Compare stated purpose with actual competitive effects
Watch whether incumbents support the supposed constraint on them

situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: Regulatory capture warns heavily regulated niches may already be wired to protect incumbents who helped write the entry requirements themselves.
situation_notes.competitor-price-war: Regulatory capture reveals large rivals may welcome costly rules because they can absorb compliance expenses that would bankrupt you.
situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: Regulatory capture teaches skepticism when industry funded experts praise rules that conveniently raise barriers against their own future competitors.

case_seeds: Interstate Commerce Commission railroad regulation and abolition 1995
Stigler theory of economic regulation 1971
origin: Marver Bernstein described an agency life cycle ending in industry alignment in Regulating Business by Independent Commission in 1955. George Stigler gave the idea its economic form in The Theory of Economic Regulation in 1971, arguing that regulation is often acquired by an industry and operated for its benefit. Sam Peltzman and Gary Becker later refined the theory to include competing interest groups.
mechanism_deep: Capture rarely begins with bribery. It begins with dependence. A regulator needs technical data, risk models, and staff expertise that only the regulated industry holds in depth, so daily work requires constant cooperative contact with industry specialists. The industry, facing profits that hinge on specific rules, can afford permanent legal and lobbying teams, while consumers harmed by a few units of currency each cannot justify organising. Career incentives complete the alignment: expertise in a niche industry is most valuable back inside that industry, creating the revolving door between agency and firm. A subtler form, cultural capture, needs no job offers at all; regulators simply absorb the worldview of the people they meet every day. The loop self-reinforces because favourable rules raise industry profits, which fund more influence capacity. Capture weakens when agencies rotate staff, publish data that outsiders can analyse, face competing expert bodies, or operate under transparency rules that expose contacts. It also varies by issue salience: a disaster or scandal briefly empowers the diffuse public, opening a window in which genuinely restrictive rules can pass before attention fades.
examples_extra: After the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico in 2010, investigations and press reporting documented close social and professional ties between the United States Minerals Management Service and the offshore industry it regulated. The agency was subsequently reorganised and split into separate bureaus separating resource management, leasing, and safety enforcement functions.

Following the crashes of Lion Air Flight 610 in 2018 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 in 2019, investigations examined how the United States Federal Aviation Administration had delegated substantial certification work on the Boeing 737 MAX to Boeing employees under its designation programme. Congress passed certification reform legislation in 2020 increasing direct agency oversight of delegated functions.
misconceptions: Many people think capture requires bribery or secret deals — in reality, dependence on industry data, careers, and shared worldview can align a regulator without any illegal payment.
Many people think industry support for a rule proves capture — in reality, firms sometimes support rules for genuine safety reasons; capture is shown by effects and mechanisms, not support alone.
Many people think all regulation is captured — in reality, agencies vary widely, and salience, transparency, and competing experts can keep a regulator independent for long periods.

practice.title: Revolving-door check
practice.instructions: Choose one regulator in the news. Search for where its last three senior leaders worked before and after office, and list any industry meetings or consultations reported. Then ask whether the pattern shows expertise flowing in, influence flowing out, or both.

cross_domain: In business, an internal audit team that depends on one division for data, budget, and future transfers can drift into approving that division's practices. In professional sport, leagues that both promote events and discipline participants face the same referee-player overlap, which is why independent anti-doping bodies were created. In online communities, moderation teams funded or staffed by the largest creators tend to write rules those creators can absorb, reproducing capture without any government involved.

name_vi: Quy luật sắt của bộ máy quan liêu
definition: Organizations tend over time to prioritize their own survival, procedures, and growth over the mission they were originally created to serve.
mechanism: Staff are rewarded for avoiding blame, following procedure, and expanding headcount, not for solving problems so well the department becomes unnecessary. Rules multiply because each failure adds a safeguard and no one is rewarded for removing one. Jerry Pournelle popularized this iron law, observing that people devoted to the organization itself eventually control it over people devoted to its stated purpose.
classic_example: The March of Dimes was founded in 1938 to fight polio. After the Salk vaccine conquered polio in 1955, the organization did not disband but adopted new missions around birth defects. Critics and admirers both cite it as bureaucracy instinctively preserving itself after its founding purpose disappeared.
modern_example: A company approval process that began as one signature becomes five forms and three committees after a single mistake. Each layer protects someone from blame while customers wait weeks. Employees feel the law personally when following the process becomes safer than producing the outcome the process was built for.
failure_mode: Procedures also prevent real fraud, accidents, and chaos, and some mission drift is legitimate adaptation to new needs. Small or young organizations often show the opposite problem, too little structure. The model should prompt scrutiny of incentives, not automatic contempt for every rule or administrator.
apply_steps: Ask whether this rule serves mission or self protection
Find who is rewarded for adding process layers
Sunset procedures unless someone rejustifies them periodically
Reward solving problems, not merely following steps correctly

situation_notes.idea-rejected-by-boss: The iron law explains bosses may reject ideas threatening headcount, budget, or routine even when the idea clearly serves customers.
situation_notes.presenting-to-leadership: The iron law shows proposals succeed when they protect approvers from blame as carefully as they promise organizational gains ahead.
situation_notes.asking-for-budget: The iron law reveals departments defend budgets fiercely at year end because unspent money signals they need less next year.

case_seeds: March of Dimes mission change after polio vaccine 1955
source_ref: Jerry Pournelle — Iron Law of Bureaucracy
origin: American writer Jerry Pournelle popularised the iron law in his computing columns and essays in the 1980s, distinguishing staff devoted to an organisation itself from staff devoted to its goals. The idea descends from Robert Michels, who proposed an iron law of oligarchy in Political Parties in 1911, and from Max Weber's earlier analysis of bureaucracy as a self-perpetuating form of organisation.
mechanism_deep: The engine is asymmetric reward. An official who approves something that fails is visibly blamed, while an official who blocks something that would have succeeded pays almost no price, because the lost success is invisible. Rational staff therefore multiply approvals, documentation, and precedent checks. Each incident adds a rule, but no career incentive rewards removing rules, so procedure only ratchets in one direction. Budget systems reinforce the drift: money unspent this year signals a smaller need next year, so units spend to protect their baseline regardless of mission value. Over time, selection does the deeper work. People who enjoy process and internal politics stay and rise, while mission-focused staff who find procedure stifling leave, gradually changing who leads the organisation. The law weakens in small teams with direct contact with users, in organisations with sunset clauses and genuine outcome measurement, and during founding or crisis periods when survival visibly depends on results. It strengthens with size, monopoly provision, and distance from the people served, which is why the same pattern appears in ministries, corporations, universities, and charities alike.
examples_extra: Eastman Kodak invented an early digital camera in 1975, yet its committee-driven management repeatedly protected the highly profitable film business and delayed a full digital commitment. Kodak filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in January 2012. Business histories cite its layered approval culture and defence of existing divisions as central reasons a technology leader failed to convert its own invention into a new core business.

General Motors entered bankruptcy in June 2009 after decades in which internal reports and later government reviews described a culture of committees, slow escalation, and reluctance to carry bad news upward. The United States government-backed restructuring that followed replaced senior leadership and explicitly targeted bureaucratic decision processes alongside the company's financial problems.
misconceptions: Many people think bureaucracy grows because officials are lazy — in reality, procedure grows because avoiding blame and protecting budgets are rational responses to how staff are rewarded.
Many people think all procedure is bureaucratic waste — in reality, some process prevents fraud and accidents; the law targets procedure that survives after its protective purpose has gone.
Many people think the law applies only to government — in reality, any large organisation with internal promotion and blame asymmetry, including firms and charities, shows the same drift.

practice.title: Sunset one rule
practice.instructions: List three procedures your team follows and find the incident or reason each was created. If nobody can name the problem a rule solves, propose a dated trial suspension with a review point. Record what actually happens instead of debating what might.

practice.title: Count the signatures
practice.instructions: Trace one routine decision from request to approval and count every hand it passes through. For each hand, write what risk that person actually removes. Hands that remove no identifiable risk are candidates for removal or delegation.

cross_domain: In software companies, the law appears as review boards and compliance gates that persist after the product has changed, slowing releases while headcount in coordination roles grows. In nonprofit organisations, grant-reporting staff and fundraising machinery can expand faster than the programmes donors intended to fund. In online communities, moderation rulebooks grow after every dispute until enforcing the ruleset itself becomes the community's main activity, crowding out the discussion the rules were meant to protect.

name_vi: Cửa sổ Overton
definition: The Overton window is the range of ideas considered acceptable in public debate at a given time, and that range can shift.
mechanism: Politicians rarely adopt ideas outside what voters currently find sensible, so change agents work on the window itself. Repeated discussion, crises, research, and visible examples move proposals from unthinkable to radical to acceptable to popular. Joseph Overton developed the concept at the Mackinac Center in the 1990s. The mechanism matters because arguing only within todays limits concedes the boundary, while pushing ideas just beyond it gradually relocates the center.
classic_example: Same sex marriage in the United States moved from a fringe proposal in the 1990s to majority public support within two decades, culminating in the Supreme Court Obergefell versus Hodges ruling in 2015. Activists, media representation, and state level wins shifted what mainstream politicians could safely endorse step by step.
modern_example: Remote work was considered a risky perk by most employers before 2020, then became an enforced experiment during the pandemic, and afterward a normal expectation in many industries. A professional proposing fully remote arrangements in 2018 sounded radical, while by 2023 companies advertised flexibility to compete for talent.
failure_mode: Not every fringe idea deserves mainstreaming, and window shifting can normalize harmful or false claims as easily as liberating ones. The model also tempts activists to overestimate discourse effects when material events and demographics drive change. Pushing too far too fast can backlash and shrink the window.
apply_steps: Map what is currently considered sensible versus radical
Introduce ideas one step beyond current acceptability
Repeat through credible voices, examples, and pilots
Convert shifted opinion into policy while momentum lasts

situation_notes.idea-rejected-by-boss: The Overton window reveals a rejected idea may be too far outside current comfort, needing smaller pilot steps first.
situation_notes.persuading-stubborn-person: The Overton window shows persuasion works by moving someone one acceptable step at a time, not demanding total conversion instantly.
situation_notes.presenting-to-leadership: The Overton window explains framing a bold proposal as an extension of already accepted practice dramatically raises its approval chances.
situation_notes.online-arguments: The Overton window warns extreme voices online can drag perceived normal opinion even when most silent people disagree with them.

case_seeds: Obergefell versus Hodges Supreme Court ruling 2015
Shift to mainstream remote work after 2020
origin: Joseph P. Overton, a vice president at the Mackinac Center for Public Policy in Michigan, developed the concept in the 1990s while explaining to donors how think tanks shift what politicians can support. Overton died in a plane crash in 2003, and colleagues at the centre named and published the model after his death.
mechanism_deep: The window rests on a simple asymmetry between politicians and ideas. Most elected officials are punished more reliably for endorsing something voters consider extreme than they are rewarded for being right early, so they continuously read public acceptability and position themselves just inside its edge. That makes the boundary itself the strategic prize. Overton described positions moving through degrees of acceptance, roughly from unthinkable, to radical, to acceptable, to sensible, to popular, and finally to enacted policy. Movement between degrees is driven by several reinforcing mechanisms. Repetition through credible voices makes an idea cognitively available, so it stops sounding strange even before it persuades. Visible examples convert abstraction into precedent: one city, company, or country adopting a policy supplies evidence that opponents must now argue against rather than merely dismiss. Elite cues matter because most citizens take shortcuts from trusted figures, so when experts, professional bodies, or figures from both political camps endorse a step, hesitant supporters gain permission to agree publicly. Preference falsification sustains the old boundary until that permission arrives; many people privately accept an idea while believing they are in a minority, so each public defection reveals support and triggers further defections in a cascade. Crises accelerate everything by discrediting the status quo and compressing years of discussion into weeks, which is why Milton Friedman observed that change depends on ideas lying around when a crisis hits. The same machinery can run in reverse: a policy failure, a scandal attached to a proposal, or a backlash mobilisation can move an idea back out of the window, and skilled opponents deliberately attach extreme versions to moderate proposals to drag them outside it. The model weakens in fragmented media environments, where there is no single public but several audiences with separate windows, so an idea can be policy in one community and unthinkable in another at the same time. It also weakens when material conditions change faster than discourse, when adoption is driven by courts or markets rather than voters, or when a determined executive accepts the electoral cost and acts anyway. Finally, the window describes perceived acceptability, not majority opinion measured privately, and confusing the two leads strategists to mistake loud visibility for genuine movement, or silence for genuine opposition. Organised shifters exploit this deliberately. Think tanks, campaign groups, and sympathetic commentators keep a more radical version of a proposal in circulation so that the version they actually seek looks moderate by comparison, a positioning effect sometimes described as a radical flank. They also sequence demands, asking first for a study, then a pilot, then a local exception, and only then a general rule, because each granted step redefines what counts as the reasonable middle for the next negotiation. Opponents counter with the mirror tactics: publicising the most extreme supporters of a change, demanding its advocates defend the final destination rather than the current step, and holding referendums early, before examples can accumulate. Which side prevails usually depends less on argument quality than on who supplies the first credible working example, since a functioning case converts the debate from speculation about consequences into observation of them, and observation is far harder for the other side to move.
examples_extra: Ireland became the first country to introduce a comprehensive workplace smoking ban in March 2004, a step widely treated beforehand as politically impossible in a country associated with pub culture. Compliance was high, other European countries followed within a few years, and indoor smoking moved from normal to unacceptable across much of Europe within a decade. The Irish precedent supplied the visible example that shifted debate elsewhere from principle to practicality.

In the United States, Colorado and Washington voters approved recreational cannabis legalisation in November 2012, the first states to do so after decades in which legalisation sat outside mainstream politics. State-level medical programmes since California's Proposition 215 in 1996 had gradually normalised regulated access. Further states followed through ballot measures and legislatures during the following decade, while federal prohibition remained in place.
misconceptions: Many people think the Overton window is a conspiracy technique used by manipulators — in reality, it is a descriptive model of perceived acceptability that shifts through ordinary advocacy, events, and example.

Many people think moving the window means persuading a majority — in reality, politicians respond to perceived acceptability, which can shift well before or well after private majority opinion changes.
Many people think any idea can be mainstreamed with enough messaging — in reality, material events, failed pilots, and backlash can move the window backwards or close it entirely.

practice.title: Map one window at three dates
practice.instructions: Choose a topic such as remote work or a local policy. Find headlines, speeches, or platform positions from roughly twenty years ago, ten years ago, and today. Label each position unthinkable, radical, acceptable, sensible, or popular, and identify the events or examples that moved it between labels.

practice.title: Place your own proposal
practice.instructions: Write your proposal in one sentence and honestly label where it sits today for the audience you need. Then design the one-step-smaller version that sits just inside acceptable, and decide what pilot or example would make the full version look sensible next time.

cross_domain: In business, pricing follows a window: one firm normalises a subscription or a higher price point with a visible success, and competitors who called it impossible adopt it within a few cycles. In product design, features move from radical to expected the same way, as touchscreens did after 2007. In workplace culture, practices such as four-day weeks or meeting-free days travel from fringe experiments to recruitment standards through the identical sequence of example, repetition, and permission.

name_vi: Vấn đề hành động tập thể
definition: Groups often fail to act together for a shared benefit because each member prefers letting others pay the cost.
mechanism: If the benefit arrives whether or not I contribute, my rational move is to free ride. When everyone reasons this way, the benefit never materializes, even though all would pay a small share for it. Mancur Olson formalized this in The Logic of Collective Action in 1965, showing small concentrated groups organize easily while large diffuse groups struggle without selective incentives, coercion, or social norms sustaining contribution.
classic_example: Mancur Olson published The Logic of Collective Action in 1965, explaining why large groups like consumers rarely lobby effectively while small producer groups do. His logic explained patterns from union organizing to why taxpayers lose policy fights against industries with concentrated stakes in the outcome.
modern_example: Everyone in an apartment building wants a cleaner shared hallway, but each household hopes neighbors will organize the roster. Open source projects face the same trap: millions benefit, few contribute code or money. Systems that make contribution visible, small, and socially rewarded escape the trap more reliably.
failure_mode: Humans also cooperate from identity, duty, and reciprocity, not calculation alone, so the model underpredicts movements, volunteering, and sacrifice in wars or disasters. Digital tools have lowered organizing costs dramatically. Treating free riding as inevitable can become a self fulfilling excuse for never attempting collective efforts.
apply_steps: Define the shared benefit and its total cost
Make individual contributions visible and socially recognized
Lower the smallest first contribution to near zero
Add selective rewards for contributors or consequences for free riders

situation_notes.team-conflict: The collective action problem reveals shared chores go undone because everyone benefits from them but nobody owns the cost.
situation_notes.channel-not-growing: The collective action problem explains audiences rarely share content spontaneously, so creators must make sharing easy, visible, and rewarding.
situation_notes.online-arguments: The collective action problem shows good commenters stay silent because correcting misinformation costs them time while benefits spread to strangers.

case_seeds: Olson The Logic of Collective Action 1965
origin: Mancur Olson, an economist at the University of Maryland, formalised the problem in The Logic of Collective Action, published by Harvard University Press in 1965. Writing against the assumption that shared interests automatically produce organised groups, Olson showed that group size and selective incentives determine whether a latent interest ever becomes collective action. The book reshaped political science and the study of interest groups.
mechanism_deep: The core is a gap between individual and group arithmetic. In a large group, one contribution is too small to visibly change the outcome, yet the contributor pays the full personal cost, so withholding effort dominates regardless of what others do. Olson showed this logic weakens as groups grow: small groups can monitor each other, apply social pressure, and sometimes contain a privileged member who values the good enough to provide it alone. Large latent groups act only when organisers attach selective incentives, meaning private benefits available only to contributors, such as insurance, discounts, status, or access, or when coercion such as mandatory dues solves the assurance problem. Technology changes the cost side rather than the logic: cheap communication lowers organising costs dramatically, which is why online movements form fast, but the same cheapness lowers commitment, so digitally assembled groups often dissolve just as fast. Norms and identity can substitute for material incentives by making contribution a marker of belonging and defection a reputational cost. The model weakens in repeated, small-scale settings with visible contributions and trusted enforcement, and it underpredicts action driven by moral shock, where a single event temporarily makes people value participation itself more than the outcome it buys.
examples_extra: Climate policy illustrates the problem at global scale. The Paris Agreement, adopted in December 2015, relies on voluntary national pledges rather than enforceable quotas, because every country benefits from global emissions cuts whether or not it bears the cost of its own reductions. Negotiations since then have repeatedly centred on finance and burden-sharing, reflecting each government's incentive to let others move first.

Within NATO, the allies agreed a guideline in 2006 that members should spend two percent of gross domestic product on defence, and reaffirmed it in the Wales Summit Declaration in 2014. For many years only a minority of members met the target, while all members benefited from the alliance's collective deterrence. Spending rose sharply across the alliance after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
misconceptions: Many people think collective action fails because people are selfish or apathetic — in reality, it can fail even when everyone is well intentioned, because each person's contribution barely changes the outcome.
Many people think a larger group is always stronger — in reality, Olson showed large diffuse groups are often weaker than small concentrated ones because monitoring and incentives break down.
Many people think awareness solves the problem — in reality, knowing about an issue does not change the payoff for contributing; incentives, visibility, or norms must change.

practice.title: Diagnose a stalled group effort
practice.instructions: Pick a shared task that keeps failing, such as a residents' project or open-source fund. Write down the total benefit, the cost per contributor, and whether anyone can tell who contributed. Then redesign one element: make contributions visible, shrink the first step, or add a contributor-only benefit.

cross_domain: In business, industry standards show the same pattern: every firm benefits from a common standard, yet each prefers rivals to fund the standards body, so consortia survive on selective benefits like certification and early access. In academia, peer review depends on unpaid referees whose individual effort is invisible, and journals struggle with shortages for exactly Olson's reasons. In online communities, a tiny minority creates most content while the majority consumes it, because creation costs are personal and benefits are shared.

name_vi: Tìm kiếm đặc lợi / trục lợi chính sách
definition: Rent seeking is spending effort to capture existing wealth through favors, licenses, or rules, instead of creating new wealth through production.
mechanism: When governments can grant monopolies, tariffs, subsidies, or exclusive licenses, those privileges become prizes worth lobbying for. Resources flow into lawyers, lobbyists, and connections rather than better products, so society loses twice: the transfer itself plus the wasted effort chasing it. Gordon Tullock introduced the core insight in 1967, and Anne Krueger coined the term rent seeking in 1974, transforming analysis of corruption and protectionism.
classic_example: Anne Krueger coined the term in her 1974 paper on the political economy of the rent seeking society, studying import licenses in India and Turkey. Firms spent heavily competing for licenses that created no new goods, and she estimated such rents consumed a significant share of national income.
modern_example: A local business spending months chasing an exclusive permit to block competitors, instead of improving its product, is rent seeking at small scale. Taxi medallion owners in New York lobbied against ride hailing to protect medallion values that once exceeded one million dollars before collapsing as Uber expanded.
failure_mode: Not all engagement with government is rent seeking. Firms legitimately seek patents for real inventions, safety standards, or redress of genuine harms. The label gets abused to smear any policy one dislikes. Distinguishing value creation from privilege capture requires examining effects, not merely noticing that someone lobbied.
apply_steps: Ask whether profit comes from creating or capturing value
Follow which rule or license protects this income
Count resources spent on influence versus production
Support rules that are general rather than favor granting

situation_notes.choosing-a-niche: Rent seeking warns niches profitable only through licenses or connections collapse when the political favor or loophole disappears suddenly.
situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: Rent seeking reveals industry praise for new rules may reflect captured privilege rather than genuine consumer benefit from regulation.
situation_notes.competitor-price-war: Rent seeking shows some rivals fight through lobbying and complaints to authorities instead of competing on product and price.

case_seeds: Krueger rent seeking paper 1974
New York taxi medallion value collapse after Uber expansion
origin: Gordon Tullock introduced the central insight in his 1967 paper The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft, showing that the social cost of a privilege includes the resources spent competing to obtain it. Anne Krueger coined the term rent seeking in The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society, published in The American Economic Review in 1974, drawing on import licensing in India and Turkey.
mechanism_deep: A rent exists whenever income depends on a restriction rather than on production: a licence limited in number, a tariff that excludes rivals, a subsidy tied to political criteria. Once such a prize exists, rational actors compare the cost of influence with the value of the privilege, and spending on lobbyists, lawyers, donations, and revolving-door careers becomes an investment with an expected return. Tullock's deeper point was about dissipation: if many competitors chase one privilege, their combined spending can approach or even exceed the rent itself, so society loses both the distortion and the talent diverted into chasing it. The activity self-reinforces because winners use part of the rent to defend and extend the privilege, while losers learn that competing on product alone is insufficient and join the influence contest. Rent seeking weakens where rules are general, automatic, and hard to tailor, where allocation uses transparent auctions or lotteries, and where privileges carry expiry dates that force re-justification. It also depends on discretion: officials who must grant or deny individual cases hold something worth buying, while a simple rule available to everyone on equal terms offers no rent to capture.
examples_extra: In March 2002 the United States imposed tariffs of up to thirty percent on a range of imported steel, following intensive lobbying by domestic steel producers and steelworker unions. Trading partners challenged the measures at the World Trade Organization, which ruled against them, and the tariffs were withdrawn in December 2003. Studies of the episode debated effects on steel-using manufacturers, who employed far more workers than steel production itself.

The United States Renewable Fuel Standard, created by the Energy Policy Act of 2005 and expanded in 2007, required set volumes of biofuels such as corn ethanol to be blended into transport fuel. The mandate created a guaranteed market whose value depended on a regulatory decision, and farm, refining, and fuel groups have lobbied continuously over the annual volume requirements ever since.
misconceptions: Many people think rent seeking is just another word for lobbying — in reality, lobbying to inform or to defend general rules differs from spending to obtain an exclusive privilege at others' expense.

Many people think the harm is only the money transferred to the winner — in reality, Tullock showed the resources burned by all competitors chasing the transfer are an additional, often larger, social loss.
Many people think high profit proves rent seeking — in reality, profit from a better product is value creation; rent seeking is identified by dependence on a favour, licence, or restriction.

practice.title: Creation or capture audit
practice.instructions: Take one profitable business you know and split its advantage into two lists: things customers would pay for even if all special rules vanished, and advantages that depend on a licence, quota, or exclusive right. The second list is its rent exposure, and it tells you how political its profits really are.

cross_domain: In business strategy, firms practise a private version when they invest in exclusive shelf space, default placement, or patent portfolios mainly to block rivals rather than to serve customers better. In academia, grant-chasing shapes research agendas toward what funding committees reward, diverting effort from questions scholars judge most important. In online platforms, creators who optimise for algorithm loopholes and policy exceptions rather than audience value are rent seeking on the platform's rulebook, and their advantage vanishes when the rule changes.

name_vi: Nguyên tắc bổ trợ / quyết định ở cấp gần nhất
definition: Decisions should be made at the smallest, closest level capable of handling them, with higher levels only supporting when lower levels cannot.
mechanism: Local decision makers hold local knowledge about needs, culture, and constraints that distant centers cannot see, and they face consequences directly, sharpening accountability. Centralizing everything creates delays and one size fits all errors. Subsidiarity reserves higher levels for problems that cross boundaries or exceed local capacity. The principle is embedded in European Union law through the Treaty of Maastricht in 1992 and has older roots in Catholic social teaching.
classic_example: The Treaty of Maastricht, signed in 1992, wrote subsidiarity into European Union law, stating the Union should act only when member states cannot achieve objectives sufficiently themselves. The clause aimed to protect national and local decision making against steady centralization of power in Brussels institutions.
modern_example: A company where every small refund needs headquarters approval frustrates customers and staff alike. Giving front line teams a clear budget to resolve problems on the spot uses their direct knowledge and speeds resolution. Headquarters keeps only fraud patterns and policy design, where its wider view genuinely adds value.
failure_mode: Local control can entrench local tyranny, discrimination, or incompetence, and some problems like pandemics or pollution spill across borders and demand central coordination. Subsidiarity does not specify exactly which level is competent, so actors invoke it selectively to grab or dodge responsibility as suits them.
apply_steps: Ask who is closest to this problem and affected
Check if that level has capacity to act
Push decision down, keep support and guardrails up
Escalate only cross boundary or capacity exceeding issues

situation_notes.team-conflict: Subsidiarity suggests resolving conflicts at team level first because those closest hold context headquarters mediation would likely flatten or miss.
situation_notes.scaling-decision: Subsidiarity reveals scaling works when local units decide daily matters within guardrails rather than routing everything through founders slowly.
situation_notes.asking-for-budget: Subsidiarity strengthens budget requests showing decisions and accountability sit locally, with central funds only enabling what teams cannot fund.

case_seeds: Treaty of Maastricht subsidiarity principle 1992
origin: Pope Pius XI gave subsidiarity its classic statement in the encyclical Quadragesimo Anno in 1931, arguing that higher associations should not take over functions smaller communities can perform. The principle has older roots in Johannes Althusius and in federal thought, entered European Union law through the Treaty of Maastricht in 1992, and remains a test for when the Union may act.
mechanism_deep: Subsidiarity works through two channels: information and accountability. Information about local conditions is detailed, current, and largely tacit, and it decays as it travels upward through reports and summaries, so central decisions systematically miss context that local actors use without effort. Accountability sharpens at small scale because decision-makers live with the consequences and face the affected people repeatedly, making poor performance visible and personal. Higher levels still hold real advantages: they can internalise spillovers, pool risk, fund redistribution, and set minimum standards that stop local races to the bottom. The principle therefore functions as a burden-of-proof rule rather than an answer: the centraliser must show that the lower level cannot achieve the goal, or that the problem crosses boundaries in ways local action cannot handle. The arrangement self-reinforces when local units build competence by deciding, which strengthens the case for keeping decisions local. It weakens when local capacity is genuinely thin, when local elites capture institutions without outside scrutiny, or when higher levels use funding conditions to control decisions they formally delegated, producing subsidiarity on paper and centralisation in practice.
examples_extra: In Switzerland, the twenty-six cantons retain primary responsibility for areas such as education, health care organisation, and policing under the federal constitution, while the Confederation handles defence, foreign affairs, and other enumerated tasks. Cantons also implement much federal law. The structure is frequently cited in comparative federalism research as a working example of decisions taken at the lowest competent level.

In Germany, the Basic Law of 1949 assigns education and cultural affairs primarily to the sixteen Länder, which is why school systems, curricula details, and university governance differ between states. Policing is also mainly a Land responsibility. Federal coordination occurs through conferences of state ministers rather than through direct federal administration of schools.
misconceptions: Many people think subsidiarity means the central government should do nothing — in reality, it assigns higher levels a supporting role and reserves them for problems lower levels demonstrably cannot handle.
Many people think subsidiarity is identical to decentralisation — in reality, decentralisation describes where power sits, while subsidiarity supplies a test for where each decision ought to sit.
Many people think local decisions are always better — in reality, local control can entrench capture or discrimination, which is precisely why higher-level guardrails remain part of the principle.

practice.title: Lowest competent level test
practice.instructions: List three decisions currently made above your team. For each, ask who holds the relevant daily information, who bears the consequences, and whether effects spill outside the team. Move down only the decisions where information and consequences are both local, and keep a guardrail metric the higher level reviews.

cross_domain: In software architecture, subsidiarity appears as autonomous service teams that own their components end to end, with central platforms supplying only shared infrastructure and standards. In nonprofit federations, local chapters run programmes adapted to their communities while the national body handles brand, training, and safeguarding floors. In families and schools, the same logic grants children decisions proportionate to demonstrated competence, expanding autonomy as capacity grows rather than by age or by central permission alone.

name_vi: Tính chính danh
definition: Legitimacy is the shared belief that an authority has the right to rule, making people obey willingly rather than only from fear.
mechanism: Power based only on coercion is expensive and brittle, requiring constant surveillance and punishment. When people accept authority as rightful, through tradition, law, elections, or competence, compliance becomes largely voluntary and institutions survive crises and unpopular decisions. Max Weber classified legitimacy sources as traditional, charismatic, and legal rational. Losing legitimacy does not immediately topple rulers, but it raises the cost of every action they take.
classic_example: When the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989, East German border guards hesitated to use force and the regime collapsed within a year. The government still possessed weapons and police, but its legitimacy had evaporated among citizens and even its own officials, leaving coercion without belief to sustain it.
modern_example: A team leader promoted through a transparent process can deliver hard feedback and be trusted, while an appointed favorite giving identical feedback triggers suspicion and resistance. Managers, creators, and brands all run on perceived right to lead. Once audiences decide success was rigged, every later achievement gets discounted.
failure_mode: Legitimacy is a perception, not proof of justice; popular and traditional authorities have committed grave wrongs with full public acceptance. Charismatic legitimacy is especially unstable and personal. The model describes why people obey, not whether they should, so it cannot substitute for moral judgment about a regime.
apply_steps: Identify the source of this authority claim
Check whether affected people actually accept that source
Maintain fair process visibly, especially in hard decisions
Repair legitimacy early before compliance requires constant force

situation_notes.presenting-to-leadership: Legitimacy shows proposals from trusted, fairly chosen presenters get heard generously while identical ideas from doubted sources face extra scrutiny.
situation_notes.stronger-colleague-threat: Legitimacy explains a stronger colleague threatens you most when others begin seeing them as the rightful voice on your territory.
situation_notes.reading-a-new-partner: Legitimacy reveals partners who win status through transparent competence stay trusted longer than those relying on titles or connections alone.

case_seeds: Fall of the Berlin Wall 1989
Weber typology of legitimate authority
origin: Max Weber systematised legitimacy in Economy and Society, published posthumously in 1922, distinguishing traditional, charismatic, and legal-rational grounds on which people accept domination as valid. The problem is older: John Locke argued in the Second Treatise of Government in 1689 that government rests on consent, making the source of a ruler's right to command a central question of political theory.
mechanism_deep: Legitimacy is best understood as a discount on enforcement. A legitimate authority issues an unpopular ruling and most people comply while reserving the right to complain, because they accept the process that produced it. Research on procedural justice associated with Tom Tyler shows people judge fairness of treatment and voice as heavily as outcomes when deciding whether an authority deserves obedience. This creates a reservoir: institutions with deep legitimacy can survive scandals, defeats, and austerity that would shatter a purely feared regime, because citizens separate the office from its current holder. Succession is the stress test. Traditional and legal-rational systems routinise transfer, while charismatic legitimacy, attached to a person, faces a crisis at every succession unless it is converted into institutions. Performance can substitute for procedure for a time, as growth or security buys tolerance, but performance legitimacy is hostage to results and evaporates in downturns precisely when rulers need compliance most. The loss process is nonlinear: each visible act of impunity or rigged process teaches observers that others no longer believe, and once the belief in shared belief collapses, compliance can fall suddenly rather than gradually.
examples_extra: South Africa held its first election under universal suffrage in April 1994, with queues of first-time voters widely reported. The African National Congress won and Nelson Mandela became president in May 1994. The transfer grounded the new state's authority in a franchise from which the majority had previously been excluded, and the outgoing government handed over power through the process it had negotiated.

The United States election of 1800 ended with Thomas Jefferson, of the Democratic-Republican Party, succeeding John Adams, a Federalist, as president in March 1801 after a contested count resolved in the House of Representatives. Historians treat the peaceful transfer between rival parties as an early demonstration that electoral legitimacy could survive a change of governing faction.
misconceptions: Many people think legitimacy means popularity — in reality, an authority can be legitimate while making unpopular decisions, if people accept its right to decide through a fair process.
Many people think legitimacy means an authority is just or wise — in reality, legitimacy describes whether people believe in its right to rule, which is a sociological fact, not a moral verdict.
Many people think losing an election destroys legitimacy — in reality, systems are legitimate precisely when losers accept results and expect a fair chance to win next time.

practice.title: Name the source
practice.instructions: Choose an authority whose decision you recently obeyed or resisted, such as a manager, platform, or council. Identify which Weberian source its claim rests on: tradition, charisma, or legal-rational process. Then write down what single event would most damage that specific source.

practice.title: Reservoir check
practice.instructions: After a hard decision in your team, note whether people complied while disagreeing, complied only under monitoring, or quietly worked around it. The first pattern signals a legitimacy reservoir; the third signals that formal authority remains but belief has already drained.

cross_domain: In companies, a chief executive appointed through a credible board process can deliver restructuring news that an owner's relative, appointed without process, cannot deliver with the same words. In professional communities, standards bodies govern without legal force because members accept their procedures as fair and expert. In online platforms, creators accept demonetisation or ranking changes from systems they see as consistently applied, and revolt against identical outcomes they believe were decided by favouritism.

quote.text: Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
quote.author: Lord Acton

name_vi: Quyền lực mềm
definition: Soft power is the ability to influence others through attraction and example, rather than through force, threats, or payments.
mechanism: When a country, company, or person is admired for values, culture, and competence, others voluntarily adopt their preferences and standards. That attraction lowers resistance, builds alliances cheaply, and makes leadership feel natural. Joseph Nye coined the term in 1990, distinguishing attraction from the hard power of military and economic coercion. Soft power compounds slowly through credibility, so hypocrisy damages it disproportionately.
classic_example: Joseph Nye introduced soft power in his 1990 book Bound to Lead and a Foreign Policy article the same year. He argued American influence rested partly on universities, films, and ideals attracting others. South Korea later demonstrated it vividly as Korean dramas and K pop built global goodwill governments could not buy directly.
modern_example: A marketer whose free content genuinely helps strangers builds an audience that trusts product recommendations without heavy advertising. That attraction is personal soft power. Companies experience the same effect when a respected employer brand makes hiring easier, while firms known for mistreating staff must overpay for every recruit.
failure_mode: Attraction cannot stop an invasion or settle every conflict, and it is slow to build when urgent outcomes are needed. Soft power is also hard to control: cultural exports may spread messages governments dislike. Measuring it precisely is difficult, inviting vague claims that everything popular counts as influence.
apply_steps: Identify what others genuinely admire about you
Demonstrate values consistently before promoting them loudly
Invest in culture, craft, and credibility over coercion
Avoid hypocrisy that destroys attraction faster than force

situation_notes.channel-not-growing: Soft power reveals channels grow when audiences are attracted by consistent values and craft, not pushed by constant promotional pressure.
situation_notes.writing-sales-copy: Soft power shows sales copy converts better after attraction and trust are built, making the offer feel like a natural next step.
situation_notes.stronger-colleague-threat: Soft power explains colleagues gain influence through admired competence and generosity that formal authority alone cannot easily counter or copy.

case_seeds: Joseph Nye coining soft power 1990
Global spread of Korean culture and Hallyu wave
origin: Harvard political scientist Joseph S. Nye Jr. coined soft power in his 1990 book Bound to Lead and in a Foreign Policy article titled Soft Power that same year. Writing as the Cold War ended, Nye argued that the United States also led through the attraction of its universities, culture, and ideals, not only through military and economic instruments.
mechanism_deep: Nye identified three sources: culture that others find attractive, political values actually practised at home and abroad, and foreign policies seen as legitimate and considerate of others' interests. The conversion mechanism is agenda attraction: when others admire a model, they voluntarily learn its language, adopt its standards, send students to its universities, and frame their own ambitions in its terms, so the attractive party's preferences spread without orders or payments. This lowers the cost of leadership because coalitions form around shared framing rather than needing side payments for every issue. Credibility is the bottleneck resource. Attraction depends on perceived consistency, so a visible gap between professed values and behaviour damages soft power faster than it damages material power, because the asset is belief itself. Soft power is also only partly controlled by governments: films, firms, universities, diasporas, and individual creators generate most of it, and their output can contradict official messaging. It weakens when culture is read as arrogance, when exchange and media channels close, or when security threats make audiences prioritise protection over admiration, and it converts poorly into specific concessions unless combined with harder instruments, the combination Nye later called smart power.
examples_extra: The United States Fulbright Program, established by legislation in 1946, funds academic exchanges between the United States and other countries and counts hundreds of thousands of alumni. Exchange programmes of this kind are standard soft power examples because participants build long-term familiarity and professional networks, and alumni have included dozens of future heads of government identified in programme histories.

The BBC World Service began broadcasting in 1932 as the BBC Empire Service and built an international reputation for reporting that audiences in closed media environments treated as comparatively reliable. Britain's cultural relations organisation, the British Council, founded in 1934, runs language teaching and cultural programmes abroad. Both institutions are routinely cited in public diplomacy research as long-horizon attraction assets.
misconceptions: Many people think soft power is just popularity or entertainment exports — in reality, attraction only counts as power when it helps obtain desired outcomes, and admired culture with no political effect is not yet power.

Many people think governments can manufacture soft power by messaging campaigns — in reality, most attraction comes from civil society and practised values, and propaganda perceived as such usually reduces credibility.
Many people think soft power replaces hard power — in reality, Nye argued the two combine; attraction cannot stop aggression, and coercion without attraction is unusually expensive to sustain.

practice.title: Attraction inventory
practice.instructions: List what outsiders already admire about your team, school, or country without exaggeration: a craft, a value consistently practised, a place people want to join. For each item, note one behaviour that would destroy it. Protect the destroyers list before spending anything on promotion.

cross_domain: In business, employer brands reproduce the mechanism: firms admired for craft and fair dealing receive stronger applicants at lower salaries than firms that must compensate for reputation. In the nonprofit sector, organisations whose methods others copy voluntarily set field standards without any regulatory authority. In online communities, creators who consistently teach useful skills attract collaborations and audience trust that paid promotion cannot buy, while a single exposed hypocrisy, such as secretly selling the products they criticise, burns the asset quickly.

name_vi: Kiểm soát diễn ngôn và tuyên truyền
definition: Whoever controls the dominant story about events shapes what people believe happened, who is to blame, and what responses seem reasonable.
mechanism: Humans understand events through stories with heroes, villains, and causes, not raw data. Propaganda exploits this by repeating selected facts, loaded labels, and emotional frames through controlled channels until alternatives feel fringe. Edward Bernays described engineering consent in his 1928 book Propaganda. The mechanism works because repetition builds familiarity, familiarity feels like truth, and most people never encounter the omitted evidence.
classic_example: Edward Bernays published Propaganda in 1928, openly describing how organized persuasion shapes democratic publics. His 1929 torches of freedom campaign reframed cigarettes for women as symbols of emancipation, linking a product to a liberation story. Tobacco sales to women rose as the narrative, not the product, changed minds.
modern_example: In workplace conflicts, the person who frames events first in a message to leadership often anchors how everyone later interprets the facts. On social media, a viral clip with a confident caption can define an incident for millions before fuller footage appears. Checking who benefits from the framing is a daily survival skill.
failure_mode: Not every persuasive story is propaganda, and labeling opponents narratives as manipulation can become its own manipulation. Audiences are not passive; leaks, satire, and lived experience regularly break official stories. Overestimating narrative control leads to conspiratorial thinking where material facts and genuine disagreement disappear from analysis.
apply_steps: Ask who is telling this story and why
Identify heroes, villains, and omitted facts in framing
Seek the same events from an independent source
Notice repetition and loaded labels replacing evidence

situation_notes.online-arguments: Narrative control reveals online fights are usually over framing and labels, so arguing facts alone rarely shifts the dominant story.
situation_notes.evaluating-news-and-courses: Narrative control teaches checking who funds and benefits from a story before accepting its heroes, villains, and conclusions.
situation_notes.persuading-stubborn-person: Narrative control shows stubborn people defend identity stories, so new facts must fit a face saving alternative narrative first.
situation_notes.presenting-to-leadership: Narrative control explains the first clear framing of results often anchors leadership memory more strongly than later detailed corrections do.

case_seeds: Bernays Propaganda book 1928
Bernays torches of freedom campaign 1929
