origin: Edward Bernays crystallised the practice in Propaganda in 1928, drawing on his work for the United States Committee on Public Information during the First World War and on his uncle Sigmund Freud's psychology. Walter Lippmann had supplied much of the theory in Public Opinion in 1922, describing the pictures in our heads and the manufacture of consent in modern democracies.
mechanism_deep: The mechanism operates at three levels. First, selection: gatekeepers decide which events become news at all, and agenda-setting research by Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw in 1968 showed that media emphasis strongly predicts which issues the public ranks as important, even when opinions on those issues differ. Second, framing: within a covered event, labels assign causation and blame, so the same act described as reform, crackdown, or chaos primes different remedies before any evidence is weighed. Third, repetition: repeated claims gain fluency, and the illusory truth effect means familiar statements feel more accurate, which is why slogans and talking points are synchronised across speakers. Emotional stories outperform statistics because a single identified victim or villain organises memory and motivates sharing. Modern distribution intensifies each level, since engagement-ranked feeds promote the most activating frame rather than the most accurate one, and corrections travel more slowly than the original story. Control weakens when audiences have direct experience contradicting the story, when rival gatekeepers with comparable reach contest the frame early, and when overclaiming produces a visible gap between narrative and lived reality that satire and leaks can exploit.
examples_extra: The poster known as Rosie the Riveter, painted by J. Howard Miller for Westinghouse in 1943, formed part of a broader United States campaign to recruit women into wartime factory work while men served overseas. Women's employment in defence industries rose sharply during the war. The image was little known after the war and became an enduring cultural symbol only after its rediscovery in the 1980s.

Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines began broadcasting in Rwanda in 1993 and aired dehumanising propaganda against Tutsi during the 1994 genocide. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda later convicted senior figures associated with the station and other media in the Media Case, concluding that broadcasts had directly incited violence. The case is a standard reference in international law on media responsibility.
misconceptions: Many people think propaganda must consist of lies — in reality, effective propaganda often uses true facts, selectively chosen, labelled, and repeated until they crowd out the rest of the picture.
Many people think only governments produce propaganda — in reality, companies, movements, and influencers use the same selection, framing, and repetition machinery for commercial and cultural ends.

Many people think audiences are helpless against narrative control — in reality, direct experience, rival sources, and visible narrative failures regularly break official stories, especially over long periods.

practice.title: Strip the frame
practice.instructions: Take one strongly worded news story and rewrite its headline three times using neutral verbs and no adjectives. List the facts that survive every version and the claims that depended on wording. Then find how one source with a different interest framed the same event.

practice.title: Count the repetition
practice.instructions: For one week, note each time you encounter the same phrase or claim about a topic and where it came from. At the end, ask whether your confidence in the claim grew from new evidence or only from familiarity. Separate the two lists explicitly.

cross_domain: In corporate life, the first account of a failed project to reach senior leadership usually becomes the template for reviews and promotions, so teams invest in framing results before rivals do. In consumer markets, category narratives decide which product attribute counts as quality, letting a brand win by redefining the story rather than improving specifications. In online communities, a pinned post or popular thread sets the interpretive frame for an incident, and later evidence is read through it by everyone who arrives afterwards.
